title: MasDrift: Benchmarking Authorization Preservation Across Multi-Agent Architectures
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) decompose long-horizon tasks across supervisors and subagents, but delegated goals do not necessarily carry their original authorization boundaries. Existing safety benchmarks mainly study adversarial compromise, while work on constraint drift lacks controlled architecture-level evaluation. We introduce MasDrift, a benchmark of 600 benign productivity tasks across eight domains. Each task pairs required work with reserved actions. MasDrift compares single-agent, centralized, and decentralized coordination while varying hierarchy depth and peer width, measuring task completion and authorization preservation. Across generic multi-agent conditions, centralized hierarchies achieve 93.9--98.6% task completion versus 85.7--87.0% for peer networks, while unauthorized actions occur in 2.7--19.8% of tasks versus 0.6--0.8%, a gap that widens with hierarchy depth. We further compare two defenses that differ in where authorization evidence resides. One re-anchors every pending call to the original user request. The other carries an attenuated policy along the delegation chain. Re-anchoring reduces unauthorized actions in every model configuration we evaluate, at a cost of 1.6 points of pooled completion. Chain propagation blocks required work instead, forfeiting up to 36.3 points. A heterogeneous case study confirms that the failure follows from coordination rather than model strength. MasDrift exposes a centralization tradeoff and makes authorization preservation a measurable property of MAS design.

AI.tldr: MasDrift is a benchmark for measuring authorization preservation in multi-agent systems, revealing that centralized hierarchies complete more tasks but cause more unauthorized actions compared to peer networks, with re-anchoring defenses being most effective.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems delegate tasks across agents but goals may not preserve original authorization boundaries. Current safety benchmarks focus on adversarial compromise, while constraint drift lacks controlled architecture-level evaluation.
AI.method: Introduced MasDrift benchmark with 600 benign productivity tasks across 8 domains, each pairing required work with reserved actions. Compared single-agent, centralized, and decentralized coordination while varying hierarchy depth and peer width, measuring task completion and authorization preservation. Evaluated two defenses: re-anchoring calls to original user requests vs. carrying attenuated policy along delegation chain.
AI.result: Centralized hierarchies achieved 93.9-98.6% task completion vs 85.7-87.0% for peer networks. Unauthorized actions occurred in 2.7-19.8% of tasks for centralized vs 0.6-0.8% for peers. Re-anchoring reduced unauthorized actions in all configurations (costing 1.6 points of completion), while chain propagation blocked required work (forfeiting up to 36.3 points).
AI.conclusion: MasDrift exposes a centralization tradeoff and makes authorization preservation a measurable property of MAS design. The failure patterns result from coordination issues rather than model strength.

title: Mobility, Memory, and Network Structure in Agent-Based Models of Convention Tipping and Convergence
comment: Under review at the Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation (JASSS)
summary: Tipping-point dynamics describe the critical conditions under which a committed minority drives a population to abandon an established convention in favor of a new one. We present a transparent agent-based model of this process, in which agents hold one of two behavioral states and a mobile committed minority attempts to overturn the incumbent convention. Our goal was to examine how localized mobility, bounded agent memory, and network topology jointly influence the tipping threshold. Using a custom agent-based simulation framework, we found that in many configurations, tipping becomes effectively inevitable: given sufficient time, the population always converges to the minority state. This observation motivated a complementary analysis focused on the pace of convergence rather than its feasibility. We introduce a unified predictive model that accurately estimates how structural and behavioral parameters determine the time required for complete adoption, showing that mobility is the dominant accelerator while memory and connectivity modulate convergence in systematic ways. Together, these results extend classical tipping-point research by linking structural and behavioral factors not only to the likelihood of convention change but also to the timescale on which it unfolds. While we frame the model in terms of convention-like binary behavioral adoption, the same mechanisms bear on norm change and other contagion-like social processes.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an agent-based model showing how a committed minority can overturn established conventions, finding tipping becomes inevitable with sufficient time and mobility accelerates convergence while memory and connectivity modulate it.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand how localized mobility, bounded agent memory, and network topology jointly influence tipping thresholds in social convention change, extending classical tipping-point research by linking structural and behavioral factors to both likelihood and timescale of change.
AI.method: The researchers used a transparent agent-based model where agents hold one of two behavioral states, with a mobile committed minority attempting to overturn the incumbent convention. They employed a custom agent-based simulation framework to examine how different parameters affect tipping thresholds and convergence times.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) In many configurations, tipping becomes effectively inevitable - given sufficient time, the population always converges to the minority state; (2) A unified predictive model accurately estimates how structural and behavioral parameters determine the time required for complete adoption; (3) Mobility is the dominant accelerator of convergence while memory and connectivity modulate convergence in systematic ways.
AI.conclusion: The study extends classical tipping-point research by linking structural and behavioral factors not only to the likelihood of convention change but also to the timescale on which it unfolds. While framed in terms of binary behavioral adoption, the mechanisms also apply to norm change and other contagion-like social processes.

title: Per-Shipment Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Intermodal Freight Routing Under Hurricane Disruption
summary: Intermodal freight networks face growing disruption risk from climate extremes that degrade multiple corridors simultaneously. To address this, we formulate freight routing as a Dec-POMDP with per-shipment action granularity and train Independent PPO (IPPO) under Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution, comparing against two heuristic baselines with privileged state access on a 15-hub network under hurricane disruption. Across 30 matched episodes, no single policy dominates: IPPO achieves the highest throughput ($+12.7\%$) and delivery rate while a capacity-aware heuristic leads on Resilience Index (RI) and delay. Under demand surge (2.9:1 capacity ratio), IPPO's RI advantage grows to $+6.4\%$, suggesting learned routing is most valuable when capacity is scarce. A Multi-Agent PPO (MAPPO) variant collapses under train-eval queue mismatch ($\mathrm{RI} = 0.811$); retraining recovers RI to $1.018$ but IPPO still leads on throughput, pointing to residual limitations in centralized critics under per-shipment dispatch.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Dec-POMDP formulation for freight routing under hurricane disruptions, training Independent PPO agents that achieve higher throughput but heuristic methods lead on resilience metrics.
AI.motivation: Climate extremes increasingly disrupt intermodal freight networks by degrading multiple corridors simultaneously, creating a need for robust routing solutions.
AI.method: Formulates freight routing as Dec-POMDP with per-shipment granularity, trains Independent PPO (IPPO) under Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution, compares against heuristic baselines on 15-hub network under hurricane disruption.
AI.result: No single policy dominates: IPPO achieves highest throughput (+12.7%) and delivery rate, while capacity-aware heuristic leads on Resilience Index and delay. Under demand surge, IPPO's RI advantage grows to +6.4%. MAPPO variant fails initially but recovers with retraining.
AI.conclusion: Learned routing (IPPO) is most valuable when capacity is scarce, but heuristic methods remain competitive on certain resilience metrics. Centralized critics (like in MAPPO) may have limitations under per-shipment dispatch scenarios.

title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Urban Traffic Management via Spatio-Temporal Mobility Profile Planning
summary: As modern cities face increasingly severe traffic congestion, connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) have emerged as a crucial enabling technology for next-generation intelligent traffic management. However, fully realizing this potential is hindered by the limitations of current paradigms. Existing approaches typically optimize localized interactions rather than system-wide efficiency, incur severe communication overhead, or lack the deterministic guarantees required for safe kinematic execution. Furthermore, current multi-agent adaptations are frequently restricted to small predefined scenarios, failing to scale across large and complex urban networks. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces VeloCity, a decentralized multi-agent spatio-temporal mobility profile planning framework designed for CAVs operating in arbitrary urban areas. To minimize vehicles' travel times, VeloCity distributes mobility profile optimization directly to individual CAVs. Vehicles query a localized traffic coordinator for a reservation table, independently compute their fastest conflict-free mobility profile, and reserve their requested space-time slots back with the coordinator. By natively adapting to any arbitrary road topology, the framework manages highly irregular urban areas without requiring scenario-specific tuning, all while guaranteeing collision-free and physically executable vehicle trajectories. Extensive simulations across four large-scale real-world urban maps (Tokyo, Manhattan, Rome, and Bologna) demonstrate the framework's scalability. Compared to established state-of-the-art models, VeloCity yields drastically lower travel times, tightly bounds delay variance, and successfully prevents congestion gridlocks even under extremely high vehicular densities.

AI.tldr: VeloCity is a decentralized multi-agent spatio-temporal mobility profile planning framework for CAVs that enables scalable, collision-free traffic management in arbitrary urban areas with reduced travel times and congestion prevention.
AI.motivation: Current CAV traffic management approaches have several limitations: they optimize only localized interactions rather than system-wide efficiency, incur severe communication overhead, lack deterministic safety guarantees, and fail to scale across large complex urban networks. Existing multi-agent adaptations are restricted to small predefined scenarios.
AI.method: A decentralized framework where individual CAVs optimize their own mobility profiles. Vehicles query a localized traffic coordinator for reservation tables, independently compute their fastest conflict-free mobility profiles, and reserve space-time slots back with the coordinator. The framework natively adapts to any arbitrary road topology without scenario-specific tuning.
AI.result: Extensive simulations across four large-scale real-world urban maps (Tokyo, Manhattan, Rome, and Bologna) show VeloCity achieves drastically lower travel times compared to state-of-the-art models, tightly bounds delay variance, and successfully prevents congestion gridlocks even under extremely high vehicular densities.
AI.conclusion: VeloCity bridges the gap between current CAV traffic management limitations and the requirements for scalable urban traffic optimization by providing a decentralized approach that guarantees collision-free execution while adapting to arbitrary urban topologies and achieving significant performance improvements.

title: Application of Artificial Intelligence for Fraudulent Banking Operations Recognition
summary: This study considers the task of applying artificial intelligence to recognize bank fraud. In recent years, due to the COVID19 pandemic, bank fraud has become even more common due to the massive transition of many operations to online platforms and the creation of many charitable funds that criminals can use to deceive users. The present work focuses on machine learning algorithms as a tool well suited for analyzing and recognizing online banking transactions. The study`s scientific novelty is the development of machine learning models for identifying fraudulent banking transactions and techniques for preprocessing bank data for further comparison and selection of the best results. This paper also details various methods for improving detection accuracy, i.e., handling highly imbalanced datasets, feature transformation, and feature engineering. The proposed model, which is based on an artificial neural network, effectively improves the accuracy of fraudulent transaction detection. The results of the different algorithms are visualized, and the logistic regression algorithm performs the best, with an output AUC value of approximately 0,946. The stacked generalization shows a better AUC of 0.954. The recognition of banking fraud using artificial intelligence algorithms is a topical issue in our digital society.

AI.tldr: The study applies AI and machine learning to detect bank fraud, finding that stacked generalization achieves the best performance with AUC 0.954, while logistic regression alone gets AUC 0.946.
AI.motivation: Bank fraud has increased significantly due to the COVID-19 pandemic's shift to online operations and creation of charitable funds that criminals exploit. There's a need for effective AI solutions to analyze online banking transactions.
AI.method: Uses machine learning algorithms to analyze online banking transactions, with focus on data preprocessing techniques, handling imbalanced datasets, feature transformation, and feature engineering. The main model is based on artificial neural networks, with comparison to other algorithms.
AI.result: The artificial neural network effectively improves fraud detection accuracy. Logistic regression performs best among individual algorithms with AUC 0.946, while stacked generalization achieves even better performance with AUC 0.954.
AI.conclusion: AI algorithms are highly relevant for banking fraud detection in our digital society. The study demonstrates that proper preprocessing and algorithm selection can significantly improve fraud detection accuracy, with stacked generalization showing the best performance.

title: Towards an Argumentative Foundation for Evaluative AI
summary: Evaluative AI (EAI) has been recently proposed as a way to support human decision-making, not by producing a single recommendation, but by presenting competing hypotheses together with evidence for and against each. In this position paper, we advocate (computational) argumentation as a particularly suitable paradigm to provide a formal, computable foundation for forms of EAI that are explainable and contestable, setting the ground for a long-term research agenda towards distributed and human-centred EAI systems.

AI.tldr: Argumentation is proposed as a formal foundation for Evaluative AI (EAI) systems that support human decision-making through competing hypotheses and evidence, enabling explainable and contestable AI.
AI.motivation: Need for AI systems that support human decision-making without just giving single recommendations, but by presenting competing hypotheses with evidence. This supports distributed and human-centered AI approaches.
AI.method: Advocates for computational argumentation as the formal, computable foundation for Evaluative AI (EAI) systems. This is a position paper setting a research agenda rather than presenting a specific implemented method.
AI.result: Proposes argumentation as a suitable paradigm for creating explainable and contestable EAI systems. Establishes the groundwork for future research in distributed, human-centered EAI.
AI.conclusion: Computational argumentation provides the necessary formal foundations for developing next-generation Evaluative AI systems that are explainable, contestable, and truly human-centered, paving the way for a long-term research agenda in this direction.

title: AOC-CBS: Anytime-Optimal Continuous-time Conflict-Based Search for Generalised Multi-Agent Path Finding
summary: Many research fields share a common structure: a set of agents, each pursuing its own goal, whose actions must be coordinated so that no two of them conflict. Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) is a concrete instance of this structure, with applications from warehouses to road traffic and airports. Much of MAPF research assumes discrete time, circular agents sharing one spatial graph, a single goal per agent, and that an agent must remain at its goal once reached, precluding heterogeneous fleets, non-geometric conflicts, task sequences, and agents that move on after completing them. We generalise the MAPF formulation to lift these assumptions, and present Anytime-Optimal Continuous-time Conflict-Based Search (AOC-CBS), an exact and solution-complete solver for it. AOC-CBS guarantees the eventual return of an optimal solution, while reporting an incumbent with a known optimality gap upper bound throughout its runtime; it is configurable with a portfolio of repair functions, one of which we introduce (Tier-Prioritized Safe Interval Path Planning), and can exploit multiple processor cores. We demonstrate AOC-CBS on a mixed fleet of non-convex agents moving along smooth, kinodynamically feasible trajectories. Preliminary experiments against the exact solver OC-CBS, on well-known benchmarks and roadmaps we sample from them, show AOC-CBS is comparable at finding optimal solutions while extending scalability from the tens to the hundreds of agents when a bounded optimality gap is accepted.

AI.tldr: AOC-CBS extends traditional MAPF by lifting assumptions about discrete time, circular agents, single goals, and mandatory goal staying, enabling heterogeneous fleets, continuous time, and task sequences while providing anytime-optimal solutions.
AI.motivation: Traditional Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) makes restrictive assumptions: discrete time, circular agents, single spatial graph, one goal per agent, and mandatory goal staying. These assumptions preclude real-world applications like heterogeneous fleets, non-geometric conflicts, task sequences, and agents that move on after completing tasks.
AI.method: AOC-CBS (Anytime-Optimal Continuous-time Conflict-Based Search) is an exact, solution-complete solver that generalizes MAPF formulation. It uses a portfolio of repair functions including a newly introduced Tier-Prioritized Safe Interval Path Planning, supports continuous time, and can exploit multiple processor cores. It works with mixed fleets of non-convex agents moving along smooth, kinodynamically feasible trajectories.
AI.result: Preliminary experiments show AOC-CBS is comparable to exact solver OC-CBS on finding optimal solutions while extending scalability from tens to hundreds of agents when accepting bounded optimality gaps. It maintains an incumbent solution with known optimality gap upper bound throughout runtime.
AI.conclusion: AOC-CBS successfully lifts traditional MAPF limitations to handle more realistic scenarios including heterogeneous fleets, continuous time, and task sequences while providing anytime-optimal solutions with scalability improvements.

title: Data-Driven Fire-Zone Segmentation for Improved Short-Term Wildfire Prediction
summary: Wildfire prediction models typically discretize study areas into uniform grids, ignoring the heterogeneous spatial distribution of ignitions. We challenge this paradigm by showing that how data is discretized matters more than which model is used. We propose an unsupervised fire-zone segmentation algorithm combining watershed detection with K-means clustering to define prediction units directly from historical fire patterns. Experiments across six French departments and six forecasting models show that fire-zone segmentation consistently outperforms grid-based approaches, with mean IoU improvements of +3--6% depending on spatial scale. The method is computationally lightweight (<10s per configuration) and fully parallelizable. Our results demonstrate that optimizing spatial discretization yields significant, reproducible performance gains for short-term wildfire forecasting.

AI.tldr: Fire-zone segmentation based on historical fire patterns consistently outperforms uniform grids for wildfire prediction, showing that spatial discretization optimization matters more than model choice.
AI.motivation: Traditional wildfire prediction models use uniform grid discretization which ignores heterogeneous spatial distribution of ignitions. The authors challenge this paradigm by showing that data discretization matters more than model selection.
AI.method: Proposed an unsupervised fire-zone segmentation algorithm combining watershed detection with K-means clustering to define prediction units directly from historical fire patterns. The method is computationally lightweight (<10s per configuration) and fully parallelizable.
AI.result: Experiments across six French departments and six forecasting models show fire-zone segmentation consistently outperforms grid-based approaches, with mean IoU improvements of +3-6% depending on spatial scale.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing spatial discretization yields significant, reproducible performance gains for short-term wildfire forecasting, demonstrating that how data is discretized matters more than which model is used.

title: Flow-by-Flow:Content-Judgment Bypass for Governing AI Output in High-Loss Domains
summary: Prior work showed that human-in-the-loop oversight becomes structurally untenable in high-loss domains when AI output velocity V exceeds human cognitive capacity C_max. The operative constraint, however, is not V alone but V x L, where L denotes per-item cognitive load. L consists of triage, judgment, and response, which respond asymmetrically to AI capability improvement. Triage cost does not decline as models become more capable, because semantic indeterminacy is inherent in general-purpose design. Response cost is invariant to accuracy improvements. Only judgment cost faces downward pressure, and this pressure often operates by inducing omission rather than genuine reduction. Capability improvement therefore restructures L rather than reducing it. Governance mechanisms based on evaluating whether AI output is correct either delegate that evaluation to AI and inherit hallucination risk, or delegate it to humans and face the V x L ceiling. We propose Flow-by-Flow, a governance paradigm that controls supervisory load without evaluating content. A cognitive cost score based on formal, countable features imposes nonlinear costs on high-volume production, while an institutional capacity cap keeps processing volume within C_max. We derive four design invariants for any content-judgment-bypass exceedance pathway: no content judgment, no scalable consumption of examiner capacity, identity-bound per-application friction, and no batch clearance. One reference implementation is discussed to show that these invariants are jointly satisfiable, while its practical difficulties are explicitly acknowledged. An illustrative Monte Carlo analysis across 1,000 parameter draws suggests that composite multi-metric flow control outperforms supervision reinforcement alone in 90.8% of trials.

AI.tldr: Prior human oversight becomes unworkable when AI output velocity exceeds human cognitive capacity. The paper proposes Flow-by-Flow governance that controls supervisory load without evaluating content, using formal metrics and capacity caps instead of judgment-based oversight.
AI.motivation: Existing human-in-the-loop oversight fails in high-loss domains when AI output velocity exceeds human cognitive capacity. The problem is V x L (velocity times per-item cognitive load), where L components (triage, judgment, response) don't scale well with AI improvements. Content-based evaluation approaches either delegate judgment to AI (risking hallucinations) or to humans (hitting capacity ceilings.
AI.method: Proposes Flow-by-Flow governance paradigm that bypasses content judgment entirely. Uses cognitive cost scores based on formal, countable features to impose nonlinear costs on high-volume production. Includes institutional capacity caps to keep processing within cognitive limits. Establishes four design invariants: no content judgment, no scalable consumption of examiner capacity, identity-bound friction, and no batch clearance.
AI.result: Monte Carlo analysis across 1,000 parameter draws shows composite multi-metric flow control outperforms supervision reinforcement alone in 90.8% of trials. A reference implementation demonstrates the four design invariants are jointly satisfiable, though practical difficulties are acknowledged.
AI.conclusion: Content-based governance approaches face fundamental scalability limits. Flow-by-Flow offers a viable alternative by shifting from evaluating whether AI output is correct to controlling supervisory load through formal, non-content metrics and capacity constraints, enabling governance in high-velocity AI environments.

title: Fluid Structure, Rigid Record: A Layered Organizational Design Framework for Agent-Native Organizations
summary: An agentic organization should not be a set of model instances with corporate titles, despite most MAS still operationalizing organization as a conversational topology, a role prompt, or a fixed workflow. This paper develops an agent-native organizational structure framework that separates the persistent and dynamic layers of operations. The persistent layer consists of a four-store record architecture and a pool of resident specialization agents. A coordination layer defines Permission as the boundary of the operational world available to an agent, and Privilege as the set of organizational state changes that the agent is authorized to initiate. Together, these mechanisms compile task-specific operational worlds. A runtime layer combines an external Workflow Protocol with an isolated runtime store to dynamically assemble Task Groups. A human-interaction layer exposes the organization through a Control Plane mediated by a non-decision-making Translation Agent. Three orthogonal Role Groups further separate Operation, Review, and Supervision. Operators execute within narrowly scoped leases; reviewers receive elevated but demand-activated authority to modify organizational state; supervisors retain broad observational access while holding limited modification authority. The resulting architecture is fluid at the execution surface but structurally rigid underneath: tasks and events may alter team composition, topology, views, tools, and workflows, while records, write constraints, authority boundaries, and separation of powers remain persistent. The architecture has been implemented as a prototype and evaluated in small-sample experiments. Large-scale empirical validation remains incomplete, therefore no general performance claimed is made yet. Instead, the contribution is a coherent and falsifiable framework for designing, governing, recovering, and evaluating agent-native organizations.

AI.tldr: A framework for agent-native organizational structures separating persistent and dynamic layers, with four-store architecture, coordination mechanisms, runtime task groups, and human interaction through a Control Plane.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent systems treat organizations simplistically as conversational topologies, role prompts, or fixed workflows, lacking proper organizational structures for agentic systems. There's a need for agent-native organizational frameworks that separate persistent and dynamic operational layers.
AI.method: Develops a framework with: 1) Persistent layer with four-store record architecture and resident specialization agents; 2) Coordination layer defining Permission (operational world access) and Privilege (state change authorization); 3) Runtime layer combining external Workflow Protocol with isolated runtime store for Task Groups; 4) Human-interaction layer with Control Plane mediated by Translation Agent; plus three orthogonal Role Groups (Operation, Review, Supervision).
AI.result: Architecture creates fluid execution surface with structural rigidity underneath: tasks/events can alter team composition, topology, views, tools, and workflows while maintaining persistent records, write constraints, authority boundaries, and separation of powers. Implemented as prototype with small-sample experimental evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale empirical validation incomplete, so no general performance claims made. Main contribution is a coherent, falsifiable framework for designing, governing, recovering, and evaluating agent-native organizations that separates persistent organizational structure from dynamic operations.

title: Evolving Safety Landscape of Multi-modal Large Language Models: A Survey of Emerging Threats and Safeguards
comment: Accepted at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Principled Design for Trustworthy AI
summary: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) integrate heterogeneous modalities through modality alignment and fusion, enabling stronger understanding and reasoning. However, this architectural shift reshapes the safety landscape of machine learning. Increased model complexity and cross-modal interactions give rise to novel threats, including compromised modality integration, modality misalignment, and fused safety risks, reflecting shifts in threat modeling beyond uni-modal assumptions. These shifts, in turn, impose new constraints on safety solutions not captured by existing frameworks rooted in uni-modal learning. Motivated by these challenges, this survey provides a systematic analysis of the evolving safety landscape of MLLMs. We first propose a multimodal grounded taxonomy of safety threats and analyze shifts in threat models, covering adversarial attacks, data poisoning, jailbreaks, and hallucinations. We then summarize updated safety assumptions and organize recent advances in MLLM safety strategies accordingly. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions to inform the development of more principled and scalable safety mechanisms for multimodal systems.

AI.tldr: This survey systematically analyzes the evolving safety landscape of multimodal large language models, identifying novel threats from cross-modal interactions and proposing updated safety frameworks beyond uni-modal assumptions.
AI.motivation: The integration of heterogeneous modalities in MLLMs reshapes the safety landscape, creating new threats like compromised modality integration, modality misalignment, and fused safety risks that existing uni-modal safety frameworks fail to address adequately.
AI.method: Proposes a multimodal grounded taxonomy of safety threats covering adversarial attacks, data poisoning, jailbreaks, and hallucinations; analyzes threat model shifts; summarizes updated safety assumptions; and organizes recent safety strategies accordingly.
AI.result: Provides systematic analysis of MLLM safety evolution, identifies key threat model shifts, organizes safety strategies into updated framework, and highlights gaps in current approaches to multimodal safety.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes by discussing open challenges and future directions for developing more principled and scalable safety mechanisms tailored to the unique characteristics of multimodal systems.

title: Determinization in Structure Theories: A Unified Framework via Closure, Comparability, and Joint Admissibility
comment: Formal framework paper on canonicalization and determinization in structure theories; version v2.16.4; 29 pages
summary:
We develop a formal framework for constructing canonical interpretations from plural structure theories. A structure theory is a triple T = (Σ, A, I) consisting of a signature, axioms, and an inference policy, whose admissible interpretation family collects all globally consistent assignments of structural conclusions.
  We distinguish three levels of canonicalization: closure stabilization (per-seed convergence), global completion (seed-independent convergence), and determinization (a unique admissible interpretation). Non-determinism is classified into epistemic plurality (Type E) and structural plurality (Type S), with a refined Type S-strong subclass characterized by the absence of common upper bounds.
  Two canonicalization mechanisms arise: operator-based completion and selector-based construction. We provide sufficient structural conditions under which these mechanisms exist, and show that pure inference-based completion reduces to a saturated closure operator under positive, non-retractive rules with an additional soundness condition. For Type E theories, closure stabilization is established, while full determinization depends on a global confluence property that remains open. For Type S-strong theories, determinization is achieved via canonical selection.
  We further show that multi-level canonicalization forms a structurally non-commutative system via staged operators, and provide a conditional classification theorem reducing theory-intrinsic mechanisms to closure or selection. The framework also applies to LLM-assisted reasoning, where hallucination can be viewed as unsupported canonicalization.

AI.tldr: A formal framework for constructing canonical interpretations from plural structure theories, distinguishing three canonicalization levels and two mechanisms, with applications to non-determinism classification and LLM reasoning.
AI.motivation: To develop a formal framework for understanding how to construct canonical interpretations from theories with multiple admissible interpretations (plural structure theories), addressing the problem of non-determinism in structural reasoning and its applications.
AI.method: Develops a formal framework using structure theories (triples of signature, axioms, inference policy), distinguishes three canonicalization levels (closure stabilization, global completion, determinization), classifies non-determinism into Type E (epistemic) and Type S (structural), and proposes two canonicalization mechanisms (operator-based completion and selector-based construction).
AI.result: Establishes sufficient structural conditions for canonicalization mechanisms, shows pure inference-based completion reduces to saturated closure operator under specific conditions, proves closure stabilization for Type E theories, achieves determinization for Type S-strong theories via canonical selection, demonstrates multi-level canonicalization forms structurally non-commutative system, and applies framework to LLM reasoning where hallucination is unsupported canonicalization.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a formal foundation for canonicalization in plural structure theories, offering mechanisms to resolve non-determinism, with practical applications to reasoning systems including LLMs, though global confluence for Type E theories remains an open problem.

title: Muscle Memory for Agents: Compile not Merely Retrieve
summary: Memory for LLM agents has converged on a single architectural pattern: store experience as text, embeddings, reflections, or rules; retrieve at inference time; let a general-purpose orchestrator interpret what to do. This paper argues that the pattern is the wrong default for personalization. We position Muscle Memory - the practice of compiling recurring user intent into purpose-built specialist agents - as a distinct memory paradigm from retrieval, and we argue that compilation is a better fit for the workloads where current assistants impose a multi-turn tax on their users: making them repeatedly correct format, depth, and scope to obtain a domain-appropriate answer. We support the position with a reference implementation and empirical evidence. The implementation is a four-phase pipeline (Harvest $\rightarrow$ Analyze $\rightarrow$ Augment $\rightarrow$ Evaluate) that mines conversational history, separates behavioral from task patterns, and emits quality-gated executable compiled specialists with two-stage trigger matching. On 90 held-out scenarios across five user personas, the augmented assistant wins 32 of 36 cases where a specialist fires, an 88.9% win rate, with a +2.05 personalization gain and only a $-0.28$ accuracy cost on a 1-4 scale. We discuss why compilation is better suited than retrieval in this regime, what the result implies for the broader memory design space, and what open problems remain.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Muscle Memory - compiling recurring user patterns into specialist agents instead of retrieving from memory, showing significant personalization improvements with minimal accuracy trade-off.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agent memory architecture (storing and retrieving experiences) imposes a "multi-turn tax" on users who must repeatedly correct format, depth, and scope. This pattern is argued to be wrong for personalization workloads where users face repeated friction in obtaining domain-appropriate answers.
AI.method: Four-phase pipeline: Harvest (mine conversational history) → Analyze (separate behavioral from task patterns) → Augment (emit executable compiled specialists) → Evaluate (quality-gated with two-stage trigger matching). Reference implementation creates purpose-built specialist agents from recurring user intents.
AI.result: On 90 held-out scenarios across five user personas: 88.9% win rate (32 of 36 cases) when specialists fire, +2.05 personalization gain on 1-4 scale, with only -0.28 accuracy cost. Shows compilation outperforms retrieval for personalization tasks.
AI.conclusion: Muscle Memory (compilation) is a distinct and superior memory paradigm to retrieval for personalization workloads. The approach reduces user friction significantly, suggesting a broader rethinking of memory design space is needed for LLM agents.

title: Tracing sources of epistemic uncertainty in deep learning predictions: homo- and hetero-scedastic linearized estimators
summary: We adapt two classical statistical estimators for quantifying uncertainty to modern deep learning, in order to provide clearer insights into uncertainty attributable to two sources : aleatoric uncertainty, or locally scarce data. Our approach leverages recent advances in approximate Fisher Information Matrices, to enable scaling to actual architectures. Experimental results demonstrate how each test points is differentially impacted by both sources, highlighting the practical utility of our estimators in improving the robustness of real-world applications.

AI.tldr: Proposes uncertainty estimators for deep learning that distinguish between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty using Fisher Information Matrices.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models need better uncertainty quantification to distinguish between model uncertainty (epistemic) and data noise uncertainty (aleatoric). Current methods don't clearly separate these uncertainty sources or don't scale to modern architectures.
AI.method: Adapt classical statistical uncertainty estimators to deep learning using recent advances in approximate Fisher Information Matrices, enabling scaling to practical neural network architectures.
AI.result: Experimental results show each test point is differentially affected by both uncertainty sources, demonstrating practical utility in improving robustness for real-world applications.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scalable uncertainty estimators successfully separate epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty in deep learning, providing clearer insights into uncertainty sources and enhancing model robustness.

title: Emotion in an active inference model of human driving
summary: Active inference has emerged as a principled framework for modeling adaptive behavior by balancing goal-directed action with uncertainty reduction. It has been successfully applied across biological and artificial systems, including recent work on human driving. However, existing active inference models of driving have yet to address an important determinant of behavior in traffic: affective state, which significantly influences decision-making. Prior work in non-traffic domains has explored active inference agents in which emotions are represented along the axes of valence and arousal in the circumplex model. However, this work has been limited to simplified settings with discrete state spaces. In this work, we propose an expanded formulation of valence and arousal that can be extracted from a more complex active inference model of driving with continuous states. In particular, we condition affective estimates not only on the current state but also on predicted future outcomes. We evaluate the proposed approach in two interactive driving scenarios and show that the resulting emotion signals correspond to affective patterns reported in similar scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an expanded active inference model for driving that incorporates affective states (valence and arousal) conditioned on current and predicted future states, validated in interactive driving scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing active inference models of driving don't account for affective state, which is an important determinant of behavior in traffic. While prior work has explored emotions in simplified discrete state spaces, there's a need to model emotions in more complex continuous-state driving scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose an expanded formulation of valence and arousal that can be extracted from a complex active inference model of driving with continuous states. They condition affective estimates not only on current state but also on predicted future outcomes.
AI.result: The proposed approach was evaluated in two interactive driving scenarios, showing that the resulting emotion signals correspond to affective patterns reported in similar real-world scenarios.
AI.conclusion: This work successfully integrates affective states into active inference models of driving, bridging the gap between computational modeling and emotion-influenced decision-making in traffic scenarios.

title: Beyond Tier Labels: Role- and Deployment-Dependent Model Substitution in Multi-Call LLM Workflows
summary: Large multi-call LLM systems pose a scientific problem that query-level routing does not capture: the value of a model depends on where it enters a dependent computation and on the deployment that surrounds that call. Existing routers typically decide \emph{where} to spend a stronger model while treating the benefit of the substitution itself as known. We separate these two decisions through a predicate-action factorization and evaluate it in controlled solve-merge-verify workflows spanning 8-64 solve calls and four three-tier model ladders. The resulting evidence reveals a consistent principle beneath apparently conflicting outcomes. On numeric frequency counting, all-strong reduces RMSE from 4.818 to 1.538 in the Mixed Qwen/GPT ladder, whereas the average Qwen-only ordering reverses. Input-matched interventions further show that the same medium-to-strong action has sharply different value across roles and scales. A semantic task-and-contract shift reverses the Mixed ordering again, while allocation ablations distinguish useful sparse placement from under-coverage and indiscriminate escalation. Together, these results establish model substitution as a deployment-conditioned action rather than a property implied by a tier label, and they provide a practical sequence for large-scale workflow routing: calibrate the action, resolve its role-conditioned effect, and then optimize its placement.

AI.tldr: Large multi-call LLM systems require more sophisticated routing than simple query-level decisions because a model's value depends on its position in computational workflows and surrounding deployment context. The paper introduces a predicate-action factorization approach and shows through experiments that model substitution effectiveness varies by role and scale, requiring systematic calibration before placement optimization.
AI.motivation: Current LLM routing approaches treat model substitution benefits as fixed and known, but this doesn't capture the reality that a model's value depends on where it enters a dependent computation and the surrounding deployment context. There's a need to understand model substitution as a deployment-conditioned action rather than a simple property implied by tier labels.
AI.method: The paper separates routing decisions through a predicate-action factorization and evaluates this approach in controlled solve-merge-verify workflows spanning 8-64 solve calls across four three-tier model ladders (including Mixed Qwen/GPT configurations). Experiments include input-matched interventions, semantic task-and-contract shifts, and allocation ablations to distinguish effective placement strategies.
AI.result: Results show model substitution effectiveness varies dramatically: on numeric frequency counting, all-strong models reduced RMSE from 4.818 to 1.538 in Mixed Qwen/GPT ladder, but average Qwen-only ordering reversed. Input-matched interventions revealed the same medium-to-strong action had sharply different value across roles and scales. Semantic task shifts reversed the Mixed ordering again. Allocation ablations distinguished useful sparse placement from under-coverage and indiscriminate escalation.
AI.conclusion: Model substitution should be treated as a deployment-conditioned action rather than a property implied by tier labels. For large-scale workflow routing, a practical sequence emerges: first calibrate the action, then resolve its role-conditioned effect, and finally optimize its placement. This approach reveals consistent principles beneath apparently conflicting outcomes in multi-call LLM systems.

title: SkillConsist: Detecting Inconsistencies in Agent Skills via Bidirectional Graph Alignment
summary: Agent Skills provide reusable capabilities to LLM agents. Agent Skill inconsistencies can expose undisclosed dangerous behavior or cause wrong Skill selection. Recent Agent Skill research has increasingly examined Agent Skill consistency detection. Existing methods evaluate behaviors or security-property graphs against predefined categories or declared scopes. More recently, PL-HCL uses an LLM-based model to learn consistency across metadata, instructions, and resources. However, declaration and implementation behavior can be mixed across text and code, and a concise declaration can correspond to multiple connected implementation steps. We present SkillConsist to address both challenges. An LLM separates declaration and implementation content into behavior records on the implementation and declaration sides, while static analysis supplements implementation records. These records form declaration and implementation behavior graphs, respectively. Starting from a behavior record on either side, bidirectional graph alignment searches the other graph for a candidate subgraph and expands it along behavior relations until it completely expresses the source-side behavior. Graph differencing identifies conflicts between aligned subgraphs and outputs the detection results. We construct a 633-Skill benchmark from ClawHub's 500 most-downloaded public Skills and 133 Skill-Inject packages. The benchmark contains 319 inconsistent and 314 consistent Skills and 442 localized inconsistency annotations. On this benchmark, SkillConsist achieves 86.85% precision, 89.03% recall, and 87.93% F1 for package-level detection, improving F1 over the best baseline by 20.43 percentage points. For localization, it achieves 67.60% precision, 58.14% recall, and 62.52% F1.

AI.tldr: SkillConsist is a novel approach for detecting inconsistencies between Agent Skill declarations and implementations using LLM-powered behavior graph alignment and differencing, significantly outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Agent Skill inconsistencies pose serious risks - they can expose dangerous behaviors or cause wrong Skill selection. Existing methods have limitations: they either evaluate against predefined categories/declared scopes or use LLMs that struggle with mixed text-code content and complex implementation mappings.
AI.method: 1) LLM separates declaration/implementation content into behavior records, supplemented by static analysis for implementations. 2) Creates declaration and implementation behavior graphs. 3) Bidirectional graph alignment searches for matching subgraphs across graphs. 4) Graph differencing identifies conflicts between aligned subgraphs to detect inconsistencies.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 633 Skills (319 inconsistent, 314 consistent), SkillConsist achieved: Package-level detection - 86.85% precision, 89.03% recall, 87.93% F1 (improving over best baseline by 20.43 points). Localization - 67.60% precision, 58.14% recall, 62.52% F1.
AI.conclusion: SkillConsist effectively addresses the challenges of mixed text-code content and complex declaration-implementation mappings, providing superior inconsistency detection for Agent Skills through its graph-based alignment approach.

title: Training Variable Long Sequences with Data-Centric Parallel
summary: Training deep learning models on variable long sequences poses significant computational challenges. Existing methods force a difficult trade-off between efficiency and ease-of-use. Simple approaches use static configurations that cause workload imbalance low efficiency, while complex methods introduces significant complexity and code change for new models. To break this trade-off, we introduce Data-Centric Parallel (DCP). Its core principle is to let the data itself drive the runtime. It achieves this by dynamically adjusting direct runtime settings (e.g., parallel size, gradient accumulation, recomputation) based on each batch's sequence length. Empirical results demonstrate that our method achieves up to a 2.88$\times$ speedup on 32 H200 GPUs. Designed for generalization, it can be integrated into any model with 10 lines of code. We anticipate this simple yet effective approach will serve as a robust baseline and facilitate future advancements in distributed training for variable long sequences.

AI.tldr: DCP (Data-Centric Parallel) is a simple runtime system that dynamically adjusts parallel configurations based on sequence length per batch to efficiently train models on variable-length sequences.
AI.motivation: Training deep learning models on variable long sequences creates computational challenges with existing methods forcing a trade-off between efficiency and ease-of-use. Simple static configurations cause workload imbalance and low efficiency, while complex methods introduce significant complexity and code changes.
AI.method: Data-Centric Parallel (DCP) lets the data itself drive the runtime by dynamically adjusting direct runtime settings (parallel size, gradient accumulation, recomputation) based on each batch's sequence length. It's designed for generalization and can be integrated into any model with just 10 lines of code.
AI.result: Empirical results show DCP achieves up to 2.88× speedup on 32 H200 GPUs compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: DCP breaks the efficiency-ease-of-use trade-off for training on variable-length sequences. This simple yet effective approach can serve as a robust baseline and facilitate future advancements in distributed training for variable long sequences.

title: MoRSE: Task-Oriented Multi-Agent System with Mixture of Role-Subtask Experts
summary: Large language model-based multi-agent systems have recently shown strong potential for complex, long-horizon tasks. However, existing methods mainly rely on coarse prompt-level differentiation without parameter adaptation for diverse subtasks, resulting in insufficient inter-agent heterogeneity and limited specialized capability that bottleneck performance on tasks with complex requirements. To address this, we introduce a Task-Oriented Multi-Agent System with Mixture of Role-Subtask Experts (MoRSE) that distinguishes agents with (role, subtask)-conditional specialization at both the task structure and parameter levels. To make agents' responsibility explicit at the task structure level, we formulate a task-oriented multi-agent system that decomposes each task into a dependency-aware Directed Acyclic Graph of subtasks and assigns each agent a specific (role, subtask), introducing task-level specialization across collaborating agents. Additionally, to address the diverse role and subtask parameter adaptation demands, we propose a dynamic Mixture of (role, subtask) LoRA Experts module with a prototype-based semantic router for subtasks, augmenting agents with parameter-level specialization on a shared LLM substrate cost-effectively. Then, to co-optimize experts and router stably under sparse task rewards, we further propose a hierarchical group-relative policy optimization with two-layer credit assignment that isolates expert updates from the cross-route variance introduced by routing decisions, disentangling expert quality from routing quality. Experiments on code-generation benchmarks across three backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, with improvements in both whole-task and step-wise performance, and the gains from trained specialization generalize across held-out task categories and domains.

AI.tldr: MoRSE introduces a multi-agent system with specialized agents for different roles and subtasks using task decomposition graphs and parameter-level specialization through dynamic LoRA experts.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM systems lack sufficient inter-agent heterogeneity and specialized capabilities due to relying only on prompt-level differentiation without parameter adaptation, limiting performance on complex tasks.
AI.method: 1) Task-oriented multi-agent system with dependency-aware DAG subtask decomposition; 2) Dynamic Mixture of (role, subtask) LoRA Experts with prototype-based semantic router; 3) Hierarchical group-relative policy optimization with two-layer credit assignment for stable training.
AI.result: Experiments on code-generation benchmarks across three backbones show improvements in whole-task and step-wise performance, with gains generalizing across held-out task categories and domains.
AI.conclusion: MoRSE effectively addresses the heterogeneity and specialization limitations of current multi-agent LLM systems through both task structure and parameter-level specialization, enabling better performance on complex tasks with generalization capabilities.

title: PhysAttNet: Enhancing Predictive Performance in Industrial and Astrophysical Time Series via Physics-Informed Attention
summary: Accurate and robust time series forecasting is essential in many applications involving physical processes, such as manufacturing monitoring and astrophysical event detection. In these settings, predictive models must remain reliable under noise, variability, and measurement uncertainty while capturing temporally localized structures corresponding to physically meaningful events. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely used for such tasks due to their computational efficiency and strong representational capacity. However, their learned temporal representations often exhibit unstable or physically inconsistent attention patterns, reducing robustness, generalization, and interpretability. This paper introduces PhysAttNet, a physics-informed attention framework for time series forecasting. PhysAttNet augments a lightweight CNN forecaster with an attention head guided by domain-informed regularization reflecting the structural properties of physical signals. Specifically, three complementary constraints are imposed during training: an alignment regularization that encourages attention to follow smooth, peak-centered temporal structures derived from the input signal, a smoothness regularization that enforces continuous temporal evolution, and a sparsity regularization that promotes selective focus on informative intervals. These differentiable regularization terms introduce physics-guided inductive bias without requiring annotated explanations or manual supervision. Experiments on two distinct applications, namely predicting cutting forces during milling and forecasting flares in blazar time series, demonstrate that PhysAttNet improves forecasting accuracy, generalization, and prediction performance on structurally important events.

AI.tldr: PhysAttNet is a physics-informed attention framework for time series forecasting that enhances CNN models with domain-guided regularization to improve robustness and interpretability in physical signal prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Current CNN models for physical time series forecasting often exhibit unstable or physically inconsistent attention patterns, reducing robustness, generalization, and interpretability in applications like manufacturing monitoring and astrophysical event detection where models must handle noise and variability while capturing meaningful physical events.
AI.method: The paper introduces PhysAttNet, which augments a lightweight CNN forecaster with an attention head guided by three complementary differentiable regularization terms: alignment regularization (encourages attention to follow smooth, peak-centered temporal structures), smoothness regularization (enforces continuous temporal evolution), and sparsity regularization (promotes selective focus on informative intervals).
AI.result: Experiments on cutting force prediction in milling and blazar flare forecasting demonstrate that PhysAttNet improves forecasting accuracy, generalization, and prediction performance on structurally important events without requiring annotated explanations or manual supervision.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed attention regularization effectively introduces domain knowledge into neural network forecasting models, enhancing their reliability, interpretability, and performance on physical signal prediction tasks while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: The Knowing-Saying Gap: When Probes See Errors that Confidence Misses
summary: Linear probes detect corrupted context in language models with near-perfect accuracy, yet this does not translate into reliable failure prediction. The result is a dissociation with direct implications for deployment monitoring. Across multi-hop arithmetic chains, probes that detect corruption turn out to be uninformative about final answer correctness; models forced into structured confidence formats collapse to two values with indistinguishable error rates; and probe persistence across hops fails to separate correct from incorrect outcomes, refuting our pre-registered "persistence beats peak" hypothesis. This pattern of knowing but not saying generalises across model families including reasoning models. As a real-time monitor, probe-based interventions are sharply model and error-type dependent: branch-and-pick is net-positive across models and uniquely non-breaking on Llama-3.1-8B (4 rescued, 0 broken), while reprompt and replace-prior break correct traces at roughly the rate they rescue wrong ones. Probe-based monitoring is a necessary complement to verbalised confidence, but no single intervention dominates, and the deployable answer is model-aware, error-type-aware routing.

AI.tldr: Linear probes can detect corrupted context in language models with near-perfect accuracy, but this detection doesn't reliably predict model failures or enable effective interventions, requiring model-aware and error-type-aware routing for deployment.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the dissociation between linear probes' ability to detect corrupted context in language models and their inability to reliably predict model failures, which has important implications for deployment monitoring and safety.
AI.method: The study uses linear probes on multi-hop arithmetic chains across different model families, testing probe persistence across reasoning hops, structured confidence formats, and various intervention strategies (branch-and-pick, reprompt, replace-prior) to evaluate failure prediction capabilities.
AI.result: Probes detect corruption with near-perfect accuracy but fail to predict final answer correctness. Models forced into structured confidence formats collapse to binary outputs with indistinguishable error rates. Probe persistence doesn't separate correct from incorrect outcomes. Intervention effectiveness is model and error-type dependent: branch-and-pick works best across models, while reprompt and replace-prior break correct traces as often as they rescue wrong ones.
AI.conclusion: Probe-based monitoring is necessary but insufficient alone. No single intervention dominates across models. Effective deployment requires model-aware, error-type-aware routing strategies that combine probe monitoring with verbalized confidence, as models exhibit a "knowing but not saying" pattern that persists across model families including reasoning models.

title: Distributed Team Orchestration via Supervisor Networks: Convergence, Optimality, and Resilience
summary: In this paper, we study zero-sum potential team games with a supervisor network, where agents rely on supervisor-provided belief information rather than accurate common beliefs. The main challenge is that such belief information can be inaccurate because of supervisors' belief-estimation errors and the misreporting of joint actions by Byzantine teams. We propose the distributed team-orchestrating algorithm (DTOA), which combines team fictitious play with supervisor-based distributed belief learning. We prove the convergence of supervisors' belief estimates and establish that the induced learning dynamics converge to a near team-Nash equilibrium (TNE) in terms of the team-Nash gap (TNG). In the Byzantine setting, we consider a misreporting attack model and develop a Byzantine-resilient DTOA. We further provide probabilistic guarantees for Byzantine-team identification and establish an asymptotic bound on the honest TNG. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical findings, compare DTOA with baseline learning methods, and evaluate its performance in a Markov decision process setting.

AI.tldr: Proposes DTOA algorithm for zero-sum potential team games with supervisor networks, handling inaccurate belief information and Byzantine attacks, with convergence guarantees to near team-Nash equilibrium.
AI.motivation: In team games with supervisor networks, agents rely on supervisor-provided belief information, which can be inaccurate due to supervisors' belief-estimation errors and Byzantine teams misreporting joint actions, requiring robust algorithms that handle these challenges.
AI.method: Proposes distributed team-orchestrating algorithm (DTOA) combining team fictitious play with supervisor-based distributed belief learning. For Byzantine settings, develops Byzantine-resilient DTOA with probabilistic guarantees for Byzantine-team identification.
AI.result: Proves convergence of supervisors' belief estimates and shows learning dynamics converge to near team-Nash equilibrium in terms of team-Nash gap. Provides asymptotic bound on honest TNG in Byzantine settings. Numerical experiments validate theoretical findings and compare with baselines.
AI.conclusion: DTOA effectively addresses challenges in zero-sum potential team games with supervisor networks, providing theoretical guarantees for convergence and Byzantine resilience, with practical performance demonstrated in simulations.

authors: Abu Sa-Adat Mohamed Moon-Im Al Ahsan
title: CODS: Iterative Bellman-Residual Data Selection for Reusable Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline reinforcement learning repeatedly trains policies from a fixed transition pool, making redundant data costly across seeds and hyperparameters, while naive subsampling can remove rare transitions needed for long-horizon credit assignment. We introduce CODS, a critic-guided selector that alternates between fitting an algorithm-matched critic and acquiring high-residual transitions before freezing a reusable subset. Unlike prioritized replay, CODS produces a static artifact; unlike one-shot residual selection, it refreshes scores as the critic changes. At a 10\% budget, CODS retains 96.6\% of eligible-pool performance across 20 valid D4RL task--algorithm cells. It exceeds ReDOR and OPER on 19/20 cells and every other subset baseline on 20/20; all six subset advantages remain significant under predeclared hierarchical inference with Holm correction. Holding total selector updates fixed, five acquisition rounds improve four representative cells by 11.23 points over one round and saturate thereafter. Equal-pass and equal-hour evaluations clarify that reuse, rather than a single-run speedup, creates the compute advantage. Mechanism and corruption interventions expose both useful sparse-reward enrichment and sensitivity to outliers. Finally, a whole-trace extension retains 95.4\% of pooled ALFWorld success and 96.5\% of pooled GSM8K exact match. CODS is therefore a reusable selection procedure, not a formal coreset guarantee.

AI.tldr: CODS is a critic-guided offline RL data selection method that alternates between fitting a critic and selecting high-residual transitions to create reusable data subsets, achieving strong performance at 10% budget across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Offline RL requires repeated training from fixed data pools, making redundant data expensive across seeds and hyperparameters, while naive subsampling can remove rare transitions needed for long-horizon credit assignment.
AI.method: CODS alternates between: 1) fitting an algorithm-matched critic, 2) acquiring high-residual transitions, then freezes a reusable subset. Unlike prioritized replay (dynamic) or one-shot residual selection, it updates scores as the critic improves through multiple acquisition rounds.
AI.result: At 10% budget, CODS retains 96.6% of full-pool performance across 20 D4RL task-algorithm cells, outperforms ReDOR and OPER on 19/20 cells, beats all subset baselines on 20/20, and shows significant improvements with multiple acquisition rounds. Extensions show strong performance on ALFWorld and GSM8K.
AI.conclusion: CODS provides an effective reusable data selection procedure for offline RL that offers computational advantages through data reuse rather than single-run speedups, though it's a practical selection method rather than a formal coreset guarantee.

title: NL2SHACL-Bench: A Benchmark Suite for Natural Language to SHACL Translation
summary: SHACL is a core technology for validating the conformance of RDF knowledge graphs (KGs). Yet, authoring SHACL shapes requires technical expertise that most domain experts lack. Translating natural language requirements into SHACL (NL2SHACL) would lower this barrier. However, there is no dedicated benchmark for NL2SHACL, and evaluating generated shapes requires methods beyond string comparison, as semantically equivalent shapes can differ in serialisation and structure. To tackle these challenges, we present NL2SHACL-Bench, a benchmark suite for natural language to SHACL translation. Using NL2SHACL-Bench, we evaluate four state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) for this task. Our results show that current LLMs are highly capable of generating syntactically valid SHACL, but still struggle to produce semantically equivalent constraints for complex logical and structural patterns. This indicates that NL2SHACL-Bench provides a meaningful basis for measuring advances in the NL2SHACL state of the art.

AI.tldr: A benchmark suite called NL2SHACL-Bench is introduced to evaluate natural language to SHACL translation, revealing that while LLMs generate syntactically valid SHACL, they struggle with semantically equivalent constraints for complex patterns.
AI.motivation: SHACL validation of RDF knowledge graphs requires technical expertise that domain experts lack, creating a barrier. There is no dedicated benchmark for NL2SHACL (natural language to SHACL), and evaluating generated shapes requires methods beyond string comparison since semantically equivalent shapes can differ in serialization and structure.
AI.method: The authors present NL2SHACL-Bench, a benchmark suite for natural language to SHACL translation. Using this benchmark, they evaluate four state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) for the NL2SHACL task.
AI.result: Current LLMs are highly capable of generating syntactically valid SHACL, but struggle to produce semantically equivalent constraints for complex logical and structural patterns. The benchmark provides a meaningful basis for measuring advances in NL2SHACL state of the art.
AI.conclusion: NL2SHACL-Bench addresses the lack of a dedicated benchmark for natural language to SHACL translation and shows that while LLMs have made progress in generating valid SHACL syntax, significant challenges remain in achieving semantic equivalence for complex constraints.

title: An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding
summary:
Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

AI.tldr: MSEval is a new benchmark that evaluates multi-agent coding systems using real-world projects and measures practical performance metrics including functional success, latency, and token costs.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent coding benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical costs (time and money), conflate reasoning with communication, and only reward superficial task completion rather than actual software quality.
AI.method: Created MSEval benchmark with 10 authentic full-stack projects across 10 domains. Uses LegoGent execution engine to test 10 collaboration topologies with periodic sync intervals and native CI/CD deployment. Employs automated grader TAgent to dynamically probe implementations and measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token costs.
AI.result: Across 100 runs, MSEval shows that organizational topology is as important as model capability in shaping the speed-cost-quality trade-off. Varying topology for identical tasks and models shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with highest quality, while heavy managerial oversight degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software, demonstrating that team organization structure rivals model capability in determining performance outcomes.

title: Neural Operators for Immersed-Boundary Soft Swimmers Locomotion
summary: High-fidelity immersed-boundary simulation resolves the coupled motion of a deforming swimmer and its surrounding flow, but the resulting cost limits repeated evaluations for engineering design, parameter studies, and control. We develop neural-operator surrogates for temporal prediction of the hydrodynamic fields generated by planar and volumetric eel swimmers. The surrogates are trained on regular-grid fields exported from adaptive fluid--structure simulations and are conditioned on swimmer geometry and Reynolds number. The planar model jointly predicts two velocity components, scalar vorticity, and pressure. On five held-out high-Reynolds-number trajectories, its full-domain global relative L^2 error is 3.51 %. The volumetric formulation uses three target-specific models with a common multichannel input: one model predicts three-dimensional velocity, one predicts vorticity, and one predicts pressure. Their full-domain global relative L^2 errors on five held-out within-range trajectories are 3.44 %, 5.58 %, and 19.2 %. Together, the results demonstrate the feasibility of field-resolved neural surrogates for moving-boundary swimmer flows while identifying pressure accuracy and physical consistency as priorities for further development.

AI.tldr: Neural-operator surrogates are developed to predict hydrodynamic fields around deforming swimmers, significantly reducing computational costs compared to traditional high-fidelity simulations.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity immersed-boundary simulations of swimming dynamics are computationally expensive, limiting their use for engineering design, parameter studies, and control applications where repeated evaluations are needed.
AI.method: Develop neural-operator surrogates trained on regular-grid fields from adaptive fluid-structure simulations, conditioned on swimmer geometry and Reynolds number. Use separate models: a planar model predicting 2D velocity, vorticity, and pressure, and volumetric models with target-specific networks for 3D velocity, vorticity, and pressure.
AI.result: Planar model achieved 3.51% global relative L² error on held-out high-Reynolds-number trajectories. Volumetric models achieved 3.44% error for velocity, 5.58% for vorticity, and 19.2% for pressure on held-out within-range trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Field-resolved neural surrogates are feasible for moving-boundary swimmer flows, but pressure accuracy and physical consistency need improvement for further development.

title: Dynamic Coalition Formation and Communication Pricing in Skill-Based Agentic AI Systems
summary: Modern agentic AI systems combine multiple large language model agents with heterogeneous skills, yet most architectures either fix communication in advance or allow full broadcast. Both can be inefficient because token cost, latency, redundancy, and error propagation increase with the number of active agents and communication links. We model agent selection and communication as a cooperative game with task-conditioned net utility $U(C\mid x)=V(C\mid x)-\sum_{i\in C}c_i$, separating coalition-level costs from agent activation costs. We propose a marginal-value activation rule and greedy router, extend the model to optimize communication edges with per-edge costs, and use estimated Shapley values to predict which agents are worth contacting before and during execution. We connect the problem to submodular maximization and prove two limited guarantees: a curvature-refined bound for a monotone, cardinality-constrained special case, and a tight $1/2$-approximation, with a correction for signed objectives, for an unconstrained non-monotone case via double greedy. Neither guarantee applies directly to the main router, which remains a heuristic. We also prove a Shapley-submodularity sandwich bound linking the error of marginal-value routing to a per-agent diminishing-returns quantity. In synthetic experiments, greedy routing achieves $99.5%$ of brute-force-optimal utility while activating $1.96$ of $8$ agents on average, compared with $38.8%$ for full broadcast. Performance is robust to activation cost and redundancy weight but falls to $66%$ under strong violations of submodularity or noisy value estimates. We distinguish the framework from Shapley pricing, hedonic coalition formation, and communication-graph pruning, and propose evaluation on real multi-agent LLM benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A framework for efficient communication in multi-agent LLM systems using cooperative game theory and Shapley values to optimize agent selection and reduce token costs.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent LLM architectures either use fixed communication patterns or full broadcast, which are inefficient due to increasing token costs, latency, redundancy, and error propagation as more agents and communication links are added.
AI.method: Models agent selection and communication as cooperative game with task-conditioned net utility function, proposes marginal-value activation rule and greedy router, extends to optimize communication edges with per-edge costs, uses estimated Shapley values to predict worthwhile agents to contact, connects to submodular maximization with theoretical guarantees for special cases.
AI.result: In synthetic experiments, greedy routing achieves 99.5% of brute-force optimal utility while activating only 1.96 of 8 agents on average (vs. 38.8% for full broadcast), robust to activation costs but performance degrades to 66% under strong submodularity violations or noisy value estimates.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides efficient communication routing for multi-agent LLM systems, distinguishes from related approaches like Shapley pricing and coalition formation, and offers theoretical insights while remaining a practical heuristic approach for real-world applications.

authors: Abu Sa-Adat Mohamed Moon-Im Al Ahsan
title: Finite Constant Frontiers and Auditable Regret Certificates for Average-Reward Reinforcement Learning
summary: Average-reward reinforcement-learning regret is known up to logarithmic factors, but the numerical content of published guarantees is difficult to compare because probability mode, structural parameter, logarithmic normalization, prior information, and planning assumptions differ. We introduce a constant-aware comparison protocol and derive an explicit finite lower certificate for communicating MDPs. The construction is a binary tree of two-state blocks; its proof uses exact trajectory-level Bernoulli KL divergence and keeps action budget, diameter, occupancy, navigation cost, and terminal bias explicit. A common closed-form envelope improves the published coefficient $0.015$ across a finite frontier: $0.0200$ in a moderate regime and up to $0.0291$ under stronger action, diameter, and horizon conditions, a $94\%$ increase. The limiting coefficient is $\frac1{32}\sqrt{(A-3)/A}$.
