AI.conclusion: EasyBalance provides an effective cross-layer load balancing solution for MoE inference that offers instant adaptability and minimal overhead compared to existing expert replication/migration approaches, significantly improving inference efficiency through smart workload scheduling across layers.

title: Who Built This Model? Tracing LLM Lineage via Spectral Fingerprints in Weight Space
summary: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly developed through complex, multi-stage pipelines, leading to intricate lineage relationships that reflect model origin, ownership, and evolution. Understanding these relationships is important for model provenance, governance, and supply-chain integrity. In this work, we investigate the notion of LLM "biometrics" (analogous to human biometrics) to ask whether LLMs exhibit intrinsic fingerprints in weight space alone, without access to input data, that reveal their origin and lineage. We formulate this as a lineage discrimination problem, distinguishing among independent-origin, same-series, and shared-base models. To characterize these relationships, we propose a unified geometric fingerprinting framework that analyzes weight matrices from two complementary perspectives: (i) spectral energy, captured by singular value distributions to encode global magnitude patterns, and (ii) subspace alignment, quantified via subspace deviations to capture directional geometry. Our analysis uncovers a clear hierarchy of structural similarity in weight space: spectral energy reliably distinguishes independently trained models and different model families, while subspace alignment enables fine-grained discrimination among closely related models, including variations in dataset scale and post-training procedures. Extensive experiments on over 110 diverse open-weight LLM pairs demonstrate that weight-space geometry provides a robust and interpretable signal for model lineage, enabling coarse-grained regime separation and fine-grained discrimination within shared-base models.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit intrinsic "biometric" fingerprints in weight space that can reveal model origin and lineage through analysis of spectral energy and subspace alignment, enabling discrimination between different lineage relationships without access to input data.
AI.motivation: Open-weight LLMs are increasingly developed through complex multi-stage pipelines, creating intricate lineage relationships important for model provenance, governance, and supply-chain integrity. Understanding these relationships is crucial but challenging.
AI.method: Proposes a unified geometric fingerprinting framework that analyzes weight matrices from two complementary perspectives: (1) spectral energy (captured by singular value distributions encoding global magnitude patterns) and (2) subspace alignment (quantified via subspace deviations capturing directional geometry).
AI.result: Analysis of over 110 diverse open-weight LLM pairs reveals a clear hierarchy of structural similarity: spectral energy reliably distinguishes independently trained models and different model families, while subspace alignment enables fine-grained discrimination among closely related models, including variations in dataset scale and post-training procedures.
AI.conclusion: Weight-space geometry provides a robust and interpretable signal for model lineage, enabling both coarse-grained regime separation and fine-grained discrimination within shared-base models, establishing the concept of LLM "biometrics" analogous to human biometrics for model provenance.

title: ZeroLock: Concurrent Memory-Efficient LLM Training via Modular Update Decoupling
summary: Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning at the edge adapts the model to scenario-specific data while preserving privacy. Although existing studies proposed pipeline parallelism to address the limited memory and computing resources of edge devices, they commonly rely on backpropagation (BP) training, which has a fundamental limitation of update locking and could experience severe throughput and memory bottlenecks. In this work, we propose a BP-free algorithm, called ZeroLock, that decouples the model updates into independent chunk updates by local objective construction. It breaks the update locking of BP and hence can improve throughput at the algorithm level and lower memory usage by reducing activation storage. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first theoretical framework for such local objective construction-based approaches under general model chunk division by mapping local objectives to the global objective. We prove that ZeroLock has a convergence rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\sqrt{T})$, which differs from BP only by polylogarithmic factors. We design a system for ZeroLock and build real-world prototypes, incorporating techniques such as early forwarding and failure recovery for efficient and robust implementation. Experiments on the prototype show that compared to BP-based baselines, ZeroLock reduces the memory by 26.5% and improves throughput by 4.9%.

AI.tldr: ZeroLock: A BP-free algorithm for LLM fine-tuning at the edge that decouples model updates into independent chunk updates using local objective construction, breaking backpropagation's update locking to improve throughput and reduce memory usage.
AI.motivation: LLM fine-tuning at the edge addresses privacy concerns but faces resource limitations. Existing pipeline parallelism approaches rely on backpropagation training which suffers from update locking, causing throughput and memory bottlenecks that need to be addressed.
AI.method: Proposes ZeroLock algorithm that constructs local objectives for independent chunk updates, eliminating backpropagation's update locking. Includes theoretical framework mapping local objectives to global objective, system design with early forwarding and failure recovery techniques, and real-world prototype implementation.
AI.result: Experimental results show 26.5% memory reduction and 4.9% throughput improvement compared to BP-based baselines. Theoretical analysis proves convergence rate of Õ(1/√T), differing from BP only by polylogarithmic factors.
AI.conclusion: ZeroLock successfully addresses backpropagation limitations for edge LLM fine-tuning by providing a BP-free algorithm with theoretical guarantees and practical performance improvements in both memory efficiency and throughput.

title: CliniCARE-Bench: Clinical Calibrated Audit of Medical Reasoning in EHR
summary: Large language models perform strongly on medical knowledge benchmarks, but reliable clinical deployment requires agents to conduct defensible investigations over heterogeneous, longitudinal records: determining what evidence is needed, retrieving and reconciling structured and free-text data, grounding conclusions in verifiable evidence, and deferring cases that cannot be resolved reliably. We introduce CliniCARE-Bench (Clinical Calibrated Audit of Medical Reasoning in EHR), a benchmark for retrospective clinical audit: 25 clinician-validated scenarios instantiated as 750 patient-specific cases over real-patient-derived MIMIC-IV data. Systems investigate each case through a governed, logged tool environment for record retrieval, computation, and policy access, and return one of four verdicts---Yes, No, Indeterminate: Lack of Data, or Indeterminate: Medically Ambiguous---the last two separating missing evidence from residual medical ambiguity. Beyond verdict accuracy, we score patient-evidence and policy grounding, process adherence, calibrated abstention, reliability, and efficiency against case-level reference verdicts produced by independent multi-model adjudication and calibrated against Clinical Board review. Every retrieval, computation, and report is replayable, so the investigation trace is inspectable and scorable. To our knowledge, CliniCARE-Bench is the first deployment-oriented clinical-agent benchmark to jointly evaluate real longitudinal EHR investigation, claim-level evidence grounding, governing-policy use, process adherence, and calibrated abstention within a common patient-level adjudication framework. Across 16 agentic systems, four-way accuracy spans 65.3-76.1%, but raw accuracy overstates investigation quality. Defect-free accuracy, which credits a verdict only when correct and free of prohibited shortcuts, is 4.8-14.8 points lower and reorders the leaderboard.

AI.tldr: CliniCARE-Bench is a novel clinical audit benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on longitudinal EHR investigations with calibrated abstention, evidence grounding, and process adherence requirements.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs perform well on medical knowledge benchmarks but lack reliable clinical deployment capabilities for defensible investigations over heterogeneous, longitudinal medical records. There's a need to evaluate systems that can determine required evidence, retrieve structured and free-text data, ground conclusions in verifiable evidence, and appropriately defer uncertain cases.
AI.method: Created CliniCARE-Bench with 25 clinician-validated scenarios instantiated as 750 patient-specific cases using real-patient MIMIC-IV data. Systems investigate cases through a governed tool environment for record retrieval, computation, and policy access. They return one of four verdicts: Yes, No, Indeterminate: Lack of Data, or Indeterminate: Medically Ambiguous. Evaluation scores include verdict accuracy, patient-evidence/policy grounding, process adherence, calibrated abstention, reliability, and efficiency.
AI.result: Across 16 agentic systems, four-way accuracy ranged from 65.3% to 76.1%. However, defect-free accuracy (which credits verdicts only when correct and free of prohibited shortcuts) was 4.8-14.8 points lower and reordered the leaderboard, showing that raw accuracy overstates investigation quality.
AI.conclusion: CliniCARE-Bench is the first deployment-oriented clinical benchmark that jointly evaluates real longitudinal EHR investigation, evidence grounding, policy use, process adherence, and calibrated abstention. The results demonstrate that comprehensive evaluation metrics beyond simple accuracy are crucial for assessing clinical readiness of AI agents.

title: Evaluator Ensembles Under Reward Hacking: Covariance Geometry and Finite-Search Guarantees
summary: Language-model judges and reward models enable scalable supervision, but finite optimization can exploit evaluator errors rather than improve response quality. We characterize this failure through the covariance geometry of evaluator ensembles. For calibrated judges, the ensemble mean retains common-mode error along the all-ones direction, whereas cross-judge disagreement captures only orthogonal error. Consequently, disagreement can be high despite robust aggregation, or low while shared response-dependent errors persist. We prove that common-mode error is not identifiable from internal judge scores alone. Under a joint sub-Gaussian model, we bound best-of-K selection overstatement and target-quality regret, extending the guarantees to predictably adaptive search under conditional calibration. The resulting search terms scale as the square root of log K and are asymptotically tight for Gaussian projected errors. We further show that noisy quality proxies introduce artificial rank-one covariance without changing disagreement, and propose a bounded two-anchor Bernstein certificate for finite-search error and regret. Fixed-seed Gaussian stress tests over 120 (J, rho, K) configurations and real-model audits validate the theory while revealing the limits of disagreement-based diagnostics under increasing search pressure.

AI.tldr: Paper shows that using ensembles of language model judges/reward models can still fail due to shared errors, and proposes mathematical analysis of when disagreement metrics misrepresent actual error patterns.
AI.motivation: Language model judges and reward models enable scalable supervision, but optimization can exploit evaluator errors rather than improve response quality. Existing approaches using judge ensembles can fail due to common-mode errors that aren't captured by simple disagreement metrics.
AI.method: Characterizes failure through covariance geometry of evaluator ensembles. Uses mathematical proofs to show common-mode error is not identifiable from internal judge scores alone. Develops bounds for best-of-K selection overstatement and target-quality regret under joint sub-Gaussian models. Proposes bounded two-anchor Bernstein certificate for finite-search error analysis.
AI.result: Proves that ensemble mean retains common-mode error along all-ones direction while cross-judge disagreement captures only orthogonal error. Shows disagreement can be high despite robust aggregation, or low while shared errors persist. Provides tight asymptotic bounds for Gaussian projected errors. Validates theory through fixed-seed Gaussian stress tests over 120 configurations and real-model audits.
AI.conclusion: Disagreement-based diagnostics have limitations under increasing search pressure, and common-mode errors in judge ensembles pose fundamental identifiability challenges that require new certification methods like the proposed two-anchor Bernstein certificate.

title: CausalNav: Reliability-Certified Causal World Models for Control under Physical-Parameter Shift
summary: A world model is only useful for physical AI if it changes what the agent does, and only safe if it declines to do so when it is wrong. We study both halves of that requirement with CausalNav, a controller built around a signed, action-conditioned transition graph over identified state coordinates. At deployment CausalNav simulates a small library of intervention sequences, converts their objective error into policy-logit advice, and admits that advice only when a scale-free predictive-reliability certificate, a policy-margin gate, and an argmax-agreement gate all pass; otherwise it falls back exactly to its own model-based base controller. We evaluate against nine controlled baselines (transformer, recurrent, split-latent, graph, causal-induction, and three recent model-based reasoning modules) on CartPole-v1 and discretized Pendulum-v1 with physical-parameter shifts, under one shared PPO trainer, one interaction budget, and ten held-out seeds (200 runs). CausalNav attains the best average rank (1.25 of ten). The diagnostic result is more informative than the ranking: the learned graph recovers structure well above chance (CartPole F1 = 0.59 +/- 0.09), yet per-seed structural fidelity is uncorrelated with per-seed control benefit (r = -0.15, p = 0.67), and the certificate abstains on 10/10 Pendulum seeds, where forcing the planner on costs return. Model fidelity did not predict downstream control utility in our setting; certified abstention, not better prediction, is what made the world model safe to deploy.

AI.tldr: CausalNav is a safety-certified controller that uses a causal graph world model with multiple gates (reliability certificate, policy-margin gate, argmax-agreement gate) to decide when to trust its predictions, falling back to a base controller when uncertain, achieving best average rank in physical control tasks.
AI.motivation: World models for physical AI should only influence agent behavior when they're accurate and useful, and abstain when they're wrong to ensure safety. The paper aims to create a world model that can both improve performance when correct and safely decline when uncertain.
AI.method: CausalNav builds a signed, action-conditioned transition graph over identified state coordinates. At deployment, it simulates intervention sequences, converts prediction errors into policy-logit advice, and only admits this advice when three conditions pass: 1) scale-free predictive-reliability certificate, 2) policy-margin gate, and 3) argmax-agreement gate. Otherwise, it falls back to a model-based base controller.
AI.result: CausalNav achieved best average rank (1.25 of ten) across 200 runs on CartPole-v1 and discretized Pendulum-v1 with physical-parameter shifts. The learned graph recovered structure significantly above chance (CartPole F1 = 0.59 ± 0.09), but structural fidelity didn't correlate with control benefit (r = -0.15, p = 0.67). The certificate successfully abstained on 10/10 Pendulum seeds where forcing the planner would have reduced performance.
AI.conclusion: Model fidelity alone didn't predict downstream control utility in this setting. The key to safety was certified abstention - knowing when not to use the world model - rather than simply having better predictions. The proposed multi-gate certification mechanism enables safe deployment of world models in physical AI systems.

title: Quality-Diversity Stress Tests for Process Reward Models:What Archive Coverage Can and Cannot Certify
summary: Process reward models (PRMs) score intermediate reasoning steps and are widely used for search, ranking, and training, but optimization can exploit these learned proxies by increasing reward while turning correct reasoning into incorrect reasoning. We formulate PRM stress testing as a quality-diversity search problem using MAP-Elites, retaining the most severe correctness-flipping edit in each behavior-space region while separating search coverage from exploit coverage. We characterize what such archives certify: finite-cell repair bounds covered-cell tail risk and average residual severity but cannot bound the worst remaining cell from covered fraction alone; under Lipschitz post-repair loss and metric-cover auditing, the residual is bounded by archive fitting error plus the Lipschitz constant times the covering radius. A controlled landscape validates this certificate and the impossibility of any fraction-only worst-case guarantee. On real PRMs, the search reveals an aggregation-dependent vulnerability in Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B: padding yields 44 strict exploits with maximum gain 0.294 under mean pooling versus one exploit under minimum readout; a matched syntactic control isolates the mechanism, and an RLHFlow value-head model shows the same qualitative effect with maximum gain 0.005. A predeclared paired LoRA repair protocol reduces exploit rates from 0.148 to 0.037 to 0.074, lowers the worst attack from 0.333 to 0.177 to 0.212, improves ranking AUROC without degrading best-of-4 accuracy, attributes gains to adversarial fine-tuning rather than archive diversity, and is confirmed by independent unpaired replications (44 to 1, clean-split worst gain 0.0092, MATH-500 41 to 0, clean ranking 40/40).

AI.tldr: Process reward models can be exploited to increase reward while making reasoning incorrect; this paper develops a quality-diversity search method to find these exploits, characterizes certification bounds, demonstrates vulnerabilities in real PRMs, and proposes a repair protocol that reduces exploits.
AI.motivation: Process reward models are widely used but can be exploited by increasing reward while turning correct reasoning into incorrect reasoning, creating safety vulnerabilities that need to be systematically identified and repaired.
AI.method: Formulate PRM stress testing as quality-diversity search using MAP-Elites to find correctness-flipping edits, characterize certification bounds theoretically, validate on controlled landscapes, and apply to real PRMs to reveal aggregation-dependent vulnerabilities.
AI.result: Revealed aggregation-dependent vulnerability in Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B (44 strict exploits with mean pooling vs. 1 with min readout), proposed LoRA repair protocol reduces exploit rates from 0.148 to 0.037-0.074 and worst attack from 0.333 to 0.177-0.212 while improving ranking AUROC without degrading accuracy.
AI.conclusion: PRMs have systematic vulnerabilities that can be exploited, quality-diversity search effectively identifies them with certifiable bounds, and targeted repairs can substantially reduce exploitability while maintaining performance, though fraction-only certification is insufficient.

title: When the Judge Should Not Decide: Evidence-Locked, Non-Compensatory Selection Bounds LLM-Judge Failure in Reasoning Pipelines
summary: An LLM judge deployed inside a reasoning pipeline does not merely measure quality, it decides which answer ships. We show that the cost of that decision depends less on judge accuracy than on the decision rule the judge is embedded in. On frozen candidate pools from four GRPO policies, an unconstrained scalar DeepSeek-R1-7B judge buys almost nothing over answer-level majority vote (+1.0 pp on 500 GSM8K questions, +0.34 EM on 300 HotpotQA questions), and on a frozen-rule 30-question confirmation split it is 10 points worse than majority, a judge that destroys accuracy while scoring candidates confidently. We then subordinate the same judge to Evidence-Locked Derive-Gate-Repair (EL-DGR), a task-adaptive non-compensatory rule under which a judge preference may override evidence-supported consensus only with an extractive evidence certificate, and a repair only when neither alternative is certified and the repair is. With no change to the judge, the candidates, or the budget, EL-DGR reaches 58.2% on GSM8K (vs. 56.8% judge, 55.8% majority, 55.4% first candidate) and 17.33 EM / 25.46 F1 on HotpotQA (vs. 15.67/23.49, 15.33/23.19, 15.33/22.97), improving on first-candidate GRPO by +2.8 pp (exact McNemar p=0.0026) and +2.00 EM (p=0.070, borderline). A decision audit shows why: EL-DGR overturns consensus on only 8 of 30 pilot questions and never converts a correct consensus into an incorrect answer. We also report what did not work: the same seven-channel decomposition used as a step-level gated training reward is null, and corrected channel-drop ablations show no channel is individually necessary (p=1.0 throughout). The practitioner-facing finding is negative about judges and positive about admissibility, bound the judge's blast radius rather than trying to make it accurate.

AI.tldr: LLM judges in reasoning pipelines need to be embedded in proper decision rules rather than just optimized for accuracy - the Evidence-Locked Derive-Gate-Repair (EL-DGR) rule significantly outperforms simple voting or judge scoring alone by constraining judge decisions with evidence requirements.
AI.motivation: LLM judges are increasingly used to select final answers in reasoning pipelines, but simply improving judge accuracy may not translate to better decisions. The paper investigates how the decision rules that embed judges affect overall performance more than judge accuracy itself.
AI.method: The paper evaluates an unconstrained scalar DeepSeek-R1-7B judge against answer-level majority voting on frozen candidate pools from GRPO policies. It then introduces Evidence-Locked Derive-Gate-Repair (EL-DGR), a task-adaptive non-compensatory rule where judges can only override evidence-supported consensus with extractive evidence certificates, and can only repair when neither alternative is certified but the repair is.
AI.result: EL-DGR achieves 58.2% on GSM8K (vs. 56.8% judge, 55.8% majority, 55.4% first candidate) and 17.33 EM / 25.46 F1 on HotpotQA (vs. 15.67/23.49, 15.33/23.19, 15.33/22.97), improving on first-candidate GRPO by +2.8 pp (p=0.0026) and +2.00 EM (p=0.070). Decision audit shows EL-DGR only overturns consensus on 8 of 30 pilot questions and never converts correct consensus into incorrect answers.
AI.conclusion: The key finding is that practitioners should focus on bounding the judge's decision authority (blast radius) through proper admissibility rules like EL-DGR rather than trying to maximize judge accuracy. The decomposition used as step-level gated training reward was ineffective, and no single channel was individually necessary.

title: Ground-Truth Neighborhood Regularization for Reinforcement Learning Post-Training of Time Series Foundation Models
summary: Time series forecasting (TSF) plays an important role in a wide range of real-world applications. Recently, time series foundation models (TSFMs), pretrained on large-scale datasets, have demonstrated strong generalization capabilities and emerged as an important paradigm for TSF. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has consequently attracted growing attention as a means of further improving their performance on downstream tasks. However, we find that, in certain forecast regions, RL post-training may gradually shift the output distributions of TSFMs away from the ground truth, thereby limiting their performance. We refer to this phenomenon as \textbf{suboptimal collapse}. Our analysis suggests that difficulty in initially sampling high-quality trajectories near the ground truth is an important contributing factor to suboptimal collapse. To address this issue, we propose Ground-Truth Neighborhood Regularization (GTN-R) for RL post-training of TSFMs. GTN-R uses the ground truth as a reference for locating high-quality regions and guides the model's probability mass toward the ground-truth neighborhood. This increases the probability of sampling high-quality trajectories, mitigates suboptimal collapse, and improves performance. Moreover, GTN-R can be flexibly integrated into various RL methods for TSFMs. Extensive experiments show its effectiveness.

AI.tldr: GTN-R addresses suboptimal collapse in RL post-training of time series foundation models by guiding probability mass toward ground-truth neighborhoods to improve forecasting performance.
AI.motivation: The paper identifies that reinforcement learning post-training of time series foundation models can sometimes cause "suboptimal collapse" - where model outputs gradually shift away from ground truth distributions, limiting performance improvements despite RL fine-tuning.
AI.method: Proposes Ground-Truth Neighborhood Regularization (GTN-R), which uses ground truth as reference to locate high-quality regions and guides the model's probability distribution toward these ground-truth neighborhoods. This increases sampling probability of high-quality trajectories.
AI.result: GTN-R effectively mitigates suboptimal collapse, improves RL post-training performance of time series foundation models, and can be flexibly integrated with various RL methods as demonstrated through extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: GTN-R is an effective regularization approach for RL post-training of time series foundation models that addresses the suboptimal collapse problem by leveraging ground-truth information to guide sampling toward high-quality regions.

title: Counterfactual Benchmarking and Training for Factuality Consistency and Order-Robust Grounded Reasoning in LLMs over Heterogeneous Knowledge
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have increasingly supported response generation grounded in user-provided knowledge spanning heterogeneous structures. However, existing benchmarks provide limited assessment of whether LLMs can faithfully perform multi-hop reasoning chains across such knowledge contexts while remaining robust to variations in their input order. We introduce TKFQA, a factuality consistency benchmark comprising 10,130 question-answering (QA) pairs grounded in tables, texts, and knowledge graphs (KGs). Each example is constructed from an explicit counterfactual reasoning chain, enabling the joint evaluation of answer correctness, reasoning-chain accuracy, and robustness to different input-order. An extensive evaluation of 14 open- and closed-source LLMs reveals that state-of-the-art models exhibit limited reasoning-chain accuracy and remain sensitive to variations in the input order of heterogeneous knowledge contexts. To address these limitations, we propose ORLF, an LLM-agnostic training framework that models cross-context topological relations through knowledge-specific latent vectors. ORLF integrates context-wise position encoding, a latent-bridge attention mask, and topological knowledge bias to preserve knowledge-specific bias and encode topological semantics. Experiments across four LLM backbones show that ORLF outperforms competitive training-free and LoRA-based baselines, improving average Exact Match and Reasoning-Chain Accuracy by 2.15% and 4.29%, respectively, while reducing order-induced performance standard deviation by 0.04% to 3.01%.

AI.tldr: TKFQA benchmark evaluates LLMs' factuality consistency across heterogeneous knowledge structures, showing current models struggle with multi-hop reasoning and input order sensitivity. ORLF framework improves performance by encoding topological relations.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks inadequately assess LLMs' ability to perform faithful multi-hop reasoning across heterogeneous knowledge structures (tables, texts, KGs) while being robust to variations in input order.
AI.method: Introduced TKFQA benchmark with 10,130 QA pairs grounded in tables, texts, and KGs using explicit counterfactual reasoning chains. Proposed ORLF framework with context-wise position encoding, latent-bridge attention mask, and topological knowledge bias to model cross-context topological relations.
AI.result: Evaluation of 14 LLMs revealed limited reasoning-chain accuracy and sensitivity to input order variations. ORLF outperformed baselines, improving average Exact Match by 2.15% and Reasoning-Chain Accuracy by 4.29%, while reducing order-induced performance standard deviation by 0.04-3.01%.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs have limitations in faithful multi-hop reasoning across heterogeneous knowledge and robustness to input order. ORLF effectively addresses these issues by encoding topological semantics and preserving knowledge-specific bias.

title: Do All LLMs Know When They're Being Harmful? A Reproducibility Study of Latent-Space Safety Probes Across Model Families
summary: Khatri et al. (2026) [DOI: 10.1109/DSN-W70714.2026.00027] show that lightweight MLP probes on final-layer activations of a single 8B model (LLaMA-3.1-8B) detect harmful prompts at F1 competitive with guard models 1000x larger, using one probe per benchmark. We reproduce this pipeline end-to-end and extend it along two axes the original study leaves open. First, we test whether the result generalizes across other model architecture and scale by training identical probes on activations from models like Gemma-4-E4B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen2-7B, using the three benchmarks (WildJailbreak, BeaverTails, AEGIS 2.0). Second, we test how much of the reported performance is affected by non-determinism during inference by repeating extraction under five random seeds and measuring the variance of F1 scores. Our results reproduce the original LLaMA model benchmarks within 0.37 percentage points of the original F1 scores (and within 0.2 points on BeaverTails). We find that the original MLP probe architecture extends to other model families with F1 scores within a point of the values reported for LLaMA-3.1-8B. Our experiments varying seed values reveal an interesting observation: final token latent vectors remained the same for all tested architectures irrespective of the seed values used.

AI.tldr: Lightweight MLP probes on final-layer activations detect harmful prompts competitively with guard models 1000x larger; this generalizes across model architectures and seeds.
AI.motivation: To reproduce and extend Khatri et al.'s finding that lightweight MLP probes on final-layer activations can detect harmful prompts effectively, and to test whether this result generalizes across different model architectures and scales, as well as to investigate the impact of non-determinism during inference.
AI.method: Reproduced the original pipeline end-to-end and extended it by: 1) training identical MLP probes on activations from various model architectures (Gemma-4-E4B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Qwen2-7B) using three benchmarks (WildJailbreak, BeaverTails, AEGIS 2.0), and 2) testing the impact of non-determinism by repeating extraction under five random seeds and measuring F1 score variance.
AI.result: Successfully reproduced original LLaMA model benchmarks within 0.37 percentage points of original F1 scores. Found that MLP probe architecture extends to other model families with F1 scores within a point of values reported for LLaMA-3.1-8B. Discovered that final token latent vectors remained identical across all tested architectures regardless of seed values used.
AI.conclusion: The effectiveness of lightweight MLP probes for harmful prompt detection is robust across different model architectures and scales, and is not significantly affected by inference non-determinism, making it a practical and efficient alternative to much larger guard models.

title: Back to the Future: A workbook time machine for spread sheet creation benchmarks
summary: We introduce the workbook time machine, a pipeline that automatically creates benchmarks evaluating the ability of language models to create derived objects in spreadsheets (formulas, charts, pivot tables, and conditional formatting). Applied to public workbook corpora, it produces wtmcorpus--a collection of (input workbook, output workbook, query) triples spanning four artifact types and varying complexity. From this corpus we curate wtmbench, a 150-task evaluation benchmark with queries at three levels of specificity. We evaluate existing spreadsheet manipulation agents and baselines on wtmbench across artifact types, step complexity, and instruction granularity. Our evaluations show that query specificity, agent orchestration, and interface API used to control spreadsheets play a big role in LLM performance on Excel tasks.

AI.tldr: A pipeline called "workbook time machine" automatically creates benchmarks for evaluating language models' ability to create derived objects in spreadsheets, producing a corpus and 150-task benchmark for comprehensive evaluation of spreadsheet manipulation agents.
AI.motivation: There's a need to systematically evaluate language models' ability to manipulate spreadsheets and create derived objects like formulas, charts, pivot tables, and conditional formatting, as existing evaluation methods may not adequately assess these complex spreadsheet manipulation capabilities.
AI.method: The authors develop the "workbook time machine" pipeline that automatically generates benchmarks from public workbook corpora, creating wtmcorpus (a collection of input-output-query triples) and curating wtmbench (a 150-task evaluation benchmark). The benchmark includes queries at three specificity levels and spans four artifact types.
AI.result: The pipeline successfully creates wtmcorpus and wtmbench. Evaluation of existing spreadsheet manipulation agents shows that query specificity, agent orchestration, and interface APIs significantly impact LLM performance on Excel tasks, revealing key factors affecting spreadsheet manipulation capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The workbook time machine provides a valuable framework for benchmarking LLMs' spreadsheet manipulation abilities, revealing important design considerations for spreadsheet agents including query granularity, system architecture, and API interfaces for optimal performance.

title: CLAM: Causal Spatial Disaggregation to Infer Local Effects From Coarse Data
summary: Learning fine-grained spatial patterns from coarse-resolution data is challenging, especially in causal settings where high-resolution effects must be inferred from aggregated interventions and outcomes. We introduce CLAM, a method for estimating localized causal effects from coarse observations by exploiting high-resolution contextual covariates that modulate these effects. By jointly learning the causal mechanism and a disaggregation mapping, CLAM captures interactions that are missed when addressing these problems independently. The method supports localized effect estimation, counterfactual reasoning, and principled outcome disaggregation, and reliably captures spatially varying causal effects across diverse settings. This is particularly relevant for applications such as public health and environmental policy, where decisions are made at broad scales despite substantial local heterogeneity. Code is available at https://github.com/gerritgr/clam

AI.tldr: CLAM is a method for estimating localized causal effects from coarse-resolution data by jointly learning causal mechanisms and disaggregation mappings using high-resolution contextual covariates.
AI.motivation: In many real-world applications like public health and environmental policy, interventions and outcomes are observed at coarse scales (aggregated data), but substantial local heterogeneity exists. This creates a challenge: how to estimate fine-grained spatial causal effects when we only have coarse-resolution interventions and outcomes.
AI.method: CLAM jointly learns the causal mechanism and a disaggregation mapping by exploiting high-resolution contextual covariates that modulate causal effects. This allows the method to capture interactions between causal effects and spatial patterns that are missed when addressing these problems independently.
AI.result: The method reliably captures spatially varying causal effects across diverse settings. It supports localized effect estimation, counterfactual reasoning, and principled outcome disaggregation, outperforming approaches that handle causal inference and disaggregation separately.
AI.conclusion: CLAM provides a principled approach to inferring high-resolution causal effects from coarse data, addressing the practical challenge of spatial aggregation in policy-relevant domains where local heterogeneity matters but only aggregated data is available.

title: SurgLAT: Surgical Latent Attention Tracking for Depth-Aware Robotic Laparoscope Control
summary: Autonomous laparoscopic camera control requires continuous understanding of the surgeon's operative intent in dynamic surgical scenes, where the target operative region is not a stable physical object but a latent and temporally evolving attention state. In this work, we present Surgical Latent Attention Tracking (SurgLAT), a causal online framework for latent surgical attention modeling and autonomous laparoscopic view control. SurgLAT uses a frozen DINOv3 encoder and a state-conditioned spatial token mixer to extract operative evidence under a memory-guided spatial prior, while a selective causal latent memory module jointly models short-term motion continuity and long-horizon surgical intent evolution through dynamic retrieval of current, recent, and historical latent states. The learned latent surgical attention state is decoded into a probabilistic attention heatmap and operative region for downstream endoscope guidance. Beyond perception, we further introduce a robotic deployment framework with explicit laparoscopic Remote Center of Motion (RCM) constrained control based on virtual-axis formulation, together with redundancy-aware null-space initialization for stable and smooth manipulator motion. We validate the full system on real laparoscopic surgical videos and a physical robotic laparoscope platform. Experimental results demonstrate robust online operative-region tracking and stable autonomous endoscopy adjustment under occlusion, rapid motion, and target transitions, highlighting the effectiveness of latent surgical intent modeling for surgical autonomy.

AI.tldr: SurgLAT is a causal online framework that models latent surgical attention for autonomous laparoscopic camera control, using frozen DINOv3 encoder, state-conditioned token mixing, and selective causal latent memory to track operative regions and guide endoscopes with RCM-constrained robotic control.
AI.motivation: Autonomous laparoscopic camera control needs to understand the surgeon's evolving operative intent, which is a latent attention state rather than a stable physical object in dynamic surgical scenes.
AI.method: SurgLAT uses: 1) Frozen DINOv3 encoder with state-conditioned spatial token mixer to extract operative evidence under memory-guided spatial prior; 2) Selective causal latent memory module modeling short-term motion continuity and long-horizon surgical intent evolution via dynamic retrieval of current, recent, and historical latent states; 3) Learned latent attention decoded into probabilistic attention heatmaps for endoscope guidance; 4) Robotic deployment with RCM-constrained control and redundancy-aware null-space initialization for stable manipulator motion.
AI.result: The system demonstrates robust online operative-region tracking and stable autonomous endoscopy adjustment under occlusion, rapid motion, and target transitions on real laparoscopic videos and physical robotic platform.
AI.conclusion: Latent surgical intent modeling is effective for surgical autonomy, enabling reliable tracking of evolving surgical attention states for autonomous laparoscopic camera control.

title: Adaptive Symmetry Discovery for Dynamical System Identification
summary: Dynamical systems model trajectory data generated by fixed underlying dynamics, with applications ranging from biology to physics. Especially in scientific settings, dynamical systems are not generic but often exhibit symmetries imposed by physical laws, formalized through equivariance with respect to group actions. The identification problem concerns recovering the parameters of a system from observed trajectories. In this work, we study adaptive symmetry discovery for dynamical system identification and address how a system can be identified from a single trajectory when it is equivariant with respect to an unknown symmetry group. To this end, we first show that for known symmetries, the system can be identified from a significantly shorter single trajectory than in the generic setting, and we precisely characterize this improvement. We then consider the automatic symmetry discovery setting, proposing a method to learn the symmetry group directly from a single trajectory and incorporate it into the identification procedure, achieving the same optimal trajectory length as in the known-symmetry case. Our analysis relies on tools from group representation theory and the expander properties of Cayley graphs, and may be of independent interest for the study of symmetries in dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: A method for discovering unknown symmetries in dynamical systems from a single trajectory, enabling more efficient system identification than generic approaches by leveraging group representation theory.
AI.motivation: Dynamical systems in scientific applications often have symmetries imposed by physical laws, but these symmetries are frequently unknown. The identification problem - recovering system parameters from observed trajectories - becomes challenging when symmetries exist but are not known a priori, especially when only a single trajectory is available for learning.
AI.method: The authors first analyze how known symmetries allow system identification from shorter trajectories than generic approaches. Then they propose an automatic symmetry discovery method that learns the symmetry group directly from a single trajectory and incorporates it into the identification procedure. The analysis uses tools from group representation theory and expander properties of Cayley graphs.
AI.result: The method achieves the same optimal trajectory length for system identification as in the known-symmetry case, demonstrating that unknown symmetries can be discovered and leveraged without sacrificing identification efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry discovery enables efficient dynamical system identification from single trajectories, with the theoretical framework potentially having broader applications for studying symmetries in dynamical systems across scientific domains.

title: GRACE: LLM-Grounded Semantic Metric Spaces for Scalable Mixed-Data Clustering
summary: Clustering mixed tabular data requires a unified metric space to bridge the inherent heterogeneity between continuous numerical measurements and discrete categorical symbols. Traditionally, algorithms rely entirely on dataset-internal statistics to estimate categorical relationships, which confines the learned metric to empirical co-occurrences and ignores conceptually obvious yet statistically unobserved affinities. Although LLMs offer external world knowledge, applying their text-centric reasoning to highly abstract tabular concepts presents significant challenges. Bridging this modality gap to construct a semantically complete metric typically requires embedding LLMs into iterative metric learning loops to dynamically optimize cross-modality representations. This incurs intractable computational overhead, forcing a compromise between semantic enrichment and scalability. Therefore, we propose GRACE, an LLM-grounded framework for scalable mixed-data clustering. GRACE shifts semantic acquisition to the attribute-value level via a multi-perspective LLM querying strategy, mapping heterogeneous values into knowledge-informed descriptions. Crucially, this one-shot grounding extracts general-purpose semantic representations that embed heterogeneous attributes into a unified space, decoupling expensive LLM invocation from iterative optimization. Furthermore, GRACE cross-validates these external semantics against dataset-internal statistical evidence to ensure alignment with the dataset-specific cluster structure. Ultimately, GRACE matches the scalability of conventional statistics-driven baselines while achieving superior clustering accuracy and conceptual interpretability over 11 competing methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/develop-yang/GRACE-GRACE-A

AI.tldr: GRACE is an LLM-grounded framework for scalable mixed-data clustering that uses one-shot semantic grounding at the attribute-value level to bridge numerical and categorical data in a unified space, achieving better accuracy than traditional methods without iterative LLM optimization.
AI.motivation: Traditional mixed-data clustering relies on dataset-internal statistics, which misses conceptually obvious but statistically unobserved affinities between categories. While LLMs offer external knowledge, their text-centric reasoning doesn't directly apply to abstract tabular concepts, and iterative LLM optimization for metric learning is computationally prohibitive.
AI.method: GRACE uses a multi-perspective LLM querying strategy at the attribute-value level to map heterogeneous values into knowledge-informed descriptions. This one-shot semantic grounding extracts general-purpose representations, decoupling expensive LLM calls from iterative optimization. It then cross-validates external semantics against dataset-internal statistics to align with cluster structure.
AI.result: GRACE matches the scalability of conventional statistics-driven baselines while achieving superior clustering accuracy and conceptual interpretability over 11 competing methods.
AI.conclusion: GRACE successfully bridges the modality gap between numerical and categorical data through efficient one-shot LLM grounding, providing a scalable solution that combines external world knowledge with dataset-specific statistics for improved mixed-data clustering.

title: Support Selection Beyond Smooth DAG Exactness: Completion Geometry,Score Margins, and Selective Certificates
summary: Smooth acyclicity constraints answer whether a weighted support is a DAG, whereas structure learning asks which support change should be made. Existing analyses establish degeneracy for particular constraint formulas but do not isolate what follows from smooth exactness itself. At a DAG boundary, we show that minimal cycle completions generate a squarefree monomial ideal containing every restricted Taylor jet of an exact representation. If the smallest completion has $q$ edges, the first possible response has order $q$ for a vector residual and $2q$ for a nonnegative scalar. Exponentially many constant-scale cyclic manifolds exhibit the same lack of ranking away from the boundary for NOTEARS and DAGMA. We derive the exact selection time for an isolated cycle. When $Ψ'(h)\asymp h^ν$, the feasibility-only time is $T_0(\varepsilon)=Θ(\varepsilon^{-(2ν+1)})$; a score margin changes the leading dynamics at scale $T_0^{-1}$ for $ν>0$, while $ν=0$ has a logarithmic boundary layer requiring $γT_0\log(1/\varepsilon)\to0$. Experiments verify this law, and a truth-free separation statistic predicts selection time on 320 official NOTEARS/DAGMA trajectories (Spearman $-0.52$ and $-0.66$, permutation $p<10^{-4}$). For finite samples, a parent-set confidence family and forced-opposite queries certify skeleton and unshielded-collider labels shared by every population optimum of a frozen score. Across 320 runs, every regret bound covers an independent oracle-score audit. None of 3,042 certified skeleton or 2,396 collider labels disagrees with the oracle-score optimum, although 4.4% and 5.5%, respectively, disagree with the generating graph. These results separate DAG feasibility, score-based support selection, and causal identification.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes degeneracy in DAG structure learning, showing that smooth exact acyclicity constraints lead to vanishing gradients at DAG boundaries, with precise scaling laws for selection times and separation of feasibility, support selection, and causal identification.
AI.motivation: Existing analyses of smooth acyclicity constraints in DAG learning establish degeneracy for specific formulas but don't isolate what follows from smooth exactness itself. The paper aims to understand the fundamental limitations and scaling behaviors when using smooth constraints for DAG structure learning.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of DAG boundaries showing minimal cycle completions generate squarefree monomial ideals containing Taylor jets of exact representations. Derivation of exact selection times for isolated cycles with scaling laws. Empirical verification on 320 NOTEARS/DAGMA trajectories, and development of parent-set confidence families with forced-opposite queries to certify skeleton and collider labels.
AI.result: When smallest cycle completion has q edges, first possible gradient response has order q for vector residuals and 2q for nonnegative scalars. Feasibility time scales as T₀(ε)=Θ(ε^{-(2ν+1)}). Score-based selection changes dynamics at scale T₀^{-1}. Experiments show strong predictive power with Spearman correlations -0.52 to -0.66. Certification methods successfully identify skeleton and collider labels shared by all population optima.
AI.conclusion: The paper separates three aspects of DAG learning: feasibility (acyclicity constraints), score-based support selection, and causal identification. It shows fundamental limitations of smooth constraints at DAG boundaries and provides precise scaling laws and certification methods that work in practice, with verification on hundreds of runs showing no disagreement with oracle-score optima.

title: Reason Wide, Not Deep: Amortizing the Reasoning Premium into Distilled Skills
summary: Reasoning modes of language models outperform their non-reasoning counterparts on multi-step agentic tasks, but pay a 3-6x premium in output tokens on every episode -- much of it spent re-deriving procedures that are shared across episodes of the same domain. We show this recurring cost can be amortized: a coding agent analyses a small corpus of existing trajectories from a training split and compiles a compact natural-language skill that is injected into the non-reasoning model's system prompt. Across four agentic benchmarks (ALFWorld, tau$^2$-bench telecom and retail, and SpreadsheetBench-Verified), skills recover 55%-100%+ of the reasoning gap for GPT-5.4-mini on held-out tasks -- exceeding the reasoning mode outright on two of four -- while emitting 2.7-6x fewer output tokens and zero reasoning tokens. Notably, reasoning traces are not a prerequisite: skills distilled from non-reasoning trajectories alone remain competitive with skills distilled from paired reasoning/non-reasoning corpora, with domain-dependent differences between the two sources. We interpret these results through a search lens: test-time reasoning is deep search inside a single episode, re-paid at every deployment, while corpus distillation is wide search across episodes, paid once. The two recover overlapping procedural knowledge, and width over cheap trajectories is often the better buy -- with the residual gap on some domains (telecom, SpreadsheetBench) delineating where genuinely per-instance deep search remains necessary.

AI.tldr: LLM reasoning mode improves performance on agent tasks but costs 3-6x more tokens. This paper shows how to compile reusable skills from trajectory corpora, recovering most of reasoning gap with far fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Reasoning-enabled LLMs perform better on multi-step agent tasks but incur heavy token costs (3-6x) by re-deriving procedures each episode. Much of this cost is redundant as procedures are shared across episodes in the same domain.
AI.method: A coding agent analyzes existing trajectories from training data and compiles compact natural-language skills that are injected into non-reasoning models' system prompts. Skills can be distilled from either reasoning or non-reasoning trajectories.
AI.result: Across four agent benchmarks, skills recovered 55%-100%+ of the reasoning gap for GPT-5.4-mini on held-out tasks, often exceeding reasoning mode while emitting 2.7-6x fewer tokens. Skills from non-reasoning trajectories remained competitive with those from reasoning trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Corpus distillation provides efficient amortized knowledge acquisition, while test-time reasoning offers per-instance deep search. The width-based approach (corpus distillation) is often more cost-effective, with residual gaps indicating where per-instance reasoning remains necessary.

title: TSDS-Toolbox: A Toolbox for Measuring Time-Series Dataset Similarity
summary: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly accelerated research in time-series analysis, particularly in forecasting, classification, and generation tasks. Recent models, especially foundation models, benefit from time-series dataset similarity due to its significant role in source dataset selection for fine-tuning. However, many existing implementations for benchmarking time-series dataset similarity methods are fragmented and difficult to extend. To address this, we present a unified framework, the Time-Series Dataset Similarity Toolbox (TSDS-Toolbox). Our work enables (1) systematic and reproducible comparisons of time-series dataset similarity methods; (2) flexible extensibility for users to add customized datasets, similarity methods, and downstream time-series tasks; and (3) consistent evaluation of both dataset-level and series-level similarity methods through integrated time-series dataset reducers. The effectiveness of TSDS-Toolbox is validated through comprehensive experiments under diverse experimental settings. Our toolbox is publicly available.

AI.tldr: TSDS-Toolbox is a unified framework for benchmarking time-series dataset similarity methods, addressing fragmentation in existing implementations and enabling reproducible comparisons with flexible extensibility.
AI.motivation: The rapid advancement of AI in time-series analysis needs dataset similarity methods, but existing implementations are fragmented and difficult to extend, making systematic benchmarking challenging.
AI.method: Developed TSDS-Toolbox (Time-Series Dataset Similarity Toolbox) - a unified framework that allows systematic comparisons, flexible extensibility for custom datasets/methods, and consistent evaluation of both dataset-level and series-level similarity methods.
AI.result: The toolbox's effectiveness is validated through comprehensive experiments under diverse experimental settings, and the framework is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: TSDS-Toolbox successfully addresses the fragmentation problem in time-series dataset similarity benchmarking, providing a unified, extensible framework for reproducible research that benefits AI foundation models in time-series analysis.

title: TelemetrySuffBench: Is Agent Telemetry Sufficient for Failure-Origin Diagnosis?
summary: Agent systems increasingly expose execution traces, yet telemetry that reveals a failure may still be inadequate for identifying where that failure originated. We introduce TelemetrySuffBench, a controlled benchmark that separates failure detection, fault-origin localization, and safe abstention under insufficient evidence. The benchmark constructs canonical multi-component traces with delayed-binding faults and renders them as paired coarse views, seven-factor telemetry masks, and exact-equal ambiguous origin pairs. We evaluate five frontier language models using unified protocols, explicit candidate sets, invalid-output accounting, subgroup analyses, and a frozen blind holdout. With full telemetry, origin-step Top-1 accuracy ranges from 33.8% to 97.2% across models. Metadata, OpenTelemetry-compatible, and OpenInference-compatible views retain 99.5% to 100% detection F1 while limiting origin-step accuracy to at most 0.5%, exposing a robust detection-localization gap. Factor ablations further show that removing decision content reduces origin-step accuracy to zero for every model, while provenance removal also causes large model-dependent losses. On rich ambiguous inputs that require abstention, evidence gating reduces unsupported unique-origin answers by 12.5 to 48.6 percentage points for three models, whereas two models still answer every case, revealing strong model dependence in safe abstention. Results on the frozen holdout reproduce the central pattern within the same generator family. These findings show that terminal status can support detection, whereas reliable causal attribution requires explicit decision-to-provenance links and abstention safeguards that remain effective across models. The dataset and benchmark implementation are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TelemetrySuffBench-E635/README.md.

AI.tldr: TelemetrySuffBench is a new benchmark that separates failure detection, fault localization, and safe abstention in agent systems with delayed-binding faults, revealing a significant gap between detecting failures and identifying their origins.
AI.motivation: Agent systems increasingly expose execution traces, but telemetry that reveals failures may still be inadequate for identifying where those failures originated. There's a need to understand the limitations of current telemetry approaches for reliable causal attribution.
AI.method: Created TelemetrySuffBench with controlled multi-component traces containing delayed-binding faults, rendered as paired coarse views, seven-factor telemetry masks, and exact-equal ambiguous origin pairs. Evaluated five frontier language models using unified protocols, explicit candidate sets, invalid-output accounting, subgroup analyses, and a frozen blind holdout.
AI.result: With full telemetry, origin-step accuracy ranged 33.8% to 97.2% across models. Metadata and standard telemetry views retained 99.5% to 100% detection F1 but limited origin-step accuracy to ≤0.5%. Removing decision content reduced origin-step accuracy to zero for all models. Evidence gating reduced unsupported answers by 12.5 to 48.6 percentage points for some models, but two models still answered every case.
AI.conclusion: Terminal status can support failure detection, but reliable causal attribution requires explicit decision-to-provenance links and abstention safeguards that remain effective across models. The detection-localization gap is robust, and model behavior varies significantly in safe abstention scenarios.

title: Accurate Ensembles, Fragile Narratives: Multi-Scale Stacking and a Fidelity Audit of LLM-Generated Explanations for Credit Risk
summary: Credit scoring increasingly relies on models whose decision logic cannot be read off their parameters, in tension with supervisory expectations that adverse decisions be explainable. A common proposal closes that gap with a language model: compute feature attributions, hand them to an LLM, and let it write the rationale. We build such a system end to end and test whether the second half of the promise holds. The predictive component is a multi-scale stacking ensemble fusing four differently regularised gradient-boosting learners with a residual network through a neural meta-learner trained on out-of-fold predictions. On a public 32,581-application credit dataset it reaches test ROC-AUC 0.9539 (95% CI [0.9462, 0.9616]) and PR-AUC 0.9137, beating the best single model by Delta-AUC = 0.0143 (p = 0.016 under a conservative independence assumption). Our central finding is asymmetric. The ranking gain is real but operationally small: at the F1-optimal threshold the ensemble avoids only six additional missed defaults out of 1,422 against a tuned random forest, cutting cost-weighted loss by under 2%. The narrative layer fails in a way prompt engineering alone does not fix. In an audited case the model named three factors as risk-increasing that the supplied attributions scored as risk-reducing, omitted the dominant driver, and introduced a feature never given to it. We trace this to properties we measure rather than assume: SHAP and LIME agree on which features matter (overlap@10 = 0.80) but not on their order (tau = 0.43, p = 0.18), and the attribution sign for the model's most sensitive input is near a coin flip across applicants (modal-sign share 0.53). Calibration (ECS = 0.117) and perturbation stability (DPD = 0.078) both fall short of our own thresholds. Constrained prompting is necessary but not sufficient: grounding must be verified after generation, not assumed.

AI.tldr: Researchers built an advanced credit scoring ensemble model with explainability via LLMs, finding that while the model achieved small performance gains, the LLM-based explanation layer produced unreliable rationales despite sophisticated prompt engineering.
AI.motivation: There's a tension between using complex, non-interpretable machine learning models for credit scoring (which perform well) and regulatory requirements for explainable adverse decisions. A common solution is to use LLMs to generate explanations from feature attributions, but it's unclear if this actually produces reliable rationales.
AI.method: Built a multi-scale stacking ensemble combining four differently regularized gradient-boosting learners with a residual network through a neural meta-learner trained on out-of-fold predictions. Tested on a public credit dataset of 32,581 applications. Used SHAP and LIME for feature attributions fed to LLMs for explanation generation, with rigorous auditing of the resulting narratives.
AI.result: The ensemble achieved test ROC-AUC 0.9539 and PR-AUC 0.9137, beating the best single model by ΔAUC = 0.0143 (p=0.016). However, the performance gain was operationally small - at F1-optimal threshold, it avoided only 6 additional missed defaults out of 1,422, cutting cost-weighted loss by <2%. More critically, the LLM-based explanation layer failed: in one audited case, the model named three risk-increasing factors that attributions scored as risk-reducing, omitted the dominant driver, and introduced a nonexistent feature.
AI.conclusion: Constrained prompting for LLM explanations is necessary but insufficient - grounding must be verified after generation, not assumed. SHAP and LIME often disagree on feature importance ordering, and attribution signs can be unstable. The modest predictive gains of complex ensembles may not justify their operational complexity and unreliable explainability.

title: GraphThink: Graph-Enhanced LLM Thinking for Long-Horizon Embodied Task Planning
summary: Embodied agents using LLM-based planners often struggle with physical hallucinations, poor generalization to long-horizon tasks, and lack of environmental awareness. We propose GraphThink, a novel framework that integrates a task graph to provide structured knowledge for robust planning and a scene graph to maintain environmental memory for event-driven replanning. Specifically, the task graph guides LLM thinking through contextual prompting and iterative refinement, effectively mitigating planning hallucinations. Furthermore, within the GRPO framework, the task graph offers delicate reward design to train the LLM planner, enhancing long-horizon planning capabilities and improving generalization. Finally, an event-driven replanning module, powered by the scene graph, enables closed-loop environment awareness and error correction. GraphThink achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ALFRED benchmark. In particular, our high-level planner surpasses leading API-based LLMs on both the validation set and held-out long-horizon tasks, underscoring its robust zero-shot and few-shot capabilities. Additional evaluations further demonstrate strong out-of-distribution generalization to novel tasks and environments.

AI.tldr: GraphThink: A framework combining task graphs and scene graphs to improve LLM-based embodied planning by reducing hallucinations, enhancing long-horizon task generalization, and enabling event-driven replanning through environmental awareness.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based embodied agents suffer from physical hallucinations, poor generalization to long-horizon tasks, and lack of environmental awareness, limiting their practical application in real-world scenarios.
AI.method: Proposes GraphThink framework with two main components: (1) Task graph for structured knowledge representation to guide LLM thinking through contextual prompting and iterative refinement, integrated with GRPO framework for reward design; (2) Scene graph for environmental memory enabling event-driven replanning and closed-loop awareness.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on ALFRED benchmark. High-level planner surpasses leading API-based LLMs on validation set and held-out long-horizon tasks, demonstrating robust zero-shot/few-shot capabilities and strong out-of-distribution generalization to novel tasks and environments.
AI.conclusion: GraphThink effectively addresses key limitations of LLM-based embodied planning by integrating structured knowledge representations with environmental memory, enabling more robust, generalizable, and adaptive planning for complex real-world tasks.

title: DoGMA: A Central-Dogma-Guided Foundation Model for Multi-Omics Alignment and Multi-Task Learning in Oncology
summary: Attention mechanisms have been widely utilized in modern deep learning, and many existing multi-omics models inherit their conventional use to allow unrestricted bidirectional interactions. However, the fundamental logic of life is directional. Existing designs often overlook the directionality suggested by the central dogma, potentially limiting transfer across heterogeneous cancers, downstream tasks, and incomplete modality settings.In this work, we present DoGMA, a central-dogma-guided foundation model for pan-cancer multi-omics analysis, arguing that robust transfer requires representations with domain-specific inductive bias. Concretely, we build it on a Transformer-MoE architecture where directed attention biases inter-omics communication toward central-dogma information flow. We further pretrain our model with masked hierarchical omics reconstruction to guide it toward learning central-dogma-consistent interactions. Across diverse downstream tasks, including cancer representation learning, survival prediction, and metastasis prediction, DoGMA consistently demonstrates strong predictive performance. Ablations and analyses further suggest that the performance gains arise from the synergy between central-dogma-guided directed attention and reconstruction-based pretraining, which together promote more biologically consistent cross-omics information exchange. Overall, DoGMA demonstrates that domain-specific inductive biases can improve the robustness and transferability of multi-omics foundation models, offering new insights into the design of attention mechanisms for multi-omics representation learning.

AI.tldr: DoGMA is a central-dogma-guided foundation model for pan-cancer multi-omics analysis that uses directed attention and masked hierarchical reconstruction to learn biologically consistent cross-omics interactions, improving transferability across cancers and tasks.
AI.motivation: Current multi-omics models use conventional bidirectional attention mechanisms that overlook the fundamental directional logic of life (central dogma - DNA→RNA→protein). This lack of domain-specific inductive bias limits transfer across heterogeneous cancers, downstream tasks, and incomplete modality settings.
AI.method: Transformer-MoE architecture with directed attention that biases inter-omics communication toward central-dogma information flow, plus masked hierarchical omics reconstruction pretraining to learn central-dogma-consistent interactions.
AI.result: Strong predictive performance across diverse downstream tasks including cancer representation learning, survival prediction, and metastasis prediction. Ablations show performance gains come from synergy between central-dogma-guided directed attention and reconstruction-based pretraining.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific inductive biases (like central-dogma guidance) improve robustness and transferability of multi-omics foundation models, offering new insights for attention mechanism design in multi-omics representation learning.

title: When Is Benchmark Contamination Detectable? Information Limits and Power-Calibrated Audits
summary: Behavioral contamination detectors can return "no evidence" either because a benchmark is clean or because the audit has little power. We formalize this distinction for a benchmark in which an unknown fraction alpha of items was seen during training. With matched clean and seen controls, the behavioral channel is the sparse mixture Q_alpha = (1 - alpha) P_0 + alpha P_1, and an exact second-moment argument shows that detectability is governed by alpha * rho * sqrt(m), where rho^2 = chi^2(P_1 || P_0) measures behavioral separability. Any scalar detector reduces to its efficacy, ef = |E_1 f - E_0 f| / sqrt(Var_0(f)) <= rho, which can be estimated from controls before the audit is run. A separate sample-split certificate lower-bounds alpha distribution-free, without requiring an orientation assumption. Our empirical finding is two-sided. Frozen calibration efficacy predicts held-out power curves, with R^2 = 0.83-0.98 across six exact-permutation channels, but the efficacy-only Gaussian budget is miscalibrated at the small sample sizes it prescribes, failing in 9/9 gate-passing channels even though efficacy itself transports. The failure is in the inversion, not the calibration. A predeclared two-stage planner that simulates the deployed test repairs the budgets, is uniformly conservative, and abstains when its probe does not transport. The certificate is valid but vacuous at audit scale, and a five-seed paired injection study recovers the mechanism ordering verbatim > paraphrase > surface, in which the apparent answer-only signal is explained by baseline drift. We report the audit contract and its failures together: a non-rejection is interpretable only alongside the efficacy, budget, and validity gates that produced it.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes behavioral contamination detection, distinguishing between clean benchmarks and low-power audits using a sparse mixture model with efficacy measures, provides distribution-free certification, and identifies budget miscalibration issues that can be repaired with two-stage planning.
AI.motivation: To address the ambiguity in behavioral contamination detection where "no evidence" can mean either a clean benchmark or an audit with low power, requiring formal methods to distinguish these cases and ensure interpretable audit results.
AI.method: Formalizes detection using a sparse mixture model Q_α = (1-α)P₀ + αP₁ with matched controls, introduces efficacy measure ef = |E₁f - E₀f|/√Var₀(f) ≤ ρ, provides distribution-free certification via sample splitting, and develops a two-stage planner to repair budget miscalibration by simulating deployed tests.
AI.result: Frozen calibration efficacy predicts held-out power with R² = 0.83-0.98 across six exact-permutation channels, but efficacy-only Gaussian budget fails in 9/9 gate-passing channels. Two-stage planner repairs budgets and is uniformly conservative. Five-seed paired injection study reveals mechanism ordering: verbatim > paraphrase > surface, with apparent answer-only signal explained by baseline drift.
AI.conclusion: Audit contracts must be reported with their failures - a non-rejection is only interpretable alongside efficacy, budget, and validity gates. Two-stage planning with transport verification enables valid audit budgets, addressing the failure of efficacy-only approaches while maintaining conservative guarantees.

title: A Hybrid Nested Harness for Decoupling Structure and Parameters in LLM-Driven Optimization
comment: Published as a conference paper at LM4Sci Workshop @ COLM 2026
summary: In evolutionary algorithms powered by language models, the LLM acts as a single operator that simultaneously updates structural components (like control flow) and continuous parameters. While LLMs can be good at the first, they are not efficient at the second, wasting tokens taking discrete jumps inside a trial and error loop. We resolve this by formalizing a hybrid nested search, in which an outer loop has the LLM propose a structural sketch, with numeric gaps, and an inner numerical optimizer tunes the sketch. Both the outer and inner solvers are pluggable: any text-based optimizer can be combined with a zero-order optimizer (CMA-ES), gradient-based routines, or MCMC samplers. We validate our framework across three scientific domains: (i) meta-optimizers on closed-form test functions, (ii) code-based policies for systems research and social dilemmas; and (iii) approximate Bayesian inference tasks. Across all three, the hybrid optimizer is superior to both vanilla LLM-driven search and pure numerical optimization baselines. Code at: https://github.com/vicgalle/hybrid-nested-search

AI.tldr: Hybrid nested search framework combines LLMs for structural optimization with numerical methods for parameter tuning, outperforming pure LLM-based or numerical optimization approaches across multiple scientific domains.
AI.motivation: LLMs in evolutionary algorithms simultaneously handle both structural components (like control flow) and continuous parameters, but they're inefficient at continuous parameter optimization, wasting tokens on trial-and-error discrete jumps. There's a need to leverage LLMs' strengths in structural reasoning while using more efficient methods for numerical optimization.
AI.method: Formalized hybrid nested search with an outer loop where LLMs propose structural sketches with numeric gaps (placeholders), and an inner numerical optimizer tunes those gaps. Both solvers are pluggable - any text-based optimizer can be combined with zero-order optimizers (like CMA-ES), gradient-based routines, or MCMC samplers.
AI.result: The hybrid optimizer was superior to both vanilla LLM-driven search and pure numerical optimization baselines across three scientific domains: (1) meta-optimizers on closed-form test functions, (2) code-based policies for systems research and social dilemmas, and (3) approximate Bayesian inference tasks.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid nested search framework effectively resolves the inefficiency of LLMs in continuous parameter optimization by separating structural and numerical optimization, creating a synergistic approach that outperforms both component methods individually across diverse applications.

title: TongGuOCR: A Layout-Aware and Token-Augmented OCR Framework for Chinese Historical Documents
summary: Chinese historical documents preserve valuable cultural heritage, but many collections remain accessible only as scanned page images, preventing full-text retrieval, collation, and computational analysis. Optical character recognition (OCR) can bridge this gap, but accurate transcription remains challenging because historical documents often contain complex layouts, rare characters, and nontrivial reading orders. We propose TongGuOCR, a layout-aware and token-augmented OCR framework for Chinese historical documents. First, a Layout-Aware Preprocessing module constructs and refines locally coherent recognition blocks to preserve local context while reducing interference across regions. Second, a Token-Augmented Recognition module augments the transcription target at two complementary levels: character-level vocabulary expansion gives each rare glyph a direct one-token representation and shortens its decoding path, while line-to-line transition modeling injects discrete spatial displacement tokens that guide the decoder along complex reading paths without requiring precise coordinates. Experiments on two Chinese historical document OCR benchmarks show that TongGuOCR outperforms representative traditional task-specific OCR models, general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and OCR-oriented MLLMs. On the more challenging M5HisDoc benchmark, TongGuOCR achieves 93.76 AR and reduces NED from 10.43 to 6.15 and RO-ED from 7.53 to 3.49 relative to the best competing score for each metric. An online demo is available at https://jzzh2004.github.io/TongGuOCR.

AI.tldr: TongGuOCR is a layout-aware, token-augmented OCR framework for Chinese historical documents that outperforms existing methods by using improved layout preprocessing and dual-level token augmentation.
AI.motivation: Chinese historical documents are often only available as scanned images, preventing full-text retrieval and computational analysis. Accurate OCR transcription is challenging due to complex layouts, rare characters, and nontrivial reading orders in these documents.
AI.method: The framework has two main components: 1) Layout-Aware Preprocessing module that constructs and refines locally coherent recognition blocks to preserve context while reducing interference; 2) Token-Augmented Recognition module with character-level vocabulary expansion (giving rare glyphs direct token representations) and line-to-line transition modeling (using spatial displacement tokens to guide decoding along complex reading paths).
AI.result: TongGuOCR outperforms traditional task-specific OCR models, general-purpose multimodal LLMs, and OCR-oriented MLLMs on two Chinese historical document benchmarks. On the M5HisDoc benchmark, it achieves 93.76 AR and reduces NED from 10.43 to 6.15 and RO-ED from 7.53 to 3.49 relative to best competing scores.
AI.conclusion: TongGuOCR effectively addresses OCR challenges for Chinese historical documents through layout-aware preprocessing and token-augmented recognition, providing superior performance and enabling better computational analysis of cultural heritage materials.

title: Predicting blood clot growth from sparse post-onset measurements with latent neural differential equations
summary: Computational models of blood clotting improve understanding of thrombus formation, but their clinical application remains limited because many model inputs are difficult to measure and patient-specific data are often sparse. We present a computational framework based on latent neural differential equations that infers unknown model parameters from sparse measurements and forecasts thrombosis progression. We demonstrate the framework using data generated from a multiphysics blood-clotting model in which clot growth is governed by the coagulation cascade and diffusion.
