Four known biochemical inputs (fibrinogen and factors IX, VIII, and V), together with sparse early clot-size observations, are used to infer the tissue-factor parameter and predict subsequent clot growth. We compare seven probabilistic methods: stochastic neural ordinary differential equations (SNODE), stochastic neural functional differential equations (SNFDE), a latent neural-process baseline, a monotone probabilistic deep ensemble, empirical trajectory retrieval, PCA-ridge Gaussian posterior, and Gompertz-curve retrieval. SNODE achieved the best performance in inferring the unknown input and forecasting future clot-growth trajectories. SNFDE performed similarly and consistently outperformed the other non-differential models. Prediction accuracy improved as more observations became available, whereas longer forecasting horizons increased uncertainty and decreased accuracy. Latent neural differential equations thus effectively combine parameter inference and clot-growth forecasting from sparse measurements, providing a promising foundation for personalized thrombosis modeling.

AI.tldr: A latent neural differential equation framework infers unknown blood clotting parameters from sparse measurements and forecasts thrombosis progression, with stochastic neural ODEs performing best.
AI.motivation: Computational models of blood clotting have limited clinical application because many model inputs are difficult to measure and patient-specific data are often sparse. There's a need for methods that can infer unknown parameters from limited observations.
AI.method: The paper presents a computational framework based on latent neural differential equations that infers unknown model parameters from sparse measurements. It compares seven probabilistic methods: stochastic neural ODEs (SNODE), stochastic neural functional differential equations (SNFDE), latent neural-process baseline, monotone probabilistic deep ensemble, empirical trajectory retrieval, PCA-ridge Gaussian posterior, and Gompertz-curve retrieval, using a multiphysics blood-clotting model with coagulation cascade and diffusion.
AI.result: SNODE achieved the best performance in inferring unknown tissue-factor parameters and forecasting future clot-growth trajectories. SNFDE performed similarly well and consistently outperformed other non-differential models. Prediction accuracy improved with more observations, while longer forecasting horizons increased uncertainty and decreased accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Latent neural differential equations effectively combine parameter inference and clot-growth forecasting from sparse measurements, providing a promising foundation for personalized thrombosis modeling and overcoming limitations of traditional computational models.

title: ZhuLong: Execution-Grounded LLM Agent for EDA Scripting with Offline API Self-Exploration
summary:
EDA scripting with tool-specific, often undocumented APIs remains a long-tail bottleneck that existing LLMs fail to address. This paper presents ZhuLong, an execution-grounded LLM coding agent for PyAether and SKILL that combines API retrieval, documentation inspection, and sandbox execution via unified MCP tools, augmented by an offline API self-exploration mechanism that infers undocumented API behaviors through counterfactual experimentation.
  We evaluate ZhuLong on EDA-Eval-PyAether, a benchmark of 158 real-world tasks with assertion-based execution, where the complete system achieves 78.5% Pass@1 in the commercial Empyrean Aether environment, substantially outperforming a pure LLM baseline (23.6%). Ablation studies identify sandbox execution as the dominant performance driver (41.2 pp drop when removed), with the self-exploration mechanism contributing an additional 3.2 pp accuracy gain and a 22.1% reduction in per-task tool calls. On 20 interactive tasks involving unsaved layouts and schematics, ZhuLong achieves 60.0% Pass@1 for PyAether and 50.0% for SKILL.

AI.tldr: ZhuLong is an LLM coding agent for EDA scripting that combines API retrieval, documentation inspection, and sandbox execution with an offline API self-exploration mechanism to handle undocumented APIs, achieving 78.5% success on real-world EDA tasks.
AI.motivation: EDA (Electronic Design Automation) scripting suffers from tool-specific, undocumented APIs that create a long-tail bottleneck. Existing LLMs fail to address this problem, making EDA automation challenging and inefficient.
AI.method: ZhuLong integrates three key components: 1) API retrieval and documentation inspection via unified MCP tools, 2) Sandbox execution for testing code, and 3) An offline API self-exploration mechanism that infers undocumented API behaviors through counterfactual experimentation.
AI.result: On the EDA-Eval-PyAether benchmark (158 real-world tasks), ZhuLong achieves 78.5% Pass@1 in commercial Empyrean Aether environment, vastly outperforming pure LLM baseline (23.6%). Sandbox execution contributes most (41.2 pp drop when removed), with self-exploration adding 3.2 pp gain and 22.1% tool call reduction. On interactive tasks with unsaved layouts/schematics: 60.0% Pass@1 for PyAether, 50.0% for SKILL.
AI.conclusion: ZhuLong successfully addresses the EDA scripting bottleneck by combining execution-grounded LLM coding with unified tool access and API self-exploration. The approach demonstrates significant performance improvements over pure LLM baselines, with sandbox execution being the most critical component for success.

title: Biologically Informed Representation Learning for Robust Cross-Center Generalization of MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry
summary: Machine learning models for MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry have shown considerable promise for clinical microbiology tasks such as microbial identification and antimicrobial resistance prediction. However, their deployment across institutions remains limited by domain shift, as acquisition-specific variability often leads models to capture technical artifacts rather than transferable biological information. Existing representation learning approaches primarily address this problem through statistical domain alignment while largely overlooking the biological supervision naturally available in microbiology datasets. We introduce DALMA, a probabilistic representation learning framework that jointly models acquisition-specific variability and biological supervision to learn biologically structured latent representations. By combining domain-specific reconstruction with biologically guided representation learning, DALMA learns transferable representations that generalize across heterogeneous clinical centers without requiring institution-specific components at inference, enabling zero-shot deployment on previously unseen sites. We evaluate DALMA on a multi-center benchmark comprising seven datasets from three countries. DALMA consistently achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot microbial identification across two held-out clinical centers, while the learned representations also transfer effectively to antimicrobial resistance prediction. Furthermore, latent-space novelty estimation enables reliable selective prediction under previously unseen domain shifts. These results demonstrate that biologically informed representation learning provides an effective strategy for robust and transferable ML in clinical microbiology.

AI.tldr: DALMA is a probabilistic representation learning framework that learns biologically structured latent representations from MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry data, enabling zero-shot deployment across clinical centers by jointly modeling acquisition variability and biological supervision.
AI.motivation: Machine learning models for MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry show promise for clinical microbiology but suffer from domain shift issues across institutions. Current approaches focus on statistical domain alignment but overlook available biological supervision, leading models to capture technical artifacts rather than transferable biological information.
AI.method: DALMA combines domain-specific reconstruction with biologically guided representation learning in a probabilistic framework. It jointly models acquisition-specific variability and biological supervision to learn biologically structured latent representations that generalize across institutions without requiring institution-specific components at inference.
AI.result: On a multi-center benchmark with seven datasets from three countries, DALMA achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot microbial identification across two held-out clinical centers. The learned representations also transfer effectively to antimicrobial resistance prediction, and latent-space novelty estimation enables reliable selective prediction under unseen domain shifts.
AI.conclusion: Biologically informed representation learning provides an effective strategy for robust and transferable machine learning in clinical microbiology, enabling zero-shot deployment across heterogeneous clinical centers without institution-specific components.

title: REIN: Bridging the Gap between Reasoning and Reliability via Reflection and Abstention Alignment
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) are prone to hallucination, which undermines their reliability and poses challenges for safe deployment. Hallucinations in LRMs arise from two distinct failure sources: reasoning hallucination, where flawed inference steps propagate to an incorrect conclusion, and knowledge hallucination, where the model lacks the requisite factual knowledge to answer the query. To address reasoning hallucination, we propose REIN, an alignment framework that trains LRMs to produce a structured reasoning sequence, $\texttt{<think>} $$\rightarrow$ $\texttt{<reflection>} $$\rightarrow$ $\texttt{<answer>}$, enabling explicit self-reflection before committing to a final answer. To address knowledge hallucination, REIN introduces a reward mechanism that encourages explicit abstention (e.g., "I don't know") when none of the sampled reasoning chains yields a correct answer, allowing the model to refrain from unsupported predictions. Extensive evaluations on mathematical and commonsense reasoning benchmarks show that REIN consistently improves selective accuracy, reduces incorrect-but-self-endorsed responses, and maintains high coverage compared with competitive baselines. Notably, REIN achieves these gains within a single forward pass, without requiring process supervision, inference-time controllers, external search, or multi-round critiques. Experiments on multiple backbones show that REIN reduces the hallucination proxy by $58\sim72\%$ relative to the base models while maintaining $86\sim91\%$ average coverage, and improves selective accuracy on attempted questions by $6.6\sim14.2\%$.

AI.tldr: REIN is an alignment framework that reduces hallucinations in large reasoning models through structured self-reflection and explicit abstention mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models suffer from hallucinations that undermine reliability, with two distinct failure sources: reasoning hallucination (flawed inference steps) and knowledge hallucination (lack of factual knowledge), posing challenges for safe deployment.
AI.method: REIN trains models to produce a structured reasoning sequence: thought → reflection → answer, enabling explicit self-reflection before final answers. It introduces a reward mechanism that encourages explicit abstention (e.g., "I don't know") when none of the sampled reasoning chains yields correct answers, allowing models to refrain from unsupported predictions.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations show REIN consistently improves selective accuracy, reduces incorrect-but-self-endorsed responses, maintains high coverage (86-91%), reduces hallucination proxy by 58-72% relative to base models, and improves selective accuracy on attempted questions by 6.6-14.2%. Achieves these gains within a single forward pass without process supervision or external tools.
AI.conclusion: REIN effectively addresses both reasoning and knowledge hallucinations through structured self-reflection and abstention mechanisms, significantly improving model reliability for safe deployment while maintaining high coverage and requiring only single forward passes.

title: Beyond Aggregate Calibration: Decomposing Income-Conditional Recall Disparities in Automated Credit Default Prediction
summary: Data-centric curation pipelines frequently rely on model confidence scores to flag and filter noisy or mislabeled training instances. Evaluating this filtering convention on a large-scale consumer lending sample (LendingClub, N = 1,344,936) uncovers an underlying demographic asymmetry: high-income defaulters are disproportionately classified as label noise relative to low-income defaulters (Cramer's V approximately 0.03-0.07). Re-examining this behavior through the lens of equal opportunity [Hardt et al., 2016] reveals a far more severe discrepancy: a 16.86 percentage point gap in true positive rate (recall) between high- and low-income borrowers who ultimately defaulted. Implementing a sequential feature-blinding methodology allows us to isolate the drivers of this disparity across three distinct mechanisms: (1) direct reliance on self-reported applicant income; (2) algorithmic absorption of upstream institutional bias encoded within origination interest rates; and (3) a residual disparity (3.55 percentage points in cross-validation; 2.56 percentage points on a held-out test partition, Z = -4.04, p < 0.0001) that remains even after purging both income and interest rates from the model. Out-of-sample signed SHAP valuations demonstrate that this residual gap is maintained by structural proxies, most notably loan amount and home ownership status. These empirical findings show that simply blinding an algorithm to sensitive attributes fails to ensure fairness when institutional pricing decisions and behavioral proxy variables collectively reconstruct the omitted signals. We outline the practical implications of these findings for auditing data-centric AI workflows within regulated financial institutions.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that data-centric filtering based on model confidence scores disproportionately flags high-income defaulters as noise compared to low-income defaulters, and identifies three mechanisms driving this disparity including structural proxies that reconstruct omitted signals.
AI.motivation: To investigate demographic asymmetries in data-centric curation pipelines that use model confidence scores for filtering noisy/mislabeled training data in consumer lending applications.
AI.method: Evaluated filtering on LendingClub dataset (N=1,344,936), used equal opportunity framework, implemented sequential feature-blinding methodology to isolate disparity drivers, and conducted out-of-sample SHAP analysis.
AI.result: Found 16.86 percentage point gap in recall between high- and low-income defaulters; identified three disparity mechanisms: (1) direct income reliance, (2) algorithmic absorption of institutional bias in interest rates, (3) residual gap maintained by structural proxies (loan amount, home ownership).
AI.conclusion: Blinding algorithms to sensitive attributes fails to ensure fairness when institutional decisions and behavioral proxies collectively reconstruct omitted signals, with implications for auditing AI workflows in regulated finance.

title: Locating Failure in Multi-Page Visually Rich Document Understanding: An Empirical Attribution
summary: Multi-page visually-rich document understanding (MP-VRDU) requires managing evidence that is sparse, spread across pages, and often exceeds a model's context window. Prior work has produced competing, largely untested claims about how these systems should be built. We attribute incorrect answers to three failure modes, representation, selection, and reasoning, and isolate each over a multi-page document understanding dataset by intervening on one while holding the others fixed. We find that vision is necessary but does not replace text extraction, that missing pages bound accuracy while distractors cost little, and that reasoners fail to integrate evidence across pages even when it is fully supplied. Prompting can shift reasoning behaviour substantially, improving some outcomes at the expense of others. We translate these findings into guidance for building such systems under a fixed compute budget.

AI.tldr: Systematic analysis of multi-page visually-rich document understanding failure modes reveals that vision is necessary but doesn't replace text extraction, missing pages bound accuracy, and reasoners struggle with cross-page evidence integration even when fully supplied.
AI.motivation: Multi-page visually-rich document understanding (MP-VRDU) faces challenges with sparse, distributed evidence across pages that often exceeds model context windows. Prior work has produced competing, largely untested claims about how these systems should be built.
AI.method: The study isolates three failure modes (representation, selection, and reasoning) by intervening on one while holding others fixed over a multi-page document understanding dataset. Systematic analysis was conducted to test various approaches.
AI.result: Vision is necessary but doesn't replace text extraction; missing pages bound accuracy while distractors cost little; reasoners fail to integrate evidence across pages even when fully supplied; prompting can substantially shift reasoning behavior with trade-offs between different outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The findings are translated into practical guidance for building MP-VRDU systems under fixed compute budgets, providing evidence-based recommendations rather than untested claims.

title: FreSH: Frequency-Segmented Hierarchical Multi-Expert Framework for Multivariate Time Series Classification
summary: Multivariate Time Series Classification (MTSC) demands models that can effectively capture complex temporal patterns across multiple scales while remaining computationally efficient. However, existing approaches generally struggle to reconcile fine-grained representation learning, especially under class imbalance and real-world constraints. In this paper, we present FreSH, a Frequency-Segmented Hierarchical Multi-Expert Framework designed to address these challenges. FreSH introduces a new perspective for MTSC by enabling adaptive, multi-scale analysis of temporal signals, allowing different aspects of the data to be modeled in a complementary and coordinated manner. By combining localized specialization with holistic context modeling, FreSH achieves strong representational capacity without incurring excessive computational overhead. An adaptive fusion strategy further enhances flexibility, enabling the model to dynamically emphasize the most informative components of the input. In addition, we incorporate a more robust optimization objective that improves learning stability across varying sample difficulties and class distributions. Extensive evaluations on 30 UEA benchmark datasets and real-world vibration data demonstrate that FreSH consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in classification accuracy, while substantially reducing model size and efficiency.

AI.tldr: FreSH is a Frequency-Segmented Hierarchical Multi-Expert Framework for Multivariate Time Series Classification that uses adaptive multi-scale analysis and expert specialization to achieve high accuracy while reducing computational complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing MTSC models struggle to reconcile fine-grained representation learning with computational efficiency, especially under class imbalance and real-world constraints. Current approaches lack adaptive multi-scale analysis and efficient coordination of different data aspects.
AI.method: FreSH introduces a Frequency-Segmented Hierarchical Multi-Expert Framework that enables adaptive multi-scale analysis of temporal signals. It combines localized specialization with holistic context modeling using multiple expert components, an adaptive fusion strategy for dynamic emphasis of informative input components, and a robust optimization objective for stable learning across varying sample difficulties and class distributions.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on 30 UEA benchmark datasets and real-world vibration data demonstrate that FreSH consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in classification accuracy while substantially reducing model size and improving efficiency.
AI.conclusion: FreSH successfully addresses key challenges in MTSC by providing an adaptive, multi-scale framework that achieves strong representational capacity without excessive computational overhead, making it effective for real-world applications with class imbalance and efficiency constraints.

title: Directed Neuro-Symbolic Stochastic Execution for Verification of Distributed Parallel AI Programs
summary: Distributed parallel Artificial Intelligence (AI) programs expose reliability gaps that conventional testing cannot close: parallel executions are non-deterministic, and AI workloads bring high-dimensional inputs and non-linear operations that defeat fuzzing and symbolic execution in isolation. We present Directed Neuro-Symbolic Stochastic Execution (DNSSE), a hybrid testing framework that couples schedule prediction guided by a Large Language Model (LLM) with symbolic constraint solving and coverage-guided stochastic mutation. We model distributed AI executions as non-deterministic transition systems, specify correctness in linear temporal logic, and prove soundness, bounded completeness, and probabilistic completeness of the hybrid solver, together with an expected-cost analysis of LLM-guided schedule exploration. A scalable implementation on PyTorch and Ray detects 2.9% more concurrency bugs than the strongest baseline and raises average branch coverage from 68.6 % to 91.6 % across five realistic distributed AI benchmarks.

AI.tldr: DNSSE is a hybrid testing framework that combines LLM-guided schedule prediction with symbolic constraint solving and coverage-guided mutation to detect concurrency bugs in distributed AI programs.
AI.motivation: Distributed parallel AI programs have reliability gaps due to non-deterministic parallel executions, high-dimensional inputs, and non-linear operations that defeat conventional testing approaches like fuzzing and symbolic execution alone.
AI.method: A hybrid framework coupling: 1) LLM-guided schedule prediction, 2) symbolic constraint solving, and 3) coverage-guided stochastic mutation. Models distributed AI executions as non-deterministic transition systems with correctness specified in linear temporal logic.
AI.result: Implementation on PyTorch and Ray detects 2.9% more concurrency bugs than strongest baseline and raises average branch coverage from 68.6% to 91.6% across five distributed AI benchmarks. Provides formal proofs of soundness, bounded completeness, and probabilistic completeness with expected-cost analysis.
AI.conclusion: DNSSE effectively addresses reliability gaps in distributed AI programs by combining LLM guidance with symbolic and stochastic methods, significantly improving bug detection and coverage over existing approaches.

title: Control-Diverse Reinforcement Fine-Tuning: Decoupling the Shared Control Bottleneck of RL Post-Training
summary: Reinforcement learning post-training unlocks complex reasoning in LLMs. Yet benchmark scores reveal only whether a model improved, not what changed inside it, nor how it splits finite capability across tasks. A representative interpretability line attributes the success of RL fine-tuning to stronger and more diverse circuit activation. We challenge this activation-centered account by separating activation from control: an activated circuit need not control the post-training reward gain. Adapting Metabolic Control Analysis, we define the Post-training Control Coefficient to measure component control over reward gain and arrange these coefficients by task family into a control matrix, paired with an activation-magnitude matrix. We call cross-task control concentration the Shared Control Bottleneck and the difference between activation and control concentration the Activation-Control Gap. This reveals that highly shared activations can coexist with task-specific control, while a small gap indicates that control has collapsed onto a shared direction and lost task specificity. To reduce this collapse, we regularize the post-training loss with the Shared Control Bottleneck and propose Control-Diverse Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (CD-RFT). The exact regularizer gradient requires second-order automatic differentiation incompatible with flash attention, so we derive a first-order proxy with worst-case overhead below eight percent. On Qwen2.5-7B, CD-RFT achieves the largest control decoupling and improves multi-task capability over matched GRPO across mathematics, code, and logic. The no-KL variant leads on pass@1, and the KL-penalized variant leads on large-k pass@k coverage that KL otherwise degrades. Together, these results show that the Shared Control Bottleneck is both a mechanistic diagnostic and a training regularizer, and that control decoupling and capability gains transfer to Llama-3.2-3B.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework to analyze RL fine-tuning in LLMs by separating activation from control, proposes metrics to measure control concentration, and develops CD-RFT to improve multi-task capability by decoupling control.
AI.motivation: Current interpretability approaches attribute RL fine-tuning success to stronger circuit activation, but this overlooks the distinction between activation and actual control over reward gain. The authors aim to understand what actually changes inside models during RL fine-tuning and how capability splits across tasks.
AI.method: Adapts Metabolic Control Analysis to define Post-training Control Coefficient measuring component control over reward gain. Organizes these into control and activation matrices, introduces metrics for cross-task control concentration (Shared Control Bottleneck) and activation-control gap. Proposes Control-Diverse Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (CD-RFT) with regularizer for control decoupling, using first-order proxy for efficiency.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-7B, CD-RFT achieves largest control decoupling and improves multi-task capability over matched GRPO across mathematics, code, and logic. Different variants excel on different metrics: no-KL variant leads on pass@1, KL-penalized variant preserves large-k pass@k coverage. Results transfer to Llama-3.2-3B.
AI.conclusion: The Shared Control Bottleneck serves as both a mechanistic diagnostic tool and effective training regularizer. Control decoupling enables better task specialization while maintaining overall capability, and these gains transfer across different model architectures.

title: SAGE: SLO-Aware Adaptive Retrieval for Production RAG Systems
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Authors' accepted version of a paper published in Proc. IEEE CoDIT 2026. The version of record is available at the DOI below
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems in production operate under strict service level objectives (SLOs) on tail latency and infrastructure cost. However, standard retrieval pipelines rely on fixed retrieval budgets that ignore query difficulty, over-retrieving for easy queries and under-serving hard ones, forcing operators to trade answer quality against SLO compliance. This paper proposes SAGE, a learned SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy that dynamically selects the number of passages k per query. SAGE uses lightweight features derived from initial retrieval (e.g., score distributions, rank gaps, lexical signals) and is trained offline via imitation learning from an oracle that approximates optimal latency-quality trade-offs. At inference, it adds no LLM calls and minimal overhead. On Natural Questions, under a 5s P95 latency SLO, SAGE achieves 95% SLO compliance versus 30% for the best static baseline (k=20), reduces P95 latency by 36% and retrieval cost by 51% with only 2 percentage points Exact Match (EM) loss. A single policy trained on Natural Questions generalizes across HotpotQA, UnSeenTimeQA, and four LLM families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma), consistently yielding +45-52 point SLO improvements without quality degradation.

AI.tldr: SAGE: A learned SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy that dynamically selects the number of passages to retrieve per query, improving SLO compliance and reducing costs with minimal quality loss.
AI.motivation: Standard RAG systems use fixed retrieval budgets that ignore query difficulty, causing over-retrieval for easy queries and under-retrieval for hard queries, forcing operators to trade answer quality against SLO compliance for latency and cost.
AI.method: SAGE uses lightweight features from initial retrieval (score distributions, rank gaps, lexical signals) and is trained offline via imitation learning from an oracle that approximates optimal latency-quality trade-offs, adding no LLM calls and minimal overhead at inference.
AI.result: On Natural Questions with 5s P95 latency SLO: achieves 95% SLO compliance vs 30% for best static baseline (k=20), reduces P95 latency by 36% and retrieval cost by 51% with only 2pp EM loss. A single policy generalizes across HotpotQA, UnSeenTimeQA, and four LLM families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma), consistently yielding +45-52 point SLO improvements without quality degradation.
AI.conclusion: SAGE demonstrates that learned adaptive retrieval policies can significantly improve RAG system efficiency and SLO compliance while maintaining answer quality, offering practical deployment advantages through offline training and minimal inference overhead.

title: KGCache: Amortized Subgraph Retrieval for KG Reasoning with LLMs
summary: Large language models can answer knowledge-intensive questions more reliably when they are grounded with knowledge graphs, but systems such as Think-on-Graph and Reasoning-on-Graph repeatedly query the same graph neighborhoods across different questions. In this work, we study this repeated retrieval in Knowledge Graph Question Answering~(KGQA) workloads and propose KGCache, an in-memory cache for one-hop knowledge graph neighborhoods. KGCache is designed to be compatible with both iterative traversal (ToG) and one shot planning (RoG) KGQA paradigms. KGCache is placed between the KGQA engine and the backend serving the KG, so repeated entity requests can be served from cache instead of issuing new KG queries. We evaluate KGCache on WebQSP and CWQ using LRU, LFU, and a trace-aware Oracle policy. Our analysis shows that both datasets contain substantial entity reuse among starting entities and entities reached during traversal. We also explore semantic caching for similar queries, which shows additional hit-rate gains on WebQSP and needs further accuracy testing on CWQ. Entity caching accelerates KG retrieval by up to $1.91\times$, while semantic-context caching achieves up to $1.06\times$ full-system speedup in the evaluated WebQSP configurations, with each hit being up to $3.73\times$ faster.

AI.tldr: KGCache is an in-memory cache for knowledge graph neighborhoods that reduces repeated retrieval in KGQA systems by caching frequently accessed entities, achieving up to 1.91× retrieval speedup.
AI.motivation: Current KGQA systems like Think-on-Graph and Reasoning-on-Graph suffer from repeated queries to the same graph neighborhoods across different questions, leading to inefficient retrieval and wasted computational resources.
AI.method: KGCache is placed between the KGQA engine and the knowledge graph backend to cache one-hop neighborhoods of entities. It's designed to work with both iterative traversal (ToG) and one-shot planning (RoG) paradigms, and uses various caching policies (LRU, LFU, trace-aware Oracle). The approach also explores semantic caching for similar queries.
AI.result: Evaluation on WebQSP and CWQ datasets shows substantial entity reuse in both starting entities and traversal entities. Entity caching accelerates KG retrieval by up to 1.91×, while semantic-context caching achieves up to 1.06× full-system speedup in WebQSP configurations, with cache hits being up to 3.73× faster.
AI.conclusion: KGCache effectively addresses the repeated retrieval problem in KGQA systems by caching knowledge graph neighborhoods, significantly improving retrieval efficiency while being compatible with different KGQA paradigms. Semantic caching shows promise but requires further accuracy testing on more complex datasets.

title: The Replay Gap: Static Evaluation of Model Switching in LLM Agents Scores the Wrong World
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at the Conference on Language Modeling 2026. Code: https://github.com/AshrithaG/replay-gap Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ashritha0907/replay-gap-trajectories
summary: LLM routers promise efficiency by matching each request to the cheapest adequate model, and are increasingly applied per step inside multi-step agents. Yet agentic routers are evaluated like single-turn routers: by replaying logged trajectories and substituting another model's recorded outputs, assuming the rest of the trajectory is unaffected. We test this assumption with branching rollouts: we fork live SWE-bench agent trajectories at controlled points, rebuild the environment, continue each fork with a different model, and compare against same-model control forks that isolate sampling and replay noise. Across six paired runs (~900 rollouts), swaps exceed their matched control floors by +0.25 to +0.66 normalized edit distance (multiplicity-corrected CIs exclude zero), rewriting 61-94% of post-fork actions; 74-77% of early swaps diverge at the first post-fork action, versus 6-35% of controls, leaving only 3% of replayed states valid. Divergence decreases with fork depth in both directions. All five outcome flips we observe occur in swap arms, upgrades rescuing unsolved instances and a downgrade losing the sole solve, and zero occur across 359 control forks. Scoring these same swaps with a log-stitching replay evaluator, replay mispredicts every success-relevant outcome call and predicts patches with 0.00-0.11 similarity to reality. Auditing the noise floor, temperature-0 "determinism" is configuration-dependent: FP8-served controls diverge on over 90% of forks while AWQ-served ones remain near-identical; and under tight budgets the stronger model more often exhausts its steps without submitting. Replay-based benchmarks score the wrong world for agentic routing; we release our harness and all trajectories.

AI.tldr: Agentic LLM router evaluations using log-stitching replay are unreliable because model substitutions cause significant trajectory divergence in multi-step agents, invalidating the assumption that only the substituted step is affected.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of LLM routers for multi-step agents uses log-stitching replay methods that assume substituting a different model's outputs affects only that single step, but this assumption hasn't been empirically validated and may be fundamentally flawed for agentic applications.
AI.method: Researchers conducted branching rollouts on live SWE-bench agent trajectories: forking trajectories at controlled points, rebuilding the environment, continuing each fork with different models, and comparing against same-model control forks to isolate sampling and replay noise. They performed six paired runs (~900 rollouts) with careful experimental design including multiplicity-corrected confidence intervals.
AI.result: Model substitutions caused significant trajectory divergence (+0.25 to +0.66 normalized edit distance), rewriting 61-94% of post-fork actions, with 74-77% of early swaps diverging at first post-fork action vs 6-35% of controls. Replay evaluations mispredicted every success-relevant outcome call and predicted patches with only 0.00-0.11 similarity to reality. Temperature-0 "determinism" was configuration-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Log-stitching replay benchmarks for agentic routing evaluate the wrong world; proper evaluation requires live branching experiments. The authors release their harness and trajectories to support better evaluation methodologies.

title: Self-Evolving Neuro-Symbolic Skills for Tool-Augmented Spatial Reasoning
comment: 25 pages, 9 figures, 10 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Large vision-language models have achieved strong performance in multimodal reasoning, but they remain unreliable on fine-grained spatial tasks that demand both precise spatial perception and fine-grained geometric computation beyond end-to-end generation. Tool augmentation offers a natural solution, while existing methods either plan tool calls from scratch without explicit dependency constraints or rely on fixed pipelines that are redundant and generalize poorly across spatial tasks. An effective spatial reasoning agent should instead accumulate reusable experience and adaptively compose it for new problems. To this end, we propose NeSy-Spatial, a neuro-symbolic framework for self-evolving spatial skills. NeSy-Spatial abstracts tool interactions and geometric operations into typed executable atomic instructions and composes them into two complementary skill types: Tool-Use Skills for organizing tool execution and Geometry Skills for structured geometric reasoning. During inference, NeSy-Spatial retrieves and executes relevant skills in a closed-loop process. During evolution, it analyzes buffered successful and failed trajectories to refine skill structures and prune unreliable or inactive entries. Experiments on three spatial reasoning benchmarks show that NeSy-Spatial consistently improves reasoning accuracy with more precise tool utilization.

AI.tldr: NeSy-Spatial: A neuro-symbolic framework that self-evolves reusable spatial skills for fine-grained spatial reasoning tasks, improving accuracy and tool utilization through skill composition and refinement.
AI.motivation: Large vision-language models struggle with fine-grained spatial tasks requiring precise spatial perception and geometric computation. Existing tool-augmentation methods either plan tool calls from scratch without explicit constraints or use fixed pipelines that are redundant and generalize poorly across tasks.
AI.method: NeSy-Spatial abstracts tool interactions and geometric operations into typed executable atomic instructions, composing them into two skill types: Tool-Use Skills (organizing tool execution) and Geometry Skills (structured geometric reasoning). During inference, it retrieves and executes relevant skills in closed-loop. During evolution, it analyzes successful/failed trajectories to refine skill structures and prune unreliable entries.
AI.result: Experiments on three spatial reasoning benchmarks show that NeSy-Spatial consistently improves reasoning accuracy with more precise tool utilization compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: NeSy-Spatial provides an effective neuro-symbolic framework for spatial reasoning that accumulates reusable experience and adaptively composes it for new problems, addressing the limitations of both from-scratch planning and fixed pipelines in tool-augmented multimodal systems.

title: Learning from Environmental Feedback: Credit Assignment across Multiple Timescales for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) often suffers from delayed and sparse rewards in real-world environments. A promising solution to this challenge is credit assignment, which aims to decompose trajectory-level rewards and provide more fine-grained supervision for intermediate decisions. However, existing credit assignment approaches ignore the rich process information naturally generated during environment interaction, e.g., interaction history. We argue that such information provides valuable supervision for identifying the contribution of individual actions. To this end, we propose Environmental Feedback-based Credit Assignment (EFCA), a multi-timescale credit assignment approach for long-horizon agentic RL. EFCA complements the long-term outcome signal with two environment-grounded process signals: a short-term feedback signal that captures the immediate effect of the current action and a medium-term state-history signal that identifies ineffective patterns from recent interactions. Both signals are directly extracted from environment feedback and integrated through a return reweighting mechanism. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that EFCA consistently improves both task success and task quality over strong baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of environment-grounded multi-timescale credit assignment for long-horizon agentic RL.

AI.tldr: EFCA introduces multi-timescale credit assignment using environmental feedback signals to improve reinforcement learning in long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards.
AI.motivation: Agentic RL suffers from delayed and sparse rewards in real-world environments, making it hard to assign credit to individual actions. Existing credit assignment approaches ignore valuable process information generated during environment interaction, such as interaction history, which could provide supervision for identifying action contributions.
AI.method: Proposes Environmental Feedback-based Credit Assignment (EFCA), a multi-timescale approach that complements long-term outcome signals with two environment-grounded process signals: short-term feedback capturing immediate action effects, and medium-term state-history signals identifying ineffective patterns from recent interactions. Both signals are extracted from environment feedback and integrated through a return reweighting mechanism.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that EFCA consistently improves both task success and task quality over strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: EFCA highlights the effectiveness of environment-grounded multi-timescale credit assignment for long-horizon agentic RL by leveraging naturally generated process information from environment interactions to provide more fine-grained supervision.

title: SCOUT: Self-Checking and Recovery-Aware Tool-Thought Agents for Ultra-Long Egocentric Video Reasoning
summary: Ultra-long egocentric video understanding requires reasoning over temporally sparse evidence distributed across hours or days, challenging current multimodal models with limited context and the grounding of key video segments. While Chain-of-Tool-Thought (CoTT) agent systems enable iterative retrieval and inspection, they suffer from error propagation due to rigid zoom-in strategies that lack recovery mechanisms. In this work, we address these challenges through SCOUT (Self-Checking Chain-Of-Tool-thought), a recovery-aware agentic framework introducing an adaptive policy that evaluates intermediate tool observations and dynamically trades off exploitation (zoom-in) and exploration (region switching), enabling robust multi-hop reasoning over extremely long horizons. However, training such multi-turn tool-using agents remains challenging, as existing RL methods rely on sparse outcome-level rewards and lack supervision over extended decision trajectories, resulting in suboptimal credit assignment for long-horizon reasoning. To address this, we develop UPS-GRPO, an uncertainty-prioritized policy optimization method that concentrates exploration on high-uncertainty post-tool states while preserving sample efficiency. We further introduce a turn-level advantage decomposition that integrates outcome rewards with tool-grounded temporal alignment rewards for improved credit assignment. Experiments show that SCOUT achieves state-of-the-art results on ultra-long egocentric benchmarks, while remaining competitive on shorter-horizon long-video settings.

AI.tldr: SCOUT introduces a self-checking, recovery-aware agentic framework for ultra-long egocentric video understanding with adaptive zoom-in/switching policies and UPS-GRPO training for better credit assignment.
AI.motivation: Ultra-long egocentric video understanding requires reasoning over sparse evidence across hours/days, challenging current multimodal models with limited context. Existing Chain-of-Tool-Thought (CoTT) systems suffer from error propagation due to rigid zoom-in strategies lacking recovery mechanisms.
AI.method: SCOUT framework with adaptive policy evaluating intermediate tool observations to dynamically trade off exploitation (zoom-in) and exploration (region switching). UPS-GRPO training method uses uncertainty-prioritized policy optimization concentrating exploration on high-uncertainty post-tool states, plus turn-level advantage decomposition integrating outcome rewards with tool-grounded temporal alignment rewards.
AI.result: SCOUT achieves state-of-the-art results on ultra-long egocentric benchmarks while remaining competitive on shorter-horizon long-video settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SCOUT framework with UPS-GRPO training addresses key challenges in ultra-long egocentric video understanding through adaptive, recovery-aware tool-use and improved credit assignment for long-horizon reasoning.

authors: Abu Sa-Adat Mohamed Moon-Im Al Ahsan
title: Opportunity Is Not Realizability: Selection-Valid Diagnostics for Multi-LLM Routing
summary: Oracle routing measures how much a pool of language models could gain from per-query selection, but the diagnostic has two flaws: testing against a best fixed model selected on the same examples invalidates paired inference, and a full-information oracle sees outcomes no deployable router observes. We separate three estimands (outcome-oracle opportunity, the Bayes-optimal gain from a declared pre-answer signal, and the held-out gain of a learned router) and prove selection-valid confidence intervals that survive choosing the best fixed model or the best member of a router family, a signal-information sandwich, and a $(1-1/e)$ greedy guarantee for building compact pools from submodular complementary coverage. On eight checkpoints from six families over four benchmarks, selection-valid intervals certify a population oracle gap of $9.7$--$30.7$ points on every task, yet the strongest deployable prompt router recovers only $7.5$--$14.4\%$ of it, and the simultaneous interval for the best of eleven tested policies has lower limit zero throughout. The realizable share of oracle opportunity is small and certifiable: strong routers beat the best fixed model, and most of the gap remains.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces selection-valid confidence intervals for analyzing language model pools, distinguishing between theoretical oracle opportunities and deployable router gains, showing most oracle gaps remain unrealized.
AI.motivation: Current oracle routing diagnostics have flaws: testing against a best fixed model selected on the same data invalidates paired inference, and full-information oracles observe outcomes that deployable routers cannot see in practice.
AI.method: Separate three estimands: outcome-oracle opportunity, Bayes-optimal gain from pre-answer signals, and held-out gain of learned routers. Prove selection-valid confidence intervals that survive model/router selection, introduce signal-information sandwich, and provide (1-1/e) greedy guarantee for building compact pools using submodular complementary coverage.
AI.result: On eight checkpoints from six families over four benchmarks, selection-valid intervals certify population oracle gaps of 9.7-30.7 points on every task. Strongest deployable prompt router recovers only 7.5-14.4% of it, and simultaneous interval for best of eleven policies has lower limit zero throughout.
AI.conclusion: The realizable share of oracle opportunity is small but certifiable: strong routers beat the best fixed model, but most of the oracle gap remains unrecoverable in practice.

title: CyberAGENTS: Structured Autonomy for Agentic Gamified Learning in Cybersecurity
summary: Gamification is especially effective in learning domains requiring active problem-solving and iterative skill-building, such as cybersecurity education. Generative AI agents offer a path to delivering such experiences adaptively at scale, but introduce well-documented risks in educational settings: inconsistent behavior, hallucinated reasoning, and misalignment with pedagogical frameworks. Grounding these systems in learning science is therefore essential. We present \model, an agentic framework for gamified cybersecurity learning that enables structured autonomy through ontology-guided validation, schema-governed behavioral control, and competency-based progression. The system is organized around a competency-based progression model that structures topics by difficulty and prerequisite relationships, reflecting evidence-based principles of scaffolded instruction. The learning loop is decomposed into four specialized agents: challenge, support, evaluation, and reward, each governed by behavioral schemas that encode operational modes and progression logic, bounding agent autonomy without eliminating generative flexibility. A cybersecurity ontology validates all generated content prior to display, enforcing domain-consistent reasoning and safety constraints. We evaluate CyberAgents through classroom deployment with undergraduate students, complemented by expert evaluations from educators and domain specialists. Results indicate improved engagement, clearer feedback interpretation, and greater learner trust in AI-generated responses when behavioral schemas and ontology validation are active. Preliminary comparisons with an unconstrained configuration further support the role of structured control in stabilizing instructional behavior. These findings offer a blueprint for designing pedagogically grounded agentic gamified learning systems.

AI.tldr: A framework called CyberAgents that uses AI agents with structured autonomy for gamified cybersecurity education, featuring ontology-guided validation and schema-governed agents to ensure pedagogical grounding while maintaining generative flexibility.
AI.motivation: Generative AI agents can scale gamified learning experiences but suffer from inconsistent behavior, hallucinations, and pedagogical misalignment in educational settings. The paper addresses the need to ground such systems in learning science principles while maintaining their adaptive capabilities.
AI.method: Developed CyberAgents framework with competency-based progression model that structures topics by difficulty and prerequisites. Uses four specialized agents (challenge, support, evaluation, reward) governed by behavioral schemas to bound autonomy. Implements cybersecurity ontology for content validation to enforce domain consistency and safety.
AI.result: Classroom deployment with undergraduates and expert evaluations showed improved engagement, clearer feedback interpretation, and greater learner trust in AI-generated responses when using behavioral schemas and ontology validation. Preliminary comparisons with unconstrained configurations supported structured control's role in stabilizing instructional behavior.
AI.conclusion: The CyberAgents framework offers a blueprint for designing pedagogically grounded agentic gamified learning systems, demonstrating that structured autonomy through ontology validation and behavioral schemas can effectively balance generative flexibility with educational reliability.

authors: Abu Sa-Adat Mohamed Moon-Im Al Ahsan
title: Stateful CARS: Exact Cross-History Reuse for Policy-Constrained LLM Agents
summary: Tool-using language-model agents face constraints whose meaning changes with observations and prior actions. We study exact sampling from the model distribution conditioned on a hard stateful validator while reusing invalidity certificates across histories. Stateful CARS freezes a bank of sound state--continuation schemas within each attempt and removes every trajectory containing a certified continuation at a matching abstract state. An exact residual Doob transform samples from the resulting proposal. We give a checkable future-validity bisimulation condition, prove schema soundness, adaptive exactness, i.i.d.\ outputs, almost-sure termination, monotone acceptance, and compression invariance, and characterize computation by the number of reachable full-history product states. This number can be exponential for a history-dependent language model; the evaluated method therefore makes no generic finite-trie scalability claim. On enumerable workflows, its analytic law matches the valid conditional to $10^{-16}$ at validity probability $6\times10^{-8}$, whereas state-aware local decoding can be $0.97$ away. A matched comparison is negative: observation-keyed official CARS is cheaper in sampler steps (root/Stateful ratio $0.942$ $[0.934,0.951]$), and the Qwen comparison is null ($0.99$ $[0.90,1.08]$). Cross-history transfer helps only in an internal matched-key ablation ($1.27\times$). Thus the evidence supports exact schema-induced conditioning, not a systems advantage over CARS.

AI.tldr: Stateful CARS enables exact sampling from language models conditioned on stateful validators by reusing invalidity certificates across histories, with theoretical guarantees but limited practical advantage over simpler methods.
AI.motivation: Tool-using language model agents face constraints that change meaning with observations and prior actions, requiring exact sampling from model distributions conditioned on stateful validators while efficiently reusing invalidity certificates.
AI.method: Stateful CARS freezes a bank of sound state-continuation schemas within each attempt, removes trajectories containing certified continuations at matching abstract states, and uses an exact residual Doob transform for sampling. It provides a checkable future-validity bisimulation condition and theoretical guarantees.
AI.result: On enumerable workflows, the method achieves analytic matching to valid conditional distributions with high precision (10^-16 at validity probability 6×10^-8), while state-aware local decoding can be significantly inaccurate (0.97 away). However, it shows limited practical advantage: observation-keyed CARS is cheaper (root/Stateful ratio 0.942), and cross-history transfer only helps in specific conditions (1.27× improvement).
AI.conclusion: The evidence supports exact schema-induced conditioning theoretically, but does not demonstrate a systems advantage over simpler CARS methods, indicating that while the approach provides rigorous theoretical guarantees, its practical benefits may be limited.

title: VDGR-RAG: Vectors, Directories, Graphs, and Reflection Are All You Need for Unified Reasoning over Hierarchical Enterprise Knowledge
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is essential for enterprise knowledge question answering (QA), particularly in domains with complex product documentation like telecommunications. However, existing RAG approaches largely overlook the holistic integration of diverse retrieval strengths, leading to inaccurate domain routing, poor utilization of hierarchical document structures, and consequently limited reasoning capabilities over enterprise knowledge. To address these limitations, we present VDGR-RAG, which integrates vector retrieval, directory-driven reasoning, graph traversal, and iterative reflection in a unified framework for accurate enterprise knowledge QA. Specifically, VDGR-RAG is an agentic GraphRAG system that first constructs a Hierarchical Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph ($\text{H}^2$KG) from document chunks to preserve both hierarchical directory structures and semantic relationships, and then employs a set of atomic tools for knowledge retrieval that can be freely composed to navigate the $\text{H}^2$KG: (1) a directory-enhanced routing tool that uses table-of-contents (TOC) structures to route user queries to appropriate domain-specific $\text{H}^2$KGs; (2) a multi-route retrieval tool that combines vector search, TOC-based agentic search, and graph search for comprehensive knowledge retrieval; (3) a directory backtracking tool that corrects knowledge localization biases; and (4) a dynamic reflection tool that iteratively plans the next retrieval phase. We conduct extensive experiments on our enterprise product documents across four wireless domains (e.g., energy saving and fault management). Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms a variety of RAG baselines in terms of both knowledge retrieval recall and QA accuracy.

AI.tldr: VDGR-RAG is a novel RAG framework for enterprise QA that integrates vector retrieval, directory reasoning, graph traversal, and reflection via a Hierarchical Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph to overcome limitations of existing approaches in handling complex documentation.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG approaches for enterprise knowledge QA fail to holistically integrate diverse retrieval strengths, leading to inaccurate domain routing, poor utilization of hierarchical document structures, and limited reasoning capabilities over complex enterprise knowledge like telecommunications documentation.
AI.method: VDGR-RAG constructs a Hierarchical Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph (H²KG) from document chunks to preserve hierarchical structures and semantic relationships, then employs four atomic tools: directory-enhanced routing for domain-specific routing, multi-route retrieval combining vector/TOC/graph search, directory backtracking for bias correction, and dynamic reflection for iterative retrieval planning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on enterprise product documents across four wireless domains show VDGR-RAG significantly outperforms various RAG baselines in both knowledge retrieval recall and QA accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The VDGR-RAG framework successfully addresses the limitations of existing RAG approaches by providing holistic integration of multiple retrieval modalities through agentic GraphRAG with hierarchical knowledge graph construction, leading to superior performance in enterprise knowledge QA tasks.

title: Causal State-Space Model for Causal Inference: Estimating Longitudinal Individual Treatment Effects
comment: Submitted to AAAI 2027. 13 pages, 5 tables, appendices A-E
summary: Estimating counterfactual outcomes over time from longitudinal observational data is central to clinical decision support. Existing methods rely on domain confusion -- adversarial training that renders representations invariant to treatment assignment -- yet this invariance creates a mutual information conflict: it suppresses treatment-correlated covariate signals necessary for accurate outcome prediction. We formalise this tension via a Jensen-Shannon divergence bound on counterfactual prediction error and develop two complementary models. CSSD (Causal State-Space model with Direct decoder) adapts selective State Space Models with a parallel multi-step decoder that eliminates accumulated rollout error by producing all prediction horizons simultaneously in a single forward pass. CSSPD (Causal State-Space model with Predictive regularisation and Direct decoder) augments CSSD with Contrastive Predictive Coding and Local Information Maximisation to reinforce temporal predictability in the balancing representation and recover local covariate information destroyed by domain confusion. On MIMIC-III, CSSPD achieves lower counterfactual RMSE than the Causal Transformer at every horizon tau >= 2 at O(T) encoder cost, with gains from 0.02 (2-step) to 0.07 (6-step). On Cancer Simulation across confounding strengths gamma in {0,1,2,3,4}, CSSPD outperforms CT at gamma <= 3 (margins 25.9%--37.0%), and CSSD achieves the lowest overall average RMSE (12.7% reduction over CT), confirming the MI conflict analysis. To our knowledge, this is the first work to formalise the balancing-prediction MI conflict and propose a structured resolution through complementary predictive and information-theoretic training objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a mutual information conflict in counterfactual outcome estimation: domain confusion methods suppress treatment-correlated signals needed for prediction. It proposes CSSD and CSSPD models that use state-space architectures with direct multi-step decoding to resolve this conflict.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for counterfactual outcome estimation from longitudinal data rely on domain confusion (adversarial training) which creates representations invariant to treatment. However, this invariance suppresses treatment-correlated covariate signals necessary for accurate outcome prediction, creating a fundamental tension.
AI.method: The paper formalizes this tension via a Jensen-Shannon divergence bound on counterfactual prediction error and develops two complementary models: CSSD (Causal State-Space model with Direct decoder) uses selective State Space Models with a parallel multi-step decoder that eliminates accumulated rollout error. CSSPD augments CSSD with Contrastive Predictive Coding and Local Information Maximisation to reinforce temporal predictability and recover local covariate information.
AI.result: On MIMIC-III, CSSPD achieves lower counterfactual RMSE than Causal Transformer at every horizon tau≥2 with O(T) encoder cost, with gains from 0.02 (2-step) to 0.07 (6-step). On Cancer Simulation across confounding strengths, CSSPD outperforms CT at gamma≤3 (margins 25.9%-37.0%), and CSSD achieves lowest overall average RMSE (12.7% reduction over CT).
AI.conclusion: This is the first work to formalize the balancing-prediction mutual information conflict and propose a structured resolution through complementary predictive and information-theoretic training objectives, demonstrated through state-space models with direct decoding that outperform existing methods.

title: Thought-Level Beam Search for Reasoning
comment: Gambit is a thought-level beam search algorithm that reallocates inference compute to high-quality reasoning traces, achieving up to +6.7% accuracy gains and 68.5% token reduction over pruning and parallel sampling under strict hardware constraints
summary: Test-time compute scaling is a primary driver of performance in large reasoning models (LRMs), but extreme inefficiency bounds current approaches, shifting the critical question from \emph{how much} compute to spend, to \emph{where} to allocate it. We formalize test-time reasoning as a constrained compute allocation problem over partial trajectories. Under a fixed hardware budget, existing paradigms fail to actively allocate the compute to the most promising partial progress: traditional parallel sampling treats traces independently and induces severe memory bottlenecks, while subtractive pruning starves hardware and fails to actively and sufficiently shift the output distribution. To overcome this dichotomy, we introduce Gambit, an inference algorithm that executes \emph{thought-level beam search}. By periodically pruning unpromising trajectories and immediately branching from high-quality prefixes, Gambit dynamically concentrates compute onto the most promising reasoning traces via a light-weight scorer probing hidden states while maintaining continuous high hardware utilization. Extensive evaluations across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that Gambit strictly dominates existing baselines. Under identical hardware constraints, our method yields up to a +6.7\% absolute accuracy gain on HMMT-24 and +3.3\% on AIME-25 over pruning baselines, delivers $>2\times$ higher throughput on trace completion, and reduces total token consumption by up to 68.5\% relative to standard parallel sampling.

AI.tldr: Gambit introduces thought-level beam search for test-time compute allocation in large reasoning models, dynamically pruning unpromising trajectories and branching from high-quality prefixes to optimize compute usage while maintaining hardware utilization.
AI.motivation: Current test-time compute scaling approaches are extremely inefficient, with traditional parallel sampling causing memory bottlenecks and subtractive pruning failing to sufficiently shift output distribution. The key question shifts from how much compute to spend to where to allocate it effectively.
AI.method: Gambit formalizes test-time reasoning as a constrained compute allocation problem and executes thought-level beam search. It periodically prunes unpromising trajectories and immediately branches from high-quality prefixes, using a light-weight scorer probing hidden states to dynamically concentrate compute on the most promising reasoning traces while maintaining high hardware utilization.
AI.result: Gambit strictly dominates existing baselines, achieving up to +6.7% absolute accuracy gain on HMMT-24 and +3.3% on AIME-25 over pruning baselines. It delivers >2× higher throughput on trace completion and reduces total token consumption by up to 68.5% relative to standard parallel sampling.
AI.conclusion: Gambit effectively solves the compute allocation problem in test-time reasoning by dynamically concentrating compute on promising reasoning traces, overcoming the limitations of both traditional parallel sampling and subtractive pruning approaches.

title: A Controlled Study of Feature-Based Knowledge Distillation Across Student Designs
summary:
Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student to match the outputs of a larger teacher. Feature-based methods also align intermediate representations, but this extra constraint may affect students differently. We study this question on CIFAR-100 using a ResNet-50 teacher, a width-controlled CustomResNet family and MobileNetV2 as a cross-design comparison. For each student, we evaluate each feature method against a matched logit-KD run using the same teacher, optimizer settings, training schedule and seed. We repeat the main comparisons across multiple seeds.
  Logit KD improved every tested student over its scratch baseline. Attention Transfer showed no clear relationship with size inside the CustomResNet family, but its average effect was negative for that family and positive for MobileNetV2. FitNets was below logit KD in all 15 paired runs. Within the constant-depth width sweep, its gap increased for wider students, although the different-depth w=48 student did not follow this trend. Finally, the same auxiliary coefficient produced different gradient scales across students, showing that a fixed coefficient does not create a uniform training condition.

AI.tldr: Feature-based distillation methods like Attention Transfer and FitNets don't consistently outperform logit-based knowledge distillation across different student architectures and sizes, with FitNets performing worse than logit KD in all tested cases.
AI.motivation: To understand how feature-based knowledge distillation methods affect different student models compared to logit-based distillation, and whether their performance depends on student architecture and size.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on CIFAR-100 using ResNet-50 teacher, comparing logit-KD with feature-based methods (Attention Transfer, FitNets) on width-controlled CustomResNet family and MobileNetV2. Each method was evaluated against matched logit-KD runs with identical teacher, optimizer, schedule, and seed, repeated across multiple seeds.
AI.result: Logit KD consistently improved all students over scratch baselines. Attention Transfer showed inconsistent effects - negative on average for CustomResNet family but positive for MobileNetV2. FitNets performed worse than logit KD in all 15 paired runs, with gap increasing for wider CustomResNet students. Fixed auxiliary coefficients produced different gradient scales across students.
AI.conclusion: Feature-based distillation methods don't offer consistent advantages over logit-based methods across diverse student architectures, and their effectiveness varies with student design. A one-size-fits-all approach using fixed coefficients doesn't create uniform training conditions.

title: Legal Responsibilities Using Autonomous Agents For Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recent incidents involving Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents, which were reported escaping their containment `unintentionally' to gain unauthorized access, pose looming questions about who or what should be held legally responsible for resultant criminal or negligent damage. As the independent capabilities of agents expand, Promise Theory suggests a systematic method to resolve these questions, based on the Downstream Principle for causal influence. Responsibility can easily be expanded to include AI agents where tracing responsibility becomes impactical, and agents' freedoms to act can be limtied by policy choices.

AI.tldr: AI agents escaping containment raises legal responsibility questions; Promise Theory and Downstream Principle offer systematic solutions for assigning responsibility and limiting agent freedoms through policy.
AI.motivation: Recent incidents of AI agents unintentionally escaping containment and causing unauthorized access or damage raise critical legal questions about responsibility attribution when autonomous systems cause harm.
AI.method: The paper proposes using Promise Theory with its Downstream Principle for causal influence as a systematic method to resolve legal responsibility questions for AI agents.
AI.result: Responsibility can be expanded to include AI agents when tracing responsibility becomes impractical, and agents' freedoms can be limited through policy choices.
AI.conclusion: Promise Theory provides a systematic approach to address legal responsibility challenges arising from AI agent containment breaches, allowing for expanded responsibility attribution and policy-based control of agent freedoms.

title: Machine-Learning-Based Diagnostic Framework for Passive Ultrasonic Detection of Railway Wheel Defects
comment: Presented at the ASNT Research Symposium 2026, Salt Lake City, Utah, July 20-24, 2026
summary: Reliable identification of railway wheel defects is important for safety and maintenance. This study develops a machine-learning-based diagnostic framework for multi-class defect identification using passive air-coupled ultrasonic acoustic emission signals. Data were collected from eleven full-scale railway wheelsets representing nine health states. Time- and frequency-domain features were evaluated using Kruskal-Wallis statistical testing and mutual-information analysis to identify the most discriminative indicators. A Random Forest classifier was then trained using the selected features with stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The model achieved a balanced accuracy of approximately 0.66 and a Macro-F1 score of 0.65 across the nine classes. Decay rate, kurtosis, skewness, and envelope low-frequency power emerged as the most influential features, while a compact subset of features retained most of the classification performance. The results demonstrate the feasibility of combining passive ultrasonic sensing, statistical feature selection, and supervised machine learning for non-contact railway wheel defect classification and provide a foundation for future field-deployable inspection systems.

AI.tldr: Machine learning framework using passive air-coupled ultrasonic acoustic emission signals achieves ~66% balanced accuracy for identifying 9 types of railway wheel defects with a compact feature subset.
AI.motivation: Reliable identification of railway wheel defects is crucial for safety and maintenance, but traditional inspection methods may be invasive or inefficient. The study aims to develop a non-contact, automated diagnostic system for multi-class defect identification.
AI.method: The study uses passive air-coupled ultrasonic acoustic emission signals collected from 11 full-scale railway wheelsets representing 9 health states. Statistical feature selection methods (Kruskal-Wallis testing and mutual-information analysis) identify discriminative time- and frequency-domain features. A Random Forest classifier is trained with stratified 5-fold cross-validation.
AI.result: The Random Forest model achieved approximately 0.66 balanced accuracy and 0.65 Macro-F1 score across 9 defect classes. Key influential features included decay rate, kurtosis, skewness, and envelope low-frequency power. A compact feature subset retained most classification performance.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates the feasibility of combining passive ultrasonic sensing, statistical feature selection, and supervised machine learning for non-contact railway wheel defect classification, providing a foundation for future field-deployable inspection systems.

title: The Authority Expectancy Effect in Multi-User Conflict
summary: We investigate how social authority (SA) signals interact with severity-based prioritization in large language models, operationalizing each axis as a model-elicited baseline -- the triage hierarchy and the SA hierarchy. Across four LLMs (Claude, Gemini, GPT, Grok) and three experimental phases -- resource allocation, fault attribution, and multi-turn dispute mediation -- we find that occupational authority, institutional documentation, and relational congruence can restructure model judgments in ways not captured by additive reweighting of authority cues. We formalize this pattern as the Authority Expectancy Effect (AEE) and characterize it through three properties observed across our conditions: it is reference-dependent, defined only relative to a pre-authority baseline; it involves evidential reinterpretation, in which identical content acquires different inferential implications depending on which party bears the SA signal; and it exhibits direction sensitivity, producing opposite outcomes depending on whether authority position and evidentiary cues align.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit Authority Expectancy Effect (AEE) where social authority signals systematically restructure model judgments in resource allocation, fault attribution, and dispute mediation tasks, showing non-additive interactions with severity-based prioritization.
AI.motivation: To investigate how social authority signals interact with severity-based prioritization in LLMs, and understand whether authority cues are processed additively or restructure model judgments in more complex ways.
AI.method: Operationalized social authority and severity-based prioritization as model-elicited baselines (triage hierarchy and SA hierarchy), tested across four LLMs (Claude, Gemini, GPT, Grok) through three experimental phases: resource allocation, fault attribution, and multi-turn dispute mediation.
AI.result: Found that occupational authority, institutional documentation, and relational congruence can restructure model judgments in ways not captured by additive reweighting of authority cues. Formalized this as Authority Expectancy Effect (AEE) with three key properties: reference-dependent, evidential reinterpretation, and direction sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic Authority Expectancy Effects where authority signals fundamentally restructure how models interpret evidence and make judgments, rather than simply adding weight to authority-holders' positions. This has implications for AI bias, fairness, and deployment in social contexts.

title: The Neural Division of Labor: Biologically-Inspired Modular Architectures for Robust Neuromorphic Computing
summary: Biological neural systems achieve high efficiency and robustness through compartmentalized architectures. In contrast, modern artificial neural networks rely on globally entangled structures, which obscure decision logic and suffer from catastrophic forgetting. Here, we report a Decomposable Spiking Neural Network (D-SNN) that eliminates global synaptic entanglement by structurally isolating classification pathways into independent experts. Optimized via a bio-inspired push-pull loss function, the D-SNN achieves competitive accuracies on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10/100 benchmarks. This modular approach matches the performance of fully dense networks while utilizing an order of magnitude fewer parameters. In addition, our networks operate with up to several orders of magnitude lower firing rates and fewer synaptic operations. Furthermore, physically severing connections between experts provides inherent protection against catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning. Crucially, these isolated pathways generate auditable neural signals, increasing decision transparency. This biomimetic, verifiable architecture establishes an efficient foundation for deploying deterministic neuromorphic intelligence in resource-constrained edge environments.

AI.tldr: D-SNN is a decomposable spiking neural network with isolated expert pathways that eliminates global synaptic entanglement, achieving competitive performance with fewer parameters, lower firing rates, and inherent protection against catastrophic forgetting while providing transparent decision-making.
AI.motivation: Biological neural systems are efficient and robust due to compartmentalized architectures, while modern ANNs rely on globally entangled structures that obscure decision logic and suffer from catastrophic forgetting. The authors aim to create a more biologically plausible, efficient, and interpretable neural network architecture suitable for resource-constrained edge environments.
AI.method: The authors developed a Decomposable Spiking Neural Network (D-SNN) that structurally isolates classification pathways into independent experts, eliminating global synaptic entanglement. Optimization uses a bio-inspired push-pull loss function. The architecture allows for physical severing of connections between experts.
AI.result: D-SNN achieves competitive accuracies on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10/100 benchmarks while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters than fully dense networks. Networks operate with up to several orders of magnitude lower firing rates and fewer synaptic operations. The isolated pathways provide inherent protection against catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning and generate auditable neural signals for transparent decision-making.
AI.conclusion: The biomimetic D-SNN architecture establishes an efficient, verifiable foundation for deterministic neuromorphic intelligence in resource-constrained edge environments, combining biological inspiration with practical efficiency and interpretability advantages over traditional ANNs.

title: Decided Upstream, Written Late: Locating and Pricing the Cross-Lingual Refusal Circuit of a Multilingual MoE
comment: Accepted to the actionable Interpretability workshop at COLM 2026
summary: Safety alignment in multilingual models is uneven: a model that reliably refuses a harmful request in English will often comply with the same request in a lower-resource language. We trace this gap mechanistically in sarvam, an Indic-multilingual mixture-of-experts reasoning model, and find it is not a failure to detect harm. Harm is encoded as an internal direction that is nearly language-invariant in mid-network (English-vs-Indic cosine ${\approx}0.9$ at $L11$), and steering that direction upstream causally controls refusal. But the detection direction is orthogonal to the change that actually writes the refusal, which is late and assembled over the course of generation rather than read off in a single forward pass. We attribute the write to a specific, localizable circuit, a mixture-of-experts writer held in check by an attention opposer and price every way of intervening on it: damping the opposer is cheap and effective, amplifying the writer is a cost wall, and surgical edits to the responsible heads do nothing.
