AI.motivation: There's a need to establish language model provenance (base checkpoint and training data overlap) for governance purposes, as metadata alone is insufficient to determine relationships between models.
AI.method: The method creates fingerprints based on top-k vocabulary projections of late hidden states from 250 fixed knowledge probes, compared using Jaccard overlap over decoded token strings. No training required.
AI.result: The fingerprint shows a similarity ladder following model relatedness, can identify exact documented bases in lineage retrieval, strengthens toward output layers, and remains stable under quantization (0.92 Jaccard similarity under int8).
AI.conclusion: The training-free fingerprint method effectively establishes language model provenance across different architectures and organizations, providing a practical solution for model governance and lineage tracking.

title: When Skills Meet Safety: Benchmarking and Characterizing the Adaptive Jailbreak Robustness of Skill-Merged LLMs
summary: Model merging has become the default way to give an aligned language model new skills without retraining: a practitioner folds task vectors from math, code, or domain specialists into a safety-aligned base using task arithmetic, TIES, or DARE. This convenience is known to carry a safety cost, but almost all of that evidence rests on static refusal tests: fixed harmful prompts scored for compliance. We argue this is misleading. Because safety alignment is "shallow," concentrated in the first few generated tokens, a merged model's static refusal can stay clean while a real adaptive attack still breaks it. We introduce SkillSafe-Bench, a controlled benchmark that scores skill-merged models on static refusal, adaptive jailbreak robustness, and capability retention under a conservative two-judge AND rule. Across six open-weight bases (five families, two scales), static safety does not predict robustness to attack: under a semantic template attack, safe-looking merges on the fragile bases (both Qwen scales and Gemma) are jailbroken 60-76% of the time while others (Llama, Phi-4) stay robust. We further show the static effect of merging is base-conditional, characterize same-recipe abliteration-style safety erosion through a data-free geometric signal (the overlap of a task vector with a safety subspace), and outline SubSafe-Merge, which projects this overlap away to remove that erosion at held capability. Adaptive evaluation is not optional for merged LLMs: the models that most need it look safe under static screening.

AI.tldr: Model merging for LLMs can appear safe in static tests but remains vulnerable to adaptive attacks due to shallow safety alignment; static safety doesn't predict real-world robustness, requiring adaptive evaluation.
AI.motivation: Model merging is widely used to add new skills to aligned LLMs, but current safety evaluation relies on static refusal tests that may be misleading. The researchers want to demonstrate that models that appear safe in static tests can still be jailbroken through adaptive attacks.
AI.method: Created SkillSafe-Bench benchmark to evaluate merged models across three dimensions: static refusal, adaptive jailbreak robustness, and capability retention using conservative two-judge AND rule. Tested six open-weight bases across five families and two scales under semantic template attacks. Analyzed geometric properties of task vectors in relation to safety subspaces.
AI.result: Static safety scores don't predict adaptive attack robustness: safe-looking merges on fragile bases (Qwen, Gemma) were jailbroken 60-76% of the time, while others (Llama, Phi-4) remained robust. Found merging's safety effect is base-dependent, identified geometric signal for safety erosion (task vector overlap with safety subspace), and proposed SubSafe-Merge to project away this overlap while preserving capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive evaluation is essential for merged LLMs because static safety screening is insufficient. Models that appear safest in static tests may be most vulnerable to real attacks, requiring new evaluation methods and mitigation approaches like SubSafe-Merge.

title: Long SKILL Compliance as Logical Reasoning: Closure-Grounded Detection with Scaling-Guided On-Policy Distillation
summary: The increasing complexity of enterprise business scenarios has promoted the widespread adoption of long SKILL documents in agent systems, posing new challenges for compliance detection: large models incur substantial inference costs, while small models may fail to maintain detection accuracy. To address this gap, we propose SkillCDG, a graph-based framework for long SKILL compliance detection. SkillCDG represents complex business policies as a two-layer constraint dependency graph, where the upper layer indexes SKILL descriptions for scenario routing and the lower layer captures dependencies among atomic constraints within each SKILL. During inference, two-level retrieval followed by dependency closure supports compliance judgment and source traceability. We comprehensively evaluate the framework on three enterprise datasets and two controlled public benchmark variants. Experimental results demonstrate that SkillCDG outperforms baseline methods by up to 12.8 percentage points in detection F1 score, while reducing token consumption by a maximum 64.3\%. Moreover, we further investigate the inherent relationships among policy-graph complexity, model scale, and detection performance. Comparative experiments conducted on four checkpoints from a single model family validate a concise and effective scaling trend: end-to-end detection correctness exhibits a complexity-differentiated scaling pattern, and the complexity metric derived from the constraint dependency graph can effectively quantify instance difficulty and the performance improvement potential of models. Leveraging this insightful scaling trend, we conduct adaptive training sample selection and adopt on-policy distillation to efficiently enhance the compliance detection capability of small-scale models.

AI.tldr: SkillCDG: A graph-based framework for efficient compliance detection in long SKILL documents using constraint dependency graphs to balance accuracy and cost.
AI.motivation: Enterprise business scenarios increasingly use long SKILL documents, creating a challenge where large models are expensive for compliance detection while small models sacrifice accuracy.
AI.method: SkillCDG represents business policies as a two-layer constraint dependency graph: upper layer indexes SKILL descriptions for scenario routing, lower layer captures dependencies among atomic constraints within each SKILL. Uses two-level retrieval with dependency closure for compliance judgment and traceability.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines by up to 12.8 percentage points in F1 score while reducing token consumption by maximum 64.3%. Shows complexity-differentiated scaling pattern where constraint dependency graph metrics effectively quantify instance difficulty and model improvement potential.
AI.conclusion: SkillCDG effectively addresses the cost-accuracy trade-off in long SKILL compliance detection, provides insights into policy-graph complexity effects, and enables efficient enhancement of small models through adaptive training and distillation.

title: Neural Message Passing on Structural Interaction Graphs for Fully-Inductive Graph Neural Networks
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure in the main body. 12 pages, 5 figures in appendix. Submitted to AAAI 2027 (main track) and currently under review
summary: A central obstacle in building graph foundation models is the input heterogeneity in terms of feature space dimensionality, semantics, and structure. Such heterogeneity limits the capability of graph neural networks to generalize to new graphs with unseen feature spaces. We address the transferability challenge with SIGIL, a framework that maps any attributed graph to a unified representation space of fixed dimension. Given a graph, SIGIL lifts it to a structural interaction graph, where nodes are the input feature dimensions and weighted, typed edges encode feature alignment across multiple orders of the graph's connectivity. A relational message-passing network embeds each feature dimension into a shared space, transforming the original node features, of arbitrary dimensionality, into representations transferable to any downstream graph. By construction, SIGIL is equivariant to permutations of nodes, feature dimensions, and labels. Additionally, when the input features are one-hot indicators of discrete relations, SIGIL recovers and strictly generalizes existing foundation models for knowledge graph reasoning. A single SIGIL model, pretrained on one graph, delivers strong fully-inductive link prediction. Also, SIGIL can be used to implement existing knowledge graph foundation models. As such, SIGIL unifies several existing regimes in graph foundation model design under a single framework

AI.tldr: SIGIL is a framework that maps any attributed graph to a unified fixed-dimension representation space, enabling transfer learning across graphs with different feature spaces by transforming node features into transferable representations.
AI.motivation: The main motivation is to address the input heterogeneity problem in graph foundation models, where graphs have different feature space dimensionalities, semantics, and structures, which limits the generalization capability of graph neural networks to new graphs with unseen feature spaces.
AI.method: SIGIL lifts input graphs to structural interaction graphs where nodes represent input feature dimensions and weighted typed edges encode feature alignment across multiple orders of connectivity. A relational message-passing network then embeds each feature dimension into a shared space, transforming original node features of arbitrary dimensionality into transferable representations.
AI.result: SIGIL achieves strong fully-inductive link prediction with a single model pretrained on one graph, and can implement existing knowledge graph foundation models. It provides permutation equivariance to nodes, feature dimensions, and labels, and strictly generalizes existing foundation models for knowledge graph reasoning when input features are one-hot indicators.
AI.conclusion: SIGIL successfully addresses transferability challenges in graph foundation models by unifying different graph representation regimes under a single framework that can handle heterogeneous graph inputs while maintaining strong generalization capabilities.

title: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Reward Shaping in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Sparse, delayed, and weakly informative rewards remain central obstacles to efficient reinforcement learning. Reward shaping addresses these limitations by supplementing the task reward with an auxiliary signal that can accelerate learning while, in the classical setting, the original objective remains the evaluation criterion. Established theory guarantees safety for fixed shaping signals: potential-based reward shaping preserves optimal policies when the auxiliary term is the discounted difference of a time-invariant potential. In contemporary reinforcement learning systems, however, both the learner and the information available for guidance evolve during training: value estimates improve, novelty diminishes, feedback shifts, and predictive models are refined. Adaptive reward mechanisms occur across exploration, Bayesian inference, human-in-the-loop learning, automated reward design, and foundation-model-based approaches. This study introduces a unified analytical framework for comparing dynamic reward shaping and neighbouring adaptive reward mechanisms. The proposed framework distinguishes parametric revision from state-dependent variation, separates additive shaping from reward replacement and reward-adjacent guidance, and organises existing methods along temporal, informational, and theoretical dimensions. Using this framework, twelve method families are comparatively analysed. The framework further highlights the conditions under which optimality guarantees survive contemporary deep reinforcement learning pipelines, replay buffers, bootstrapped critics, and reward normalisation, while exposing the unresolved relationship between adaptation rate and learner stability.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a unified analytical framework for dynamic reward shaping and adaptive reward mechanisms in reinforcement learning, analyzing how evolving guidance signals interact with learning systems while maintaining theoretical guarantees.
AI.motivation: Sparse, delayed, and weakly informative rewards create efficiency problems in reinforcement learning. While classical reward shaping theory works for fixed signals, modern RL systems have evolving learners and available guidance information (value estimates, feedback, predictive models), but there's no unified framework to analyze these dynamic adaptive reward mechanisms.
AI.method: The paper proposes a unified analytical framework that distinguishes between parametric revision vs state-dependent variation, separates additive shaping from reward replacement and reward-adjacent guidance, and organizes methods along temporal, informational, and theoretical dimensions. The framework is used to comparatively analyze twelve method families.
AI.result: The framework reveals conditions under which optimality guarantees survive modern deep RL pipelines with replay buffers, bootstrapped critics, and reward normalization. It also exposes the unresolved relationship between adaptation rate and learner stability, providing a systematic way to compare dynamic reward shaping approaches across different applications.
AI.conclusion: A unified framework is needed to understand adaptive reward mechanisms in modern RL, as both learners and guidance evolve during training. The proposed framework organizes existing methods and reveals where theoretical guarantees hold, while highlighting key open problems like adaptation rate stability.

title: Robust Reputation-Driven Crowdsourced Federated Learning
comment: Accepted for presentation at the HotDiSec Workshop, co-located with ESORICS'26
summary: Crowdsourced Federated Learning (CrowdFL) extends traditional federated learning by enabling open and heterogeneous participation through a crowdsourcing paradigm. In this setting, reputation-driven incentive mechanisms are commonly employed to guide worker selection and enhance trustworthiness. While such approaches improve participant reliability, existing frameworks largely overlook the quantification of their robustness against stealthy adversaries, particularly those capable of evading standard detection mechanisms. To fill this gap, this paper proposes R2CFL, a robust reputation-driven CrowdFL framework. R2CFL introduces a robust reputation model coupled with a nearest neighbor mixing (R2-NNM) defense mechanism that links reputation evolution with the filtering of updates during aggregation. The proposed mechanism prevents stealthy attackers from gradually accumulating trust and influencing future tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that R2-NNM matches or surpasses state-of-the-art Byzantine-robust and backdoor defense mechanisms against adaptive attackers. Furthermore, when integrated with existing detect-and-filter defenses, the proposed reputation model faithfully captures the statistical robustness of the underlying defense by producing reputation scores that closely reflect its true positive and false positive characteristics.

AI.tldr: R2CFL is a robust reputation-driven crowdsourced federated learning framework that introduces a reputation model with nearest neighbor mixing defense to protect against stealthy adversaries that evade traditional detection mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Existing crowdsourced federated learning frameworks with reputation-driven incentives overlook robustness quantification against stealthy adversaries. Current approaches don't adequately address attackers who can evade standard detection mechanisms and gradually accumulate trust to influence future tasks.
AI.method: Proposes R2CFL framework with robust reputation model and nearest neighbor mixing (R2-NNM) defense mechanism. Links reputation evolution with filtering of updates during aggregation to prevent stealthy attackers from accumulating trust.
AI.result: R2-NNM matches or surpasses state-of-the-art Byzantine-robust and backdoor defense mechanisms against adaptive attackers. When integrated with existing detect-and-filter defenses, the reputation model faithfully captures statistical robustness by producing reputation scores that reflect true positive and false positive characteristics.
AI.conclusion: R2CFL provides an effective framework for robust crowdsourced federated learning that addresses the vulnerability of reputation systems to stealthy adversaries, offering both theoretical robustness and practical performance improvements.

title: When Is a Steerable Concept Representation Real? Measurement Confounds in a Cross-Family Audit of Neuroscience Parallels in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly reported to exhibit human-like neural and cognitive signatures, including concept cells, mental number lines, and cognitive maps. These claims often rely on linear probing and activation steering applied to a single model, yet both methods are highly sensitive to measurement choices. A reported parallel may therefore reflect the model, the measurement procedure, or both. We audit four representative neuroscience-inspired paradigms across 17 models from five families, spanning $0.6$B to $72$B parameters. Our main experiment examines the causal steerability of concept directions. With raw activation units and a fixed layer and coefficient, steerability appears to increase with model scale, resembling an emergent capability. However, this pattern is produced by an uncalibrated pipeline rather than by a claim established in the steering literature. The trend depends jointly on raw units, the readout metric, and the operating point; correcting any one of these removes it. With residual-norm-comparable interventions and held-out operating-point selection, concept steering remains significant at every scale, but shows no significant trend across the Qwen3 series, although the confidence interval does not rule out a moderate positive slope. The remaining results are mixed. A linear geographic world map is consistently decodable in every tested checkpoint up to $72$B. Number magnitude is strongly encoded, but whether individual neurons appear bell-shaped or monotonic depends on the selection criterion. Language-specific structure is localizable, but the direction of the cross-lingual asymmetry reverses under a different attribution method. These results suggest that the main constraint on AI neuroscience is not a lack of phenomena, but a lack of comparable measurements and adequate controls. We release the protocol, stimuli, and code.

AI.tldr: LLM neuroscience findings are highly sensitive to measurement choices; scale-dependent patterns may be artifacts of uncalibrated pipelines rather than emergent capabilities.
AI.motivation: To assess whether reported human-like neural signatures in LLMs reflect genuine model properties or measurement artifacts, by auditing neuroscience-inspired paradigms across diverse models.
AI.method: Audited four representative neuroscience-inspired paradigms across 17 models from five families (0.6B to 72B parameters). Examined causal steerability of concept directions with proper calibration controls. Investigated geographic world map decoding, number magnitude encoding, and language-specific structure localization with varying measurement approaches.
AI.result: Scale-dependent concept steerability trend disappears after calibration corrections. Geographic world map consistently decodable across all scales. Number magnitude strongly encoded but neuron shape depends on selection criterion. Language-specific structure localizable but cross-lingual asymmetry direction reverses with different attribution methods.
AI.conclusion: Main constraint on AI neuroscience is not lack of phenomena but lack of comparable measurements and adequate controls. Reported parallels may reflect measurement procedures rather than model properties.

title: When Can Fraud Operations Authorize Automation? A Decision-Support Framework for Fresh Audit Evidence and Review Workload
summary: Fraud operations must allocate events among automatic approval, analyst review, and automatic blocking even though the labels needed to evaluate these actions are selective and delayed. Predictive scores order cases, but they do not show whether the evidence is current and representative enough to delegate an action to the model. We develop freshness-constrained audit capacity (FCAC), a decision-support framework that treats automation as an authorization decision constrained by action risk, evidence freshness, and shared review capacity. It evaluates candidate action regions from mature randomized audits and a prespecified temporal allowance. Supported regions are automated; unsupported regions remain in review. The resulting decision record reports evidence age, audit demand, total review workload, value exposure, and compatible temporal change. We show that current action risk is unidentified without restricting unobserved label evolution. Under representative randomized audits, label-independent evidence windows, and a prespecified condition linking historical and current action risk, we derive simultaneous finite-sample control of unsafe authorization. Chronological evaluations with simulated audits on IEEE-CIS, ULB-Worldline, and Elliptic++ yield zero-drift automation rates of 84.4%, 67.4%, and 81.3%, with total review workloads of 24.1%, 46.0%, and 43.1%. The experiments reveal an audit-capacity trade-off: sparse auditing delays authorization, whereas intensive auditing eventually increases workload. A separately specified BAF stress test further indicates that fallback thresholds must reflect candidate-specific evidence rather than a common fraction of the risk limit. These findings identify audit freshness and analyst capacity as joint design considerations for fraud decision support.

AI.tldr: FCAC framework automates fraud decisions while controlling risk through freshness-constrained audit capacity, balancing automation rates with review workloads.
AI.motivation: Fraud systems need to allocate events between automatic approval, review, and blocking, but face challenges with selective/delayed labels and uncertain evidence freshness. Predictive scores alone don't indicate whether evidence is current/representative enough for automation.
AI.method: Developed freshness-constrained audit capacity (FCAC) framework that treats automation as authorization decision constrained by action risk, evidence freshness, and shared review capacity. Uses candidate action regions from randomized audits and temporal allowance. Evaluates evidence age, audit demand, workload, value exposure, and temporal change compatibility.
AI.result: Chronological evaluations on IEEE-CIS, ULB-Worldline, and Elliptic++ datasets show zero-drift automation rates of 84.4%, 67.4%, and 81.3% with total review workloads of 24.1%, 46.0%, and 43.1%. Reveals audit-capacity trade-off: sparse auditing delays authorization while intensive auditing increases workload.
AI.conclusion: Audit freshness and analyst capacity must be jointly designed for fraud decision support. Fallback thresholds should reflect candidate-specific evidence rather than common risk fractions. FCAC provides controlled automation with quantifiable risk bounds.

title: Agentic AI-driven Immersive Simulation: A Knowledge-Aware Virtual Training Platform forHigh Dose Rate (HDR) Brachytherapy
summary: The convergence of the Metaverse and Large Language Model (LLM)-based AI agent is catalyzing a shift toward autonomous, immersive, and personalized pedagogical frameworks in medical education. This paper presents a novel agentic AI-driven immersive simulation specifically designed for High Dose Rate (HDR) vaginal cylinder (VC) brachytherapy in cancer care. By integrating Virtual Reality (VR) and mobile computing, the system establishes a high-fidelity, risk-free environment that allows trainees to master complex procedural skills without the facility or safety constraints posed by physical anatomy or live radioactive sources. A core contribution of this work is the seamless integration of a knowledge-aware assistant leveraging Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to ground agent interactions in authoritative clinical guidelines. This architecture also enables an interactive agent to provide natural language interfaces and hands-free, real-time guidance during intricate medical maneuvers. We validate the proposed system through a prototype deployment comprising a Meta Quest 3 interface linked to a local GPU-accelerated AI backend, demonstrating a feasible architecture for HDR brachytherapy simulation. Experimental results indicate that the system maintains suitable end-to-end latency and high context precision, answer completeness, and relevance in the RAG-enhanced pedagogical support.

AI.tldr: A novel AI-driven VR simulation system combining LLM agents with RAG for HDR brachytherapy training, enabling risk-free procedural learning in immersive environments.
AI.motivation: Medical education faces challenges with complex procedures like HDR brachytherapy due to facility constraints, safety risks with radioactive sources, and the need for personalized, immersive training. Traditional methods lack interactive guidance and risk-free practice environments.
AI.method: Integrates VR with mobile computing and LLM-based AI agents using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to ground responses in clinical guidelines. Features a Meta Quest 3 interface connected to a local GPU-accelerated AI backend, providing natural language interfaces and hands-free real-time guidance.
AI.result: The system maintains suitable end-to-end latency and demonstrates high context precision, answer completeness, and relevance in RAG-enhanced pedagogical support. The prototype shows feasibility for HDR brachytherapy simulation.
AI.conclusion: This agentic AI-driven immersive simulation represents a significant advancement in medical education, enabling autonomous, risk-free training for complex procedures like HDR vaginal cylinder brachytherapy through the convergence of Metaverse technologies and LLM-based AI agents.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Agent-Specific Preference
comment: This article has been accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering. This is the author's version, which has not been fully edited, and the content may change prior to final publication. \c{opyright} 2026 IEEE. All rights reserved, including rights for text and data mining and training of artificial intelligence and similar technologies
summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is a powerful framework for solving complex collaborative tasks, but it relies heavily on well-defined global reward functions. Designing such rewards is challenging, especially in systems with heterogeneous agents, where a single scalar objective may fail to capture diverse behaviors. In this paper, we introduce Multi-AGent Preference-Integrated lEarning (MAGPIE), which addresses these challenges through agent-specific preference modeling. Each agent is evaluated by a dedicated expert through preference signals, eliminating the need for global evaluation. We theoretically prove that optimizing these decentralized preferences converges to a Nash equilibrium policy. To integrate local preferences into a coherent global objective, we construct agent-specific reward models from preference data and combine them via a monotonic aggregation mechanism. We further prove that optimizing this aggregate reward model is equivalent to training the Nash equilibrium policy. Extensive experiments on benchmark multi-agent tasks and a sequential production line task show that MAGPIE achieves performance comparable to reward-engineered baselines, demonstrating its potential to facilitate policy learning in scenarios where precise reward engineering is impractical.

AI.tldr: MAGPIE (Multi-AGent Preference-Integrated lEarning) is a MARL framework that uses agent-specific preference modeling instead of global rewards, converging to Nash equilibrium policies and matching reward-engineered baselines.
AI.motivation: Designing global reward functions in multi-agent reinforcement learning is challenging, especially with heterogeneous agents where a single scalar objective may fail to capture diverse behaviors and their contributions to the global task.
AI.method: MAGPIE uses agent-specific preference modeling where each agent is evaluated by a dedicated expert through preference signals (eliminating global evaluation). The method constructs agent-specific reward models from preference data and combines them via a monotonic aggregation mechanism to create a coherent global objective.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark multi-agent tasks and a sequential production line task show that MAGPIE achieves performance comparable to reward-engineered baselines, demonstrating effectiveness in scenarios where precise reward engineering is impractical.
AI.conclusion: MAGPIE provides a practical alternative to reward engineering in MARL by using decentralized preference modeling, theoretically converging to Nash equilibrium policies and achieving competitive performance with traditional reward-based approaches.

title: Matching Supervision to the Student's Learning Capacity: A Unified Framework for On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary:
On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves the reasoning abilities of LLMs by internalizing privileged context into model parameters through self-distillation.
  Two recent research lines promote vanilla OPSD by choosing which tokens to learn from and by controlling how much privileged information the teacher receives, respectively.
  However, we show that each line optimizes one variable while holding the other fixed, which leads to a suboptimal solution.
  We argue that the two variables are coupled through the student's learning capacity: the privileged information sets the per-token divergence the teacher prescribes, while token weighting selects which of these the student must absorb.
  We formalize the two lines of work into a unified optimization framework, which maximizes the aggregate teacher--student divergence, subject to a budget on the aggregate learning difficulty the student can absorb.
  Under this modelling, we propose Unified On-Policy Self-Distillation (USD), a lightweight online algorithm to solve the Lagrangian.
  USD reveals that a single dual variable governs both decisions: at one price for learning difficulty, it simultaneously sets the token-selection threshold and the direction of privileged-information adjustment, keeping supervision matched to the student's evolving capacity.
  Through extensive experiments, USD consistently demonstrates superior performance over OPSD and token- and PI-side baselines across various model scales on various reasoning benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/lauvlalala/USD.

AI.tldr: USD is a unified on-policy self-distillation framework that jointly optimizes token selection and privileged information adjustment through a single dual variable, outperforming existing methods across various reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) methods either optimize token selection or privileged information adjustment separately, leading to suboptimal solutions. The authors identify that these two variables are coupled through the student's learning capacity and need to be optimized jointly.
AI.method: The authors formalize existing approaches into a unified optimization framework that maximizes aggregate teacher-student divergence subject to a budget on aggregate learning difficulty. They propose USD (Unified On-Policy Self-Distillation), a lightweight online algorithm to solve the Lagrangian optimization problem using a single dual variable that governs both token selection and privileged information adjustment.
AI.result: USD consistently demonstrates superior performance over vanilla OPSD and token-side/PI-side baselines across various model scales on various reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The unified optimization framework successfully addresses the limitations of existing OPSD methods by jointly optimizing token selection and privileged information adjustment through a single dual variable, leading to improved reasoning abilities in LLMs while maintaining alignment with the student's evolving learning capacity.

title: Domain-Aware Pruning: Sparsity and Domain Generalization via Regularized Probabilistic Masking
summary: Domain generalization (DG) and neural network pruning are conventionally treated as distinct objectives, targeting out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness and model efficiency, respectively. In this work, we bridge this gap by introducing Domain-Aware Pruning (DAP), a framework that leverages network sparsity as a mechanism to implicitly enhance generalization to unseen domains. Diverging from standard binary mask optimization, DAP learns a continuous parameter retention probability $p \in [0, 1]$, framing network compression as a continuous probabilistic masking problem. By introducing a regularization objective that actively penalizes the retention of domain-sensitive weights during the mask training, DAP identifies a domain-invariant subnetwork. Empirical results across five DG benchmark datasets demonstrate that DAP achieves significant sparsity while consistently matching or exceeding the OOD performance of its dense counterparts. Crucially, DAP is an algorithm-agnostic framework that integrates seamlessly with existing DG pipelines without necessitating post-hoc fine-tuning. Beyond efficiency and generalization, we show that DAP natively provides increased robustness to adversarial perturbations and yields highly interpretable models, where the retained weights reliably encapsulate the most domain-invariant and task-critical representations.

AI.tldr: Domain-Aware Pruning (DAP) bridges domain generalization and network pruning by learning continuous probabilistic masks that retain domain-invariant weights, achieving both sparsity and improved out-of-distribution performance without post-hoc fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Domain generalization (DG) and neural network pruning have traditionally been separate objectives - DG focuses on out-of-distribution robustness while pruning focuses on model efficiency. The authors aim to bridge this gap by exploring whether network sparsity can implicitly enhance generalization to unseen domains.
AI.method: DAP introduces continuous parameter retention probabilities (p ∈ [0,1]) instead of binary masks, framing pruning as a continuous probabilistic masking problem. It includes a regularization objective that penalizes retention of domain-sensitive weights during mask training, identifying domain-invariant subnetworks. The framework is algorithm-agnostic and integrates with existing DG pipelines.
AI.result: Empirical results across five DG benchmark datasets show DAP achieves significant sparsity while matching or exceeding OOD performance of dense counterparts. The method also provides increased adversarial robustness and yields interpretable models where retained weights reliably encapsulate domain-invariant and task-critical representations.
AI.conclusion: DAP successfully bridges domain generalization and network pruning, demonstrating that network sparsity can serve as a mechanism to enhance OOD robustness while maintaining efficiency. The approach works without requiring post-hoc fine-tuning and provides additional benefits like adversarial robustness and model interpretability.

title: Large Multimodal Agents for Intelligent Transportation Systems: Architectures, Evidence, and Deployment Challenges
summary: Large multimodal agents (LMAs) are increasingly proposed for intelligent transportation systems (ITS), but existing studies often conflate multimodality, agency, empirical performance, and deployment readiness. This review provides an auditable evidence map of 42 primary study families released between January 2023 and 3 August 2026 within a corpus of 91 mapped sources. It distinguishes model-level, system-level, and hybrid multimodality and classifies each family by system architecture and action authority. Evidence is assessed independently through functional capability (C0-C3), validation setting (E0-E4), three evidence propositions (P1-P3), and eight methodological-concern domains (Q1-Q8). Transportation semantics (P1) are directly evaluated in 23 families and multidimensional integration (P3) in 24; 19 families directly evaluate both. Evidence reconciliation (P2) remains unresolved because no family demonstrates the complete provenance-challenge-handling-comparison-outcome chain. Fourteen families reach C3, but 13 remain at E2; only one reaches E3 and none reaches E4. Across ITS domains, LMAs are best supported for semantic interpretation, intent translation, evidence organisation, scenario authoring, explanation, and specialist-tool coordination. Numerical forecasting, optimisation, simulation fidelity, hard constraints, low-level control, safety fallback, and final authority should remain with independently verifiable specialist systems or accountable humans. The review therefore supports bounded orchestration rather than replacement and provides a matched comparative evaluation protocol and staged roadmap for accountable deployment. The living evidence repository is available at https://github.com/pangjunbiao/ITS-LMA-Review.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 42 large multimodal agent (LMA) study families in intelligent transportation systems (ITS), mapping evidence and capabilities to identify current limitations and propose bounded orchestration rather than full replacement of existing systems.
AI.motivation: Existing studies on LMAs in ITS often conflate multiple aspects like multimodality, agency, empirical performance, and deployment readiness. There's a need for a systematic evidence map to clarify what capabilities have actually been demonstrated and what gaps remain for accountable deployment.
AI.method: Conducted an auditable evidence map of 42 primary study families (from 91 sources, Jan 2023-Aug 2026), distinguishing model-level, system-level, and hybrid multimodality. Classified families by system architecture and action authority, assessed independently through functional capability levels (C0-C3), validation settings (E0-E4), three evidence propositions (P1-P3), and eight methodological-concern domains (Q1-Q8).
AI.result: Transportation semantics (P1) evaluated in 23 families, multidimensional integration (P3) in 24, with 19 evaluating both. Evidence reconciliation (P2) remains unresolved. 14 families reached C3 but only 13 at E2; just one reached E3, none reached E4. LMAs best supported for semantic interpretation, intent translation, evidence organisation, scenario authoring, explanation, and specialist-tool coordination. Numerical forecasting, optimization, simulation fidelity, hard constraints, low-level control, safety fallback, and final authority should remain with specialist systems or humans.
AI.conclusion: Supports bounded orchestration rather than replacement of existing ITS systems, providing a comparative evaluation protocol and staged roadmap for accountable deployment. LMAs should augment rather than replace specialized systems, with the living evidence repository available for ongoing updates.

title: Trajectory Design and Budgeted Querying for Digital Twin Calibration
comment: Accepted at the CDEL 2026 workshop at ECCV 2026 (non-archival)
summary: Digital-twin calibration requires interaction data that is expensive to collect. We study two acquisition decisions: which trajectories to generate, and when to spend a limited budget on privileged parameter measurements. Our framework couples an excitation-oriented reinforcement learning controller, a recurrent parameter estimator with predictive uncertainty, and a budgeted query policy. In Pendulum, a Random Forest diagnostic recovers gravity only weakly from task-oriented trajectories and does not recover mass or length, while a GRU trained on excitation-oriented trajectories reaches a mean absolute error of 0.0066 with no queries. We then withdraw continuous oracle access partway through an episode, so that the twin must run on the estimator's output for the remainder. The estimator-plus-policy pipeline achieves a terminal error of 0.0092 under a three-query budget, against 0.2031 for an uncalibrated twin. In partially observable Waterworld, five controllers produce different observed error profiles across three hidden parameters, and an estimator trained on a five-controller mixture reaches online normalized errors of roughly 4-5%. These exploratory case studies are not controlled ablations, but they motivate treating trajectory design and query allocation as explicit design variables in data-scarce calibration.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for budgeted digital-twin calibration that combines excitation-oriented trajectory generation with selective parameter queries to efficiently learn system parameters with limited data collection budget.
AI.motivation: Digital-twin calibration requires expensive data collection, particularly when system parameters need to be learned. The paper addresses the challenge of efficient data acquisition with limited budget for both trajectory generation and privileged parameter measurements.
AI.method: The proposed framework integrates three components: 1) an excitation-oriented RL controller for generating informative trajectories, 2) a recurrent parameter estimator (GRU-based) with predictive uncertainty, and 3) a budgeted query policy that decides when to spend budget on privileged parameter measurements.
AI.result: In Pendulum experiments: GRU trained on excitation-oriented trajectories achieved MAE of 0.0066 with no queries vs. Random Forest's weak recovery. With 3-query budget and partial oracle withdrawal, the pipeline achieved terminal error of 0.0092 vs. 0.2031 for uncalibrated twin. In Waterworld: estimator trained on mixed controller trajectories reached 4-5% normalized error across three hidden parameters.
AI.conclusion: The exploratory studies (not controlled ablations) demonstrate that treating trajectory design and query allocation as explicit design variables can significantly improve data-scarce calibration performance, motivating more systematic approaches to data acquisition in digital-twin systems.

title: Quantization Degradation in Large Language Models: A Signal-Noise Perspective
summary: Post-training quantization reduces the deployment cost of large language models, yet how severely a quantized model degrades is not determined by bit-width alone. We systematically study weight-only post-training quantization across bit-widths, quantization methods, model scales and downstream tasks on multiple model families. We observe that such degradation varies substantially across these factors: 4-bit quantization usually preserves performance, 2-bit often causes broad degradation, and at 3-bit, degradation becomes apparent but varies markedly with task type, quantization method and model scale. To explain this variability, we use the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to measure how strongly quantization perturbs full-precision representations. We trace degradation back to two linked processes: how quantization errors arise within individual modules, and how they accumulate across layers. First, a source SNR decomposition shows that newly introduced errors depend on three factors: the magnitude of the weight error, the strength of the task-specific signal, and how strongly the quantization error aligns with task-specific activations. Different factors affect these components in distinct ways. Second, a cross-layer propagation analysis shows that these errors can be attenuated, preserved, or amplified as they pass across layers, and that larger models benefit from weaker error amplification. Together, these results establish that quantization degradation is governed by how errors are introduced at the source and how they accumulate across the network.

AI.tldr: Weight-only post-training quantization degradation varies significantly with bit-width, quantization method, model scale, and downstream tasks, governed by how quantization errors are introduced at source and accumulate across layers.
AI.motivation: To understand why quantization degradation varies substantially even at the same bit-width, and to systematically study the factors affecting weight-only post-training quantization performance across different scenarios.
AI.method: Systematic study of weight-only post-training quantization across bit-widths, quantization methods, model scales, and downstream tasks on multiple model families, using signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to measure quantization perturbation effects.
AI.result: 4-bit quantization generally preserves performance, 2-bit causes broad degradation, and 3-bit degradation varies significantly. Quantization degradation depends on how errors are introduced (source SNR decomposition) and how they propagate across layers, with larger models benefiting from weaker error amplification.
AI.conclusion: Quantization degradation is governed by both how quantization errors arise within individual modules and how these errors accumulate across layers, with degradation patterns varying substantially based on bit-width, task type, quantization method, and model scale.

title: Exact Rank-Space KL Projection for Shared-Marginal Low-Rank Factors: Application to Doubly Stochastic Clustering
summary: We study exact Kullback--Leibler (KL) projection for low-rank factorizations whose two nonnegative factors have prescribed row marginals and a shared, learned column marginal. For arbitrary positive row marginals of equal total mass, the joint KL projection reduces exactly to a strictly convex gauge-fixed dual with only $r-1$ effective variables; its Hessian is a sum of categorical covariance terms and admits $O((n+m)r)$ matrix-free Hessian--vector products. The projection theorem is objective-independent. We then specialize this geometry to doubly stochastic (DS) graph learning through $W=U\operatorname{Diag}(g)^{-1}V^\top$, where row-simplex factors with a common column mass induce an exactly DS graph without materializing an $n\times n$ optimization variable. Combined with observed-edge sparse fitting, a stochastic anchor-reduced manifold regularizer, and Bregman backtracking, the resulting mirror-descent method preserves exact feasibility at every accepted step. Under a nonvanishing latent-mass condition, it satisfies sufficient decrease and an $O(1/N)$ mirror-stationarity bound, while strictly positive accumulation points are KKT stationary. Matched clustering experiments show competitive accuracy, feasibility residuals near numerical precision, and favorable anytime behavior without a dense learned graph.

AI.tldr: TLDR: An efficient exact KL projection method for low-rank factorizations with prescribed marginals, specialized to doubly stochastic graph learning with exact feasibility preservation and competitive performance in clustering tasks.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of learning doubly stochastic graphs without materializing large n×n optimization variables. It aims to develop efficient methods for graph learning with exact feasibility constraints while maintaining competitive performance in practical applications like clustering.
AI.method: The method uses exact KL projection for low-rank factorizations where two nonnegative factors have prescribed row marginals and a shared learned column marginal. It reduces the joint KL projection to a strictly convex gauge-fixed dual with only r-1 effective variables. For doubly stochastic graph learning, it employs W=U Diag(g)^{-1} V^⊤ factorization where row-simplex factors with common column mass induce exact DS graphs. Combines observed-edge sparse fitting, stochastic anchor-reduced manifold regularization, and Bregman backtracking mirror-descent method that preserves exact feasibility at every accepted step.
AI.result: The projection reduces exactly to a strictly convex gauge-fixed dual with only r-1 effective variables, with Hessian admitting O((n+m)r) matrix-free Hessian-vector products. Under nonvanishing latent-mass condition, the method satisfies sufficient decrease and O(1/N) mirror-stationarity bound, with strictly positive accumulation points being KKT stationary. Experimental results show competitive accuracy, feasibility residuals near numerical precision, and favorable anytime behavior without dense learned graph.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a theoretically grounded and computationally efficient framework for doubly stochastic graph learning that maintains exact feasibility constraints while achieving competitive performance in practical applications. The method avoids large optimization variables through low-rank factorizations and provides strong theoretical guarantees with practical benefits.

title: Janus: An Algorithm-Evaluator Co-Evolution Framework for LLM-Driven Discovery under Expensive Evaluation Budgets
summary: LLM-driven program discovery relies on rapid evaluator feedback, but many scientific and engineering tasks require high-fidelity simulations, hardware execution, or physical experiments, making each evaluation expensive. Cheap surrogate evaluators can reduce this cost, yet fixed surrogates are vulnerable to search-induced distribution shift and are difficult to fit reliably from sparse, search-biased labels. We introduce Janus, a framework that uses LLMs to co-evolve target programs and executable proxy evaluators. To address label scarcity, Janus leverages domain knowledge encoded in LLMs to generate task-specific evaluator programs and calibrates them using real outcomes. To mitigate distribution shift, Janus evolves evaluators alongside target programs, selects them using a promotion-aligned objective, and maintains region-conditioned portfolios with online credit updates. Because proxy predictions remain fallible, Janus uses them only to prioritize candidates and requires real validation before candidates can enter the target-program population or update the incumbent. Across five scientific and engineering design tasks, Janus achieves a larger area under the best-so-far improvement curve over the real-evaluation budget and higher final performance than a matched baseline that evolves only target programs. On average, Janus reaches 99/% of the baseline's final improvement with 59.1/% fewer real evaluations. Evolved proxy evaluators also rank promising candidates more accurately than their seed versions. Together, these results extend evaluator-guided LLM discovery from tasks with cheap, scalable feedback to scientific domains where trustworthy evaluation is scarce and expensive.

AI.tldr: LLMs co-evolve target programs and executable proxy evaluators to reduce expensive real evaluations in scientific discovery tasks.
AI.motivation: Scientific and engineering tasks require expensive high-fidelity simulations or physical experiments, making LLM-driven program discovery slow. Fixed surrogate evaluators suffer from distribution shift and sparse label problems.
AI.method: Janus framework co-evolves target programs and executable proxy evaluators using LLMs. It generates task-specific evaluators, calibrates them with real outcomes, maintains region-conditioned portfolios with online credit updates, and uses proxies only for candidate prioritization.
AI.result: Across five scientific/engineering tasks, Janus achieves larger area under improvement curve and higher final performance than baselines. Reaches 99% of baseline's improvement with 59.1% fewer real evaluations. Evolved proxies rank candidates more accurately than seed versions.
AI.conclusion: Janus extends evaluator-guided LLM discovery to scientific domains with expensive evaluations by co-evolving programs and proxies, demonstrating efficient use of scarce real evaluations while maintaining trustworthy validation.

title: Path-dependent Discrete Amortized Inference
summary: We consider the problem of sampling compositional and discrete objects from a given unnormalized posterior distribution. Notably, recent studies have shown that this problem can be efficiently solved by learning a deterministic Markov Decision Process (MDP) that progressively builds each object in proportion to the posterior. In this work, however, we demonstrate that the Markovian assumption can both hamper signal propagation during training and catastrophically reduce the learned sampler's expressivity due to state aliasing. To address these issues, we propose lifting the MDP with a learnable latent dynamical system that allows the underlying policy to depend on the entire past trajectory---and not only on the current state. In view of this, we refer to the resulting method as path-dependent discrete amortized inference. Importantly, we provably extend existing learning algorithms for discrete amortized samplers to our setting. In experiments on standard benchmark problems, we also show that our approach often leads to faster learning convergence and improved state space exploration relatively to prior techniques.

AI.tldr: Proposes path-dependent discrete amortized inference using learnable latent dynamics to overcome limitations of Markovian assumptions in sampling discrete objects, enabling faster learning and better exploration.
AI.motivation: The Markovian assumption in existing deterministic MDP-based samplers can hamper signal propagation during training and catastrophically reduce expressivity due to state aliasing. This limits effectiveness when sampling compositional discrete objects from unnormalized posterior distributions.
AI.method: Lifts the MDP framework with a learnable latent dynamical system that allows the policy to depend on the entire past trajectory rather than just the current state. Extends existing learning algorithms for discrete amortized samplers to this path-dependent setting.
AI.result: Experimental results on standard benchmark problems show that the proposed approach leads to faster learning convergence and improved state space exploration compared to prior techniques.
AI.conclusion: Path-dependent amortized inference with learnable latent dynamics effectively addresses limitations of Markovian assumptions, improving training efficiency and sampler expressivity for sampling discrete compositional objects.

title: A Minimal $κ$--$τ$ Logic for Risk-Sensitive Abduction
comment: 44 pages, 2 figures. Submitted to Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence (IOS Press/Sage)
summary: Standard approaches to abductive reasoning can retain multiple candidate explanations, but they do not generally combine explicit compositional cross-hypothesis interaction with an internal, rival-sensitive commitment judgment. This paper argues that in risk-sensitive domains -- where premature commitment carries asymmetric downside costs -- the timing of commitment is itself a governed decision that the inferential apparatus should formally represent. We present a minimal $κ$--$τ$ logical framework built on two primitives: epistemic interaction among hypotheses ($κ$) and a normative commitment threshold ($τ$). Hypotheses may coexist, reinforce or inhibit one another, and form emergent composite explanations, while collapse into committed conclusions is regulated by governance constraints rather than forced by inference alone. The logic is developed in two complementary modes sharing the interaction relation and the governance apparatus: a synthetic mode, in which atomic hypotheses are composed upward into emergent explanations, and an analytic mode, in which complex observed states of affairs are decomposed into causal clusters of latent factors, with commitment governed at both the cluster and the factor level. The framework provides formal machinery for domains in which the distinction between highly likely and commit-worthy is operationally consequential. The $κ$--$τ$ logic is positioned as the symbolic governance layer of a neurosymbolic architecture: its epistemic parameters are naturally estimated by neural components -- semantic embeddings and generative models, as demonstrated in existing computational realizations -- while its normative parameters remain under explicit human governance, yielding transparent and auditable abductive reasoning for deployment in high-stakes settings.

AI.tldr: A logical framework (κ-τ) for abductive reasoning that separates epistemic interaction among hypotheses from commitment decisions, enabling controlled reasoning in risk-sensitive domains.
AI.motivation: Standard abductive reasoning lacks formal mechanisms for cross-hypothesis interaction combined with controlled commitment timing, which is critical in risk-sensitive domains where premature commitment carries asymmetric downside costs.
AI.method: Developed a κ-τ logical framework with two primitives: κ for epistemic interaction among hypotheses (reinforcement/inhibition/composition), and τ for normative commitment threshold. Implemented in two complementary modes: synthetic (bottom-up composition) and analytic (top-down decomposition).
AI.result: Created a formal logic that distinguishes between likelihood and commitment-worthiness, allowing hypotheses to interact while commitment decisions are governed rather than forced, providing transparent abductive reasoning suitable for high-stakes settings.
AI.conclusion: The κ-τ logic serves as a symbolic governance layer in neurosymbolic architectures, where neural components estimate epistemic parameters while normative parameters remain under human governance, enabling auditable reasoning in high-stakes domains.

title: Multi-Relational Knowledge Graph Enhanced Embedding for Trajectory-User Linking
summary: Trajectory-User Linking (TUL) aims to identify the owner of an anonymous trajectory from a set of candidate users, providing a basis for user mobility analysis and personalized location-aware services. Existing methods often learn Point of Interest (POI), temporal, and semantic features independently, make limited use of structural knowledge shared across trajectories, and compress structural and sequential information before classification. To address these issues, we propose Multi-Relational Knowledge Graph Enhanced Embedding for Trajectory-User Linking (MakeTUL), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first attempt to introduce knowledge graph representation learning into TUL. MakeTUL organizes visit-time, POI-category, and transfer-speed information as typed relations in a multi-relational mobility knowledge graph, allowing heterogeneous mobility semantics to jointly constrain the learned embeddings. The resulting POI representations are further enriched with high-order co-occurrence patterns extracted from the trajectory collection, providing structural prior knowledge for sparse and overlapping trajectories. By integrating these prior-enhanced representations with temporal, category, and transfer information, the trajectory sequence learning module captures ordered mobility patterns, while a dual-branch classification layer preserves and combines global structural evidence and sequential evidence at the decision level.

AI.tldr: MakeTUL introduces knowledge graph representation learning to Trajectory-User Linking, creating a multi-relational mobility knowledge graph that captures heterogeneous mobility semantics and enriches POI representations with structural prior knowledge for better user identification.
AI.motivation: Existing TUL methods have limitations: they learn POI, temporal, and semantic features independently, make limited use of structural knowledge shared across trajectories, and compress structural/sequential information before classification. There's a need for better integration of heterogeneous mobility semantics and structural knowledge.
AI.method: MakeTUL organizes visit-time, POI-category, and transfer-speed information as typed relations in a multi-relational mobility knowledge graph. It enriches POI representations with high-order co-occurrence patterns from trajectory collections, integrates prior-enhanced representations with temporal, category, and transfer information, and uses a dual-branch classification layer combining global structural and sequential evidence.
AI.result: MakeTUL is presented as the first attempt to introduce knowledge graph representation learning into TUL, creating a framework that allows heterogeneous mobility semantics to jointly constrain learned embeddings and better capture ordered mobility patterns.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MakeTUL framework advances TUL by introducing knowledge graph representation learning, enabling better integration of structural and sequential evidence, and providing a more comprehensive approach to capturing mobility patterns for user identification.

title: Persuasive and Compliant Tendencies Predict Group Decision-Making in Humans and Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly involved in group decision-making with other LLMs and humans. Yet it remains unclear whether their influence is driven by persuasion-oriented expression or compliance-oriented accommodation. We introduce DecisionQE, a questionnaire-based framework for measuring each model's persuasive and compliant tendencies across multiple decision scenarios, and use the Werewolf game as an interactive testbed to study their effects on social influence and group outcomes under asymmetric information. Across experiments, stronger persuasive tendency does not significantly improve group outcomes, whereas compliant-oriented models show more stable advantages in cooperation. We further reveal a dual effect of compliance: it supports cooperation in honest roles but improves concealment in adversarial roles. These findings suggest that LLM group interactions reveal not only task outcomes, but also measurable patterns of intrinsic behavioral tendency. LLMs can therefore serve as a lens for sociological observation of language-mediated interaction, while highlighting the need to incorporate behavioral tendencies into safety evaluation of LLM systems.

AI.tldr: LLM group decision-making influence stems more from compliance-oriented accommodation than persuasion-oriented expression, with compliance showing dual effects that improve cooperation in honest roles but enhance concealment in adversarial roles.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly involved in group decision-making with other LLMs and humans, but it's unclear whether their influence comes from persuasive expression or compliant accommodation. There's a need to understand these behavioral tendencies and their effects on group outcomes, especially under asymmetric information conditions.
AI.method: Introduced DecisionQE, a questionnaire-based framework for measuring persuasive and compliant tendencies across decision scenarios. Used the Werewolf game as an interactive testbed to study social influence and group outcomes under asymmetric information.
AI.result: Stronger persuasive tendency didn't significantly improve group outcomes, while compliant-oriented models showed more stable advantages in cooperation. Compliance had dual effects: supporting cooperation in honest roles but improving concealment in adversarial roles.
AI.conclusion: LLM group interactions reveal measurable patterns of intrinsic behavioral tendency, not just task outcomes. LLMs can serve as a lens for sociological observation of language-mediated interaction, highlighting the need to incorporate behavioral tendencies into safety evaluation of LLM systems.

title: LegoLM: Structured Weight Sharing for Large Language Models
summary: We present \LegoLM{}, a structured weight-sharing compression framework for large language models grounded in a systematic study of why global weight sharing fails and how to fix it. We identify two distinct failure modes. Distributional mismatch: for vector blocks of dimension d <= 2, transformer layers with heterogeneous weight scales impose a scale-mismatch penalty that grows linearly with d and cannot be resolved by increasing K, producing perplexity in the millions.Outlier dominance: for scalar blocks, a fraction ~1/K of weights lies beyond the outermost Lloyd-Max decision threshold and cannot be represented by any centroid; their misrepresentation accumulates across layers, causing catastrophic quality loss. \LegoLM{} resolves both failure modes via three data-free adaptations: 1 scalar-block encoding to eliminate the $d$-linear mismatch component, 2 percentile-selective replacement that identifies and preserves outlier weights verbatim, and 3 boundary-layer protection for the first and last transformer blocks. Across GPT-2 small (124M) and Mistral-7B, \LegoLM{} achieves +0.03% PPL degradation at 4.41X compression on Mistral-7B - outperforming PTQ-8bit in both quality and compression ratio - and -0.02% at 2.67X. Downstream evaluation on LAMBADA and HellaSwag confirms that \LegoLM{} at K=64, p=99% preserves accuracy within noise at 5.12 X compression, exceeding PTQ-8bit's compression ratio while matching its accuracy. We further discover that outlier dominance grows with model scale: full replacement at K=128 degrades GPT-2 small by only +23% but catastrophically degrades Mistral-7B by +1,134,279%, while selective replacement at p=99% rescues both models to under +15%. A controlled ablation confirms that selective replacement is the dominant mechanism: adding it to per-layer K-means also yields near-lossless quality, matching \LegoLM{} within 0.02%.

AI.tldr: LegoLM is a structured weight-sharing compression framework for LLMs that fixes global weight sharing failures via three data-free adaptations, achieving near-lossless quality at high compression ratios.
AI.motivation: Global weight sharing compression fails for LLMs due to two key problems: distributional mismatch in vector blocks (caused by scale differences between transformer layers) and outlier dominance in scalar blocks (where extreme weight values cannot be properly represented), leading to catastrophic quality degradation.
AI.method: LegoLM introduces three data-free adaptations: 1) scalar-block encoding to eliminate linear mismatch, 2) percentile-selective replacement to preserve outlier weights verbatim, and 3) boundary-layer protection for the first and last transformer blocks.
AI.result: Achieves +0.03% PPL degradation at 4.41X compression on Mistral-7B (outperforming PTQ-8bit), -0.02% at 2.67X, and maintains accuracy within noise at 5.12X compression on downstream tasks. Selective replacement rescues catastrophic degradation from +1,134,279% to under +15%.
AI.conclusion: LegoLM successfully addresses fundamental limitations of global weight sharing for LLM compression through targeted adaptations, demonstrating that selective outlier preservation is crucial for maintaining model quality at high compression ratios while exceeding existing quantization methods.

title: Illusion of Alignment: Detecting Hidden Disagreement in Collaborative Dialogue
summary: Collaborative dialogue can end with apparent agreement while participants still differ on goals, assumptions, or execution plans, creating an \textbf{illusion of alignment (IoA)}. A real-user study across 18 meetings confirms that IoA arises routinely in human collaboration. Yet IoA poses a paradox: if participants were aware of such disagreements, they would already be explicit; if not, they cannot articulate them when asked, leaving IoA invisible to both participants and observers. In this work, we make IoA detectable by generating diagnostic multiple-choice questions whose divergent answers across participants provide direct behavioral evidence of hidden disagreement. We construct \textbf{IoA-Suite}, a dataset and evaluation protocol for detecting hidden disagreement, spanning five task types and six domains. We find that even the best model attains only 49.5\% F1, with the bottleneck traced to private context that the dialogue does not surface. We then train \textbf{IoA-Prober-8B} based on IoA-Suite, reaching 51.8\% F1 on IoA-Suite. Across the aforementioned 18 real meetings, it surfaces 2.89 hidden disagreements per meeting that participants confirm they had not voiced, transferring to live human dialogue. Further, in multi-agent collaboration, pairing IoA-Prober-8B with LLM agents improves downstream task performance on BigCodeBench-Hard and HiddenBench.

AI.tldr: A framework for detecting "illusion of alignment" in collaborative dialogues using diagnostic multiple-choice questions, with models trained to surface hidden disagreements that participants haven't voiced.
AI.motivation: Collaborative dialogues often end with apparent agreement while participants still have hidden disagreements about goals, assumptions, or execution plans (illusion of alignment), which is invisible to both participants and observers, creating a paradox in collaboration.
AI.method: Generate diagnostic multiple-choice questions whose divergent answers across participants provide behavioral evidence of hidden disagreement. Create IoA-Suite dataset and evaluation protocol spanning five task types and six domains. Train IoA-Prober-8B model based on this dataset.
AI.result: Best existing models attain only 49.5% F1, bottlenecked by private context not surfaced in dialogue. IoA-Prober-8B reaches 51.8% F1 on IoA-Suite. In real meetings, it surfaces 2.89 hidden disagreements per meeting that participants confirm were unvoiced. In multi-agent collaboration, pairing IoA-Prober-8B with LLM agents improves performance on BigCodeBench-Hard and HiddenBench.
AI.conclusion: Illusion of alignment is a common problem in collaboration that can now be detected using diagnostic questioning approaches, and trained models can surface hidden disagreements in both human dialogues and multi-agent systems, improving collaborative outcomes.

title: Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Reinforcement Learning
summary: This work explores the relationship between task similarity and catastrophic forgetting in reinforcement learning. Catastrophic forgetting, the phenomenon in machine learning of losing the ability to effectively perform on previous tasks, is a significant impediment to continual learning. This study aims to understand the extent to which the similarity of a new task influences the performance on the previous task. Interpretable reinforcement learning, specifically Q-learning, is employed on graph-based tasks with the objective of minimising the number of steps to reach a goal. The study investigates the performance on a previously learned task after training on a new task, for tasks of varying relative levels of complexity. The experimental results reveal a complex dynamic between task similarity and forgetting, with significant fluctuations in forgetting severity observed across degrees of task similarities and task complexities, and are suggestive of an interdependence of forgetting on the similarity and complexity of tasks. The observations were accompanied by observations of high degrees of variability in forgetting and an uneven distribution of task similarity measures. The relationship between these variables remains unclear and no evidence of statistical significance that task similarity has an effect, independently, on forgetting is found in continual reinforcement learning. Further research is warranted to gain a comprehensive understanding of the potential interplay between task similarity and catastrophic forgetting.

AI.tldr: This study investigates how task similarity affects catastrophic forgetting in continual reinforcement learning using Q-learning on graph tasks, finding no clear evidence that task similarity independently influences forgetting, with complex interactions between similarity, complexity, and forgetting observed.
AI.motivation: Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning is a major challenge. The paper aims to understand whether and how the similarity between new and previous tasks influences forgetting of previous task performance.
AI.method: The researchers used interpretable Q-learning reinforcement learning on graph-based tasks designed to minimize steps to a goal. They trained agents on initial tasks, then on new tasks of varying similarity and complexity, measuring performance degradation on original tasks.
AI.result: Results showed complex dynamics between task similarity and forgetting, with significant fluctuations in forgetting severity across different similarity and complexity levels. No statistically significant evidence was found that task similarity independently affects forgetting. High variability in forgetting and uneven distribution of similarity measures were observed.
AI.conclusion: The relationship between task similarity and catastrophic forgetting remains unclear in continual reinforcement learning. While complexity and similarity appear interdependent in their effects on forgetting, task similarity alone doesn't show independent statistical significance. More research is needed to understand these complex interactions.

title: Harmful Content Is Not Enough: Continuation Framing Moderates In-Context Emergent Misalignment
summary: In-context learning (ICL) can induce emergent misalignment (EM), where narrow misaligned examples alter answers to unrelated questions. Existing prompts, however, conflate harmful-text exposure with an invitation to continue assistant behavior. We hold harmful answers fixed while varying their delivery as demonstrations, evidence, assistant history, or tool output. Across ten independently sampled contexts, demonstration framing raises broad EM by $30$--$32$ percentage points on a susceptible Gemini model; the gap survives domain exclusion, semantic clustering, unseen questions, and four prompt templates. Format and length-matched controls show that harmful content is necessary but insufficient. A role times continuation factorial further reveals model-dependent provenance effects: Gemini follows both assistant and tool histories, whereas Grok largely resists tool-framed continuation. Several other frontier and open-weight models show no gap. Blinded human audits confirm every main contrast and show that the model judge underestimates active-condition failures. Thus continuation framing is a strong, model-dependent moderator of ICL-EM, not a universal consequence of harmful context.

AI.tldr: In-context learning can cause emergent misalignment, but the framing of harmful content (as demonstrations vs other formats) strongly influences this effect in certain models like Gemini, while other models are unaffected.
AI.motivation: Existing research conflates exposure to harmful text with invitations to continue assistant behavior, failing to isolate how different framings of harmful content affect emergent misalignment in ICL.
AI.method: Systematically varied harmful content delivery as demonstrations, evidence, assistant history, or tool output while keeping answers fixed. Tested across ten contexts, included format/length-matched controls, conducted role × continuation factorial design, and performed blinded human audits.
AI.result: Demonstration framing increased broad emergent misalignment by 30-32 percentage points on susceptible Gemini models; this gap persisted across domain exclusion, semantic clustering, unseen questions, and prompt templates. Gemini followed both assistant and tool histories, while Grok resisted tool-framed continuation. Several other models showed no gap.
AI.conclusion: Continuation framing is a strong, model-dependent moderator of ICL-induced emergent misalignment, not a universal consequence of harmful context. Harmful content is necessary but insufficient for misalignment.

title: Backward Compatibility in Tree-Based Explanations and Enhanced CART Algorithm
summary: In the operation of machine learning models, model update is a fundamental process that requires careful consideration of its impact on downstream decision-making. Particularly when operating explainable models, changes in explanations resulting from model updates can lead to detrimental outcomes for users. Decision trees, due to their high transparency, are frequently employed in risk-sensitive decision-making and serve as a prominent example in which the aforementioned issue is evident. However, existing research addressing similar issues has focused on explanations based on feature contributions, and thus cannot handle explanations derived from tree structures. Therefore, this paper proposes the Backward Compatibility Loss in Tree-based eXplanations (BCLTX), a loss metric that suppresses changes in decision tree explanations before and after updates. Furthermore, we design CART with Backward Compatibility in Tree-based eXplanations (CART-BCTX), a lightweight algorithm that improves upon CART for the decision tree update problem under BCLTX. Experimental results using 10 real-world datasets, including both classification and regression tasks, show that CART-BCTX achieves favorable trade-offs between prediction performances and BCLTX values, with comparable computation times to CART, regardless of the task.

AI.tldr: BCLTX is a new loss metric that suppresses changes in decision tree explanations during model updates, with CART-BCTX algorithm achieving good trade-offs between prediction performance and explanation consistency.
AI.motivation: Model updates in explainable ML can cause harmful changes in explanations for users, especially for transparent models like decision trees used in risk-sensitive domains. Existing research can't handle tree-based explanations specifically.
AI.method: Proposes Backward Compatibility Loss in Tree-based eXplanations (BCLTX) metric to measure explanation changes. Designs CART with Backward Compatibility in Tree-based eXplanations (CART-BCTX), a lightweight algorithm that improves CART for decision tree updates under BCLTX constraints.
AI.result: Experiments on 10 real-world datasets for classification and regression show CART-BCTX achieves favorable trade-offs between prediction performance and BCLTX values, with computation times comparable to standard CART.
AI.conclusion: The proposed BCLTX framework and CART-BCTX algorithm effectively address the problem of explanation instability in decision tree updates, maintaining backward compatibility while preserving predictive performance across different tasks.

title: Metanormative Theory for RL-Based Moral Agents
comment: The 14th International Workshop on Engineering Multi-Agent Systems (EMAS 2026) held May 25-26, 2026 Co-located with AAMAS 2026 Paphos, Cyprus
summary: The overlapping disciplines of machine ethics and value alignment are concerned with designing artificial agents that are aligned with human values and that act in ethically acceptable ways. A recent trend in these disciplines is the use of reinforcement learning (RL) to design such agents, sidelining the philosophical literature that used to play a more central role. Against this backdrop, this paper pursues two goals.
