AI.tldr: The paper introduces metaplectic Barron spaces and neural dictionaries for approximating solutions to time-dependent Schrödinger equations, outperforming classical PINNs.
AI.motivation: To develop quantitative approximation methods for shallow neural networks using metaplectic operators, extending beyond classical Fourier-based approaches to better handle problems like time-dependent Schrödinger equations.
AI.method: 1) Extend Barron spaces using metaplectic transforms (symplectic Fourier extensions), 2) Establish embeddings between metaplectic Barron spaces and Sobolev spaces, 3) Construct neural metaplectic dictionaries, 4) Prove Monte-Carlo approximation bounds, 5) Design deep neural architecture using dictionary atoms, 6) Test on time-dependent Schrödinger equations.
AI.result: Theoretical Monte-Carlo approximation bounds for metaplectic Barron functions using finite linear combinations of dictionary atoms, and empirical validation showing better performance than classical physics informed neural networks (PINNs) for approximating Schrödinger equation solutions.
AI.conclusion: Metaplectic Barron spaces and corresponding neural dictionaries provide effective tools for approximating complex PDE solutions, particularly time-dependent Schrödinger equations, with superior performance over traditional PINN architectures.

title: Estimating Uncertainty in Galaxy Morphology Classification
summary: Astronomers classify galaxy morphology to investigate cosmic evolution. While deep foundation models are increasingly utilized in Galaxy Morphology Classification (GMC), little work has been done on evaluating the uncertainty of GMC results. Uncertainty evaluation is important because astronomical data are inherently noisy due to instrumental and environmental limitations. Also, the continuous evolution of galaxies creates intrinsic morphological ambiguity. However, current foundation models operate as deterministic point estimators, failing to quantify the uncertainty. To overcome this limitation, we propose UEGMC, a post-hoc framework of Uncertainty Estimation for Galaxy Morphology Classification. It categorizes uncertainty in GMC into distinct types by model parameters, astronomical data, reference standards, or intrinsic physical ambiguities, thereby facilitating better classification. Our framework can directly predict uncertainties from representations extracted from the frozen backbones of foundation models, without computationally expensive sampling, therefore enabling fine-grained uncertainty evaluations. Our experimental results demonstrate that UEGMC provides competitive uncertainty quantification performance compared with previous methods.

AI.tldr: UEGMC: A post-hoc uncertainty estimation framework for galaxy morphology classification that quantifies uncertainty from multiple sources without expensive sampling.
AI.motivation: Astronomical data is inherently noisy due to instrumental/environmental limitations, and galaxies have intrinsic morphological ambiguity from continuous evolution. Current foundation models for Galaxy Morphology Classification (GMC) are deterministic and don't quantify uncertainty, which is important for reliable analysis.
AI.method: UEGMC is a post-hoc framework that categorizes uncertainty in GMC into distinct types (model parameters, astronomical data, reference standards, intrinsic physical ambiguities). It can directly predict uncertainties from representations extracted from frozen backbones of foundation models without computationally expensive sampling.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that UEGMC provides competitive uncertainty quantification performance compared with previous methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed UEGMC framework enables fine-grained uncertainty evaluation for galaxy morphology classification, addressing the limitations of current deterministic foundation models by providing reliable uncertainty quantification from multiple sources.

title: DistillCache: KL-Guided Adaptive KV-Cache Eviction for Memory-Efficient LLM Inference
summary: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across many tasks, but their Key-Value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length, creating a severe memory bottleneck for long-context inference. Existing heuristic eviction methods (e.g., H$_2$O and SnapKV) rely on static attention or positional signals that often fail to capture a token's future predictive influence. We propose DistillCache, a reinforcement learning framework that formulates KV-cache eviction as a sequential decision problem. DistillCache learns a lightweight policy network using rich internal model signals (attention statistics, value norms, entropy, and position) and trains it with REINFORCE via a per-step KL-divergence reward to preserve the full-cache output distribution. On a 7B-parameter instruction-tuned Transformer (Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3), DistillCache retains 94.2% of full-cache accuracy on LongBench at a 25% cache budget, outperforming both strong heuristic baselines (H$_2$O, SnapKV) by up to 2.7 absolute points and, under our re-implementations, concurrent RL-based methods (ForesightKV, RLKV) by up to 1.4 points on long-context tasks. On reasoning benchmarks, DistillCache is competitive with the best concurrent method and surpasses it under aggressive compression. It also delivers up to 2.1x full-cache throughput while maintaining competitive practical efficiency. These results highlight the effectiveness of learned, distribution-aware policies for memory-efficient long-context LLM inference.

AI.tldr: DistillCache uses RL to optimize KV-cache eviction for long-context LLM inference, achieving high accuracy with reduced memory while outperforming heuristic and RL baselines.
AI.motivation: Transformer LLMs suffer from KV-cache memory bottlenecks for long sequences, and existing heuristic eviction methods (like H2O and SnapKV) fail to capture tokens' future predictive influence using static signals.
AI.method: Formulates KV-cache eviction as a sequential decision problem and trains a lightweight policy network using RL (REINFORCE) with KL-divergence rewards to preserve full-cache output distribution. Uses rich internal model signals including attention statistics, value norms, entropy, and position.
AI.result: Retains 94.2% of full-cache accuracy on LongBench at 25% cache budget, outperforms heuristic baselines by up to 2.7 points and concurrent RL methods by up to 1.4 points. Achieves 2.1x throughput while maintaining competitive efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Learned, distribution-aware policies are highly effective for memory-efficient long-context LLM inference, offering superior performance over both heuristic and existing RL approaches.

title: Forgotten History or Test-of-Time? Retrospect and Prospect on RAG from an IR Perspective
summary:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is widely regarded as a novel paradigm born from the limitations of large language models (LLMs)--a mechanism to ground their outputs in external knowledge. This view, however, is incomplete when considered within a broader historical context. In this paper, we argue that the core ideas underlying RAG are not new: foundational concepts such as integrating retrieval and language generation, knowledge augmentation, answer verification, and iterative query (or prompt) refinement had already been studied and instantiated in information retrieval (IR) and question answering (QA) research dating back to the early 2000s, well before the emergence of LLMs.
  We make this case by systematically tracing the intellectual lineage of modern RAG and Agentic RAG back to their classical IR and QA antecedents, and examining why this continuity has gone under-recognized -- a consequence of community fragmentation, shifting terminology, and the recency bias endemic to fast-moving fields. Rather than treating LLMs as the origin point of retrieval-augmented intelligence, we propose viewing them as a new interface layer atop a decades-old QA architecture. This reframing is not merely historical: by situating RAG within the longer trajectory of IR research, we surface underutilized prior work -- on user modeling, answer validation, and query refinement -- that can directly inform next-generation RAG design, reducing unintentional rediscovery and fostering genuine cross-community integration.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that RAG concepts are not new but have roots in early 2000s IR/QA research, viewing LLMs as just a new interface layer on old QA architectures.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing view that RAG is a novel paradigm born from LLM limitations, and to situate RAG within the broader historical context of information retrieval and question answering research.
AI.method: Systematically tracing the intellectual lineage of modern RAG and Agentic RAG back to their classical IR and QA antecedents, examining why this continuity has gone unrecognized due to community fragmentation, terminology shifts, and recency bias.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that core RAG concepts (retrieval-generation integration, knowledge augmentation, answer verification, iterative query refinement) were studied in IR/QA research dating back to early 2000s, before LLMs emerged.
AI.conclusion: RAG should be viewed not as originating from LLMs, but as LLMs providing a new interface layer atop decades-old QA architectures; this reframing allows surfacing underutilized prior work to inform next-gen RAG design and foster cross-community integration.

title: Federated Attention Autoencoders with a Stochastic Aggregation Scheme for Anomaly Detection
comment: Accepted and presented at the 3rd International Conference on Federated Learning Technologies and Applications (FLTA 2025)
summary: Outlier detection in decentralized data environments is a challenging task for many machine learning implementations, particularly in settings where data cannot be shared. Recently, there have been advances in federated outlier detection, some of which are based on the use of autoencoder networks. The introduction of attention mechanisms to autoencoders boosts their efficiency. However, the application of attention-based models in federated learning remains underdeveloped due to the absence of proper aggregation functions for these types of networks. In our work, we propose two novel aggregation functions tailored for attention-based autoencoders, which better preserve the learned information stored within the memory modules of these networks. We evaluated our approach on the KDDCUP10 dataset, and we showed that the proposed methods achieve up to 2.9\% and 5.1\% better results for F1 score and AUC ROC respectively when compared to traditional autoencoders.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two novel aggregation functions for attention-based autoencoders in federated learning, improving outlier detection performance by better preserving learned information in memory modules.
AI.motivation: Outlier detection in decentralized data environments where data cannot be shared is challenging. While attention mechanisms boost autoencoder efficiency for outlier detection, their application in federated learning remains underdeveloped due to the absence of proper aggregation functions for attention-based networks.
AI.method: The authors propose two novel aggregation functions specifically designed for attention-based autoencoders. These functions are tailored to better preserve the learned information stored within the memory modules of these networks in a federated learning setting.
AI.result: The proposed methods were evaluated on the KDDCUP10 dataset and achieved up to 2.9% better F1 score and 5.1% better AUC ROC compared to traditional autoencoders in federated outlier detection.
AI.conclusion: The novel aggregation functions for attention-based autoencoders successfully address the gap in federated learning for these networks, enabling better outlier detection performance in decentralized data environments while preserving data privacy.

title: TRACE-Memory: Public-Conditioned Retrieval and Utility-Aware Evidence Admission for Personalized Generation
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, and 6 tables. Submitted to the 41st AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI 2027)
summary: Personalized generation systems retrieve user history by request--memory relevance and inject it into the model context. Yet relevant history may concern the wrong preference aspect, duplicate public information, or provide insufficient support. We argue that personal memory should be used only when it adds utility beyond a public-only response. We propose TRACE-Memory, a two-stage framework for selective personalization. Stage 1 queries for user-specific information missing from the request and public context, then retrieves a coverage-oriented candidate pool. Stage 2 admits a compact subset of source-traceable evidence units, or the empty set, according to response-level incremental utility. We progressively train the query-generation and evidence-admission policies through structured SFT initialization, reduced-space stage-wise GRPO warm-up, and nested multi-sample Joint GRPO. Across 4,500 Controlled and Natural tasks from Goodreads, Amazon Reviews, and Reddit, TRACE-Memory consistently outperforms random and lexical memory use, improves over semantic retrieval, remains competitive with frontier-LLM memory pipelines as local generator capacity increases, and conditions evidence admission on public-context sufficiency, supporting selective rather than default personalization.

AI.tldr: TRACE-Memory is a two-stage selective personalization framework that retrieves user history only when it adds incremental utility beyond public information, improving over traditional memory-based generation.
AI.motivation: Current personalized generation systems automatically inject relevant user history, but this history may concern the wrong preference aspect, duplicate public information, or provide insufficient support. Personal memory should be used only when it adds utility beyond a public-only response.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: Stage 1 queries for user-specific information missing from request and public context, retrieving coverage-oriented candidates. Stage 2 admits a compact subset of source-traceable evidence units (or empty set) based on response-level incremental utility. Progressive training via structured SFT initialization, stage-wise GRPO warm-up, and nested multi-sample Joint GRPO.
AI.result: Outperforms random and lexical memory use, improves over semantic retrieval, remains competitive with frontier-LLM memory pipelines as local generator capacity increases. Conditions evidence admission on public-context sufficiency, supporting selective rather than default personalization across 4,500 tasks from Goodreads, Amazon Reviews, and Reddit.
AI.conclusion: TRACE-Memory successfully implements selective personalization by retrieving user history only when it provides incremental utility beyond public information, demonstrating superior performance over traditional memory-based approaches while maintaining traceability and efficiency.

title: A Domain-Structured Ensemble Framework for Perioperative Outcome Prediction Using Electronic Health Record Data
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Healthcare Informatics (ICHI 2026)
summary: Perioperative risk prediction models are often limited by narrow surgical populations, incomplete intraoperative data, poor calibration, and limited interpretability. We present a domain-structured ensemble framework for perioperative outcome prediction using routinely collected electronic health record (EHR) data. Predictors are organized into patient-related, surgery-related, and anesthetics-related domains. Domain-specific gradient boosting models generate independent risk estimates that are integrated through a logistic regression meta-learner. We demonstrate the framework using postoperative delirium (POD) in a case-control sample of 5,386 surgical encounters (2,693 cases, 2,693 controls) from a statewide health information exchange. POD required both delirium-related ICD codes and a positive Confusion Assessment Method screening within seven postoperative days; patients with preexisting dementia were excluded. The stacked meta-learner achieved AUROC 0.899 (95% CI: 0.891-0.906), precision-recall AUC 0.881, and Brier score 0.126, compared with AUROC 0.849 for the best single-stage model. Domain ablation showed improved discrimination and calibration over a surgery-only model (AUROC 0.879, Brier 0.140). Temporal validation on held-out post-2017 data yielded AUROC 0.915. Calibration was excellent, with intercept -0.006 (95% CI: -0.083 to 0.070) and slope 1.035 (95% CI: 0.982 to 1.088). Decision curve analysis, corrected for case-control sampling, showed positive net benefit across clinically plausible thresholds. The modular framework supports alternative outcomes, extension of predictor domains, and dynamic risk updating, providing a scalable foundation for interpretable, calibration-aware perioperative clinical decision support.

AI.tldr: Domain-structured ensemble framework predicts postoperative delirium using EHR data organized into patient, surgery, and anesthesia domains, achieving AUROC 0.899 with excellent calibration.
AI.motivation: Existing perioperative risk prediction models have limitations including narrow surgical populations, incomplete intraoperative data, poor calibration, and limited interpretability.
AI.method: Domain-structured ensemble framework with predictors organized into patient-related, surgery-related, and anesthetics-related domains. Domain-specific gradient boosting models generate independent risk estimates integrated through a logistic regression meta-learner.
AI.result: Stacked meta-learner achieved AUROC 0.899 (95% CI: 0.891-0.906), precision-recall AUC 0.881, and Brier score 0.126, outperforming the best single-stage model (AUROC 0.849). Excellent calibration with intercept -0.006 and slope 1.035. Temporal validation on held-out data yielded AUROC 0.915.
AI.conclusion: The modular framework provides scalable foundation for interpretable, calibration-aware perioperative clinical decision support, supporting alternative outcomes, domain extension, and dynamic risk updating.

title: What Keeps Agent Skills from Being Reusable? Evidence from 138K SKILL.md Files
summary: Under the current standard, Agent Skills are SKILL.md files that combine instructions with supporting resources, enabling Large Language Model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures beyond a single conversation. Yet many public skills appear to originate from a single task, repository, or conversation, even when they are shared as reusable components. We analyze this gap across 138,133 public SKILL.md files from 20,556 repositories using a two-tier defect taxonomy grounded in the official specification and best-practice guidance. We find that 91.8% of skills contain at least one detected defect, with stable estimates across lenient and strict thresholds (88.8-94.6%). The dominant failures are ordinary packaging problems rather than exotic attacks: weak routing metadata, bloated or non-actionable bodies, and poor resource organization. A deterministic routing stress test over 20,000 skills shows the functional impact: skills with valid routing metadata are retrieved more reliably from startup descriptions than skills with routing defects. Defect rates vary by platform and provenance: specification-aware skills contain fewer defects, while AI-marked skills show more safety and portability problems. Lightweight enforcement and repair experiments support a quality-assured generation workflow combining spec-aware prompting, lightweight linting, automated repair, and safety gating.

AI.tldr: 91.8% of public Agent Skills (SKILL.md files) contain defects, primarily due to weak routing metadata, bloated content, and poor resource organization, with functional impact on skill retrieval reliability.
AI.motivation: While Agent Skills are designed as reusable components for LLM agents, there's a gap between their intended reusability and actual practice - many skills appear derived from single tasks/conversations despite being shared as reusable assets, raising quality concerns.
AI.method: Analyzed 138,133 public SKILL.md files from 20,556 repositories using a two-tier defect taxonomy based on official specifications and best practices. Conducted deterministic routing stress test over 20,000 skills and performed enforcement/repair experiments.
AI.result: 91.8% of skills contain at least one defect (stable across lenient/strict thresholds: 88.8-94.6%). Main defects are weak routing metadata, bloated/non-actionable bodies, and poor resource organization. Skills with valid routing metadata are retrieved more reliably. Defect rates vary by platform and provenance - specification-aware skills have fewer defects, AI-marked skills show more safety/portability issues.
AI.conclusion: Agent Skills suffer from widespread quality issues affecting their functional reliability. The paper proposes a quality-assured generation workflow combining spec-aware prompting, lightweight linting, automated repair, and safety gating to improve skill quality and reliability.

title: Idea Search: Guiding Tree Search with Ideas to Explore Diverse Scientific Methods
summary: Tree Search-based test-time scaling of LLMs is a powerful tool for automated scientific coding. However, pure Tree Search sometimes struggles with systematic exploration, becoming trapped in local optima, or unproductive loops, especially in the vast search space of scientific methods. To address this limitation, we propose Idea Search, a framework that systematically integrates a dynamic "Idea Bank" into Tree Search. Idea Search involves three steps: (1) decomposing existing methods into atomic ideas, (2) sampling from this bank of ideas to guide branches of code mutations, and (3) dynamically updating the bank with new ideas discovered through execution. On single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) batch integration, Idea Search reliably breaks the plateau of a strong pure Tree Search baseline, improving the mean score from 0.678 to 0.697 and reaching a best score of 0.728. We then characterize which design choices drive these gains: bank augmentation helps bandit sampling but not random sampling, "Exploratory" prompting that prioritizes new ideas surfaces the rare best-performing solutions, while increasing sampling-level exploration is counterproductive.

AI.tldr: Idea Search enhances Tree Search for scientific coding by integrating a dynamic "Idea Bank" that decomposes methods into atomic ideas, samples from them to guide code mutations, and updates with new discoveries.
AI.motivation: Pure Tree Search for test-time scaling of LLMs in scientific coding struggles with systematic exploration, gets trapped in local optima or unproductive loops, especially in the vast search space of scientific methods.
AI.method: Idea Search framework integrates a dynamic "Idea Bank" into Tree Search with three steps: (1) decomposing existing methods into atomic ideas, (2) sampling from the idea bank to guide branches of code mutations, (3) dynamically updating the bank with new ideas discovered through execution.
AI.result: On scRNA-seq batch integration, Idea Search reliably breaks the plateau of a strong pure Tree Search baseline, improving mean score from 0.678 to 0.697 and reaching best score of 0.728. Analysis shows bank augmentation helps bandit sampling but not random sampling, "Exploratory" prompting surfaces best solutions, while increased sampling-level exploration is counterproductive.
AI.conclusion: Idea Search successfully addresses limitations of pure Tree Search for scientific coding by systematically integrating a dynamic idea bank, demonstrating significant performance improvements and providing insights into effective exploration strategies.

title: Hierarchical Self-Improvement: A Framework for Task-Specific Evolvable Agent Harnesses
summary: Modern LLM agents are often improved by modifying prompts, tools, or workflows manually, while the executable scaffold surrounding the model---the \emph{harness}---is typically treated as a fixed artifact after deployment. This work studies an alternative where the harness is \emph{task-specific and continuously evolvable}: each task family maintains its own harness, which is hot-swapped across iterations through a fixed task-injection seam and rewritten using environment feedback. We introduce \textbf{Hierarchical Self-Improvement (HSI)}, a framework in which a single frozen LLM $M$ operates across three hierarchical scopes: a task harness $H$ that executes tasks, an evolver that rewrites $H$, and a meta-evolver that rewrites the evolver's strategy code under a frozen outer anchor. A thinking-on/off design isolates the contribution of harness evolution by disabling reasoning during task execution while enabling it during self-modification. HSI is bounded by two factors: a \emph{feedback-fidelity bound}, since evolution requires informative reward signals to guide selection, and a \emph{backbone capability bound}, since harness redesign cannot overcome limitations of the frozen model. On BALROG with DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Preview as the frozen backbone, HSI achieves consistent gains over the initial harness on moderate-difficulty tasks ($+39.3$ on BabyAI, $+33.0$ on Crafter, $+25.0$ on TextWorld, and $+15.0$ on MiniHack, all in raw \% Progress), while obtaining strong held-out generalization on BabaIsAI sub-suites ($0.98$ best-test on BreakStop and $1.00$ on GoTo from a $20\%$ unseen split). On tasks beyond the backbone's capability (NLE), harness evolution provides no improvement. These results demonstrate task-specific harness evolution as a viable axis for improving frozen LLM agents under clear empirical limits. Code is available at https://github.com/TailinZhou/hsi.

AI.tldr: Hierarchical Self-Improvement (HSI) enables frozen LLMs to evolve task-specific harnesses through hierarchical self-modification, achieving significant performance gains on moderate-difficulty tasks while revealing clear empirical limits.
AI.motivation: Traditional LLM agent deployment treats the execution harness as fixed, but this work explores making harnesses task-specific and continuously evolvable to improve agent performance without model fine-tuning.
AI.method: HSI uses a frozen LLM operating across three hierarchical scopes: task harness for execution, evolver for rewriting the harness, and meta-evolver for rewriting evolution strategy. A thinking-on/off design isolates harness evolution contributions.
AI.result: HSI achieved consistent gains over initial harness on moderate-difficulty tasks (+39.3% on BabyAI, +33.0% on Crafter, +25.0% on TextWorld, +15.0% on MiniHack) with strong generalization on held-out tasks, but no improvement on tasks beyond backbone capability.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific harness evolution is a viable approach for improving frozen LLM agents within clear empirical bounds defined by feedback fidelity and backbone capability limits.

title: Gradient Under Microscope: Benchmarking Resource Utilization of Memory-Efficient Gradient Computation Methods
summary: AI training's rising resource intensity is straining electricity supplies and carbon budgets, motivating systematic study of memory-efficient training on constrained hardware. We benchmark five gradient optimizers (SGD, Adam, Adagrad, Adadelta, and Conjugate Gradient Descent) under three memory strategies (standard training, gradient checkpointing, and gradient accumulation) across four transformer architectures (ViT, ModernBERT, Llama 3.1 1B, and NanoVLM), measuring training loss, GPU utilization, training time, and memory usage. Gradient accumulation emerges as the most reliable strategy, cutting training loss by roughly an order of magnitude on the vision-language model and about four-fold on the language model without additional GPU memory. Contrary to common practice, Adam is not universally superior: Adadelta and SGD outperform it on the encoder and autoregressive architectures. Gradient checkpointing's effect is strongly architecture-dependent, improving vision transformer loss while severely degrading the encoder model, and it increases training time by up to 60% on memory-bound models. GPU utilization is governed primarily by architecture, ranging from 8-15% for the memory-bound language model to 96-99% for compute-bound vision models. These findings provide practical guidelines for optimizer and gradient-strategy selection in resource-efficient model training and deployment.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking five gradient optimizers and three memory strategies on four transformer architectures reveals gradient accumulation as the most reliable memory-efficient strategy, and challenges the assumption that Adam is universally superior for transformer training.
AI.motivation: AI training's increasing resource demands are straining electricity supplies and carbon budgets, necessitating systematic study of memory-efficient training on constrained hardware to enable sustainable AI development.
AI.method: Comprehensive benchmarking of five gradient optimizers (SGD, Adam, Adagrad, Adadelta, and Conjugate Gradient Descent) with three memory strategies (standard training, gradient checkpointing, and gradient accumulation) across four transformer architectures (ViT, ModernBERT, Llama 3.1 1B, and NanoVLM), measuring training loss, GPU utilization, training time, and memory usage.
AI.result: Gradient accumulation significantly reduces training loss (order of magnitude for vision-language model, 4x for language model) without extra GPU memory; Adam not universally superior (Adadelta/SGD better for encoder/autoregressive architectures); gradient checkpointing effects architecture-dependent; GPU utilization architecture-governed (8-15% for memory-bound LM vs 96-99% for compute-bound vision models).
AI.conclusion: Provides practical guidelines for optimizer and gradient-strategy selection in resource-efficient model training and deployment, challenging common assumptions about optimizer superiority and revealing architecture-dependent performance patterns for memory-efficient strategies.

title: LLM within MCP Matters: Measuring Inefficient Resource Utilization Driven by LLMs
comment: 4 pages, 1 table. Accepted at the AgentSearch Workshop at SIGIR 2026, Melbourne, Australia (non-archival). Code and data: https://github.com/rabqatab/llm-in-mcp-matters
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how servers expose data and tools to Large Language Models (LLMs). A common server design embeds frequently used reference data, such as identifier lookup tables, directly in the server instructions: the system-prompt text a server hands to the host application. When a query concerns an entry of the embedded table, the model can act on it immediately instead of re-discovering the same information through a search tool. We test whether client LLMs actually consume such instruction-embedded data, reporting a 54,000-trial study across 24 LLMs (9 Claude, 6 Gemini, 9 GPT) on a production legal-information MCP server. A diagnostic condition that removes the competing search tool shows that failures are dominated by behavioral preference rather than missing capability. With search unavailable, 23 of 24 models read the embedded data reliably (hit ratio at least 98%); with a search tool merely present, 9 models drop below 15%. A 2^3 factorial analysis of three instruction-level interventions reveals strong interaction effects: combining all three restores at least 86% for 20 of 24 models, but individual interventions can backfire for specific model families. Per-server prompt engineering is therefore a workaround rather than a fix; we argue that MCP host applications should provide an explicit mechanism that places server instructions ahead of tool selection in the client LLM's deliberation.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether LLMs actually use instruction-embedded data in MCP servers, finding that LLMs often prefer using search tools even when relevant data is directly available in instructions, and that prompt engineering is insufficient to fix this behavior.
AI.motivation: To understand whether Large Language Models actually consume data that's embedded in server instructions within the Model Context Protocol framework, particularly when this data could prevent redundant searches for frequently used reference information like lookup tables.
AI.method: Conducted a 54,000-trial study across 24 LLMs (9 Claude, 6 Gemini, 9 GPT) on a production legal-information MCP server. Used diagnostic conditions including removing competing search tools and a 2^3 factorial analysis of three instruction-level interventions to isolate behavioral factors.
AI.result: When search was unavailable, 23 of 24 models reliably read embedded data (hit ratio ≥98%). However, with a search tool merely present, 9 models dropped below 15% usage of embedded data. The 2^3 factorial analysis showed strong interaction effects - combining all three interventions restored at least 86% performance for 20 of 24 models, but individual interventions could backfire for specific model families.
AI.conclusion: Failures to use instruction-embedded data are dominated by behavioral preference rather than missing capability. Per-server prompt engineering is a workaround, not a fix. MCP host applications should provide an explicit mechanism to place server instructions ahead of tool selection in LLM deliberation.

title: Math-Vision Diagrams: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Mathematical Diagram Generation Capabilities
summary: The generation of mathematically precise diagrams from tex- tual prompts has emerged as a critical yet underexplored capability of Large Language Models (LLMs). This has been of interest to researchers in the areas of curriculum preparation, automated ranking of problem sets, and scientific publishing. For LLMs to achieve this, it requires per- fect coordination between Spatial Reasoning, Mathematical Reasoning, and Rendering systems. While existing benchmarks such as MathVision, MathVista are built for Math Reasoning or DiagramGenBenchmark, Mer- maidSeqBench on general purpose diagram generation, no prior work provides a standardized set of prompt, image pairs that can be used to evaluate the LLMs specifically on math diagram generation. This includes fields that span both both text-to-code and text-to-image paradigms. We introduce Math-Vision Diagrams, the first benchmark specifically designed to evaluate LLMs on mathematical diagram generation, and the first to assess text-to-code and text-to-image generation paradigms together in a single unified setting, agnostic of the underlying coding lan- guage or model type. Building on the Math-Vision benchmark, we select a subset of 2920 images out of 3040 from high-quality competition problems with essential visual context. A novel pipeline combining an ensemble of LLMs with Subject Matter Expert (SME) curation is presented, together with a suite of evaluation metrics. Testing several leading models against this benchmark, we demonstrate that LLMs struggle with math diagram generation. All code, data, curation pipeline, and evaluation scripts will be fully open-sourced.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Math-Vision Diagrams, the first benchmark for evaluating LLMs on mathematical diagram generation, covering both text-to-code and text-to-image paradigms.
AI.motivation: There's a need for mathematically precise diagram generation from textual prompts for applications in curriculum preparation, problem set ranking, and scientific publishing. Existing benchmarks focus on math reasoning or general diagram generation, but none specifically evaluate mathematical diagram generation across both text-to-code and text-to-image paradigms.
AI.method: The authors built a benchmark of 2,920 images from high-quality competition problems with essential visual context. They developed a novel pipeline combining an ensemble of LLMs with Subject Matter Expert (SME) curation, along with a suite of evaluation metrics. The benchmark is designed to be agnostic of underlying coding language or model type.
AI.result: Testing several leading models against this benchmark revealed that LLMs struggle with math diagram generation. The benchmark successfully evaluates both text-to-code and text-to-image generation paradigms in a unified setting.
AI.conclusion: Math-Vision Diagrams fills a critical gap in evaluating LLMs' mathematical diagram generation capabilities. The findings demonstrate current limitations in this area, and the authors will open-source all code, data, curation pipeline, and evaluation scripts to support further research.

title: Aero Realtime: Fully Aligned Input-Output Streams for Low-Latency Streaming Multimodal Generation
summary: Existing streaming multimodal models process observations incrementally but still follow a turn-based prefill-then-decode pattern, making them non-duplex: new observations cannot naturally enter an active generation stream. Proactive alternatives use micro-turn polling or external response gates, which fragment continuous interaction, decouple response timing from language generation, and complicate KV-cache-friendly serving. We introduce Aero Realtime, a 4B streaming multimodal model with a duplex architecture for realtime generation. Aero Realtime aligns video, audio, and textual output on a shared temporal grid, where each approximately 80-ms audio slot predicts either a lexical token or a silence token. This allows input and output to advance together, enabling one autoregressive objective to learn both when to respond and what to generate. During inference, Aero Realtime appends only the newest multimodal slot, carries forward the previous output state, and reuses the KV cache for efficient incremental execution. We further provide a complete training and serving recipe, including realtime QA construction, slot-aligned supervision, hardware-aware distributed training, and resumable inference. On four NVIDIA A6000 workstation GPUs, Aero Realtime maintains 84-ms median and 173-ms P95 processing lag over 20 minutes of a continuously streamed video, remaining within 200~ms of the source timeline. These results demonstrate the feasibility of fully aligned input-output modeling for duplex, proactive, and hardware-aligned multimodal interaction.

AI.tldr: A 4B streaming multimodal model with duplex architecture that aligns video, audio, and text on a shared temporal grid for realtime generation, enabling simultaneous input processing and output generation.
AI.motivation: Existing streaming multimodal models follow turn-based patterns that prevent new observations from entering active generation streams, requiring polling or response gates that fragment continuous interaction and complicate serving.
AI.method: Proposes Aero Realtime with duplex architecture using a shared temporal grid (80ms audio slots) where each slot predicts either a lexical token or silence token. This allows joint learning of response timing and content generation with efficient KV-cache reuse during inference.
AI.result: Achieves 84ms median and 173ms P95 processing lag over 20 minutes of continuously streamed video on four NVIDIA A6000 GPUs, staying within 200ms of source timeline.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of fully aligned input-output modeling for duplex, proactive, and hardware-aligned multimodal interaction with complete training/serving recipe including realtime QA construction and resumable inference.

title: Label-Free Parkinson's Disease Screening from Face and Voice through Mechanistic Interpretability
summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder. Typical machine learning screening methods require PD labels, but the available data is limited by privacy concerns and the need for expert annotation. We propose a label-free face-plus-voice PD screen built entirely on frozen pretrained encoders--a face-expression Vision Transformer and HuBERT--in which no PD label touches any fit; the reference is training controls only. The voice modality uses a synthetic-dysarthria contrastive activation addition (CAA) direction built from time-stretch and breathy degradation of healthy speech; the face modality uses a k-nearest-neighbor anomaly score to the control embedding cluster. We introduce the alignment principle, a post-hoc analysis showing that a synthetic-degradation CAA detector works when the cosine similarity between the synthetic and real disease directions exceeds zero. Measured on the YouTubePD benchmark, this cosine is +0.37 for voice (CAA works, AUROC 0.765) and -0.48 for face (CAA fails; anomaly succeeds, AUROC 0.751). Equal-weight late fusion reaches AUROC 0.802 (95% CI [0.70,0.89]) with NPV 0.95, supporting a rule-out triage interpretation. An overfitting audit shows the voice detector transfers cleanly, while the face-side--and thus fused--AUROC is potentially optimistic pending external validation.

AI.tldr: A label-free Parkinson's disease screening method using frozen pretrained encoders for face and voice analysis, achieving AUROC 0.802 without requiring PD-labeled training data.
AI.motivation: Parkinson's disease screening typically requires labeled PD data which is limited due to privacy concerns and need for expert annotation. Current machine learning methods need PD labels, creating data scarcity issues.
AI.method: Uses frozen pretrained encoders (face-expression Vision Transformer and HuBERT) with no PD labels in training. Voice modality uses synthetic-dysarthria contrastive activation addition from healthy speech degradation. Face modality uses k-nearest-neighbor anomaly score to control embedding cluster. Introduces alignment principle to validate synthetic degradation detectors.
AI.result: Voice CAA works (cosine similarity +0.37, AUROC 0.765), face CAA fails (-0.48) but anomaly succeeds (AUROC 0.751). Equal-weight late fusion achieves AUROC 0.802 with NPV 0.95. Voice detector transfers cleanly, face-side AUROC potentially optimistic pending validation.
AI.conclusion: Label-free PD screening using frozen pretrained encoders is feasible, achieving good performance for rule-out triage. The alignment principle validates synthetic degradation approaches. Voice modality shows clean transfer, while face results need external validation.

title: Yesterday's Shield, Today's Spear: A Self-Evolving Safety Guardrail in Production
summary: Deployed LLM safety guardrails are predominantly static: trained once and frozen at release, while new jailbreak techniques and previously un-addressed harmful categories emerge within days, leaving the defense perpetually a step behind. We present SESG (Self-Evolving Safety Guardrails), a multi-agent system running in production. SESG monitors the live traffic behind a deployed guardrail and surfaces two classes of failure: jailbreaks novel in form and harmful categories novel in content. Once a failure is confirmed, a generation agent synthesizes paired training data targeted at it; a validation agent rebalances the batch toward the direction in which the deployed model errs, so that the model's own mistakes steer its training set; and a routing agent matches the training action to the diagnosed gap and returns the next version to production. Over six rounds of live evolution (V0 to V6), a 1.7B guardrail adapts to a new threat in 16-24 hours, with about 2 hours of human effort, versus the 40-90 hours of the manual process it replaces. On six emerging threats, it outperforms static guardrails from 0.6B to 9B and an adaptive baseline while preserving its general screening competence. Since April 2026, SESG has been the primary update pipeline of Sangfor's guardrail, autonomously closing 14 of 15 new threat scenarios in two months. We release 9 test sets for the 6 new threats at https://github.com/Trams1017/SESG. Warning: This paper contains examples that may be harmful or offensive.

AI.tldr: SESG is a self-evolving safety guardrail system that autonomously adapts LLM defenses to emerging jailbreak techniques and harmful content through multi-agent monitoring, targeted data generation, and continuous model updates.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety guardrails are static - trained once and frozen, making them perpetually behind emerging jailbreak techniques and new harmful content categories that appear within days of deployment.
AI.method: A multi-agent system with: 1) Monitoring agent to detect failures (novel jailbreaks & harmful categories), 2) Generation agent to synthesize targeted training data, 3) Validation agent to rebalance batches using model's own mistakes, 4) Routing agent to match training actions to diagnosed gaps and deploy updates.
AI.result: SESG adapts to new threats in 16-24 hours with ~2 hours human effort vs 40-90 hours manual process. Outperforms static guardrails (0.6B-9B) on six emerging threats while preserving general screening competence. Successfully closed 14/15 new threat scenarios in two months of production use.
AI.conclusion: SESG demonstrates that self-evolving safety systems can effectively keep pace with rapidly emerging threats, providing continuous adaptation that static defenses cannot achieve, making it a viable production solution for LLM safety.

title: Twin Rollouts: Noise-Coupled Counterfactual Branching in Interactive Video World Models
summary: Interactive video world models generate rollouts autoregressively under an action stream, yet they are trained and evaluated almost exclusively on factual prediction. We study counterfactual generation inside the rollout: given a trajectory the model has itself generated, what would have happened had the actions differed from step t* onward? We formalize noise-coupled twin rollouts --- a factual and a counterfactual branch sharing the generated prefix and the future exogenous noise sequence, diverging only in the action stream at an intervention point. Because the factual branch is self-generated, its exogenous noise is known exactly: the abduction step of Pearl's counterfactual procedure is exact by construction, sidestepping the approximate-inversion problem faced by editing-based pipelines. Noise coupling further turns the minimal-change principle into a per-sample verifiable property: we define a spatiotemporal locality metric that penalizes divergence outside the causal descendants of the intervention, computable against simulator ground truth without a learned judge. Forking the simulator state at t* yields ground-truth counterfactual re-renders, which we use as verifiable rewards for post-training. This note establishes the formal framework, metric definitions, and positioning; experiments are forthcoming.

AI.tldr: A framework for counterfactual video generation using noise-coupled twin rollouts that enables exact abduction and verifiable minimal-change evaluation against simulator ground truth.
AI.motivation: Current interactive video world models are trained and evaluated only on factual prediction, ignoring counterfactual reasoning about "what would have happened" if actions had differed. There's a need to formalize counterfactual generation within video rollouts with verifiable evaluation metrics.
AI.method: Proposes noise-coupled twin rollouts: a factual and counterfactual branch sharing the generated prefix and future exogenous noise sequence, diverging only in actions at an intervention point. Uses exact abduction by construction since factual branch is self-generated. Defines spatiotemporal locality metric to penalize divergence outside causal descendants of intervention. Uses simulator fork for ground-truth counterfactual re-renders as verifiable rewards.
AI.result: Establishes formal framework, metric definitions, and positioning for counterfactual video generation. The method sidesteps approximate-inversion problems faced by editing-based pipelines and enables per-sample verification of minimal-change principle. Ground-truth simulator forks provide verifiable rewards for post-training.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a formal framework for counterfactual video generation that addresses key limitations of existing approaches by enabling exact abduction and verifiable evaluation against ground truth, with practical experiments planned for future work.

title: HoloAegis: Frozen Representation, Topological Inference: Minimally Parametric Safety Manifolds for Zero-Shot LLM Guardrails
summary: Current LLM safety guardrails face a fundamental tension: fine-tuning distorts pre-trained representations while generative judges incur prohibitive inference costs. We challenge the prevailing paradigm by asking: can safety be achieved through pure geometric reasoning over frozen semantic representations? We present HoloAegis, a minimally parametric topological inference framework that decouples representation from reasoning. We term our approach minimally parametric because the only free parameters are the anchor count K and the temperature tau, both fixed after construction and requiring no gradient-based training. An un-fine-tuned encoder maps text to a unit sphere, after which all decisions are purely geometric. We formalize safety evaluation as a Gibbs-Boltzmann Free Energy computation over a pre-computed System Topology Anchor Bank, and we introduce Dual Time-Scale Exponential Moving Averages to detect progressive multi-turn semantic drift. Our key theoretical insight is a Topological Boundary Stability Conjecture: we provide theoretical motivation and strong empirical evidence that sparse anchor centroids stabilize the decision boundary against high-frequency lexical perturbations far better than full vector space methods. Evaluated across 8 benchmarks, HoloAegis achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (1.0000 AUC on AuthenHallu, 0.9802 on HarmBench) with sub-millisecond latency, zero cold-start data, and cross-lingual transfer (0.9758 AUC on Chinese CHIFRAUD).

AI.tldr: HoloAegis: A minimally parametric topological inference framework for LLM safety that uses pure geometric reasoning over frozen semantic representations without fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art performance with sub-millisecond latency.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety approaches face a fundamental tension: fine-tuning distorts pre-trained representations while generative judges incur prohibitive inference costs. The paper challenges whether safety can be achieved through pure geometric reasoning over frozen semantic representations.
AI.method: HoloAegis uses a minimally parametric topological inference framework that decouples representation from reasoning. An un-fine-tuned encoder maps text to a unit sphere, then decisions are purely geometric using a Gibbs-Boltzmann Free Energy computation over a pre-computed System Topology Anchor Bank. It introduces Dual Time-Scale Exponential Moving Averages to detect progressive multi-turn semantic drift, based on a Topological Boundary Stability Conjecture that sparse anchor centroids stabilize decision boundaries against lexical perturbations.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 1.0000 AUC on AuthenHallu, 0.9802 on HarmBench, with sub-millisecond latency, zero cold-start data, and cross-lingual transfer (0.9758 AUC on Chinese CHIFRAUD). Evaluated across 8 benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that safety can be achieved through pure geometric reasoning over frozen semantic representations, offering a fundamentally different approach to LLM safety that avoids representation distortion while maintaining computational efficiency and achieving strong performance across multiple domains.

title: SoftMCC: An MCC-Brier Calibration Bridge for Threshold-Free Model Selection under Class Imbalance
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Machine Learning Research
summary: Model selection for imbalanced binary classification often uses the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), but thresholding makes validation rankings threshold-dependent. SoftMCC is a post-training MCC validation framework on established probability-valued confusion counts, coupling an MCC-specific calibrated identity with a tie-aware, shared-pool selection protocol. Its core score is a covariance-normalized probability-label association, reduces exactly to MCC for hard predictions, and is Pearson-bounded. Under perfect population calibration it equals the Brier skill score with identical candidate ordering; outside that regime the gap does not identify calibration error. Across 18 settings with 12 duplicate-safe grouped repeats, SoftMCC attains the best stability mean rank (2.31) and highest mean tie-corrected Kendall's W (0.659), with a significant Friedman test (p=0.007); Nemenyi analysis separates it from AUPRC and MCC@0.5, while 14-source-family sensitivity retains only the latter. Selected-model utility shows no advantage. Three of six prespecified comparisons have negative mean test-MCC differences, only F1@best survives Holm correction (p=0.014), and the dataset-level test is not significant (p=0.117). Label permutation lowers mean W to 0.092; temperature scaling shifts SoftMCC rankings (mean Spearman 0.851) whereas rank-based and threshold-optimized metrics remain invariant. SoftMCC is a calibration-sensitive MCC-family selector with bounded stability and utility evidence.

AI.tldr: SoftMCC is a calibration-sensitive validation framework for imbalanced binary classification that extends MCC to probability-valued predictions with stable model selection and bounded scores.
AI.motivation: Standard model selection for imbalanced binary classification using Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) suffers from threshold-dependency issues when making hard predictions. Existing thresholding approaches make validation rankings dependent on the chosen threshold, limiting reliable model comparison.
AI.method: SoftMCC is a post-training MCC validation framework operating on probability-valued confusion counts. It couples an MCC-specific calibrated identity with a tie-aware, shared-pool selection protocol. The core score is a covariance-normalized probability-label association that reduces exactly to MCC for hard predictions and is Pearson-bounded.
AI.result: SoftMCC achieved the best stability mean rank (2.31) and highest mean tie-corrected Kendall's W (0.659) across 18 settings with 12 duplicate-safe grouped repeats. It showed significant separation from AUPRC and MCC@0.5 in Nemenyi analysis. Label permutation lowered mean W to 0.092, while temperature scaling shifted SoftMCC rankings (mean Spearman 0.851). Three of six prespecified comparisons had negative mean test-MCC differences, and only F1@best survived Holm correction.
AI.conclusion: SoftMCC is a calibration-sensitive MCC-family selector with bounded stability and utility evidence. It provides a threshold-independent approach for model selection in imbalanced binary classification that maintains connections to MCC while operating on probability predictions.

title: TrustRoboReward: Preference-Ordered Isotonic Score Editing for Multi-Paradigm Robot Reward Models
summary: Reward models are a bottleneck for reinforcement learning in embodied AI. Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires scalable vision feedback beyond handcrafted rewards or task-specific annotations. Existing open-source VLM reward judges like RoboReward adopt simple 1--5 trajectory progress scoring, lacking pairwise preferences for RLHF, DPO and Bradley-Terry frameworks, while failing to optimize video scene understanding. Augmenting RoboReward with pairwise comparison and video-QA supervision causes inconsistency between pairwise preferences and pointwise scores, introducing training noise and hurting downstream performance---an issue aggregation methods such as TrustJudge cannot resolve. To address this, we propose TrustRoboReward, a multi-paradigm reward modeling framework equipped with Preference-Ordered Isotonic Score Editing (POISE). We construct a unified four-paradigm dataset with trajectory progress scoring (Score-A), video-QA answer quality scoring (Score-B), and their pairwise counterparts (Pair-A, Pair-B). Pairwise labels align better with human judgment than pointwise scores, inspiring us to calibrate pointwise scores to avoid score-pair reversals against pairwise preferences. POISE rectifies pointwise scores and eliminates cross-paradigm reversal conflicts unresolved by TrustJudge. Theoretically, POISE reduces score-pair reversal conflicts from 20.15% to 0%, whereas TrustJudge retains 20.46% conflicts on the same corpus. Evaluated on our benchmark, Qwen3-VL-4B trained with POISE achieves an overall reward score of 77.96%, nearly matching GPT-5-mini (78.09%, gap 0.13%) and outperforming the strongest RoboReward-4B baseline by 10.13%. It also lifts test-time score-pair consistency to 71.90%, exceeding RoboReward-4B (57.26%) and GPT-5-mini (68.09%). Integrating TrustJudge aggregation during inference boosts the overall score to 78.57%, surpassing the GPT-5-mini teacher model.

AI.tldr: TrustRoboReward improves reward modeling for embodied AI by addressing inconsistencies between pairwise preferences and pointwise scores through POISE calibration, achieving near GPT-5-mini performance.
AI.motivation: Reward models bottleneck reinforcement learning in embodied AI; existing open-source VLM reward judges lack pairwise preferences for RLHF/DPO frameworks and suffer from inconsistencies between pairwise preferences and pointwise scores that hurt downstream performance.
AI.method: Proposes TrustRoboReward with Preference-Ordered Isotonic Score Editing (POISE), constructs unified four-paradigm dataset (Score-A, Score-B, Pair-A, Pair-B), and calibrates pointwise scores to align with pairwise preferences to eliminate score-pair reversal conflicts.
AI.result: POISE reduces score-pair reversal conflicts from 20.15% to 0% (vs. 20.46% for TrustJudge); Qwen3-VL-4B trained with POISE achieves 77.96% overall reward score (near GPT-5-mini's 78.09%), outperforming RoboReward-4B by 10.13%; with TrustJudge inference boosts to 78.57% surpassing GPT-5-mini.
AI.conclusion: TrustRoboReward with POISE effectively resolves inconsistencies between pairwise preferences and pointwise scores, creating more reliable reward models for embodied AI that match or exceed state-of-the-art teacher models.

title: Dynamic Distribution-Aware Uncertainty Tracking in Vision-Language Representation Learning
summary: Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) aims to measure the reliability of model predictions, serving as a critical safeguard for deploying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in safety-critical scenarios. Post-hoc approaches are widely adopted due to their lightweight nature, mapping the outputs of VLMs to uncertainty measures through learnable modules or inductive summarization. However, Post-hoc approaches remain inherently confined to fitting the failure patterns of the source domain, ignoring the dynamic nature of test distributions. To address this challenge, we propose a Dynamic Distribution-Aware Uncertainty Quantification framework (DDA-UQ) that shifts the paradigm from static mapping to a dynamic distribution-aware process. During training, we leverage a Gaussian Mixture Model to model the VVLMs'embedding space and extract distributional evidence, thereby dynamically deriving uncertainty estimates. During inference, the design dynamically responds to changes in the data distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: A novel Dynamic Distribution-Aware Uncertainty Quantification (DDA-UQ) framework for Vision-Language Models that shifts from static post-hoc uncertainty estimation to dynamic, distribution-aware uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Current post-hoc UQ approaches for VLMs are inherently limited as they only fit failure patterns of the source domain and ignore the dynamic nature of test distributions, which is critical for deploying VLMs in safety-critical applications where reliability assessment is essential.
AI.method: Proposes DDA-UQ framework that shifts from static mapping to dynamic distribution-aware process. During training, uses Gaussian Mixture Model to model VLMs' embedding space and extract distributional evidence for dynamic uncertainty estimation. During inference, the design dynamically responds to changes in data distribution.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed DDA-UQ approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification methods.
AI.conclusion: The dynamic distribution-aware paradigm for uncertainty quantification represents a significant advancement over static post-hoc approaches, providing more reliable uncertainty estimates that adapt to changing data distributions, which is crucial for safety-critical applications of Vision-Language Models.

title: MathShikkha: A Controlled Study of Answer-Only and Chain-of-Thought Supervision for Bangla Mathematical Reasoning in Small Language Models
summary: Mathematical reasoning remains challenging in low-resource languages such as Bangla. We study whether teacher-generated Bangla Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision provides benefits beyond ordinary supervised fine-tuning. We construct \textsc{MathShikkha}, a Bangla mathematical reasoning dataset with GPT-5.4-generated rationales, and fine-tune four 4B--7B student models under a matched protocol in which answer-only and CoT conditions share data splits, response-only loss masking, decoding, and scoring, differing only in the training target. In-domain, CoT provides no significant improvement over answer-only fine-tuning for three stronger backbones (paired bootstrap 95\% CIs include zero; exact McNemar $p \geq 0.17$), despite generating 15--52$\times$ more tokens, but significantly improves the weaker 4B model by 18.56 points ($p < 0.0001$). On the larger, contamination-audited BanglaMATH benchmark, this pattern reverses: CoT significantly outperforms answer-only supervision for all four models by 20.1--28.1 points (all $p < 0.0001$). Answer-only fine-tuning also reduces out-of-domain accuracy below the base model for three models, whereas CoT preserves or improves it for all four. A human study with two co-author annotators, external-expert adjudication, and Cohen's $κ= 0.76$--$1.00$ finds no significant CoT improvement over the base model on reasoning-content criteria; instead, its measurable effect is target-language adherence and producing inspectable reasoning. Overall, rationale supervision's value depends on backbone capability and distribution shift: in this setting, its main benefits are Bangla adherence, auditable reasoning, and out-of-domain robustness rather than improved in-domain reasoning validity.

AI.tldr: Teacher-generated Bangla Chain-of-Thought supervision shows mixed results: no significant in-domain improvement for stronger models, helps weaker model, but significantly improves out-of-domain performance and provides better target-language adherence and inspectable reasoning.
AI.motivation: Mathematical reasoning is challenging in low-resource languages like Bangla, and there's a need to understand whether Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision provides benefits beyond ordinary supervised fine-tuning for such languages.
AI.method: Created MathShikkha dataset with GPT-5.4-generated rationales, fine-tuned four student models (4B-7B) with matched protocol comparing answer-only vs CoT supervision. Conducted in-domain and out-of-domain (BanglaMATH benchmark) evaluations, plus human study with expert adjudication.
AI.result: Mixed results: In-domain, CoT provided no significant improvement for three stronger backbones but helped weaker 4B model. On BanglaMATH benchmark, CoT significantly outperformed answer-only for all models (20.1-28.1 points). CoT preserved/improved out-of-domain accuracy while answer-only reduced it. Human study found CoT improved target-language adherence and inspectable reasoning but not reasoning validity.
AI.conclusion: CoT supervision's value depends on backbone capability and distribution shift. Main benefits are Bangla language adherence, auditable reasoning, and out-of-domain robustness rather than improved in-domain reasoning validity.

title: HOPPER: Learnable Hop Extraction for Linearized Graph Sequence Models
summary: Graph neural networks typically propagate information through repeated message-passing layers, coupling the distance over which information travels with the number of nonlinear transformations applied. This coupling can make deep architectures difficult to optimize and can lead to over-smoothing, over-squashing, and the loss of long-range information. Linearized Graph Sequence Models (LGSMs) address this issue by separating information depth from processing depth and treating the successive propagation states of each node as a sequence. However, existing LGSMs construct these sequences using fixed graph operators, limiting their ability to adapt propagation to the input graph, node features, and downstream task. We introduce HOPPER, an end-to-end learnable extension of LGSM that learns how hop sequences should be extracted before they are processed by a modern state-space model. Our framework supports feature-conditioned, structure-aware, graph- and hop-adaptive propagation mechanisms while preserving permutation equivariance. Standard adjacency-based and non-backtracking LGSM sequences arise as special cases of our proposed extractor family. We show that HOPPER is state-of-the-art or competitive across the ECHO-Synth benchmark, and that varying the maximum neighborhood size of message backtracking cancellation (i.e. structural memory window) can optimize accuracy on the LRIM physics-based long-range dependency benchmark. These results demonstrate that learnable sequence extraction provides a flexible and effective approach to long-range graph representation learning.

AI.tldr: HOPPER introduces a learnable extension to Linearized Graph Sequence Models (LGSMs) that learns adaptive hop sequences before processing with state-space models, improving long-range graph representation learning.
AI.motivation: Standard GNNs couple information propagation distance with nonlinear transformation depth, causing optimization difficulties, over-smoothing, over-squashing, and loss of long-range information. Existing LGSMs use fixed graph operators that cannot adapt propagation to input graphs, features, or tasks.
AI.method: HOPPER learns how to extract hop sequences before processing by modern state-space models, supporting feature-conditioned, structure-aware, graph- and hop-adaptive propagation while preserving permutation equivariance. It treats successive propagation states of each node as a sequence.
AI.result: HOPPER achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on ECHO-Synth benchmark and demonstrates that varying maximum neighborhood size of message backtracking cancellation can optimize accuracy on LRIM physics-based long-range dependency benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Learnable sequence extraction provides a flexible and effective approach to long-range graph representation learning, with standard LGSM sequences emerging as special cases of the proposed extractor family.

title: Understanding Calibration and Truncation Error Propagation in Training-Free Low-Rank Compression for LLMs
summary: Training-free low-rank compression frameworks have been gaining prominence for LLM compression given their effectiveness in reducing model parameter count while maintaining task-level accuracy. However, existing SOTA frameworks share two key limitations: (1) residual errors in calibration data activations accumulate across layers during compression, causing misalignment between representations simulated at compression time and those experienced at inference; (2) the assumption that layer importance distribution is preserved post-compression does not hold. Together, these two effects introduce misalignment in the compression process in relation to the deployed model. We study these effects and propose a simple, training-free methodology compatible with existing frameworks to mitigate them, comprising: (1) Layer-by-Layer Compression with Calibration Correction; (2) Iterative Compression with Rank Allocation Correction. Implemented atop an existing SOTA decomposition framework, and evaluated on Llama and Qwen3 models across various benchmarks and compression rates, our approach demonstrates up to ~1-2.5 accuracy point improvements over per-weight and joint decomposition baselines on zero-shot tasks.

AI.tldr: Proposes a training-free method to address misalignment issues in low-rank LLM compression by adding layer-by-layer compression with calibration correction and iterative compression with rank allocation correction.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free low-rank compression frameworks for LLMs have two key limitations: (1) residual errors in calibration data activations accumulate across layers during compression, causing misalignment between compression-time simulations and actual inference, and (2) the assumption that layer importance distribution is preserved post-compression doesn't hold, introducing additional misalignment in the compression process.
AI.method: A simple, training-free methodology compatible with existing frameworks consisting of two components: (1) Layer-by-Layer Compression with Calibration Correction to address activation misalignment, and (2) Iterative Compression with Rank Allocation Correction to address the distribution mismatch issue.
AI.result: Implemented on top of an existing SOTA decomposition framework and evaluated on Llama and Qwen3 models across various benchmarks and compression rates, the approach demonstrates up to ~1-2.5 accuracy point improvements over per-weight and joint decomposition baselines on zero-shot tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free methodology effectively mitigates misalignment issues in low-rank LLM compression, achieving significant accuracy improvements over existing baselines while maintaining compatibility with current frameworks.

title: F2STNet: Fair and Federated Spectral-Temporal Modeling for Graph Forecasting
summary: Spatiotemporal prediction on graph-structured data is central to traffic forecasting and environmental monitoring, yet decentralized and heterogeneous data complicate both sequence modeling and collaborative training. We propose F$^2$STNet, a federated forecasting framework that combines truncated graph-Fourier features, a lightweight diagonal state-space temporal encoder, graph convolution, and Fairness-aware Federated Aggregation (FFA). The spectral branch exposes graph-frequency structure, while the state-space layer models long temporal dependencies with linear complexity in the sequence length. FFA adjusts the FedAvg prior using client validation losses and an increasing fairness schedule. Experiments on PeMS04, HZMetro, and KnowAir show favorable forecasting accuracy relative to the evaluated baselines; federated experiments on PeMS04 additionally improve worst-client and client-dispersion metrics.

AI.tldr: F²STNet: A federated forecasting framework that combines graph-Fourier features, state-space temporal encoding, graph convolution, and fairness-aware aggregation for spatiotemporal prediction on decentralized heterogeneous data.
AI.motivation: Spatiotemporal prediction on graph-structured data (like traffic forecasting and environmental monitoring) faces challenges due to decentralized and heterogeneous data, which complicates both sequence modeling and collaborative training in federated settings.
AI.method: Proposes F²STNet framework with: 1) truncated graph-Fourier features to expose graph-frequency structure, 2) lightweight diagonal state-space temporal encoder for long temporal dependencies with linear complexity, 3) graph convolution, and 4) Fairness-aware Federated Aggregation (FFA) that adjusts FedAvg using client validation losses and increasing fairness schedule.
AI.result: Experiments on PeMS04, HZMetro, and KnowAir datasets show favorable forecasting accuracy compared to baselines. Federated experiments on PeMS04 additionally improve worst-client performance and reduce client-dispersion metrics.
AI.conclusion: F²STNet effectively addresses challenges in federated spatiotemporal forecasting by combining spectral graph analysis, efficient temporal modeling, and fairness-aware aggregation, demonstrating improved accuracy and fairness in decentralized settings.

title: Time Present and Time Past: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Temporally Evolving Document Understanding
summary: Evolving documents, such as laws, tax codes, and software documentation, are amended, replaced, and sometimes reverted over time, so a question has different correct answers at different dates. In contrast to encyclopedic knowledge, where an old fact is simply overwritten, an amendment is itself an official text that states what it replaces and when it takes effect, and the earlier version stays correct for its validity period. The central challenge is therefore version resolution, that is, identifying the version in force on the queried date. Existing temporal QA datasets treat time only as an annotation, so version resolution stays untested. We present TIDE, an expert-verified benchmark of 3,050 QA pairs over 644 official customs instruments issued between 1969 and 2025 by the Government of Bangladesh, covering eight task types over deeply code-mixed documents that are heterogeneous in layout and dated in two calendars. In addition, we evaluate nine recent LLMs under a single protocol across parametric, gold-context, and retrieval access, scored by a three-judge LLM council with a hard date gate separating correct meaning from correct time. The best macro-averaged accuracy is only 68.5%. Resolving a version from an implicit date reaches 59.7%, and detecting that the supplied version does not govern the query reaches only 26.7%. Models are more likely to find correct versions than to reject incorrect ones, and they tend to follow a confident parametric answer over the supplied authoritative text. All code and data are available at https://github.com/icsetepa44/TIDE

AI.tldr: TIDE is a temporal QA benchmark for version resolution in evolving legal documents, testing LLMs' ability to identify correct document versions based on query dates.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal QA datasets treat time only as annotation, not testing version resolution - the ability to identify which version of an evolving document was in force at a specific date, which is crucial for legal, tax, and documentation contexts.
AI.method: Created TIDE benchmark with 3,050 QA pairs over 644 official customs instruments (1969-2025) from Bangladesh Government, covering 8 task types on deeply code-mixed documents in heterogeneous layouts with dual calendar dating.
AI.result: Evaluated 9 recent LLMs: best macro-averaged accuracy only 68.5%; version resolution from implicit dates reached 59.7%; detecting irrelevant versions only 26.7%; models favor confident parametric answers over supplied authoritative text.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs struggle with temporal version resolution in legal documents, particularly at rejecting incorrect versions, highlighting need for better temporal reasoning in document understanding tasks.

title: RAVEN: Frozen Random Graph Reservoirs with Physics-Informed Interaction Fingerprints for Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction
summary: Quantitative estimation of protein-ligand binding affinity from three-dimensional complex structures is a fundamental task in structure-based computational chemistry and molecular modeling. Reliable prediction remains challenging because available structure-affinity data are limited, experimentally heterogeneous, conformation-dependent, and sensitive to dataset partitioning. RAVEN (Randomized Atomistic Views with Ensemble Neural Reservoirs) utilizes a multihead reservoir of independently initialized and fully frozen atomistic graph encoders to generate diverse structural projections without end-to-end optimization of the graph representation. These projections are integrated with a deterministic physicochemical interaction fingerprint and processed by heterogeneous supervised readers, including neural and tree-based regressors, whose outputs are combined through validation-based nonnegative fusion. The random reservoir expands structural feature coverage across independent encoder realizations, whereas the explicit physicochemical descriptors and heterogeneous readers contribute complementary information and distinct inductive biases. Evaluation on a similarity-isolated PDBbind 2020R1 split reconstructed using GEMS similarity resources, together with the protected CASF-2016 subset, demonstrated strong predictive performance. The results indicate that frozen multi-view graph representations, explicit physicochemical statistics, and heterogeneous model fusion provide a robust and flexible framework for protein-ligand binding-affinity prediction.

AI.tldr: RAVEN uses frozen multi-view graph encoders, physicochemical fingerprints, and heterogeneous regressors with validation-based fusion to predict protein-ligand binding affinity, showing strong performance on PDBbind and CASF benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Protein-ligand binding affinity prediction from 3D structures is challenging due to limited and heterogeneous data, conformation-dependency, and sensitivity to dataset partitioning, requiring robust computational methods.
AI.method: RAVEN employs: 1) Multihead reservoir of frozen, randomly initialized graph encoders for diverse structural projections, 2) Deterministic physicochemical interaction fingerprints, 3) Heterogeneous supervised readers (neural and tree-based regressors), 4) Validation-based nonnegative fusion of reader outputs.
AI.result: Evaluation on similarity-isolated PDBbind 2020R1 split and CASF-2016 subset demonstrated strong predictive performance, outperforming existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Frozen multi-view graph representations, explicit physicochemical statistics, and heterogeneous model fusion provide a robust and flexible framework for protein-ligand binding affinity prediction.

title: Reproducing and Stress-Testing Two Approaches to LLM Reasoning Reliability: Test-Time Probability Aggregation and Logic-Representation Editing
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 9 tables. Code, data, and experiment logs: https://github.com/rabqatab/llm-reasoning-reliability-reproduction
summary: We independently reproduce two recent methods for making large language model (LLM) reasoning more reliable, and stress-test them across domains and models (RPC across four new task domains with Qwen3-8B, LCF across four 7-8B models). The first, RPC, aggregates token probabilities and self-consistency at inference; the second, LCF, trains projectors that split hidden states into "content" and "logic" and edits the logic part toward a valid region. Validating such reliability claims matters because the original evaluations are run by each method's own authors and were never independently reproduced or stress-tested across models and domains, and LCF shipped no public code. We re-run RPC's published-path aggregation and re-implement LCF's projector, contrastive, and intervention pipeline, then extend both to text-to-SQL, legal extraction, fallacy identification, and precedent grading, and probe LCF's representation directly.
