RPC reproduces the original grid exactly on the authors' released reasoning paths; on four new domains its edge over self-consistency is never significant (ties or small mixed differences, paired p >= 0.28), and on BIRD, the one domain where we vary the budget, the edge grows with K as predicted but its largest gap (+2.5 accuracy at K=32, p=0.16) reverses to -0.25 when we enlarge the sample to n=200. LCF's logic-validity direction is real but weak (0.82 separability at the single best sub-layer versus 0.95 for a semantic-attribute control); its one positive effect (Qwen3 $Δ$Prob) is not significant (p=0.56), while it significantly reduces $Δ$Prob on two of the other three models.

AI.tldr: Independent reproduction and stress-testing of two LLM reasoning reliability methods (RPC and LCF) shows limited effectiveness - RPC's improvements over self-consistency are not significant, and LCF's logic-editing effects are weak and sometimes harmful.
AI.motivation: To independently validate claims about LLM reasoning reliability methods, as original evaluations were conducted by the methods' authors without independent reproduction or stress-testing across different models and domains. LCF specifically had no public code available for verification.
AI.method: Reproduced RPC's published-path aggregation and re-implemented LCF's projector, contrastive, and intervention pipeline. Extended both methods to four new task domains (text-to-SQL, legal extraction, fallacy identification, precedent grading) and tested across different models (Qwen3-8B for RPC, four 7-8B models for LCF). Also directly probed LCF's representations.
AI.result: RPC reproduced original results exactly on authors' released reasoning paths, but on four new domains showed no significant advantage over self-consistency (p >= 0.28). LCF's logic-validity direction was real but weak (0.82 separability vs 0.95 control), with one positive effect not significant (p=0.56) while significantly reducing performance on two other models.
AI.conclusion: Claims about both RPC and LCF methods are overstated - RPC doesn't provide reliable improvements over self-consistency, and LCF's logic-editing has weak effects that can actually harm model performance. Independent validation is crucial as original evaluations may not generalize across domains and models.

title: Real Data Closes Synthetic-to-Real Gap in Optical Chemical Structure Recognition
summary: Millions of chemical structures appear in patents and papers only as drawings, and using that information at scale requires reading the drawings. OCSR appears nearly solved on synthetic images yet remains difficult on real documents: the starting recognizer, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, exceeds 91% accuracy on synthetic renders but falls below 16% on three real-world benchmarks (ACS, CLEF-IP, USPTO). To identify the main source of improvement, 21 recognizers were fine-tuned on mixtures of synthetically rendered structures and labeled real depictions from patents, journal figures, and hand-drawn collections, varying the vision language model (VLM) base, the fraction of real training data, and the vision-tower adaptation strategy. Labeled real training images make the largest difference. For Qwen2.5-VL, ACS exact match rises from 0.15 with no real data to 0.37 at 9.5% and 0.46 at 50.2%; a controlled experiment across three base models reproduces the trend. A vision-tower LoRA, in contrast, does nothing for Qwen (+0.00, paired p=1.00), substantially helps InternVL3-8B (+22.8 to +34.6 pt), and modestly helps GLM-4.1V-9B (+1.0 to +9.6 pt), so its value depends on the base model. The best configuration reaches 0.96 exact match on clean renders and 0.49, 0.65, 0.84, and 0.76 on ACS, CLEF-IP, UOB, and USPTO, respectively. Gaps between base models are largest without real data (0.21), shrink to 0.06 at 70% real data, and reorder the ranking; base model and real-data mixture must therefore be selected together. Small-scale experiments on handwritten image-to-LaTeX recognition and chart-to-table conversion show that base-model rankings also vary beyond chemistry. More generally, model and adaptation choices for visual structure recognition should be evaluated on the target task.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning vision-language models with real-world training data significantly improves optical chemical structure recognition (OCSR) accuracy on patent and scientific document images, while vision-tower adaptation effectiveness depends on the base model.
AI.motivation: Millions of chemical structures appear in patents and papers only as drawings, requiring accurate OCSR at scale. While synthetic image recognition achieves >91% accuracy, real-world document performance remains poor (<16%), creating a need to identify effective improvement strategies.
AI.method: Fine-tuned 21 recognizers on mixtures of synthetic structures and labeled real depictions from patents, journal figures, and hand-drawn collections. Varied vision-language model bases (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3-8B, GLM-4.1V-9B), fraction of real training data, and vision-tower adaptation strategies (LoRA).
AI.result: Labeled real training data provides largest improvement: Qwen2.5-VL ACS exact match rises from 0.15 to 0.46 with 50.2% real data. Vision-tower LoRA effectiveness depends on base model: no effect for Qwen, substantial improvement for InternVL3-8B (+22.8-34.6 pt), modest for GLM-4.1V-9B (+1.0-9.6 pt). Best configuration achieves 0.96 on clean renders and 0.49-0.84 on real benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Base model and real-data mixture must be selected together as gaps between models shrink from 0.21 to 0.06 with increased real data. Model and adaptation choices for visual structure recognition should be evaluated on target tasks, with findings generalizing to other domains like handwritten LaTeX and chart conversion.

title: Discovering Diverse Planning Policies for Multimodal Embodied Agents with Quality-Diversity Optimization
summary: Multimodal embodied agents are increasingly required to solve long-horizon tasks by integrating visual observations, textual goals, and interaction history into closed-loop decision making. However, state-of-the-art large-model-based planners often rely on a single dominant planning style during execution. Once this execution mode becomes ineffective, the agent may remain stalled for many steps, repeatedly interacting with the environment without making meaningful progress. We address this limitation by proposing a Quality-Diversity (QD) framework for discovering diverse planning policies for multimodal embodied agents. The proposed method treats planning-policy templates as evolvable individuals and organizes them into a behavior-indexed archive rather than collapsing search to a single prompt style. In the offline stage, rollout trajectories are summarized into structured success and failure experiences, which guide policy variation through recombination and experience-guided mutation. The resulting policies are mapped into a behavior space defined by interaction intensity and goal-directedness, and the highest-quality policy in each niche is retained in the archive. In the online stage, the agent executes one policy at a time while monitoring task progress. When persistent stall is detected, the system rolls back to the latest checkpoint and switches to a behaviorally distinct archive policy to resume execution. Experiments on the ThreeDWorld transport benchmark show that the proposed framework improves both task success and interaction efficiency over representative baseline planners. These results suggest that discovering diverse policy repertoires is an effective way to support adaptive multimodal planning and online failure recovery.

AI.tldr: A Quality-Diversity framework generates diverse planning policies for multimodal embodied agents, enabling online switching between different behavior styles to recover from execution stalls.
AI.motivation: Current large-model-based planners rely on a single dominant planning style, which can lead to persistent stalls when that style becomes ineffective, causing agents to repeatedly interact without making progress.
AI.method: Uses Quality-Diversity framework to evolve planning-policy templates into a behavior-indexed archive. Offline stage: summarizes rollout trajectories into success/failure experiences to guide policy variation via recombination and mutation. Online stage: agent monitors progress, detects stalls, rolls back to checkpoints, and switches to behaviorally distinct policies from the archive.
AI.result: Experiments on ThreeDWorld transport benchmark show improvements in both task success and interaction efficiency over baseline planners.
AI.conclusion: Discovering diverse policy repertoires is an effective approach for supporting adaptive multimodal planning and online failure recovery in embodied agents.

title: A Probabilistic Circuit-Induced Pseudo-Metric for Out-of-Distribution Detection
summary: Probabilistic Circuits (PCs) are tractable generative models whose internal nodes encode a hierarchy of probabilistic sum- maries over different variable scopes. Existing PC-based out- of-distribution (OOD) detection methods ignore this hierar- chy, reducing the entire circuit to the scalar likelihood (or its uncertainty) computed at the root. We introduce Hierar- chical Likelihood Vector (HLV), a representation whose en- tries are the likelihoods associated with selected PC nodes and define the Hierarchical Likelihood Distance (HLD), a PC-induced pseudo-metric that compares the probability dis- tributions through the expectations of their HLVs. We show that HLD is an integral probability metric over a function class naturally induced by the PC and develop a principled goodness-of-fit hypothesis test for unsupervised OOD detec- tion. Unlike existing approaches, the trained PC alone serves as the representation of the in-distribution: no held-out in- distribution data are required at deployment. We further show that the quantities required by the hypothesis test can be com- puted exactly, directly from the trained circuit, yielding an ap- proximate analytic decision threshold. Experiments on tabular and MNIST datasets demonstrate that exploiting the hierarchi- cal probabilistic summaries encoded through the PC improve OOD detection over root-likelihood, uncertainty-, typicality- and kernel-based baselines, while naturally localizing distri- bution shifts to the PC nodes responsible for the shift.

AI.tldr: HLV (Hierarchical Likelihood Vector) and HLD (Hierarchical Likelihood Distance) leverage PC's hierarchical structure for OOD detection, outperforming methods that only use root likelihood.
AI.motivation: Current PC-based OOD detection methods ignore the hierarchical structure of probabilistic circuits, reducing them to just the scalar likelihood at the root node, missing valuable hierarchical information.
AI.method: Introduces HLV (hierarchical likelihood vector) containing likelihoods from selected PC nodes, and HLD (hierarchical likelihood distance) - a PC-induced pseudo-metric comparing distributions through HLV expectations. Develops a principled goodness-of-fit hypothesis test for unsupervised OOD detection.
AI.result: HLD improves OOD detection over root-likelihood, uncertainty-, typicality- and kernel-based baselines on tabular and MNIST datasets. The method localizes distribution shifts to responsible PC nodes and requires no held-out in-distribution data at deployment.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the hierarchical probabilistic summaries in PCs through HLV/HLD significantly improves OOD detection while providing interpretability about where distribution shifts occur in the circuit structure.

title: Deep probabilistic logic programming for diagnostic reasoning from incomplete information: A case study in stroke detection
comment: Accepted for presentation at IJCLR 2026. This is the accepted version, _not_ the camera-ready version for the post-proceedings of the conference
summary: In medical applications, raw data is frequently associated with significant privacy concerns, lending particular importance to the encoding of summary statistics from the literature. On the other hand, deep learning has become an invaluable tool for assessing symptoms based on visual or auditory sensor data. DeepProbLog allows for an extensible neuro-symbolic approach that accommodates connectionist components to analyse patient images within a transparent and rigorous probabilistic framework, namely probabilistic logic programming under the distribution semantics. Framed as a case study in stroke detection from multimodal data, this contribution explores the pathway from summary statistics available in the literature to a DeepProbLog-based diagnostic system. It suggests a workflow using established maximum entropy techniques to complete available probabilistic information and the probabilistic logic programming system ProbLog 2 to move from the entropy-maximising causal model to a discriminative neuro-symbolic model expressible within DeepProbLog. The relative performance of models derived from less complete data is analysed alongside the potential of the probabilistic inductive logic programming system ProbFOIL 2 for compressing large discriminative models, and the perspectives and implications of using DeepProbLog for diagnostic reasoning are discussed.

AI.tldr: The paper explores using DeepProbLog to create a neuro-symbolic diagnostic system for stroke detection from multimodal medical data, bridging from literature-based summary statistics through maximum entropy techniques to a transparent probabilistic framework.
AI.motivation: Medical applications involve privacy-sensitive data, making literature-based summary statistics important. There's a need to combine deep learning's ability to analyze visual/auditory sensor data with transparent, rigorous probabilistic reasoning for medical diagnostics.
AI.method: Proposes a workflow: 1) Use established maximum entropy techniques to complete available probabilistic information from literature, 2) Employ ProbLog 2 to move from entropy-maximizing causal models to discriminative neuro-symbolic models in DeepProbLog, 3) Analyze relative performance of models from incomplete data, 4) Explore ProbFOIL 2 for compressing large discriminative models.
AI.result: The paper presents a case study in stroke detection from multimodal data, demonstrating the pathway from literature-based summary statistics to a DeepProbLog-based diagnostic system. It analyzes model performance with incomplete data and explores model compression possibilities.
AI.conclusion: DeepProbLog offers promising potential for diagnostic reasoning by combining connectionist components for sensory data analysis with transparent probabilistic logic programming, providing an extensible neuro-symbolic approach for medical applications with privacy constraints.

title: MARA: Flow-Matching-Guided Multi-Agent Resource Allocation for Computational Resource Efficient Learning
summary: Allocating limited computation among concurrent learning tasks is difficult when each task must reach a target loss before a deadline but its required training effort is unknown. Existing approaches combine online loss prediction with adaptive resource allocation, yet commonly treat computation as continuously divisible throughput. We instead study a practical setting in which tasks arrive over time and computation is provided by discrete nodes. This setting introduces both uncertain demand and constrained sequential decisions. We propose MARA, which predicts future loss trajectories with conditional flow matching and coordinates compute nodes through a cooperative multi-agent autoregressive policy. A potential-based progress reward supplies intermediate training feedback while preserving the undiscounted task-completion objective. Across in-distribution, reinforcement-learning, and vision workloads, flow matching reduces remaining-resource prediction error relative to weighted least squares. At the scheduler's training load, MARA completes 63.46% of tasks on average, 8.54 percentage points above strong baseline Learning with Adaptive Resource Allocation (LARA), and remains ahead under unseen heavier workloads.

AI.tldr: MARA is a multi-agent autoregressive system that allocates discrete compute nodes to concurrent learning tasks with unknown training requirements and deadlines, using flow matching for loss trajectory prediction and achieving 8.54 percentage points higher task completion than baseline LARA.
AI.motivation: Existing resource allocation methods treat computation as continuously divisible throughput, but practical settings involve tasks arriving over time with computation provided by discrete nodes, creating challenges with uncertain demand and constrained sequential decisions.
AI.method: MARA uses conditional flow matching to predict future loss trajectories and coordinates compute nodes through a cooperative multi-agent autoregressive policy with potential-based progress rewards that provide intermediate training feedback while preserving the undiscounted task-completion objective.
AI.result: Flow matching reduces remaining-resource prediction error relative to weighted least squares. MARA completes 63.46% of tasks on average, which is 8.54 percentage points above the strong baseline Learning with Adaptive Resource Allocation (LARA), and maintains superiority under unseen heavier workloads.
AI.conclusion: MARA effectively addresses the challenge of allocating discrete compute nodes to concurrent learning tasks with unknown requirements and deadlines, demonstrating significant improvements over existing approaches through its combination of flow matching prediction and multi-agent coordination.

title: VoxZip: Semantic-Anchored Temporal KV Cache Compression for Long-Context Audio Inference
summary: Recent advancements in Speech Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding complex audio tasks. Despite this progress, their long-context inference remains severely bottlenecked by prohibitive KV cache memory demands. Existing text-centric compression methods struggle here, often disrupting speech continuity or discarding crucial semantic cues. To address this, we propose VoxZip, a train-free, two-stage semantic-anchored KV cache compression framework. The first stage uses automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcriptions as explicit semantic anchors to temporally align, compress, and fuse audio tokens, significantly reducing the initial KV cache while elevating token information density. To further improve the compression ratio, the second stage employs a dynamic filtering strategy based on temporally decayed accumulated attention to evict non-essential tokens while mitigating early-token bias. Comprehensive evaluations on Qwen3-Omni across six diverse audio benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our approach. VoxZip excels in long-audio reasoning and consistently maintains high-fidelity perception on short-form tasks. Notably, it sustains over 90\% of the uncompressed baseline performance even under an aggressive 20x KV cache compression in long-context scenarios. Furthermore, at a 4x compression ratio, VoxZip yields a 1.9x increase in inference throughput alongside a 3.3x reduction in peak memory overhead. Code and models will be available at https://github.com/MM-Speech/VoxZip.

AI.tldr: VoxZip is a train-free, two-stage KV cache compression framework for Speech LLMs that uses ASR transcriptions as semantic anchors and dynamic filtering to dramatically reduce memory demands while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Speech Large Language Models face prohibitive KV cache memory demands during long-context inference, and existing text-centric compression methods disrupt speech continuity or discard crucial semantic information.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: 1) Use ASR transcriptions as semantic anchors to align, compress, and fuse audio tokens, reducing KV cache while increasing token density; 2) Employ dynamic filtering based on temporally decayed accumulated attention to evict non-essential tokens and mitigate early-token bias.
AI.result: Comprehensive evaluations on Qwen3-Omni across six audio benchmarks show VoxZip maintains over 90% of baseline performance even under 20x compression in long-context scenarios. At 4x compression, it yields 1.9x inference throughput increase and 3.3x peak memory reduction.
AI.conclusion: VoxZip provides an effective solution for KV cache compression in Speech LLMs, enabling efficient long-context inference without performance degradation while being train-free and practical for deployment.

title: SwiftQK: Fast and Communication-Efficient Tensor Parallelism for Query-Key Normalization
summary: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) improves the training stability and quality of modern Large Language Models (LLMs). However, under Tensor Parallelism (TP), layerwise QK-Norm introduces additional cross-GPU communication because the normalization factor depends on the full hidden vector. We present SwiftQK, a multi-GPU RMSNorm kernel that exchanges only scalar normalization statistics and overlaps the remaining Peer-to-Peer reduction with independent element-wise computation in a deadlock-safe persistent kernel. Evaluations on recent LLMs show that SwiftQK reduces QK-Norm latency by 81.4--93.9% relative to the standard TP QK-Norm using full-vector All-Gather. In end-to-end serving, SwiftQK reduces TPOT on average by 29.5% over the All-Gather-based baseline and by 14.3% over an optimized scalar-aggregation implementation.

AI.tldr: SwiftQK is a multi-GPU RMSNorm kernel that optimizes Query-Key Normalization under Tensor Parallelism by exchanging only scalar normalization statistics instead of full vectors, significantly reducing communication overhead and improving training efficiency.
AI.motivation: QK-Norm improves LLM training stability and quality, but under Tensor Parallelism, layerwise QK-Norm requires cross-GPU communication of full hidden vectors, creating significant communication overhead that limits performance.
AI.method: SwiftQK exchanges only scalar normalization statistics between GPUs instead of full vectors, overlaps Peer-to-Peer reduction with independent element-wise computation using a deadlock-safe persistent kernel, and implements efficient multi-GPU RMSNorm.
AI.result: SwiftQK reduces QK-Norm latency by 81.4-93.9% compared to standard TP QK-Norm, reduces TPOT by 29.5% over All-Gather baseline and 14.3% over optimized scalar-aggregation implementation in end-to-end serving.
AI.conclusion: SwiftQK effectively addresses the communication bottleneck in QK-Norm under Tensor Parallelism, significantly improving training efficiency through intelligent kernel design and overlapping communication with computation.

title: FailForge: Distilling Procedural Competence from Persistent Failures into Code Agents
summary: Rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) is widely used to train code agents by generating trajectories on verifiable software engineering tasks, retaining those that pass the tests, and fine-tuning on the successful rollouts. However, even strong code agents repeatedly fail on a substantial fraction of such tasks, and standard RFT simply discards these failures. The discarded samples are precisely the hardest and most informative ones, drawn from verifiable instances that are costly to curate. Stronger base models may reduce the number of failures, but the remaining hard cases still define the frontier for further improvement. We propose FailForge, an agentic framework that converts failed rollouts into training signal. For each failed instance, an agent diagnoses the failure from error feedback and execution traces, distills the diagnosis into a concise and actionable skill, and injects the skill into the agent context for a guided second attempt. Trajectories that succeed under skill guidance are folded back into the RFT corpus. Crucially, the skill is removed at training time, so the model internalizes the recovered behavior rather than relying on external hints at inference. FailForge recovers over 26% of previously failed instances at marginal additional cost, and training Qwen3.5-4B on the augmented corpus improves the SWE-bench Verified resolve rate by 6.6 points over a strong RFT baseline, with gains concentrated on the hardest problems.

AI.tldr: FailForge converts failed code agent rollouts into training signal by diagnosing errors, creating actionable skills, guiding retries, and incorporating recovered trajectories into training without skill hints.
AI.motivation: Standard rejection sampling fine-tuning discards failed rollouts, which are the hardest and most informative cases. These discarded samples represent valuable training data from costly verifiable instances that define the frontier for agent improvement.
AI.method: For each failed instance, an agent: 1) diagnoses failure from error feedback and execution traces, 2) distills diagnosis into concise actionable skill, 3) injects skill into agent context for guided second attempt. Successful skill-guided trajectories are added to RFT corpus, but skills are removed at training time so model internalizes behavior.
AI.result: FailForge recovers over 26% of previously failed instances at marginal additional cost. Training Qwen3.5-4B on the augmented corpus improves SWE-bench Verified resolve rate by 6.6 points over strong RFT baseline, with gains concentrated on hardest problems.
AI.conclusion: FailForge successfully converts failure data into valuable training signal, improving code agent performance on hard problems without relying on external hints at inference, demonstrating the importance of leveraging failure cases in agent training.

title: Tabular Numeric Stretch Transformation
summary: Tabular data presents unique challenges for deep learning due to its heterogeneous nature, where numeric features exhibit diverse distributions, scales, and statistical properties. Although recent advances have improved how models learn from tabular data, how numeric data are transformed into model-friendly representations remains comparatively underexplored. We introduce the stretch transformation framework, which formulates numeric feature preprocessing as an optimization problem to make the target function smoother and thus more learnable. Our framework has two variants: (1) unsupervised stretch, which uniformly redistributes feature density via minimax optimization, and (2) supervised stretch, which optimizes target-aware numeric feature transformations from the perspective of target-function smoothness by minimizing the target function's Dirichlet energy in the transformed space. Our theoretical analysis further connects this framework to several popular transformations: unsupervised stretch is closely related to Piecewise Linear Encoding through a shared piecewise-linear geometry and approaches the empirical CDF transformation as the number of bins grows, while supervised stretch becomes closely related to target encoding in the fine-binning limit. Comprehensive experiments on 38 datasets from the TALENT benchmark demonstrate that supervised stretch consistently outperforms all baselines. These results show that explicitly optimizing for target function smoothness is a powerful and underexplored strategy for tabular deep learning.

AI.tldr: Stretch transformation framework optimizes numeric feature preprocessing for tabular data to make target functions smoother and more learnable, with supervised variant outperforming all baselines on 38 datasets.
AI.motivation: Tabular data presents unique challenges due to heterogeneous numeric features with diverse distributions, scales, and statistical properties. Current approaches to transforming numeric data into model-friendly representations are underexplored compared to advances in learning methods.
AI.method: Two variants: (1) unsupervised stretch uniformly redistributes feature density via minimax optimization; (2) supervised stretch optimizes target-aware transformations by minimizing the target function's Dirichlet energy in transformed space. Both formulate numeric feature preprocessing as optimization problems to make target functions smoother.
AI.result: Supervised stretch consistently outperforms all baselines on 38 datasets from the TALENT benchmark. Theoretical analysis connects unsupervised stretch to Piecewise Linear Encoding and empirical CDF transformation, while supervised stretch relates to target encoding in the fine-binning limit.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly optimizing for target function smoothness is a powerful and underexplored strategy for tabular deep learning. The stretch transformation framework provides effective numeric feature preprocessing through optimization-based smoothing.

title: SDDBMs: Soft Denoising Diffusion Bridge Models
summary: Diffusion bridge models leverage Doob's \(h\)-transform to construct stochastic transports between arbitrary endpoint distributions, and have shown strong potential in image-to-image translation and restoration. However, most existing bridge models rely on hard endpoint conditioning, which forces the terminal state to match a prescribed target exactly. This hard constraint induces terminal-boundary singularities: the terminal law collapses to a Dirac measure, and the resulting drift coefficients become ill-conditioned near the endpoint. In this paper, we propose Soft Denoising Diffusion Bridge Models (SDDBMs), a generalized framework that regularizes diffusion bridges directly at the level of their terminal constraints. Instead of imposing an exact endpoint, SDDBMs prescribe a non-degenerate Gaussian terminal marginal under the transformed path measure, with a flexible terminal center and variance. Starting from this prescribed marginal, we develop a complete closed-form construction of the soft bridge, including the Gaussian terminal reweighting and soft \(h\)-function, the induced Gaussian forward marginals and \(\mathbf{x}_0\)-free dynamics. Theoretically, SDDBMs provide a unified probabilistic perspective that encompasses existing diffusion bridge models, including DDBMs, GOUB, and UniDB, as special cases under specific parameter choices. Extensive experiments on image restoration tasks demonstrate that SDDBMs achieve improved numerical stability and superior generation quality over existing bridge-based methods.

AI.tldr: SDDBMs are a new diffusion bridge framework that replaces hard endpoint constraints with flexible Gaussian terminal distributions to avoid singularity issues and improve stability.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion bridge models suffer from terminal-boundary singularities due to hard endpoint conditioning, which forces exact target matching and causes drift coefficients to become ill-conditioned near endpoints.
AI.method: SDDBMs regularize diffusion bridges by prescribing non-degenerate Gaussian terminal marginals with flexible centers and variances, and develop closed-form constructions including Gaussian terminal reweighting, soft h-function, Gaussian forward marginals, and x₀-free dynamics.
AI.result: SDDBMs provide a unified framework that encompasses existing models (DDBMs, GOUB, UniDB) as special cases, and achieve improved numerical stability and superior generation quality in image restoration tasks.
AI.conclusion: SDDBMs offer a more flexible and stable alternative to hard-constrained diffusion bridges by allowing controlled terminal distributions, leading to better performance in practical applications.

title: A Time-Frequency Dual-Domain Multi-Scale Convolutional Neural Network for Bearing Fault Diagnosis under Strong Noise
summary: To address the degradation of bearing fault diagnosis accuracy under strong noise, this paper proposes a time-frequency dual-domain multi-scale convolutional neural network. The time-domain branch employs three parallel convolutional kernels to capture multi-scale impulse features, while the frequency-domain branch applies the Fast Fourier Transform to extract noise-robust spectral structure information. Features from both branches are fused for fault classification, yielding a compact model of 110,122 parameters. Experiments on the CWRU bearing dataset across seven signal-to-noise ratio levels demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 99.75% accuracy under clean conditions and maintains 92.50% at -4 dB SNR, representing a 7.25 percentage-point improvement over the single-domain baseline with monotonically increasing gains under stronger noise. Ablation experiments validate the independent performance contributions of the time-domain multi-scale branch and the frequency-domain branch. Comparative experiments against WDCNN, DRSN-CW, MCNN, and 1D-LeNet confirm the superiority of the proposed method under strong noise conditions.

AI.tldr: Proposes a time-frequency dual-domain multi-scale CNN for bearing fault diagnosis that maintains high accuracy under strong noise by combining time-domain multi-scale impulse features with frequency-domain spectral features.
AI.motivation: To address the degradation of bearing fault diagnosis accuracy under strong noise conditions, which is a common practical challenge in industrial applications where signals are often corrupted by noise.
AI.method: Time-frequency dual-domain multi-scale convolutional neural network with two branches: time-domain branch uses three parallel convolutional kernels to capture multi-scale impulse features; frequency-domain branch applies Fast Fourier Transform to extract noise-robust spectral structure information. Features from both branches are fused for fault classification.
AI.result: Achieves 99.75% accuracy under clean conditions and maintains 92.50% at -4 dB SNR on CWRU bearing dataset, representing 7.25 percentage-point improvement over single-domain baseline. Performance gains increase monotonically under stronger noise. Model is compact with 110,122 parameters.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-domain approach effectively improves bearing fault diagnosis accuracy under strong noise conditions by leveraging complementary time and frequency information, outperforming several existing methods including WDCNN, DRSN-CW, MCNN, and 1D-LeNet.

title: FedA2L: Adaptive layer-wise learning rate adjustment in decentralized federated learning
summary: Decentralized intelligence systems with heterogeneous devices and limited coordination increasingly rely on decentralized federated learning (DFL). However, DFL suffers from convergence inefficiency under data heterogeneity due to the use of a uniform learning rate (LR) that ignores layer-specific optimization needs. Foundational layers are responsible for maintaining network consensus, while specialized layers adapt to local data characteristics, leading to conflicting gradients and degraded performance under non-IID conditions. To address this fundamental tension, this work introduces FedA2L, a method that dynamically adjusts layer-wise LRs based on model divergence signals. By leveraging local update intensity and network consensus constraints, FedA2L seamlessly integrates into existing DFL protocols without additional communication or coordination. Extensive evaluations across DFL algorithms, various model architectures, and datasets demonstrate that FedA2L achieves up to 4.94 times faster convergence than vanilla DFL and reduces communication rounds by up to 59% compared to scheduler-based baselines. Furthermore, FedA2L exhibits resilience to severe data heterogeneity, larger network sizes, and sparse topologies, reducing communication overhead and establishing it as a versatile optimization tool for resource-constrained or large-scale distributed learning in edge and IoT deployments. The code is released at https://github.com/nclabteam/FedA2L.

AI.tldr: FedA2L is a layer-wise learning rate adaptation method for decentralized federated learning that dynamically adjusts learning rates based on model divergence, achieving faster convergence and reduced communication under data heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) suffers from convergence inefficiency under data heterogeneity due to uniform learning rates that ignore layer-specific optimization needs, where foundational layers maintain network consensus while specialized layers adapt to local data characteristics, causing conflicting gradients.
AI.method: FedA2L dynamically adjusts layer-wise learning rates based on model divergence signals, leveraging local update intensity and network consensus constraints. It integrates into existing DFL protocols without requiring additional communication or coordination.
AI.result: FedA2L achieves up to 4.94× faster convergence than vanilla DFL and reduces communication rounds by up to 59% compared to scheduler-based baselines. It exhibits resilience to severe data heterogeneity, larger networks, and sparse topologies, reducing communication overhead.
AI.conclusion: FedA2L establishes itself as a versatile optimization tool for resource-constrained or large-scale distributed learning in edge and IoT deployments, effectively addressing the fundamental tension between network consensus and local adaptation in DFL.

title: ForestBench: A Unified Graph Framework for Evaluating Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on Large Language Models (LLMs) are proliferating rapidly, but their heterogeneous execution traces provide no common basis for evaluation across methods. Outcome-only benchmarks discard collaborations, whereas LLM-as-Judge evaluation requires additional, model-dependent inference and can vary with the LLM and rubric. We introduce a generalizable evaluation framework that maps native MAS traces into a shared space of unified collaboration graphs, enabling different methods to be evaluated under the same representation, reference set, and metric panel. Candidate graphs are compared with a query-specific reference forest. Each forest is a benchmark-provided collection of verified-success graphs: it records diverse ways in which representative MAS methods can complete the task, rather than prescribing a unique optimal process. Instantiating the framework as ForestBench, we filter $844$ collaboration-necessary queries from seven public datasets, precompute ten successful target-conditioned reference graphs per query, and evaluate six representative MAS frameworks. Controlled backbone, reference-construction, and perturbation studies test the stability and scope of evaluation. Once the benchmark forests are built, ForestBench scores a trace in milliseconds without further LLM inference, providing a reusable structural basis for comparing diverse MAS collaboration traces.

AI.tldr: ForestBench introduces a unified framework for evaluating multi-agent LLM systems by mapping their execution traces to collaboration graphs, enabling fast, LLM-free comparisons using benchmark reference forests.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation methods for LLM-based multi-agent systems lack common ground: outcome-only benchmarks ignore collaboration processes, while LLM-as-Judge methods are model-dependent and inconsistent. There's no standardized way to compare heterogeneous execution traces across different MAS methods.
AI.method: The framework maps native MAS traces into unified collaboration graphs in a shared space. It uses query-specific reference forests - collections of verified-success graphs showing diverse successful approaches. ForestBench implements this by filtering collaboration-necessary queries from public datasets, precomputing reference graphs, and evaluating MAS frameworks through structural comparison.
AI.result: ForestBench achieves evaluation in milliseconds without LLM inference once benchmark forests are built. It provides stable structural evaluation through controlled studies testing backbone, reference-construction, and perturbation. The system evaluates six representative MAS frameworks using 844 collaboration-necessary queries with ten successful target-conditioned reference graphs per query.
AI.conclusion: ForestBench offers a generalizable, efficient evaluation framework that enables direct comparison of diverse MAS collaboration traces on a common structural basis, overcoming limitations of outcome-only and LLM-as-Judge approaches through reusable reference forests.

title: Beyond Solvability: Task Learnability as a Static Prior for LLM RL Post-Training
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central post-training paradigm for eliciting reasoning capabilities in large language models, yet uniform task sampling allocates compute without regard to differences in how tasks respond to optimization. Existing task-valuation methods mostly rely on snapshot-based signals such as current pass rate or reward, which estimate how solvable a task is under the current policy. However, tasks with similar current solvability can still differ substantially in how positively they respond to further training. We study this residual axis as task learnability: a regime-conditional measure of expected positive response to continued training under a fixed RL post-training regime. By analyzing per-task reward trajectories, we find that learnability is reproducible across independently sampled training contexts and predictive of downstream utility. To make this signal practical before training begins, we propose TrajVal, a lightweight probe-based estimator that approximates per-task learnability from a short probe run and two endpoint evaluations. TrajVal can be used either as a standalone static prior for task sampling or as a multiplicative prior for existing online schedulers. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks across multiple model scales show that TrajVal improves data efficiency over uniform sampling and provides complementary gains when combined with online scheduling methods.

AI.tldr: TrajVal is a method that estimates task learnability (expected positive response to continued training) using short probe runs, improving reinforcement learning data efficiency for language model reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Current RL post-training methods use uniform task sampling or snapshot-based valuations (like current pass rate), but tasks with similar current solvability can have different responses to further training. This leads to inefficient compute allocation.
AI.method: TrajVal: A lightweight probe-based estimator that approximates per-task learnability from a short probe run and two endpoint evaluations. It measures task learnability as a regime-conditional measure of expected positive response to continued training.
AI.result: TrajVal improves data efficiency over uniform sampling and provides complementary gains when combined with existing online schedulers. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks across multiple model scales demonstrate effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Task learnability is a reproducible and predictive signal for RL post-training efficiency. TrajVal enables more efficient compute allocation by identifying tasks that respond well to further training before full training begins.

title: Walking through Discussions: A Mobile Visual Analytics System for In-Situ Group Discussion Analysis
summary: Group discussion-based teaching is widely used to foster collaborative learning, yet teachers in physical classrooms often struggle to simultaneously monitor multiple groups and quickly diagnose a target group before intervening. Existing visual analytics tools primarily support post-hoc analysis on desktop, providing limited support for in-situ walk-around teaching. To address this gap, we present MobileGroupVis, a mobile visual analytics system for in-situ analysis of classroom group discussions. MobileGroupVis integrates multi-group monitoring, single-group diagnosis, and instructional intervention into a concise analytical workflow tailored for small-screen touch interaction. The system is powered by a lightweight streaming analysis pipeline that converts group audio into structured discussion data and further extracts interaction patterns, topic progression, and topic deviation through a dialogue analysis module. To enable both glanceable overview and traceable diagnosis, we design six coordinated views, including a compact glyph that visually encodes word count, interaction intensity, and topic deviation for efficient cross-group comparison and anomaly localization, along with detailed views for opinion evolution, interaction dynamics, topic coverage, and dialogue records. We evaluate MobileGroupVis through two case studies and expert interviews. The results provide preliminary evidence that MobileGroupVis supports teachers in understanding discussion processes, identifying groups in need of attention, and facilitating in-class intervention.

AI.tldr: MobileGroupVis is a mobile visual analytics system for real-time monitoring and analysis of classroom group discussions during walk-around teaching, enabling teachers to quickly identify groups needing attention through glanceable visualizations on small screens.
AI.motivation: Teachers in physical classrooms struggle to simultaneously monitor multiple discussion groups and quickly diagnose specific groups before intervening. Existing tools only support post-hoc desktop analysis, lacking support for in-situ walk-around teaching during group discussions.
AI.method: Developed MobileGroupVis, a mobile visual analytics system with a lightweight streaming pipeline that converts group audio into structured discussion data, extracts interaction patterns, topic progression, and deviation. Features six coordinated views including a compact glyph for cross-group comparison and detailed views for opinion evolution, interaction dynamics, topic coverage, and dialogue records.
AI.result: Evaluation through two case studies and expert interviews showed preliminary evidence that MobileGroupVis helps teachers understand discussion processes, identify groups needing attention, and facilitate in-class intervention during walk-around teaching.
AI.conclusion: MobileGroupVis successfully bridges the gap between post-hoc desktop analysis tools and in-situ teaching needs by providing a mobile visual analytics system that supports real-time monitoring, diagnosis, and intervention for classroom group discussions.

title: Online Learning of Scale Parameters in Score-Driven Filters
summary: Score-driven filters multiply a scaled log-likelihood score by a gain that controls the update magnitude. We treat this gain as a decision variable and study its online learning. Conditional on the current state, observation, score, and scaling rule, each admissible gain induces a reachable next state and a one-step-ahead predictive density: scalar gains govern distance along a line, while diagonal gains govern coordinatewise transmission. Gain selection is therefore a conditional predictive decision problem with a Kullback-Leibler objective. For a scalar unscaled gain, the negative raw product of consecutive scores is the stochastic gradient of this loss; positive aGAS scaling only rescales the effective step. Monotone differentiable gain links induce mirror-descent geometries on bounded gain domains, while persistence yields a Bregman pull towards a reference gain. Under convexity, compactness, and regularity conditions, we establish dynamic-regret bounds for projected and discounted mirror updates relative to time-varying, current-information comparators. Simulations illustrate the roles of scaling, link geometry, persistence, and coordinatewise transmission rates. An out-of-sample panel of equity-index volatilities shows that the bounded mirror gain generally matches or outperforms a constant gain while avoiding the extreme spikes of a nominally unbounded exponential link, with the strongest improvements observed in multi-crisis markets.

AI.tldr: The paper studies online learning of gains in score-driven filters, treating gain selection as a conditional predictive decision problem with Kullback-Leibler objective and providing dynamic regret bounds for mirror descent updates.
AI.motivation: Score-driven filters use gains to control update magnitude, but conventional approaches use constant or fixed gains. The authors propose to treat gains as decision variables that can be learned online for improved filtering performance.
AI.method: They formulate gain selection as a conditional predictive decision problem with Kullback-Leibler objective. They show that negative raw product of consecutive scores gives the stochastic gradient for scalar gains. They use mirror descent with monotone differentiable gain links and persistence terms (Bregman pull toward reference gains). Under convexity, compactness, and regularity conditions, they establish dynamic regret bounds for projected and discounted mirror updates.
AI.result: Theoretical results: dynamic regret bounds relative to time-varying comparators. Empirical results: simulations show roles of scaling, link geometry, persistence, and coordinatewise transmission. Out-of-sample application to equity-index volatilities shows bounded mirror gain matches/outperforms constant gain while avoiding extreme spikes of unbounded exponential link, with strongest improvements in multi-crisis markets.
AI.conclusion: Online learning of gains in score-driven filters via mirror descent provides robust performance improvements, especially with bounded gain domains to avoid extreme updates while maintaining or exceeding constant gain performance, particularly valuable in volatile market conditions.

title: Business Arena: Benchmarking LLM Agents in a Realistic Marketplace
summary: Running a business is a challenging form of intelligent work. Operators must infer opportunities from partial signals, commit capital under uncertainty, adapt to delayed outcomes in a changing market, and satisfy regulatory obligations before trading legally. Frontier LLM agents can increasingly complete complex workflows, yet business-related capabilities are rarely evaluated in existing agent benchmarks. We introduce \textbf{Business Arena}, a controlled environment where an AI agent runs a cross-border shop, buying from suppliers and selling to buyers over a long horizon. We ground the arena in real Alibaba.com sourcing data and market conditions calibrated from authoritative sources. Delayed and coupled consequences make individual business decisions difficult to judge, but their combined outcome is measurable through profit. Because profit alone cannot explain why an agent succeeds or fails, we compare agents with human-designed strategies to estimate available opportunity, use skill-level metrics to reveal underlying strengths and weaknesses, and trace realized gains and losses to the actions that produced them. We use mechanism ablations to establish that strong results reflect genuine business intelligence rather than neglect or simulator-specific shortcuts. We evaluate 15 frontier models and find a ninefold difference in mean final net worth. Even the best model falls behind human-designed strategies, indicating that business operation remains challenging for LLM agents. Skill-level analysis reveals operating styles, from margin-focused premium sellers to high-turnover wholesalers and customer-service specialists, while action-level attribution identifies the sourcing, pricing, and recovery decisions that create or destroy value. Together, Business Arena takes a first step toward a realistic and trustworthy testbed for evaluating end-to-end business agents.

AI.tldr: Business Arena is a new AI agent benchmark for evaluating business operation capabilities using real Alibaba.com data, measuring performance through profit while analyzing skills and decision-making patterns.
AI.motivation: Business operation is complex intelligent work involving opportunity inference, capital allocation under uncertainty, adaptation to delayed outcomes, and regulatory compliance. Existing AI agent benchmarks rarely evaluate business-related capabilities, creating a gap in assessing LLM agents' ability to handle real-world business challenges.
AI.method: The authors created Business Arena - a controlled environment where AI agents run cross-border shops with long horizons. They used real Alibaba.com sourcing data and market conditions calibrated from authoritative sources. Agents are evaluated through profit outcomes, with additional analysis including comparison to human-designed strategies, skill-level metrics, action-level attribution, and mechanism ablations to ensure genuine business intelligence rather than shortcuts.
AI.result: Evaluation of 15 frontier models showed a ninefold difference in mean final net worth. Even the best model underperformed compared to human-designed strategies, indicating business operation remains challenging for LLM agents. Skill analysis revealed distinct operating styles (margin-focused sellers, high-turnover wholesalers, customer-service specialists), and action-level attribution identified value-creating/destroying decisions in sourcing, pricing, and recovery.
AI.conclusion: Business Arena represents a first step toward creating realistic and trustworthy testbeds for evaluating end-to-end business agents, moving beyond simple profit metrics to understand underlying business intelligence, skills, and decision-making patterns.

title: FedTVD: Balancing Data Quality and Quantity for Robust Federated Learning
summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed client devices while preserving data privacy. However, FL faces significant challenges due to data heterogeneity, particularly in terms of label distribution skewness and variations in dataset sizes, which can lead to biased model updates and hinder convergence. To address this, we propose FedTVD, a novel FL algorithm that weights client contributions during aggregation by considering both data quality and quantity. Unlike traditional FL approaches such as FedAvg, which rely solely on dataset size for client weighting, FedTVD integrates Total Variation Distance (TVD) to measure the divergence between each client's local label distribution and a uniform global distribution. Clients with highly skewed distributions receive lower weights, preventing unbalanced datasets with imbalances from disproportionately influencing the global model. At the same time, dataset size is incorporated to ensure scalability and fairness. This dual-weighting mechanism effectively mitigates the impact of data imbalance, leading to more stable and generalized global models. Experimental results show that FedTVD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across all datasets (FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100) and all levels of data heterogeneity. Notably, it achieves up to 10.6% improvement over FedAvg on CIFAR-10 under highly skewed data, while maintaining top performance even under moderate and IID settings.

AI.tldr: FedTVD is a federated learning algorithm that addresses data heterogeneity by weighting client contributions using both dataset size and Total Variation Distance to measure label distribution skewness, outperforming existing methods across various datasets.
AI.motivation: Federated Learning faces challenges from data heterogeneity, particularly label distribution skewness and varying dataset sizes, which cause biased model updates and hinder convergence. Traditional methods like FedAvg only consider dataset size, failing to account for data quality issues.
AI.method: FedTVD proposes a dual-weighting mechanism during client aggregation: (1) incorporates Total Variation Distance to measure divergence between each client's local label distribution and a uniform global distribution, giving lower weights to clients with highly skewed distributions, and (2) includes dataset size for scalability and fairness considerations.
AI.result: Experimental results show FedTVD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets at all levels of data heterogeneity. Achieves up to 10.6% improvement over FedAvg on CIFAR-10 under highly skewed data while maintaining top performance even under moderate and IID settings.
AI.conclusion: FedTVD's dual-weighting approach effectively mitigates the impact of data imbalance in federated learning, leading to more stable and generalized global models by accounting for both data quality (via TVD) and quantity (dataset size) during client aggregation.

title: MedCalc-R1: Knowledge-Guided Reward Framework for Medical Mathematical Reasoning
summary: In Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) frameworks for mathematical reasoning tasks, floating-point results are typically evaluated using a tolerance-based reward. However, this strategy suffers from challenges such as difficulty in threshold calibration, unstable training dynamics, and limited accuracy, especially in clinical scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a knowledge-guided hybrid reward framework (\textsc{MedCalc-R1}). Specifically, we introduce a knowledge verification reward mechanism that enforces explicit generation of computational formulas, which are further validated by an external verifier to enhance interpretability and reasoning reliability. Furthermore, we design a hybrid soft-hard reward scheme combining a hard constraint based on clinical safety thresholds with a soft, precision-sensitive reward that progressively guides learning within the acceptable range. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines in both reasoning accuracy and generalization capability, validating the effectiveness and applicability in safety-critical domains.

AI.tldr: Proposes MedCalc-R1, a knowledge-guided hybrid reward framework for medical calculation tasks that improves upon tolerance-based rewards through explicit formula generation verification and soft-hard reward combination.
AI.motivation: Traditional Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) frameworks for mathematical reasoning use tolerance-based rewards, which suffer from threshold calibration difficulties, unstable training dynamics, limited accuracy, and are particularly problematic in clinical scenarios where safety is critical.
AI.method: Proposes MedCalc-R1 framework with two key components: 1) Knowledge verification reward mechanism that enforces explicit generation of computational formulas validated by external verifier, and 2) Hybrid soft-hard reward scheme combining hard clinical safety threshold constraints with soft, precision-sensitive reward that progressively guides learning within acceptable ranges.
AI.result: Experimental results show the method significantly outperforms existing baselines in both reasoning accuracy and generalization capability, validating effectiveness in safety-critical domains.
AI.conclusion: The proposed knowledge-guided hybrid reward framework (MedCalc-R1) effectively addresses limitations of traditional tolerance-based rewards in RLVR for mathematical reasoning, particularly enhancing interpretability, reliability, and safety in clinical applications.

title: Privileged Solutions or Context-Induced Teacher Behavior? Dissecting On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) is commonly interpreted as the transfer of privileged information: a teacher observes the verified solution to the target problem and supervises the student's trajectory. However, this interpretation conflates two effects. The reference solution not only reveals the answer to the current instance but also changes the context under which the teacher provides token-level supervision. We investigate the role of target-specific privilege with $\mathrm{OP}^{2}\mathrm{SD}$ (On-Policy Self-Distillation from Other Problems), which replaces the paired reference with a problem and solution from a different example, while preserving the student rollout, teacher, and distillation objective. Across three models and three mathematics benchmarks, $\mathrm{OP}^{2}\mathrm{SD}$ improves over the base model, remains competitive with OPSD. The success of $\mathrm{OP}^{2}\mathrm{SD}$ implies that OPSD gains do not necessarily come from access to the reference solution, and that the teacher's context-induced behavior is an important factor.

AI.tldr: OP²SD (On-Policy Self-Distillation from Other Problems) shows that self-distillation gains come more from teacher's context-induced behavior than from access to reference solutions.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the conventional interpretation that On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) works primarily through privileged access to reference solutions. It aims to disentangle two conflated effects: the actual answer information and the teacher's context-induced supervision.
AI.method: Proposes OP²SD, which replaces the reference solution with a different problem's solution while keeping the student rollout, teacher model, and distillation objective unchanged. This isolates the effect of teacher context from target-specific privilege.
AI.result: Across three models and three mathematics benchmarks, OP²SD improves over base models and remains competitive with standard OPSD, demonstrating that distillation gains don't require access to the target problem's reference solution.
AI.conclusion: The success of OP²SD shows OPSD's benefits come significantly from the teacher's context-induced behavior rather than privileged access to reference solutions, reshaping understanding of how self-distillation works.

title: UniMoMo: Expert Merging-Based MoE Acceleration for Large Recommendation Models
summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers expand recommendation capacity through conditional computation, yet a trained checkpoint still stores and routes over its full expert bank. We study a deployment problem: convert that checkpoint to a smaller standard MoE under an explicit expert budget, without adding a compression-specific online module. To address this, we introduce UniMoMo, a post-training compression framework formulated as a constrained graph coarsening problem. Rather than relying on parameter distance, UniMoMo groups experts based on their functional similarity, using an unlabeled calibration set to measure how similarly experts respond to shared recommendation states. To prevent performance degradation, we introduce a layer-adaptive protection mechanism that restricts the merging of high-traffic experts based on their routing exposure. Across Amazon Beauty, KuaiRec, and TenRec with 2, 4, and 6 MoE blocks, the final four-expert checkpoints obtain source-relative five-run mean NDCG@10 ratios of 99.92%--102.30% and measured A100 speedups of 1.28$\times$--1.63$\times$. An aggressive two-expert, top-1 operating point obtains ratios of 98.36%--104.24% and speedups of 1.47$\times$--2.21$\times$. These endpoint results evaluate the complete conversion-and-adaptation workflow and show that a trained recommendation MoE can be exported at multiple serving budgets.

AI.tldr: UniMoMo is a post-training compression framework for sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) recommendation models that groups experts by functional similarity rather than parameter distance, enabling deployment at reduced expert budgets without performance loss.
AI.motivation: Sparse MoE layers expand recommendation capacity but trained checkpoints still store and route over the full expert bank. There's a need to compress these models for deployment under explicit expert budgets without adding compression-specific online modules.
AI.method: UniMoMo formulates compression as a constrained graph coarsening problem, grouping experts based on functional similarity measured using an unlabeled calibration set. It introduces a layer-adaptive protection mechanism that restricts merging of high-traffic experts based on routing exposure.
AI.result: Compressed four-expert checkpoints achieved source-relative NDCG@10 ratios of 99.92%--102.30% with A100 speedups of 1.28×--1.63× across Amazon Beauty, KuaiRec, and TenRec datasets. Aggressive two-expert compression maintained 98.36%--104.24% NDCG ratios with 1.47×--2.21× speedups.
AI.conclusion: Trained recommendation MoE models can be effectively compressed post-training for multiple serving budgets using functional similarity-based expert grouping, maintaining performance while achieving significant inference speedups.

title: DreOPD: Degraded-Reference Extrapolative On-Policy Distillation for Flow-matching Models
summary: Flow-matching models are now a mainstream method to image generation, but its adaptation to diverse downstream scenarios typically relies on post-training, which may cause conflicts among task-specific optimization objectives. Reinforcement learning enables direct optimization of task-specific rewards beyond the original models, yet trajectory-level optimization may incur high-variance gradients and cross-task interference. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers dense and stable supervision on student rollouts, but conventional teacher matching remains imitation-based. We propose DreOPD, a Degraded-reference extrapolative OPD method for flow-matching models that bridges these two paradigms. Our DreOPD converts implicit reward extrapolation into closed-form velocity regression, enabling extrapolative post-training with the stability of OPD. It further uses a mildly degraded reference to strengthen the teacher-reference contrast, yielding a clearer extrapolation direction. Experiments on single- and multi-teacher settings show that DreOPD outperforms OPD and multi-task RL baselines in average performance, while surpassing specialized teachers on most metrics.

AI.tldr: DreOPD is a novel method that combines reinforcement learning with on-policy distillation to enhance flow-matching models for downstream tasks, using degraded references and velocity regression for stable extrapolative optimization.
AI.motivation: Current approaches for adapting flow-matching models to downstream tasks have limitations: post-training causes optimization conflicts, reinforcement learning suffers from high-variance gradients, and conventional on-policy distillation is imitation-based without extrapolation capability.
AI.method: Proposes DreOPD (Degraded-reference extrapolative OPD) that converts implicit reward extrapolation into closed-form velocity regression for flow-matching models. It uses mildly degraded references to strengthen teacher-reference contrast, providing clearer extrapolation direction while maintaining the stability of on-policy distillation.
AI.result: Experiments in single- and multi-teacher settings show DreOPD outperforms OPD and multi-task RL baselines in average performance, and surpasses specialized teachers on most metrics.
AI.conclusion: DreOPD successfully bridges reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation paradigms, enabling stable extrapolative post-training for flow-matching models that outperforms existing approaches while maintaining training stability.

title: A QUBO-Inspired Computational Framework for Airport Landside Bottleneck Diagnosis and Dynamic Dispatch Optimization
summary: Airport landside traffic centers connect terminal arrivals with taxis, ride-hailing vehicles, private cars, buses, metro services, parking facilities, and terminal-area roadways. Peak arrivals can create coupled congestion across passenger queues, vehicle queues, pickup berths, storage areas, and access roads. This study proposes a QUBO-inspired computational framework for bottleneck diagnosis and dynamic dispatch in this setting. Shanghai Pudong International Airport and Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport serve as case airports. A five-minute state model links passenger arrivals, vehicle supply, pickup berth service, vehicle storage, and road capacity. Bottleneck diagnosis uses service intensity, road demand saturation, bottleneck frequency, queue severity, shadow-price leverage, and a composite congestion severity index. Two dispatch schemes are tested under consistent demand inputs: finite-action model predictive control and quadratic-unconstrained-binary-optimization-inspired simulated annealing. In the strong-peak baseline scenario, the QUBO-inspired method reduces the final passenger queue from 3445 to 2477 passengers at Shanghai Pudong and from 2053 to 1482 passengers at Hangzhou Xiaoshan. Case results indicate different dominant bottlenecks. Shanghai Pudong is more affected by road saturation, whereas Hangzhou Xiaoshan is more affected by pickup berth service. Robustness tests under demand, supply, service, road-capacity, modal-share, and random-noise perturbations show retained queue-reduction benefits under the tested uncertainty levels.

AI.tldr: QUBO-inspired computational framework improves airport landside traffic congestion by diagnosing bottlenecks and optimizing dynamic dispatch, tested at Shanghai Pudong and Hangzhou Xiaoshan airports.
AI.motivation: Airport landside traffic centers face coupled congestion across passenger queues, vehicle queues, pickup berths, storage areas, and access roads during peak arrivals, requiring better diagnostic and dispatch methods.
AI.method: Proposes a QUBO-inspired computational framework with five-minute state model linking various system components, uses six bottleneck diagnostic metrics, and compares two dispatch schemes: finite-action MPC and QUBO-inspired simulated annealing.
AI.result: QUBO-inspired method reduced final passenger queue from 3445 to 2477 at Shanghai Pudong and from 2053 to 1482 at Hangzhou Xiaoshan; identified different dominant bottlenecks between airports; showed robustness under various perturbations.
AI.conclusion: The QUBO-inspired framework effectively diagnoses landside bottlenecks and improves dispatch decisions, with demonstrated queue reduction benefits that remain robust under uncertainty, though bottleneck dominance varies by airport characteristics.

title: Label Granularity Skew in Federated Learning with Hierarchical Image Classification
summary: Federated learning enables privacy-preserving collaboration across distributed devices without centralizing local data. However, clients may differ not only in data distributions but also in domain knowledge and annotation capabilities. In this paper, we introduce label granularity skew, a new form of statistical heterogeneity in federated hierarchical classification, in which clients provide taxonomy-consistent labels at different levels of detail within a shared class hierarchy. To model this heterogeneity, we generate client-specific local label hierarchies using a probabilistic relational neighbor classifier and construct a WordNet-guided hierarchy via silhouette score-based coarsening. Our analysis shows that strongly coupled hierarchical models are sensitive to incomplete supervision, while the conditional softmax classifier is more robust. Based on this insight, we propose Branch-wise Decoupled Fine-Tuning (BDFT) and its federated version, FedBDFT, which fine-tune branch-wise classifiers and aggregate them through federated optimization. Experiments on CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet show that FedBDFT substantially improves robustness under severe label granularity skew, with average gains of 27.9% and 56.4% at skewness levels of 0.6 and 0.9, respectively. Zero-shot results further indicate that FedBDFT better preserves hierarchical representations for unseen fine-grained classes. These findings demonstrate its effectiveness for federated hierarchical classification with heterogeneous label granularities.

AI.tldr: FedBDFT addresses label granularity skew in federated hierarchical classification by decoupling branch-wise classifiers and aggregating them through federated optimization.
AI.motivation: Federated learning faces challenges when clients differ not only in data distributions but also in domain knowledge and annotation capabilities, leading to a new form of heterogeneity called "label granularity skew" where clients provide taxonomy-consistent labels at different levels of detail within a shared class hierarchy.
AI.method: 1) Models label granularity skew by generating client-specific local label hierarchies using probabilistic relational neighbor classifier and constructing WordNet-guided hierarchy via silhouette score-based coarsening. 2) Proposes Branch-wise Decoupled Fine-Tuning (BDFT) and its federated version FedBDFT, which fine-tune branch-wise classifiers and aggregate them through federated optimization based on the insight that conditional softmax classifiers are more robust than strongly coupled hierarchical models.
AI.result: FedBDFT substantially improves robustness under severe label granularity skew, with average gains of 27.9% and 56.4% at skewness levels of 0.6 and 0.9, respectively. Zero-shot results show better preservation of hierarchical representations for unseen fine-grained classes.
AI.conclusion: FedBDFT effectively addresses federated hierarchical classification with heterogeneous label granularities, demonstrating superior robustness to label granularity skew through decoupled branch-wise optimization and federated aggregation.

title: Can Open-Weight Models Compete on Financial Text Comprehension?
comment: To be presented at the workshop International Symposium on Large Language Models for Financial Services (FinLLM@IJCAI2026)
summary: Open-weight language models from Chinese AI labs caught up on benchmarks relative to proprietary frontier models in recent months. Yet their reliability on real-world financial tasks remains largely untested. We updated the Financial Touchstone benchmark, which now has 2,967 question context-answer triplets across 495 international annual reports. We also apply a new set of models on the benchmark, expanding coverage from eleven to twenty models across ten providers, including recent open-weight models such as GLM 4.7, GLM 5, Kimi K2.6, and DeepSeek V3.2, as well as Alibaba's proprietary flagship Qwen3-Max. Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 achieves the highest accuracy (88.4%), while Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro maintains the lowest hallucination rate (0.08%). Notably, the open-weight Kimi K2.6 ranks third in accuracy, and the non-reasoning models GLM 5 and Mistral 3 rank fourth and fifth, challenging the assumption that reasoning architectures or proprietary weights are a prerequisite for strong financial comprehension. Information retrieval remains the primary bottleneck, accounting for 48.9% of all failures. We also document a new finding: geopolitical content filters in Chinese models refuse legitimate financial questions (0.08% of attempts), sometimes without clear reason, and the refusal behavior depends on the access route as much as on the model. The complete dataset and evaluation framework are publicly available.

AI.tldr: Chinese open-weight LLMs show strong financial comprehension, with Kimi K2.6 ranking third in accuracy on financial benchmarks, challenging assumptions about proprietary models and reasoning architectures.
AI.motivation: To test the real-world reliability of Chinese open-weight language models on financial tasks, despite their recent benchmark improvements, and to expand evaluation coverage to more recent models including GLM 4.7, GLM 5, Kimi K2.6, and DeepSeek V3.2.
AI.method: Updated Financial Touchstone benchmark with 2,967 question-context-answer triplets across 495 international annual reports, evaluated 20 models from 10 providers, including both open-weight and proprietary models.
AI.result: Claude Opus 4.6 achieved highest accuracy (88.4%), Gemini 2.5 Pro had lowest hallucination rate (0.08%), and open-weight Kimi K2.6 ranked third in accuracy. Information retrieval was the main bottleneck (48.9% of failures). Chinese models showed geopolitical content filters refusing legitimate financial questions (0.08% of attempts).
AI.conclusion: Open-weight models like Kimi K2.6 can achieve strong financial comprehension without proprietary weights or reasoning architectures, but information retrieval remains a key challenge, and geopolitical content filters in Chinese models affect reliability.

title: Multimodal Federated Learning under Dual-Axis Modality Missingness
summary: Multimodal federated learning (FL) supports collaborative modeling in privacy-sensitive health-sensing and medical settings, but realistic deployments often exhibit dual-axis modality missingness: clients have different modality sets, and individual samples may contain only subsets of the modalities available locally. Existing methods typically address these two axes separately. We propose Flux, a multimodal federated learning framework built around two complementary components. First, modality-aware confidence tempering learns sample-specific confidence for each modality through mask-aware unimodal supervision and fuses the confidence estimates from observed modalities into a sample-adaptive temperature that adjusts predictive sharpness according to evidence quality and completeness. Second, gradient-decoupled private adaptation applies this temperature only to a client-private prediction pathway, while training the shared federated model with a standard, untempered objective. This enables sample-specific, client-local confidence adaptation without allowing confidence-dependent gradients to perturb shared representation learning. Across four multimodal datasets, Flux achieves the highest average macro-F1 on every dataset, outperforming the strongest dataset-specific baseline by 0.8~2.2 points and by 1.6 points on average. Additional analyses demonstrate favorable calibration, temperature sensitivity to both modality missingness and input corruption, and more stable shared optimization under private-only tempering. Our code is available at https://github.com/AdibaOrz/Flux.

AI.tldr: Flux is a multimodal federated learning framework that handles dual-axis modality missingness through modality-aware confidence tempering and gradient-decoupled private adaptation, achieving state-of-the-art performance across four datasets while maintaining stable shared model optimization.
AI.motivation: Real-world multimodal federated learning deployments in health-sensing and medical settings face two key challenges: (1) clients have different modality sets, and (2) individual samples may contain only subsets of the modalities available locally. Existing methods typically address these dual-axis modality missingness issues separately rather than holistically.
AI.method: Flux consists of two complementary components: 1) Modality-aware confidence tempering learns sample-specific confidence for each modality through mask-aware unimodal supervision, fusing confidence estimates into a sample-adaptive temperature that adjusts predictive sharpness based on evidence quality and completeness. 2) Gradient-decoupled private adaptation applies this temperature only to a client-private prediction pathway while training the shared federated model with a standard, untempered objective, preventing confidence-dependent gradients from perturbing shared representation learning.
AI.result: Across four multimodal datasets, Flux achieves the highest average macro-F1 on every dataset, outperforming the strongest dataset-specific baseline by 0.8~2.2 points and by 1.6 points on average. The framework also demonstrates favorable calibration, temperature sensitivity to both modality missingness and input corruption, and more stable shared optimization under private-only tempering.
