AI.motivation: Current healthcare IT is organized around technologies rather than clinical information units. There's a need to better capture and make computable patient-specific clinical intent that exists in natural clinical communication but isn't adequately represented in existing systems and standards.
AI.method: Develop criteria for a computational layer, derive three layers (record, clinical state, and proposed intent layer), formalize the Actionable Clinical Record (ACR) as the atomic object of the intent layer, and conduct a companion feasibility study for a narrow subproblem to demonstrate tractability.
AI.result: The paper establishes computable clinical intent as a coherent research direction, introduces the ACR as a formal construct, provides a readiness ladder for implementation, and develops an executable-correctness evaluation framework. The framework distinguishes between prescribed, observed, and intended clinical processes.
AI.conclusion: Computable clinical intent represents a viable research direction with practical constructs like the ACR, readiness ladder, and evaluation framework that can be reused, extended, evaluated, or falsified in subsequent work, complementing existing standards like FHIR workflow resources, guidelines, and process mining.

title: A Mechanistic Diagnostic of Rank Collapse in Post-Norm Decoder Transformers
summary: Deep decoder-only Transformers often replace the original Post-Norm architecture with Pre-Norm variants because Post-Norm training is highly sensitive to warmup and learning rate under conventional initialization schemes. Although prior work has identified rank collapse and gradient vanishing as related symptoms, it remains poorly understood how causal attention creates high-similarity representations and why training dynamics fail to repair them. We give a two-stage analysis of Post-Norm rank collapse using token similarity as a scalar state variable. First, at initialization, causal attention acts approximately as a prefix-averaging operator that increases token similarity across depth, while the SwiGLU branch contributes only a smaller damping effect. Second, once training enters a high-similarity regime, growth of pre-normalization residual norms makes the RMSNorm backward factor contractive; under mild conditions, gradients to earlier layers decay geometrically. As a complementary result, we characterize the properties of a collapsed network: its best predictor is frequency distribution with relatively high loss floor, and gradients in collapsed layers vanish at frequency distribution. Experiments on 48-layer decoder-only Transformers trained on C4 dataset match the predicted initialization-time similarity growth and collapse-time gradient contraction, and show that collapsed runs stay near the predicted frequency loss. Together, these results distinguish the forward similarity amplification and backward repair incapacity in Post-Norm collapse, while also characterizing the behavior of collapsed networks.

AI.tldr: Post-Norm Transformer training fails due to causal attention creating highly similar token representations that RMSNorm gradient contraction cannot repair during training, unlike Pre-Norm variants that avoid this issue.
AI.motivation: Deep decoder-only Transformers use Pre-Norm instead of Post-Norm because Post-Norm training is highly sensitive to warmup and learning rate under conventional initialization. The fundamental reasons why causal attention creates high-similarity representations and why training dynamics fail to repair them remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Two-stage analysis using token similarity as a scalar state variable: 1) At initialization, causal attention acts as a prefix-averaging operator increasing token similarity, while SwiGLU provides damping; 2) During training in high-similarity regime, RMSNorm backward factor becomes contractive causing geometric gradient decay to earlier layers. Characterizes collapsed network properties predicting frequency distribution with high loss floor.
AI.result: Experiments on 48-layer decoder-only Transformers on C4 dataset confirm: 1) initialization-time similarity growth, 2) collapse-time gradient contraction, and 3) collapsed runs stay near predicted frequency loss. Distinguishes forward similarity amplification from backward repair incapacity in Post-Norm collapse.
AI.conclusion: Post-Norm collapse involves two distinct mechanisms: causal attention creates increasingly similar token representations forward in depth, while RMSNorm gradient contraction prevents backward repair during training. This explains why Post-Norm requires careful initialization and why collapsed networks predict frequency distributions with high irreducible loss.

title: Automated Generation of Complexity-Validated Decision Scenarios Using Large Language Models
summary: Cognitive decision-making research depends on diverse scenarios with carefully controlled complexity, yet manual production is slow, inconsistent, and biased. We developed an automated pipeline that uses LLms to generate structured decision scenarios and validates their complexity through a composite framework rooted in established task-complexity theory. We evaluated 4,238 scenarios across multiple domains and complexity tiers. Measurement validation met rigorous psychometric standards. Agreement among five independent model families was nearly perfect, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.997 and a kappa of 0.971. Known-groups validity demonstrated large separation between tiers, with an eta-squared of 0.587 and all pairwise comparisons significant at p less than .001. Factor analysis revealed a dominant complexity construct, with loadings between 0.87 and 0.96 across three frameworks, while interactivity formed a weaker secondary dimension at 0.34. Discriminant validity was limited by a strong relationship between complexity and text length that persisted after controlling for tier, yielding a partial correlation of 0.86. This constrains construct purity but does not undermine the instrument's tier-grading function. Model analyses showed a negative association between throughput and schema pass rate (r = -0.967, p = .007, n = 5), suggesting a speed-quality trade-off, though largely driven by one high-throughput model. Llama 4 Maverick generated scenarios fastest at 134 per minute versus 25 for DeepSeek Chat V3.2, but underproduced complex-tier scenarios, whereas DeepSeek Chat V3.2 balanced domain coverage with high schema compliance. The system demonstrated strong psychometric properties, enabling reliable classification into Simple, Moderate, and Complex tiers and providing the measurement infrastructure needed for downstream cognitive assessment of AI systems

AI.tldr: An automated pipeline using LLMs generates and validates structured decision scenarios for cognitive research, achieving reliable complexity classification with strong psychometric properties across 4,238 scenarios.
AI.motivation: Manual production of decision scenarios for cognitive research is slow, inconsistent, and biased, creating a need for automated, standardized scenario generation.
AI.method: Developed an LLM-based pipeline to generate structured decision scenarios, validated complexity using a composite framework from task-complexity theory, evaluated 4,238 scenarios across domains and complexity tiers with psychometric validation.
AI.result: Strong psychometric validation with near-perfect model agreement (ICC=0.997, kappa=0.971), large tier separation (eta-squared=0.587), dominant complexity construct (loadings 0.87-0.96), but limited discriminant validity due to correlation with text length. Llama 4 Maverick generated fastest (134/min) but underproduced complex scenarios, while DeepSeek Chat V3.2 balanced coverage with compliance.
AI.conclusion: The system provides reliable complexity classification into Simple, Moderate, and Complex tiers with strong psychometric properties, enabling measurement infrastructure for downstream AI cognitive assessment despite some construct purity limitations.

title: LITEWAY: LIghtweight HAR via Temporal Efficient highWAY
summary: Wearable human activity recognition (HAR) remains challenging due to the computational and energy constraints of deep learning models on resource-limited devices. Existing lightweight approaches often rely on recurrent architectures (e.g., GRU and LSTM), limiting parallelism and increasing inference latency. We propose LITEWAY, a modality-agnostic, fully convolutional framework for multichannel sensor time series that replaces recurrent temporal modeling with structured convolutional decomposition. LITEWAY combines lightweight convolutional blocks, strided temporal processing, and convolution-attention pooling to efficiently capture temporal dependencies while reducing computational complexity. We evaluate LITEWAY on 16 HAR datasets against TinyHAR, TinierHAR, and MLP-HAR. LITEWAY achieves competitive macro F1 while reducing model size by 4.06x-9.52x (Light) and 3.87x-9.07x (Full) compared with TinyHAR and TinierHAR. Deployment experiments further show energy reductions of 2.29x-3.14x (Light) and 1.46x-2.01x (Full) compared with TinierHAR and MLP-HAR, highlighting efficient fully convolutional temporal modeling for wearable HAR. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/dominique-nshimyimana/liteway.

AI.tldr: LITEWAY is a fully convolutional framework for wearable human activity recognition that replaces recurrent temporal modeling with structured convolutional decomposition, achieving competitive performance with significantly smaller model sizes and lower energy consumption on resource-constrained devices.
AI.motivation: Wearable human activity recognition faces computational and energy constraints on resource-limited devices. Existing lightweight approaches using recurrent architectures (GRU/LSTM) limit parallelism and increase inference latency, creating a need for more efficient temporal modeling approaches.
AI.method: LITEWAY uses a modality-agnostic, fully convolutional framework with structured convolutional decomposition to replace recurrent temporal modeling. It combines lightweight convolutional blocks, strided temporal processing, and convolution-attention pooling to efficiently capture temporal dependencies while reducing computational complexity.
AI.result: On 16 HAR datasets, LITEWAY achieves competitive macro F1 scores while reducing model size by 4.06x-9.52x (Light version) and 3.87x-9.07x (Full version) compared with TinyHAR and TinierHAR. Deployment experiments show energy reductions of 2.29x-3.14x (Light) and 1.46x-2.01x (Full) compared with baseline models.
AI.conclusion: LITEWAY demonstrates that efficient fully convolutional temporal modeling can effectively replace recurrent architectures for wearable HAR, offering significant improvements in model size and energy efficiency while maintaining competitive accuracy, making it suitable for deployment on resource-constrained wearable devices.

title: PROSLEX: A Novel Dataset for Expert-Annotated Legal Statute Prediction for Indian Judiciary
summary: Legal Statute Prediction (LSP) involves automatically identifying relevant legal statutes given factual descriptions in legal documents, typically framed as a multi-label classification task within natural language processing and information retrieval research. While recent advances have begun incorporating Large Language Models (LLMs) for statute prediction, current approaches primarily focus on accuracy metrics without addressing the critical need for legal reasoning, a fundamental requirement in judicial contexts where decisions must be explainable and justifiable. To address this research gap, we present PROSLEX (PRediction Of Statutes and LEgal eXplanation), a comprehensive dataset comprising 1,623 expert-annotated legal documents from the Indian context. Each document is paired with statute predictions and detailed explanations, totaling 7,450 explanations, capturing the underlying legal reasoning. Using this dataset, we systematically evaluate various prompting strategies, including zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and tree-of-thoughts approaches, to generate both statute predictions and their corresponding legal rationales. Our evaluation framework measures not only predictive performance but also the coherence and legal validity of generated explanations, positioning PROSLEX as a benchmark for developing explainable AI systems that can support legal practitioners while advancing research in interpretable legal NLP. To ensure reproducibility, we have made our PROSLEX dataset and model code available on GitHub: https://github.com/subinay494/Legal_Statute_Prediction_Explanation.

AI.tldr: PROSLEX introduces a comprehensive dataset with statute predictions and legal explanations, enabling evaluation of LLMs for both accuracy and legal reasoning in statute prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM approaches for Legal Statute Prediction focus only on accuracy metrics without addressing the critical need for legal reasoning and explainability required in judicial contexts.
AI.method: Created PROSLEX dataset with 1,623 expert-annotated Indian legal documents paired with statute predictions and 7,450 detailed explanations. Systematically evaluated various LLM prompting strategies including zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and tree-of-thoughts approaches.
AI.result: Developed a benchmark dataset that enables evaluation of both predictive performance and the coherence/legal validity of generated explanations. Made the dataset and code publicly available for reproducibility.
AI.conclusion: PROSLEX establishes a foundation for developing explainable AI systems that support legal practitioners and advances research in interpretable legal NLP by addressing the gap between accuracy-focused predictions and legally-justifiable reasoning.

title: How Simple Can It Get? From Interpretable Equations to Readable Rules for Financial Decision Making
summary: In regulated domains such as finance, a model that cannot be explained cannot be deployed, yet many interpretable classifiers defeat their own purpose by producing formulas with dozens of features that no regulator could read. We take the reverse direction. Starting from an interpretable classifier expressed as a single equation over the input features, we progressively simplify it into more readable forms, including a pruned monomial, a directional if--then rule, and the integer scorecards and tallies that finance already deploys. Because the equation is itself the predictive model rather than a post-hoc explanation we can directly quantify what is lost under each simplification. Across four financial datasets, we find that pruning is nearly free and that fidelity can erode faster than predictive performance, allowing simpler rules to remain effective classifiers without faithfully reproducing the original model. A human assessment shows that simplification improves perceived readability, while preferences for different representations vary by professional background. Beyond measuring these losses empirically, we show that some can be anticipated from the original model: we derive a bound on the change caused by pruning and predict how faithfully a rule retaining only the direction of each feature's effect preserves the original ranking.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes methods to simplify interpretable classifiers into more readable forms (pruned monomials, if-then rules, scorecards) while quantifying the trade-off between simplicity and predictive performance/fidelity, with empirical validation on financial datasets and human readability assessments.
AI.motivation: In regulated domains like finance, models must be explainable to be deployed, but many interpretable classifiers produce overly complex formulas with dozens of features that are not readable by regulators. There's a need for truly readable models that maintain performance while being understandable to human decision-makers.
AI.method: Starting from an interpretable classifier expressed as a single equation, the authors progressively simplify it into more readable forms: pruned monomials, directional if-then rules, and integer scorecards/tallies used in finance. They quantify what is lost under each simplification by comparing to the original predictive model (not just post-hoc explanations). They derive theoretical bounds on pruning-induced changes and analyze how well simplified rules preserve original model rankings.
AI.result: Across four financial datasets: (1) pruning is nearly free (minimal performance loss), (2) fidelity to original model can erode faster than predictive performance, allowing simpler rules to remain effective classifiers without exactly reproducing the original, (3) simplification improves perceived readability in human assessments, (4) preferences for different simplified representations vary by professional background, (5) some simplification losses can be anticipated theoretically from the original model.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a practical approach to creating truly readable models for regulated domains by simplifying interpretable classifiers while maintaining predictive performance. It provides both empirical evidence and theoretical foundations for understanding the trade-offs between model simplicity, fidelity, and predictive power, with important implications for deploying explainable AI in finance and other regulated industries.

title: Depth-adaptive Inference of Looped Language Models via Continuous Depth Batching
summary: A main promise of looped language models (LMs) is depth-adaptive inference. By iterating a block of shared layers a variable number of times, the model can use less compute for "easy" tokens and more for "hard" ones. However, this adaptivity breaks standard batching: tokens in the same batch now require a different number of loops, so there is no unified forward pass, making efficient inference difficult. Standard inference frameworks like vLLM schedule on the token level and cannot handle this because tokens need to be removed from the batch within the forward pass. Loop-level scheduling has been proposed as a solution, but never implemented end to end. The key challenge is that looped architectures also contain non-looped boundary stages (e.g., token embedding and LM head) that must be scheduled at different frequencies than the loop. We introduce continuous depth batching (CDB), which schedules at the granularity of individual loop iterations. CDB handles boundary stages and loop steps in separate priority queues, makes exit decisions one step ahead, and overlaps all scheduling work with GPU computation. On Ouro 1.4B and Huginn 3.5B, CDB can realize up to $99\%$ of the theoretical maximum speed-up from adaptive-depth, translating to $1.5$-$1.9\times$ higher offline throughput and $45$-$90\%$ lower normalized latency under dynamic serving load.

AI.tldr: Continuous Depth Batching (CDB) enables efficient inference for depth-adaptive looped language models by scheduling at individual loop iteration granularity, achieving near-theoretical maximum speed-ups.
AI.motivation: Looped LMs promise depth-adaptive inference but break standard batching since tokens require different numbers of iterations, making efficient inference difficult with existing frameworks that can't handle tokens being removed mid-forward pass.
AI.method: Continuous Depth Batching schedules at individual loop iteration granularity, uses separate priority queues for boundary stages and loop steps, makes exit decisions one step ahead, and overlaps scheduling with GPU computation.
AI.result: On Ouro 1.4B and Huginn 3.5B, CDB achieves up to 99% of theoretical maximum speed-up, delivering 1.5-1.9× higher offline throughput and 45-90% lower normalized latency under dynamic serving load.
AI.conclusion: CDB successfully solves the efficient inference challenge for depth-adaptive looped LMs by enabling continuous batching at loop iteration level, making practical deployment of such models feasible.

title: Theory-Guided Deception Detection: A RAG-Based Artificial Intelligence Exploration
summary: The current work developed seven Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models based on leading deception theories and compared how deception judgments were made relative to baseline models. Across 700 statements drawn from five published deception datasets, four large language models (gpt-4o, claude-sonnet-4-6, ollama/llama3, deepseek-v4-flash), and two run-types (RAG vs. baseline), a total of 39,200 deception judgments were rendered. Detection accuracies were consistent with typical human accuracies and not statistically different across RAG (54.5%) and baseline models (54.6%). RAG-based models (57.0%) were less truth-biased than baseline models (59.7%), but the effect size was quite small. Theoretical perspective mattered little for accuracy yet mattered substantially for response bias, which ranged from highly lie-biased (the verifiability approach, 32.2%) to highly truth-biased (truth-default theory, 88.1%). Content effects and model effects further moderated the results. Theory-guided AI judgments are unreliable with current parameters, yet they might show promise with additional datasets, model testing, and theory-to-data matching.

AI.tldr: RAG models based on deception theories don't improve detection accuracy over baseline models, showing similar performance to humans (~54.5%), but theoretical perspectives significantly affect response bias patterns.
AI.motivation: To develop theory-guided RAG models for deception detection and compare their performance against baseline models, examining whether incorporating deception theories improves AI-based deception judgments.
AI.method: Developed 7 RAG models based on leading deception theories, tested on 700 statements from 5 deception datasets using 4 large language models (GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet, Llama3, DeepSeek) with RAG vs. baseline comparisons, generating 39,200 deception judgments.
AI.result: No significant accuracy difference between RAG (54.5%) and baseline models (54.6%), both similar to human performance. RAG models showed less truth bias (57.0%) vs baseline (59.7%). Theoretical perspectives strongly influenced response bias, ranging from lie-biased (verifiability approach: 32.2%) to truth-biased (truth-default theory: 88.1%).
AI.conclusion: Theory-guided AI deception judgments are currently unreliable but show promise with better data, model testing, and theory-to-data matching. Theoretical perspectives matter more for bias patterns than accuracy improvements.

title: WDL-OPD: Weak-Driven On-Policy Distillation via Mixture-Constrained Co-Training
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) aligns a student with a teacher on trajectories sampled from the student itself, reducing the train-test state mismatch of offline distillation. The same feedback loop can nevertheless be unstable: each update changes both the policy and the states on which the next update is computed. We introduce WDL-OPD, a mixture-constrained co-training method with two trainable policies. An anchor policy generates every rollout, an auxiliary policy evaluates the same visited states, and a geometric mixture of their token distributions is matched to a frozen teacher by reverse KL. Both policies receive gradient. We show that freezing the auxiliary recovers an anchor-plus-contrast proxy target closely related to OPD$^2$ and W2S-OPD, whereas joint training creates branch-level degrees of freedom that a static delta cannot express. In recorded Qwen3 experiments at 1.7B and 4B scale, WDL-OPD produces the strongest student checkpoint in each of four scale-domain settings. It raises MATH500 accuracy from 0.630 to 0.685 at 4B and from 0.521 to 0.585 at 1.7B. In code generation, seven single-policy OPD configurations exhibit entropy growth or trajectory degradation, while co-training reaches independently re-evaluated development scores of 0.637 and 0.375. Because several comparisons differ in curriculum or initialization, these results support a stabilization hypothesis rather than a universal causal claim. We provide the exact training algorithm, failure evidence, and the controlled comparison matrix needed to test that hypothesis.

AI.tldr: WDL-OPD introduces a mixture-constrained co-training method with two trainable policies for stable on-policy distillation, overcoming instability issues in single-policy OPD through geometric mixture matching to a frozen teacher.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) suffers from instability due to the feedback loop where each update changes both the policy and the states for subsequent updates. While OPD reduces train-test state mismatch compared to offline distillation, it creates a dynamic system that can become unstable.
AI.method: WDL-OPD uses a co-training method with two trainable policies: an anchor policy generates rollouts, an auxiliary policy evaluates visited states, and their geometric mixture is matched to a frozen teacher using reverse KL divergence. Both policies receive gradients, creating branch-level degrees of freedom that static methods cannot express.
AI.result: WDL-OPD outperformed single-policy OPD configurations across experiments: improved MATH500 accuracy from 0.630 to 0.685 at 4B scale and from 0.521 to 0.585 at 1.7B scale. In code generation, while single-policy OPD showed entropy growth or trajectory degradation, co-training achieved development scores of 0.637 and 0.375. It produced the strongest student checkpoints in all four scale-domain settings tested.
AI.conclusion: The proposed WDL-OPD method effectively stabilizes on-policy distillation through co-training with two policies, overcoming the instability inherent in single-policy feedback loops. The results support a stabilization hypothesis rather than making universal causal claims, and the authors provide detailed evidence and comparisons for hypothesis testing.

title: AquiLLM: An Architecture for Supporting Tacit Knowledge Capture in Research Groups
comment: Accepted for publication in the NGEN-AI 2026 proceedings
summary: Recent advances in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and large language models (LLMs) enable researchers to integrate AI into scientific workflows. However, using proprietary commercial AI systems raises concerns about transparency, reproducibility and privacy, which are essential for scientific practices. To this end, AquiLLM was developed as an open-source modular RAG-LLM framework using open-weight models, designed to support research groups in capturing tacit knowledge. In this work, we present a series of architectural improvements and feature enhancements to AquiLLM, including local embedding and reranking, multimodal capabilities, OpenAI-compatible inference interfaces, user interface improvements, semantic and episodic memory capabilities, and skills support. These enhancements were informed by discussions with domain experts, including astrophysicists and environmental researchers, and represent a step toward AI systems more closely aligned with scientific research practices.

AI.tldr: AquiLLM is an open-source RAG-LLM framework enhanced with architectural improvements including local embedding/reranking, multimodal capabilities, OpenAI-compatible interfaces, improved UI, memory capabilities, and skills support to better support scientific research workflows.
AI.motivation: Proprietary commercial AI systems raise concerns about transparency, reproducibility, and privacy in scientific workflows, which are essential for scientific practices. There's a need for open-source AI systems that support research groups in capturing tacit knowledge while maintaining scientific standards.
AI.method: Developed AquiLLM as an open-source modular RAG-LLM framework using open-weight models. Made architectural improvements including local embedding and reranking capabilities, multimodal support, OpenAI-compatible inference interfaces, user interface enhancements, semantic and episodic memory capabilities, and skills support.
AI.result: Created an enhanced open-source RAG-LLM framework with features specifically designed for scientific workflows, informed by discussions with domain experts including astrophysicists and environmental researchers.
AI.conclusion: The enhanced AquiLLM framework represents a step toward AI systems more closely aligned with scientific research practices, addressing transparency, reproducibility, and privacy concerns while supporting the capture of tacit knowledge in research groups.

title: From Approachability Residuals to Anytime-Valid Evidence: The Online Convex Geometry of Testing by Betting
summary:
Betting-based sequential tests and Blackwell approachability are linked by a rate-explicit reduction through support-function residuals. For a compact convex target $S$ and vector observations $r_t$, an OCO learner selects a predictable normal $w_t$ and produces $q_t=\langle w_t,r_t\rangle-h_S(w_t)$. We prove the exact pathwise identity $$
  \dist(\bar r_T,S)
  =\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^Tq_t+\frac{\Reg_T}{T}. $$ When $|q_t|\leq B$, composing this identity with one-sided betting yields a finite-time transfer: if the OCO and log-wealth regrets are at most $a_T$ and $\ell_T$, respectively, then a target gap exceeding \[
  \frac{a_T}{T}
  +2B\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/α)+\ell_T}{T}} \] forces rejection by time $T$, while non-rejection certifies the converse radius. We then formulate a controlled stochastic experiment in which an action selected after $w_t$ satisfies Blackwell's supporting-halfspace condition for every null mean payoff. The resulting wealth is an e-process under adaptive nulls; sublinear OCO regret gives stochastic approachability, whereas persistent mean separation under an alternative gives exponential wealth at rate at least $δ^2/(4B^2)$. Deterministic Blackwell games and passive tests are, respectively, the noise-free and singleton-action cases of this protocol. Bounded two-sample means, kernel MMD, and active heterogeneous data sources instantiate the reduction. The resulting connection is exact algebraically, quantitative at finite time, and operational when experiments are controlled.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes an exact algebraic connection between betting-based sequential tests and Blackwell approachability via support-function residuals, with finite-time guarantees for hypothesis testing and experimental control.
AI.motivation: To create a unified framework connecting two important areas of sequential decision theory: betting-based sequential tests and Blackwell approachability, enabling quantitative finite-time guarantees and operational control in stochastic experiments.
AI.method: Develops a rate-explicit reduction through support-function residuals, using OCO learners to produce predictable normals w_t and residuals q_t = ⟨w_t,r_t⟩ - h_S(w_t). Proves an exact pathwise identity linking distance to target set with average residuals and regret.
AI.result: Establishes exact algebraic connection with finite-time transfer properties: target gap exceeding a_T/T + 2B√(log(1/α)+ℓ_T)/T forces rejection by time T. Formulates controlled stochastic experiment where resulting wealth is an e-process under adaptive nulls. Shows sublinear OCO regret gives stochastic approachability, and persistent mean separation gives exponential wealth growth.
AI.conclusion: The reduction provides an exact, quantitative, and operational connection between betting-based tests and Blackwell approachability, with applications to bounded two-sample means, kernel MMD, and active heterogeneous data sources, unifying deterministic Blackwell games and passive tests as special cases.

title: Full-bandwidth transformer
summary: Autoregressive transformers compute along two axes: horizontally across generated tokens, and vertically through model depth. Dense attention gives each token broad horizontal access to the past, but the vertical feedback channel between decoding steps remains narrow: only the sampled token returns to the bottom of the stack, while the top-layer hidden state is discarded. We introduce the \emph{full-bandwidth transformer}, which widens this channel with \emph{latent feedback}: at each decoding step, the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back as the next input. Latent feedback lets non-verbalized computation re-enter the stack with a renewed depth budget, while preserving the standard transformer architecture, KV cache, and language-modeling objective. To train full-bandwidth transformers without losing parallel teacher forcing, we use a scheduled multi-pass objective that introduces latent feedback late in pretraining and mixes a small fraction of deeper feedback passes for stability. We train 1B-parameter full-bandwidth transformers up to 400B tokens and find that latent feedback improves validation loss, 5-shot language-model evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance. With negligible per-token decoding overhead, full-bandwidth transformers match or approach standard transformers trained with roughly $1.5\times$ more tokens, and manage to produce shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy.

AI.tldr: Transformers with latent feedback that passes top-layer hidden states back to the bottom, improving efficiency and reducing token usage without changing the standard architecture.
AI.motivation: Standard transformers discard top-layer hidden states after each decoding step, losing valuable computation. Only the sampled token returns to the stack, creating a narrow vertical feedback channel that limits the reuse of non-verbalized intermediate representations.
AI.method: Introduces full-bandwidth transformers with latent feedback: previous top-layer hidden state is fused with sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back as next input. Uses scheduled multi-pass objective for training, introducing latent feedback late in pretraining with mixed deeper feedback passes for stability.
AI.result: Latent feedback improves validation loss, 5-shot language-model evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance. Full-bandwidth transformers match or approach standard transformers trained with ~1.5× more tokens, produce shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy with negligible decoding overhead.
AI.conclusion: Latent feedback effectively widens the vertical feedback channel in transformers, allowing non-verbalized computation to re-enter the stack with renewed depth budget, improving efficiency and performance while maintaining standard architecture and objectives.

title: Learning to Modulate, Not to Cycle: Soft Actor---Critic Recovers Inverter-Style Heat-Pump Control
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, Accepted at UKCI 2026, Will be published in Springer
summary: On--off cycling is the main cause of compressor wear in residential heat pumps, yet reinforcement learning (RL) controllers for buildings typically optimise only energy cost and thermal comfort, ignoring how much the learned policy cycles. We add a levelised compressor-wear term to the control reward and study how the resulting behaviour depends on the RL algorithm. Training Soft Actor---Critic (SAC) and Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) on an identical Markov decision process for the BOPTEST bestest hydronic heat pump case, we find that SAC learns a continuous modulation policy that keeps the compressor permanently engaged---the operating principle of an inverter-driven heat pump---achieving zero start-ups per day, whereas PPO collapses to bang-bang control that cycles more than the baseline. On the BOPTEST emulator the SAC policy cuts thermal discomfort by up to 90.7% for an 11.5% cost increase, while eliminating all baseline cycling.

AI.tldr: RL controllers for heat pumps can reduce compressor cycling when trained with appropriate algorithms and reward terms. SAC learns continuous modulation to eliminate cycling while maintaining comfort, while PPO fails to improve over baseline.
AI.motivation: Current RL controllers for building HVAC systems only optimize energy cost and thermal comfort, ignoring compressor wear caused by on-off cycling, which is the main cause of compressor wear in residential heat pumps.
AI.method: Added a levelised compressor-wear term to the control reward function and compared two RL algorithms (Soft Actor-Critic and Proximal Policy Optimization) trained on an identical Markov decision process for the BOPTEST bestest hydronic heat pump case study.
AI.result: SAC learned a continuous modulation policy that keeps the compressor permanently engaged (like inverter-driven heat pumps), achieving zero start-ups per day, while PPO collapsed to bang-bang control that cycles more than baseline. SAC policy reduced thermal discomfort by up to 90.7% for an 11.5% cost increase while eliminating all baseline cycling.
AI.conclusion: The choice of RL algorithm significantly impacts learned control behavior. SAC successfully learns to modulate continuously to minimize cycling, while PPO fails, showing that algorithm selection is crucial for effective compressor wear reduction in heat pump control.

title: LLM Reasoning for Subjective Tasks: Failure Modes, Mitigation, and Dynamic Reasoning Routing
summary: Recommendation systems thrive on personalization, where ''correctness'' is rarely a binary truth but a matter of subjective human preference. As Large Language Models (LLMs) are deployed as autonomous verifiers of safety and quality guidelines, they face a distinctive challenge: context-aware preference alignment. Recent gains in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) are indexed mostly on objective, mathematical tasks. Through a large-scale study spanning both proprietary and open-source models on four real-world verification tasks from a production recommender platform, we ask whether explicit reasoning generalizes to subjective, human-centric industry rubrics. We expose a fundamental vulnerability: rigid, math-centric reasoning traces actively degrade verification, and applying standard RLVR triggers a phenomenon we term reasoning collapse, in which the policy abandons deliberation in favor of rapid heuristic guessing. We introduce a conditional length-penalized post-training algorithm that intertwines verification accuracy with bounded reasoning length, halting collapse and recovering performance. Finally, we show that a reasoning trace's efficacy is tightly coupled with its socio-linguistic framing: across 1500 synthesized personas, verification accuracy swings by nearly 0.38 macro-F1 depending solely on the adopted reasoning persona---evidence that much subjective-verification error is really reasoning-style mismatch. This observation motivates a mid-training architecture that routes reasoning through contextually aligned personas. This work offers both a scalable algorithmic patch and a long-term architectural blueprint for aligning reasoning models with real-world subjective constraints.

AI.tldr: RLVR models struggle with subjective preference verification tasks, suffering from reasoning collapse and sensitivity to reasoning personas; solutions include length-penalized training and persona-aware architectures.
AI.motivation: Current RLVR models are optimized for objective mathematical tasks but fail at subjective preference verification needed in real-world recommender systems, requiring context-aware alignment with human preferences.
AI.method: Large-scale study across proprietary and open-source models on four real-world verification tasks; introduced conditional length-penalized post-training algorithm and investigated socio-linguistic framing of reasoning personas.
AI.result: Found that rigid math-centric reasoning degrades verification; standard RLVR triggers reasoning collapse; verification accuracy varies significantly (up to 0.38 macro-F1) based on reasoning persona; length-penalized training recovers performance.
AI.conclusion: Subjective verification requires reasoning-style alignment, motivating both short-term algorithmic fixes (length-penalized training) and long-term architectural solutions (persona-aware routing) for real-world preference alignment.

title: Flow-based conditional cardiac anatomy generation for virtual cohorts
summary: Cardiac digital twin research is moving from subject-specific anatomical replicas toward virtual cohorts that represent clinically relevant population subgroups. Yet access to representative imaging-derived anatomy datasets remains limited by cohort size, subgroup sparsity, and data-sharing constraints. Conditional generative models could help address this gap, but virtual cohorts are useful only if they preserve realistic, metadata-dependent anatomical variability. Existing cardiac anatomy generators largely rely on conditional variational autoencoders (cVAEs), which couple representation learning and metadata conditioning through a shared regularized latent prior. We introduce CAN-FLOW, a two-step Conditional ANatomy generation framework based on normalizing FLOWs that first learns geometry-only latent representations of diffeomorphic cardiac shape momenta and then models their sex-, age-, and body-mass-index-dependent distribution with a conditional normalizing flow. We trained CAN-FLOW on 2,208 healthy UK Biobank subjects and compared it with cVAEs across regularization strengths. CAN-FLOW generated plausible stochastic biventricular anatomies that better reproduced clinical phenotype distributions, metadata-dependent trends, subgroup variability, point-cloud coverage, and high-dimensional shape variability. Together, these results establish CAN-FLOW as a shareable framework for generating realistic, stochastically varying, metadata-conditioned biventricular anatomies for virtual cohort construction and in silico clinical trial workflows.

AI.tldr: CAN-FLOW is a two-step conditional anatomy generation framework using normalizing flows that generates realistic, metadata-dependent biventricular anatomies for virtual cohort construction, outperforming existing cVAE approaches.
AI.motivation: Current virtual cardiac cohorts face limitations due to small cohort sizes, sparse subgroup representation, and data-sharing constraints. Existing conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) approaches may not adequately preserve realistic, metadata-dependent anatomical variability needed for clinically useful virtual cohorts.
AI.method: CAN-FLOW uses a two-step approach: 1) learns geometry-only latent representations of diffeomorphic cardiac shape momenta, and 2) models their sex-, age-, and BMI-dependent distribution with a conditional normalizing flow. The framework decouples shape representation learning from metadata conditioning.
AI.result: Trained on 2,208 healthy UK Biobank subjects, CAN-FLOW generated plausible stochastic biventricular anatomies that better reproduced clinical phenotype distributions, metadata-dependent trends, subgroup variability, point-cloud coverage, and high-dimensional shape variability compared to cVAEs across regularization strengths.
AI.conclusion: CAN-FLOW establishes a shareable framework for generating realistic, stochastically varying, metadata-conditioned biventricular anatomies that can support virtual cohort construction and in silico clinical trial workflows with improved anatomical realism and population representativeness.

title: From Manuals to Maintenance: Fine-Tuning MedGemma for Multi-Modal Imaging System Support in Low-Resource Settings
comment: Accepted at the AFRICAI 2026 Workshop, a satellite event at MICCAI 2026. To appear in Springer Lecture Notes in Computer Science (LNCS)
summary: Imaging device downtime is a major barrier to healthcare delivery in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), often driven by limited access to specialized biomedical engineering support. We present a multi-modality medical equipment maintenance question-answering (QA) framework and demonstrate the fine-tuning of a medical foundation model for specialized technical troubleshooting tasks. Guided by a multi-country survey across nine LMICs, we curated technical manuals from MRI and ultrasound systems to generate the INGENZI_DatasetV1, containing 10,294 high-quality, filtered QA-context pairs. Using QLoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning, we adapted the MedGemma-4b-it model to interpret system error logs and generate step-by-step equipment repair instructions. Compared to the baseline model, the fine-tuned system achieved substantial improvements across metrics, including F1 score (0.22 to 0.38), ROUGE-2 (0.18 to 0.41), and BERTScore F1 (0.86 to 0.91). These metric gains demonstrate that the model generates significantly more precise and procedurally accurate technical responses to new troubleshooting queries. This work establishes a reliable foundation for AI-assisted diagnostic and maintenance tools in resource-constrained settings.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning MedGemma-4b-it with QLoRA on medical equipment maintenance QA pairs significantly improves troubleshooting performance for imaging devices in LMICs.
AI.motivation: Imaging device downtime in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is a major healthcare delivery barrier due to limited access to specialized biomedical engineering support.
AI.method: Created INGENZI_DatasetV1 (10,294 QA-context pairs) from MRI/ultrasound manuals, then used QLoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning to adapt MedGemma-4b-it for interpreting error logs and generating repair instructions.
AI.result: Fine-tuned model achieved substantial improvements: F1 score (0.22→0.38), ROUGE-2 (0.18→0.41), BERTScore F1 (0.86→0.91), generating more precise and procedurally accurate technical responses.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a reliable foundation for AI-assisted diagnostic and maintenance tools in resource-constrained settings, addressing equipment downtime through specialized troubleshooting AI.

title: MixFormer: Linear Transformer with Mixture of Memory Experts
summary: State Space Models (SSMs), as a mainstream research direction of linear Transformers, aim to achieve higher efficiency than standard Transformers in long-context modeling. However, existing SSMs suffer from limited input adaptivity and constrained memory capacity, leading to information loss when modeling ultra-long sequences. To address these limitations, we propose MixFormer, a novel linear Transformer that integrates a Mixture-of-Memory-Experts (MoE) mechanism. Specifically, the model maintains differentiated memory states through multiple collaborating memory experts and employs a novel Time-Aware Linear Attention (TALA) mechanism, which leverages learnable exponential decay functions and positional biases to dynamically update memory. This design enables the model to selectively reinforce important historical information while effectively mitigating memory dilution, substantially improving long-range dependency modeling. Experiments on long-sequence text and image generation tasks demonstrate that MixFormer not only achieves significant performance gains but also provides a more sustainable computational backbone for the next generation of web infrastructure.

AI.tldr: MixFormer is a novel linear Transformer that integrates a Mixture-of-Memory-Experts (MoE) mechanism with Time-Aware Linear Attention to address memory limitations in State Space Models for ultra-long sequence modeling.
AI.motivation: Existing State Space Models (linear Transformers) suffer from limited input adaptivity and constrained memory capacity, causing information loss when modeling ultra-long sequences, which hinders their effectiveness in long-context applications.
AI.method: Proposes MixFormer with: 1) Mixture-of-Memory-Experts mechanism to maintain differentiated memory states through multiple collaborating experts, and 2) Time-Aware Linear Attention using learnable exponential decay functions and positional biases to dynamically update memory and selectively reinforce important historical information.
AI.result: MixFormer achieves significant performance gains on long-sequence text and image generation tasks while providing more sustainable computational backbone for next-generation web infrastructure, effectively mitigating memory dilution and improving long-range dependency modeling.
AI.conclusion: MixFormer successfully addresses the limitations of existing SSMs by combining MoE memory management with adaptive attention mechanisms, offering an efficient solution for ultra-long sequence modeling with improved memory utilization and computational sustainability.

title: Decoding Phenotypes: A Framework for Fusing Genomic Language Models and Neuroimaging
summary: Neuroimaging and genetic testing are two important clinical references for nervous system diseases, offering complementary diagnostic information. However, integrating genomic and neuroimaging data for precise disease diagnosis is challenging due to cross-modality heterogeneity. Existing imaging-genetics approaches mainly encode genetic information as hard-coded labels, which lose the local sequence context around disease-associated variants. To address this limitation, we propose GeneFuse, a multimodal learning framework that aligns genetic representations from pre-trained Genomic Language Models (GLMs) with features extracted from images. GeneFuse integrates two components: (1) Genotype-Conditioned Feature Modulation (GCFM), a FiLM-inspired module that uses genomic embeddings to modulate image feature maps; and (2) Uncertainty-aware Genomic Residual Fusion (U-GRF), a fusion strategy that uses imaging-derived predictive uncertainty to gate the contribution of genotypic features. We evaluate GeneFuse on early cognitive decline identification (NC vs. MCI) and dementia screening (NC vs. AD). In the APOE-centered setting, GeneFuse achieves AUROCs of 0.77 and 0.83, outperforming existing imaging-genetics fusion methods. These results indicate that GLM-derived genomic embeddings provide additional information to imaging.

AI.tldr: GeneFuse is a multimodal framework that aligns genomic language model embeddings with neuroimaging features using conditioned feature modulation and uncertainty-aware fusion, achieving improved performance for cognitive decline and dementia screening.
AI.motivation: Current imaging-genetics approaches encode genetic information as simple labels, losing important local sequence context around disease-associated variants. There's a need to better integrate genomic and neuroimaging data for precise nervous system disease diagnosis despite cross-modality heterogeneity challenges.
AI.method: GeneFuse uses a multimodal learning framework with two key components: 1) Genotype-Conditioned Feature Modulation (GCFM) - a FiLM-inspired module that uses genomic embeddings to modulate image feature maps, and 2) Uncertainty-aware Genomic Residual Fusion (U-GRF) - a fusion strategy that uses imaging-derived predictive uncertainty to gate the contribution of genotypic features. The framework aligns genetic representations from pre-trained Genomic Language Models (GLMs) with image features.
AI.result: GeneFuse achieves AUROCs of 0.77 for early cognitive decline identification (NC vs. MCI) and 0.83 for dementia screening (NC vs. AD) in APOE-centered settings, outperforming existing imaging-genetics fusion methods. The results demonstrate that GLM-derived genomic embeddings provide additional information beyond imaging alone.
AI.conclusion: The proposed GeneFuse framework successfully addresses limitations of existing methods by preserving local genomic context through GLM embeddings and effectively fusing multimodal information, leading to improved diagnostic performance for neurodegenerative diseases. The work demonstrates the value of sophisticated genomic feature representation in clinical applications.

title: Hierarchical rank-evolving representation for physics-informed neural networks
summary: Recently, tensor-based physics-informed neural networks (T-PINNs) have received increasing attention. However, existing T-PINNs still face a fundamental challenge: they mainly rely on pre-specified low-rank tensor decompositions with manually tuned ranks, which limits their ability to capture the underlying structures of multivariate solution functions and hinders their practical deployment. To address this challenge, we propose a hierarchical rank-evolving (abbreviated as HRE) representation for multivariate functions, which endows us to faithfully capture the underlying structure of the targeted multivariate function accompanying with automatic rank determination. Concretely, in the hierarchical design of HRE representation, the target multivariate function is decomposed as a small-scale inner tensor with a set of univariate functions along each mode, where a customized tensor network decomposition can be readily deployed to capture the underlying structure of the small-scale inner tensor. In HRE representation, the crucial hyperparameters, ranks, can be adaptively revealed during the decomposition, freeing us from manual rank tuning and making HRE practically applicable to real-world problems. Besides, we build the HRE-PINNs correspondingly. Extensive numerical experiments, including high-dimensional static problems (Helmholtz equation and Poisson equation), nonlinear time-dependent problems (Klein-Gordon equation), and complex fluid-dynamics problems (flow mixing equation and Navier-Stokes equation), demonstrate that HRE-PINNs consistently outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches in terms of accuracy.

AI.tldr: HRE-PINNs: A hierarchical rank-evolving representation for physics-informed neural networks that automatically determines tensor ranks, overcoming manual tuning limitations in existing T-PINNs.
AI.motivation: Existing tensor-based PINNs (T-PINNs) rely on pre-specified low-rank tensor decompositions with manually tuned ranks, which limits their ability to capture underlying structures of multivariate solution functions and hinders practical deployment.
AI.method: Proposes a hierarchical rank-evolving (HRE) representation where target multivariate functions are decomposed into small-scale inner tensors with univariate functions along each mode, using customized tensor network decomposition to capture structure. Ranks are adaptively revealed during decomposition.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on high-dimensional static problems (Helmholtz, Poisson equations), nonlinear time-dependent problems (Klein-Gordon equation), and complex fluid-dynamics problems (flow mixing, Navier-Stokes equations) show HRE-PINNs consistently outperform state-of-the-art approaches in accuracy.
AI.conclusion: HRE representation enables automatic rank determination, freeing from manual tuning, making it practically applicable to real-world problems while consistently achieving better accuracy than existing methods.

title: Integrated Multimodal AI System for Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning, Object Sensing, and Damage Analysis
summary: This work presents a unified multimodal AI system for damage assessment that integrates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) models, thermal spectrum perception, vision foundation model pipelines, and exploratory wireless signal sensing. A RAG component is developed to ground a locally hosted language model in project-specific documentation, including specialized damage level classification criteria to mitigate hallucinations during inference. Controlled comparisons against static few-shot prompting demonstrate that dynamic retrieval improves grounding and factual consistency. We further compare vector-based RAG with a knowledge graph variant constructed via entity-relation extraction, and show that graph-based retrieval produces stronger responses for damage assessment queries requiring cross-document reasoning, motivating hybrid dense, sparse, and graph-aware retrieval. To address limitations of EO imagery under adverse lighting and weather conditions, infrared (IR)/thermal sensing is employed for object detection and segmentation. Our detectors generate candidate detections, yielding improved segmentation of a broad array of objects. Paired IR versus visible spectrum tracking experiments reveal failure modes, motivating multimodal fusion for robust object detection and damage analysis. Vision foundation and vision-language models are leveraged to generate synthetic damage imagery and classify damage severity with high accuracy, supporting training and validation of downstream damage assessment models. Finally, exploratory Wireless-based sensing demonstrates potential to detect presence, motion, and post-event environmental changes where EO and IR sensing are ineffective.

AI.tldr: A unified multimodal AI system for damage assessment combining RAG models, thermal sensing, vision foundation models, and wireless sensing to overcome limitations of traditional EO imagery.
AI.motivation: To improve damage assessment accuracy by addressing limitations of Earth Observation (EO) imagery under adverse conditions (poor lighting, weather) and mitigating hallucinations in AI-generated responses through better grounding in domain-specific knowledge.
AI.method: 1. RAG component to ground language models in project documentation and damage classification criteria. 2. Comparison of vector-based RAG vs. knowledge graph variant via entity-relation extraction. 3. IR/thermal sensing for object detection/segmentation under poor visual conditions. 4. Vision foundation models for synthetic damage imagery generation and damage classification. 5. Exploratory wireless sensing for environmental change detection where EO/IR are ineffective.
AI.result: 1. Dynamic RAG improves grounding/factual consistency over static few-shot prompting. 2. Graph-based retrieval outperforms vector-based for cross-document reasoning queries. 3. IR sensing enables object detection/segmentation in adverse conditions. 4. Vision models achieve high accuracy in damage severity classification. 5. Wireless sensing shows potential for environmental change detection.
AI.conclusion: The multimodal system successfully addresses limitations of traditional damage assessment methods, with hybrid dense/sparse/graph-aware retrieval, IR sensing for adverse conditions, and wireless sensing complementing EO/IR capabilities. Future work should focus on multimodal fusion for robust object detection and damage analysis.

title: When Do Task Vectors Interfere? Mapping the Validity Boundaries of Weight-Space Composition
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures; includes references and an expanded appendix
summary: Task arithmetic treats fine-tuning displacements as composable directions in weight space, yet it remains unclear when parameter addition reflects predictable changes in model function. We separate parameter geometry from functional geometry and measure pairwise functional non-additivity over a two-dimensional task-vector surface, using a first-token predictive-distribution interaction ratio conditioned on an input distribution and evaluated with norm-matched controls, three training seeds, and response-only fine-tuning. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, code+safety is more non-additive than the matched code+math control on code and instruction prompts, but not on math prompts. In a prospectively specified six-task expansion, all eight high-versus-low comparisons of unseen task pairs have the predicted sign. The primary ordering further persists under full-parameter fine-tuning at 0.5B, Qwen2.5 LoRA scale tests up to 7B, and a Llama-3.1-8B cross-architecture audit. External validation exposes a sharper boundary: raw public code, instruction, and safety prompts preserve the continuous contrast, whereas an instruction-style wrapper collapses it on the identical public-code prompts, and EvalPlus pass@1 interactions do not robustly reproduce it. Weight-space composition therefore supports coarse, input- and format-conditioned functional statements across adaptation methods, scales, and one additional model family, not a universal merging-performance predictor.

AI.tldr: Task arithmetic shows weight-space composition predicts functional behavior in coarse, input-dependent ways across models and methods, but not as a universal performance predictor.
AI.motivation: To understand when parameter addition in task arithmetic (fine-tuning displacements) actually corresponds to predictable functional changes in models, separating parameter geometry from functional geometry.
AI.method: Measure pairwise functional non-additivity using a first-token predictive-distribution interaction ratio conditioned on input distributions. Use norm-matched controls, three training seeds, and response-only fine-tuning. Test across models (Qwen2.5-1.5B to 7B, Llama-3.1-8B), adaptation methods (LoRA, full fine-tuning), and evaluate on various prompt formats.
AI.result: Code+safety task combinations show more functional non-additivity than code+math controls on code/instruction prompts, but not math prompts. In a six-task expansion, all eight high-vs-low comparisons of unseen task pairs have predicted sign. Findings persist across scales (0.5B-7B) and architectures (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), but are format-dependent: raw prompts preserve contrasts while instruction wrappers collapse them, and EvalPlus pass@1 interactions don't robustly reproduce effects.
AI.conclusion: Weight-space composition supports coarse, input- and format-conditioned functional statements across adaptation methods, scales, and model families, but does not serve as a universal merging-performance predictor.

title: Not an A11y: How Android Accessibility Exposes Mobile AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection
summary: The rise of autonomous AI agents represents a major paradigm shift in how users interact with mobile devices. Frameworks such as MobileRun and Mobile-Use can autonomously navigate Android applications and execute complex multi-step tasks. To interpret user interfaces, these frameworks rely primarily on Android accessibility (A11y) trees and secondarily on visual screenshots. In this paper, we demonstrate that this architectural dependence on unsanitized accessibility metadata, together with visual input, introduces a systemic vulnerability to indirect prompt injection. We show that adversarial prompts can cause autonomous agents to abandon their original objectives, violate context boundaries, and perform unauthorized device actions. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates goal hijacking, context drift, and unauthorized actions across visually hidden and fully exposed attack scenarios. In aggregate, MobileRun reaches an attack success rate of 0.822 with Gemma4:31B, while Mobile-Use with Qwen3.6:35B reduces this to 0.150 but does not eliminate context drift or unauthorized actions. These findings reveal that current mobile agent frameworks fail to enforce semantic context boundaries, treating passive environmental text as trusted instructions. Finally, we present a taxonomy of these attacks and discuss the need for zero-trust input validation, dedicated security agents, and strict context isolation within mobile agent architectures.

AI.tldr: Autonomous AI agents for Android apps are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection attacks through unsanitized accessibility metadata and visual inputs, causing goal hijacking, context drift, and unauthorized actions.
AI.motivation: The rise of autonomous AI agents for mobile devices introduces new security risks. These agents rely on accessibility trees and visual screenshots to navigate Android apps, but the unsanitized nature of these inputs creates systemic vulnerabilities to indirect prompt injection attacks.
AI.method: The researchers demonstrate how adversarial prompts can exploit the architectural dependence on accessibility metadata and visual inputs. They conduct empirical evaluations across visually hidden and fully exposed attack scenarios to test different mobile agent frameworks (MobileRun and Mobile-Use) with various language models.
AI.result: MobileRun achieves an attack success rate of 0.822 with Gemma4:31B, while Mobile-Use with Qwen3.6:35B reduces this to 0.150 but still suffers from context drift and unauthorized actions. Current frameworks fail to enforce semantic context boundaries and treat passive environmental text as trusted instructions.
AI.conclusion: The paper reveals critical security flaws in mobile agent architectures that treat environmental text as trusted instructions. It presents a taxonomy of attacks and recommends zero-trust input validation, dedicated security agents, and strict context isolation to address these vulnerabilities.

title: Tracking the Best Strategy in an Extensive-Form Game
summary: We consider the extensive-form bandit problem where on each trial the learner plays an extensive-form game against an oblivious adversary. We focus on the notion of switching regret, which measures the expected performance of the learner against that of any switching sequence of mixed strategies in retrospect. Our algorithm takes a parameter $ρ>0$ and achieves a switching regret of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}((1/ρ+ρK)\sqrt{H A T})$ where $K$ is the number of switches in the comparator sequence, $H$ is the maximum number of the learner's information sets that can be traversed during a play of the game and $A$ is the number of actions that the learner can possibly take. Our algorithm is extremely efficient, taking a per trial time of only $\mathcal{O}(H B)$ where $B$ is the maximum number of actions available to the learner at any of its information sets.

AI.tldr: An algorithm for extensive-form bandit problems achieves efficient switching regret with only O(HB) per-trial computation, where the regret scales with the number of switches K in the comparator sequence.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses extensive-form bandit problems where a learner plays extensive-form games against an oblivious adversary. The motivation is to develop efficient algorithms that minimize switching regret, which compares the learner's performance against any switching sequence of mixed strategies in retrospect, while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.method: The algorithm takes a parameter ρ>0 and achieves switching regret through an efficient design that only requires O(HB) computation per trial, where B is the maximum number of actions available at any of the learner's information sets. The method appears to leverage structural properties of extensive-form games to maintain efficiency.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves switching regret of Õ((1/ρ+ρK)√(HAT)), where K is the number of switches in the comparator sequence, H is the maximum number of learner's information sets traversable during play, and A is the total number of learner's possible actions. The algorithm is extremely efficient with only O(HB) per-trial computation time.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents an efficient algorithm for extensive-form bandit problems that achieves optimal switching regret with minimal computational overhead, providing a practical solution for learning in complex game-theoretic environments where the comparator may change strategies multiple times.

title: Depth-Aware Implicit Neural Representation Priors for 3D Gravity Inversion
summary: Gravimetry images subsurface density contrasts associated with geological structures, geothermal systems, and intrusive bodies. Recovering a three-dimensional density model from gravity observations is highly ill-posed because of its non-uniqueness, limited data coverage, and the attenuation of the gravity field with depth. Classical inversion methods rely on explicit regularization and parameter tuning, whereas supervised deep-learning approaches require representative gravity--density pairs that are rarely available. This paper proposes an unsupervised depth-aware implicit neural representation for 3D gravity inversion. The density volume is represented by multiple coordinate-based neural networks assigned to overlapping depth slabs and optimized directly from the observed gravity measurements through the sensitivity matrix. Slab-specific Fourier features, physics-based depth gains, and scheduled regularization provide structural priors without requiring labeled density models. Experiments on four synthetic scenarios show that the proposed method provides better overall performance in terms of RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM than the evaluated conventional and neural baselines. It also recovers more compact and spatially coherent density bodies, improves the separation of nearby anomalies, preserves internal structures, and reconstructs their vertical extent better. These results indicate that the proposed depth-aware formulation helps to mitigate the depth ambiguity inherent in gravity inversion. In the field experiment, where no ground-truth density model was available, the method produced compact, separated, and vertically coherent anomalies consistent with the observed gravity pattern.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised depth-aware implicit neural representation for 3D gravity inversion using coordinate-based networks with slab-specific Fourier features and physics-based depth gains, outperforming conventional methods without requiring labeled data.
AI.motivation: 3D gravity inversion is highly ill-posed due to non-uniqueness, limited data coverage, and field attenuation with depth. Classical methods need explicit regularization and parameter tuning, while supervised deep learning requires representative gravity-density pairs that are rarely available.
AI.method: Proposes unsupervised depth-aware implicit neural representation: density volume represented by multiple coordinate-based neural networks assigned to overlapping depth slabs, optimized directly from observed gravity measurements through sensitivity matrix. Uses slab-specific Fourier features, physics-based depth gains, and scheduled regularization as structural priors without labeled density models.
AI.result: Outperforms conventional and neural baselines in four synthetic scenarios (better RMSE, PSNR, SSIM). Recovers more compact and spatially coherent density bodies, improves separation of nearby anomalies, preserves internal structures, and reconstructs vertical extent better. Field experiment produces compact, separated, vertically coherent anomalies consistent with observed gravity patterns.
AI.conclusion: The depth-aware formulation helps mitigate the depth ambiguity inherent in gravity inversion. The unsupervised approach successfully recovers density models without requiring labeled training data, making it practical for real-world applications where ground-truth density models are unavailable.

title: Generalized Convexity and Smoothness via Conjugate Duality: Optimization Theory for Deep Neural Networks
summary: Deep neural network (DNN) training with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants achieves strong empirical performance, yet classical optimization theory does not fully explain this success. This limitation arises because conventional analyses rely on assumptions such as differentiability, convexity, or smoothness, which are often violated by DNN objectives. In this paper, we establish a unified optimization framework for DNN training by generalizing classical convexity and smoothness through Legendre functions and convex conjugation. Specifically, we introduce $\mathcal{H}(ψ)$-convexity and $\mathcal{H}(Ψ)$-smoothness, which unify convex and non-convex as well as smooth and non-smooth objectives within a single formalism and reveal a natural duality between generalized smoothness and convexity. Building on these generalized properties, we introduce generalized gradient descent (GD) and generalized SGD through convex conjugation. We theoretically prove that generalized GD admits an optimal learning rate of exactly $1$, and derive rigorous gradient-energy-based convergence rates for both proposed optimizers. We further reformulate DNN training as a composite optimization problem, demonstrating that its convergence relies on jointly reducing the gradient energy and controlling the induced norm of the network Jacobian. To characterize the practical influences of network architectures and training configurations, we introduce the gradient correlation factor and model capacity risk, and quantitatively analyze how architectural designs, batch size, and model capacity shape training convergence. Extensive experiments across diverse network architectures, datasets, optimizers, and loss functions validate our theoretical bounds and demonstrate precise alignment between our theoretical predictions and empirical training dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a unified optimization framework for DNN training using Legendre functions to generalize convexity/smoothness concepts, enabling theoretical convergence analysis that aligns with empirical training dynamics.
AI.motivation: Classical optimization theory fails to fully explain DNN training success because it relies on assumptions like differentiability, convexity, or smoothness that DNN objectives often violate, creating a gap between theory and practice.
AI.method: Introduces $\mathcal{H}(ψ)$-convexity and $\mathcal{H}(Ψ)$-smoothness using Legendre functions and convex conjugation to unify convex/non-convex and smooth/non-smooth objectives. Develops generalized GD and SGD optimizers, proves convergence rates based on gradient energy, and reformulates DNN training as composite optimization.
AI.result: Theoretically proves generalized GD has optimal learning rate of exactly 1, derives rigorous gradient-energy-based convergence rates, and shows training convergence depends on jointly reducing gradient energy and controlling network Jacobian norm. Introduces gradient correlation factor and model capacity risk to quantify architectural/configuration effects.
AI.conclusion: The unified framework successfully bridges the gap between classical optimization theory and practical DNN training, with extensive experimental validation showing precise alignment between theoretical predictions and empirical training dynamics across diverse settings.

title: Reading is not Reasoning: Bridging the Agentic Policy Gap in Vision-Text Compression
summary: Multi-step language-model agents repeatedly process growing interaction histories, leading to substantial context costs. Vision--text compression reduces these costs by rendering history as images, but the resulting modality shift creates a marked capability gap. Through controlled evaluations of history recovery, matched-state decisions, and complete trajectories, we show that this gap cannot be explained by OCR quality alone. Visual-history agents exhibit systematic drift in action selection, query formulation, stopping, and evidence use, revealing an agentic policy gap. We introduce \textbf{CAPS}, a two-stage \textbf{C}ross-modal \textbf{A}gentic \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{S}elf-distillation framework that uses the same model's stronger text-history policy to supervise its visual-history counterpart. Offline trajectory self-distillation transfers successful text-policy behavior to visual-history inputs, while online policy self-distillation provides dense supervision on states visited by the visual-history policy during reinforcement learning. On SearchQA, CAPS improves over AgentOCR by 5.0\% and 3.4\% with 3B and 7B backbones, respectively. On full-history ALFWorld, the corresponding gains are 15.6\% and 14.5\%. Across settings, CAPS reduces average memory-context cost by up to 63.3\% and peak cost by up to 83.4\% relative to matched text-history policies. These results show that explicit cross-modal policy self-distillation can preserve agent capability under vision--text compression. Our code will be made publicly available in a future release.

AI.tldr: CAPS is a cross-modal agentic policy self-distillation framework that bridges the capability gap between text-history and visual-history agents in language model systems, improving performance while reducing memory costs.
AI.motivation: Multi-step language model agents face high context costs from growing interaction histories. Vision-text compression reduces costs but creates a capability gap - visual-history agents perform worse than text-history agents, and this gap can't be explained by OCR quality alone.
AI.method: CAPS uses a two-stage cross-modal self-distillation framework: 1) Offline trajectory self-distillation transfers successful text-policy behavior to visual-history inputs, and 2) Online policy self-distillation provides dense supervision on states visited by visual-history policy during reinforcement learning.
AI.result: On SearchQA, CAPS improves over AgentOCR by 5.0% and 3.4% with 3B and 7B backbones. On ALFWorld, gains are 15.6% and 14.5%. Reduces average memory-context cost by up to 63.3% and peak cost by up to 83.4% relative to text-history policies.
AI.conclusion: Explicit cross-modal policy self-distillation can effectively preserve agent capability under vision-text compression, bridging the systematic policy gap between visual and text history representations while maintaining significant memory savings.

title: Dual-Adversarial Safety Alignment: Cultivating Intrinsic Threat Comprehension in LRMs
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve remarkable success on complex tasks but remain vulnerable to harmful prompts that induce unsafe outputs. Recent methods align LRMs using direct refusals or safety rationales, yet often focus on prompt patterns rather than intrinsic attack mechanisms. As a result, these pattern-centric alignments struggle to generalize across diverse jailbreaks, compromising adversarial robustness and reasoning utility. We propose AdvSafe, a dual-adversarial framework that enables LRMs to internalize unsafety knowledge by explicitly deconstructing adversarial mechanisms. This moves beyond pattern-dependent traces, fostering robust cognitive defense without compromising reasoning utility. Our pipeline operates via a two-phase adversarial game. First, in adversarial synthesis, an autonomous agent dynamically crafts deceptive jailbreak prompts, adapting its strategies to breach a strong teacher model. Second, in adversarial extraction, the breached teacher executes a cognitive counter-attack. For every successful jailbreak, the teacher unmasks the camouflage, explaining why the attack succeeds and how such prompts can be identified and mitigated. This dual-adversarial process yields a compact reasoning dataset capturing rich, generalizable unsafety knowledge. Student models trained on this dataset implicitly acquire safety alignment through intrinsic threat comprehension. Experiments show that with only 1K synthesized samples, AdvSafe-aligned LRMs achieve significantly stronger jailbreak robustness than existing baselines, with almost no utility degradation. Furthermore, AdvSafe improves robustness against out-of-distribution prompts, demonstrating that learning unsafety knowledge enables a superior robustness-utility trade-off and generalizes beyond seen attack patterns.

AI.tldr: AdvSafe: A dual-adversarial framework that teaches large reasoning models to internalize unsafety knowledge by deconstructing adversarial mechanisms, achieving stronger jailbreak robustness with minimal utility degradation using only 1K training samples.
AI.motivation: Large reasoning models (LRMs) are vulnerable to harmful prompts inducing unsafe outputs.
