Current alignment methods focus on prompt patterns rather than intrinsic attack mechanisms, leading to poor generalization across diverse jailbreaks and compromising both adversarial robustness and reasoning utility.
AI.method: Two-phase adversarial game: 1) Adversarial synthesis - an autonomous agent dynamically crafts deceptive jailbreak prompts to breach a strong teacher model. 2) Adversarial extraction - the breached teacher executes cognitive counter-attack by explaining why attacks succeed and how to identify/mitigate them, creating a compact reasoning dataset with generalizable unsafety knowledge.
AI.result: AdvSafe-aligned LRMs achieve significantly stronger jailbreak robustness than existing baselines with only 1K synthesized samples, showing almost no utility degradation. The method also improves robustness against out-of-distribution prompts, demonstrating superior robustness-utility trade-off and generalization beyond seen attack patterns.
AI.conclusion: AdvSafe successfully enables LRMs to internalize unsafety knowledge through explicit deconstruction of adversarial mechanisms, moving beyond pattern-dependent defenses. This approach fosters robust cognitive defense while maintaining reasoning utility, offering an effective solution to jailbreak vulnerability through intrinsic threat comprehension.

title: CoRe-UIE: Rethinking Coexisting and Region-wise Degradation for Underwater Image Enhancement
summary: Underwater images often suffer from diverse and coexisting degradations, including color distortion, scattering haze, texture attenuation, and uneven illumination. These degradations vary across regions and may coexist locally, making conventional uniform restoration difficult to adapt to different degradation patterns. To address this problem, we propose Coexisting and Region-wise Degradation for Underwater Image Enhancement (\textbf{CoRe-UIE}), a degradation-oriented expert collaboration framework. CoRe-UIE combines a content-preserving shared expert with four shared-backbone routed experts for color correction, scattering suppression, texture recovery, and illumination protection. The routed experts share the same architecture but have independent parameters, and are assigned to different regions through input-derived degradation cues and region-adaptive Top-\(k\) routing. We further introduce a Hilbert--Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC)-based representation constraint to reduce statistical dependence among expert features and alleviate redundant expert responses. Experiments on UIEB, LSUI, and U45 demonstrate that CoRe-UIE achieves competitive quantitative performance and visually balanced enhancement under diverse underwater degradation conditions.

AI.tldr: A degradation-aware underwater image enhancement framework called CoRe-UIE uses expert collaboration with shared and specialized components for different degradation types, achieving competitive performance across multiple underwater datasets.
AI.motivation: Underwater images suffer from diverse and coexisting degradations (color distortion, scattering haze, texture attenuation, uneven illumination) that vary across regions and may coexist locally. Conventional uniform restoration methods struggle to adapt to these different degradation patterns.
AI.method: CoRe-UIE is a degradation-oriented expert collaboration framework combining: 1) content-preserving shared expert, 2) four shared-backbone routed experts for color correction, scattering suppression, texture recovery, and illumination protection, 3) input-derived degradation cues with region-adaptive Top-k routing to assign experts to different regions, and 4) HSIC-based representation constraint to reduce statistical dependence among expert features and alleviate redundant responses.
AI.result: Experiments on UIEB, LSUI, and U45 datasets demonstrate competitive quantitative performance and visually balanced enhancement under diverse underwater degradation conditions.
AI.conclusion: CoRe-UIE effectively handles coexisting and region-wise degradations in underwater images through its expert collaboration framework, achieving robust performance across different underwater environments and degradation types.

title: Training-Free Universal Approximation by Prompting Random Transformers
summary: How expressive is prompting a transformer? Answering this question is important for separating the roles of prompting, architecture, and pretraining in transformer models, and for determining whether task-specific behavior must be stored in model weights or can instead be induced at inference time through the prompt. We show, in an approximation-theoretic sense, that pretraining is optional: a single-layer softmax attention network with random, untrained weights can approximate any Hölder function on a compact manifold when steered by an appropriate soft prompt. Guided by the connection between softmax attention and kernel methods, we construct explicit soft prompts (a prompt per target function, independent of the query) as solutions to linear systems matching attention logits to Gaussian kernel exponents, under which the frozen transformer emulates the classical Nadaraya-Watson kernel estimator. The construction requires only a mild rank condition on the weights, which we show holds almost surely under Gaussian initialization. The prompted network inherits the theoretical guarantees of kernel regression, leading to universal approximation theorems with minimax-optimal rates that depend on the intrinsic dimension. We further quantify the cost of prompting, exposing a tradeoff between the norm of the constructed soft prompt tokens, prompt length, and hidden dimension. Numerical experiments corroborate the constructions and predicted rates.

AI.tldr: A single-layer attention network with random untrained weights can approximate any function on a manifold when guided by an appropriate soft prompt, showing pretraining is optional for transformer expressivity.
AI.motivation: To understand the relative importance of prompting versus architecture and pretraining in transformers, and determine whether task-specific behavior must be learned in weights or can be induced at inference time through prompts.
AI.method: Shows that random untrained single-layer softmax attention networks can approximate Hölder functions on compact manifolds when steered by appropriate soft prompts. Connects softmax attention to kernel methods, constructs explicit soft prompts as solutions to linear systems matching attention logits to Gaussian kernel exponents, making the frozen transformer emulate Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression.
AI.result: The construction requires only mild rank conditions on weights (holds almost surely under Gaussian initialization). The prompted network inherits kernel regression theoretical guarantees, achieving universal approximation theorems with minimax-optimal rates dependent on intrinsic dimension. Reveals tradeoff between prompt token norm, prompt length, and hidden dimension.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining is optional for transformer expressivity - random untrained attention networks with appropriate soft prompts can approximate any function on manifolds, with theoretical guarantees matching kernel regression performance.

title: Context Is Not Authority: Structured Runtime Governance for Financial Market Agents
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 9 tables. Qiangqiang Liu and Yichi Zhang are corresponding authors
summary: Financial agents can turn correct context into an unauthorized effect: a customer-facing commitment, trade, or deployed policy. We present SAGE-Fin, a finance-specific authority-handoff contract that makes the proposed effect, not merely its text, the object of runtime control. SAGE-Fin compiles proposals into typed, adapter-bound candidates; records missing or stale institutional obligations as coverage debt; contracts authority under current market, account, policy, and dialogue state; and requires an exact-artifact receipt whose nominal type matches the consuming response, execution, or policy adapter. Evidence and workflow progress cannot substitute for effect authority, and prior authorization is rechecked after state changes. Across an authored 616-case catalog, five deterministic specifications yield 3,080 outputs; a label-isolated harness obtains 616/616 binary reference-prototype parity, including 3/3 named response-gate fixtures, while 22 tests cover selected paths. These results establish executable conformance, not independent safety accuracy. Separately, SAGE-Fin's response gate processed real customer-facing production requests at a confidential digital-asset platform. An operational team independent of the implementation team reached a strongly positive post-deployment conclusion on practical usefulness and workflow fit, and end-user feedback was also strongly positive. Disclosure permits only the review's independence, stakeholder classes, assessed dimensions, and directional conclusion, so this is qualitative field corroboration rather than an aggregate effect estimate. Three distinct de-identified predecessor failures, with independently confirmed 0/3 interception, ground repeated-emission drift, stale account evidence, and missing escalation state without estimating prevalence or treatment effect.

AI.tldr: SAGE-Fin is a finance-specific authority-handoff contract system that controls actual financial effects rather than just text, ensuring proper authorization before customer-facing commitments, trades, or policies are executed, with successful implementation at a digital-asset platform.
AI.motivation: Financial agents can transform correct context into unauthorized effects (customer commitments, trades, or policies). Current systems focus on text rather than controlling actual effects, creating security and compliance risks in financial operations.
AI.method: SAGE-Fin compiles proposals into typed, adapter-bound candidates; records institutional obligations as coverage debt; contracts authority based on current market, account, policy, and dialogue state; and requires exact-artifact receipts matching consuming responses. The system prevents workflow progress from substituting for effect authority and rechecks authorization after state changes.
AI.result: Across 616-case catalog, the system achieved 616/616 binary reference-prototype parity with deterministic specifications. SAGE-Fin successfully processed real customer-facing production requests at a digital-asset platform, receiving strongly positive feedback from independent operational teams and end-users. The system identified three distinct predecessor failures that would have been intercepted.
AI.conclusion: SAGE-Fin establishes executable conformance for financial authority-handoff through effect-based control rather than text-based authorization. The system demonstrates practical usefulness, workflow fit, and can identify and prevent various failure patterns in financial operations, though this represents qualitative field corroboration rather than aggregate effect estimation.

title: Hyperbolic Multimodal Continual Learning
summary: Hyperbolic geometry has recently emerged as a powerful representation space for multimodal learning, as it naturally captures hierarchical semantic structure across modalities. Despite this progress, how such representations behave under continual learning poses fundamentally different challenges that remain underexplored. This work provides a geometric perspective on this problem and establishes a theoretical foundation for representation preservation in hyperbolic space, showing that preventing forgetting requires cross-modal invariance under a shared hyperbolic isometry. We further show that forgetting in hyperbolic continual learning involves both semantic relation drift and hierarchy-related distortion, motivating preservation of both cross-modal relational structure and hierarchical geometry. Guided by these insights, a principled continual learning framework is derived that preserves essential geometric structure while allowing effective adaptation to new tasks. Experiments on continual multimodal benchmarks corroborate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hyperbolic geometry-based approach for continual multimodal learning that preserves cross-modal relational structure and hierarchical geometry to prevent forgetting.
AI.motivation: Hyperbolic geometry is powerful for multimodal learning due to its ability to capture hierarchical semantic structure, but its behavior under continual learning remains underexplored with fundamental challenges.
AI.method: Theoretical foundation for representation preservation in hyperbolic space, showing forgetting prevention requires cross-modal invariance under shared hyperbolic isometry. Develops a principled continual learning framework that preserves essential geometric structure while adapting to new tasks.
AI.result: Experiments on continual multimodal benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The work provides geometric insights into hyperbolic continual learning, showing forgetting involves both semantic relation drift and hierarchy-related distortion, and proposes a solution that successfully preserves both cross-modal relational structure and hierarchical geometry.

title: PolicyKG: An Agentic LLM Pipeline for Translating Institutional Policies into SHACL Knowledge Graphs
comment: 23 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Under review at IJCKG 2026, Bangkok, Thailand
summary:
Institutional policies stay in natural language while the systems that check compliance demand machine-readable constraints. Bridging that gap is still done by hand.
  PolicyKG closes the loop. It is an LLM pipeline that reads a policy PDF, classifies each sentence as an obligation, permission, or prohibition, lifts the label into first-order deontic logic, and emits SHACL constraints. Four stages run on a LangGraph state machine with per-stage validators. The piece that matters most is the Corpus Adapter: a YAML vocabulary registry that grounds LLM predicates in a target ontology. Retargeting to a new domain means swapping the registry, not retraining a model.
  On the Asian Institute of Technology Policies and Procedures corpus (1,663 sentences, 443 rules), PolicyKG reaches 86.9% deontic classification accuracy (Cohen's kappa = .709). Three annotators independently re-label a 50-item sample and agree at Fleiss' kappa = .844. SHACL shape correctness on a 69-shape subset is F1 = .866. The FOL path handles 79.2% of rules; the rest go through a direct NL-to-SHACL fallback.
  We audited every one of the 443 rules for second- or higher-order constructs. An automated regex checklist flagged none, and a first-author pass on the 92 FOL-fallback cases confirmed the same. The exact upper 95% Clopper-Pearson bound on the true HOL rate is 0.67%. This is an audit finding for one corpus, not a proof of FOL sufficiency for institutional policy.
  Swapping the AIT registry for a GDPR registry raises exact property alignment from 1/15 to 11/15 (Fisher's exact p < .001; Cohen's h = 1.53). On the LexDeMod lease-contract benchmark (N = 200), Macro F1 drops to .370 because lease English uses "shall be entitled" for permission -- exactly the vocabulary mismatch registry swap is meant to fix. Repeated runs produce hash-identical SHACL outputs.

AI.tldr: PolicyKG is an LLM pipeline that automatically converts natural language institutional policies into SHACL constraints using first-order deontic logic, with a Corpus Adapter allowing domain adaptation through vocabulary registries.
AI.motivation: There's a gap between natural language institutional policies and machine-readable constraints needed for compliance checking, which currently requires manual translation.
AI.method: Four-stage LLM pipeline: reads policy PDFs, classifies sentences as obligation/permission/prohibition, lifts labels to first-order deontic logic, emits SHACL constraints. Uses LangGraph state machine with per-stage validators and a key Corpus Adapter (YAML vocabulary registry) to ground LLM predicates in target ontologies.
AI.result: 86.9% deontic classification accuracy on AIT corpus (κ=.709), high inter-annotator agreement (κ=.844). SHACL shape correctness F1=.866. 79.2% rules handled by FOL path, rest through NL-to-SHACL fallback. Corpus audit shows low HOL rate (<0.67%). Registry swapping significantly improves property alignment (1/15→11/15).
AI.conclusion: PolicyKG effectively bridges the policy-language gap with high accuracy and domain adaptability through vocabulary registries, demonstrating practical utility for institutional policy formalization.

title: LEED: Local Embedding Evolution Distance for over-smoothing estimation and virtual node selection in GNN
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) suffer from two fundamental limitations: over-smoothing, where node representations become indistinguishable with depth, and over-squashing, where long-range information is compressed through limited message-passing channels. Existing metrics such as Dirichlet energy provide global characterizations of over-smoothing but lack the resolution to analyze node-level behavior and guide architectural improvements. In this paper, we propose LEED (Local Embedding Evolution Distance), a novel local metric that quantifies over-smoothing by tracking the evolution of individual node embeddings across layers. By operating at the node level, LEED enables fine-grained analysis of representation dynamics during training, revealing heterogeneous over-smoothing patterns that are invisible to global energy-based measures. This locality induces informative node importance scores, interpreted as embedding-driven centrality measures. We leverage LEED to design a more efficient strategy for virtual node selection. Unlike existing approaches that depend on multiple heuristic centrality measures, our method uses LEED as a unique criterion to guide the construction of Local Virtual Nodes to mitigate over-squashing. Experiments show that LEED provides more informative diagnostics than Dirichlet energy while preserving global evaluation, and enables more effective virtual node integration, improving GNN performance across datasets.

AI.tldr: A novel local metric called LEED is proposed to quantify and analyze node-level over-smoothing in GNNs, enabling better diagnostics and more effective virtual node integration to mitigate over-squashing.
AI.motivation: GNNs suffer from two fundamental limitations: over-smoothing (node representations become indistinguishable with depth) and over-squashing (long-range information compression). Existing metrics like Dirichlet energy provide only global characterizations and lack node-level resolution to guide architectural improvements.
AI.method: Proposes LEED (Local Embedding Evolution Distance), a local metric that tracks the evolution of individual node embeddings across layers. This node-level approach enables fine-grained analysis of representation dynamics and reveals heterogeneous over-smoothing patterns. LEED is then used to design a more efficient virtual node selection strategy, where it serves as the sole criterion for constructing Local Virtual Nodes to mitigate over-squashing.
AI.result: LEED provides more informative diagnostics than Dirichlet energy while preserving global evaluation capabilities. It induces informative node importance scores that function as embedding-driven centrality measures. When used for virtual node integration, it improves GNN performance across datasets compared to approaches relying on multiple heuristic centrality measures.
AI.conclusion: LEED addresses key limitations in existing GNN analysis tools by providing local, node-level insights into over-smoothing. Its ability to reveal heterogeneous patterns and guide architectural improvements makes it a valuable tool for both diagnosing and mitigating GNN limitations, leading to better performance through more effective virtual node integration.

title: DualCert: A Solver for the Traveling Salesman Problem with Constraint-Coupled Learning
summary: Large traveling salesman problem (TSP) instances require a solver to allocate limited computation while preserving the validity of its outputs. Existing neural--operations-research (OR) hybrids predict guidance without requiring learned transitions to satisfy constraints discovered during search. DualCert introduces \emph{constraint-coupled learning}, in which current degree equations and dynamically separated subtour-elimination constraints (SECs) define each learned transition. At each refinement, the degree equations and selected, strictly satisfied SEC equations, with positive slacks, define an iterate-dependent primal-slack Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) manifold. Repaired dual variables and violated SEC rows define a local cost field. An exact constrained mirror-descent step maps each finite state to a positive state on the same manifold. Where selected rows and deterministic ties remain fixed, implicit differentiation maps parameter perturbations into the manifold tangent space and reuses the forward constraint operator for the local-cost-field derivative. The terminal edge state allocates computation across Held--Karp ascent, candidate-graph edge tests, and tour construction under a fixed budget. Deterministic verification recomputes original costs and accepts only verified candidate-graph lower bounds and edge decisions. On 1,000 held-out TSP1000 instances, DualCert attains a mean tour-cost gap of \(0.0573\%\) from Lin--Kernighan--Helsgaun version 3 (LKH-3) reference tours in \(9.55\) batch-amortized seconds per instance. It returns a verified candidate-graph lower bound for every instance and achieves \(81.46\%\) edge-decision coverage. The mean gap is \(67.1\%\) smaller than the reported NeuroLKH mean gap. Thus, optimization constraints govern learning, while deterministic verification preserves output validity.

AI.tldr: DualCert introduces constraint-coupled learning for TSP, combining neural guidance with deterministic verification to maintain solution validity while improving efficiency.
AI.motivation: Large TSP instances require efficient computation while preserving output validity. Existing neural-OR hybrids don't ensure learned transitions satisfy constraints discovered during search.
AI.method: Constraint-coupled learning uses degree equations and dynamically separated SECs to define learned transitions. Creates KKT manifold, uses repaired dual variables and exact constrained mirror-descent. Implicit differentiation handles parameter perturbations.
AI.result: On TSP1000 instances: 0.0573% gap from LKH-3 reference in 9.55 seconds per instance, returns verified bounds, 81.46% edge decision coverage, 67.1% better than NeuroLKH gap.
AI.conclusion: Optimization constraints can govern learning while deterministic verification preserves output validity, enabling effective neural-OR hybrids for large TSP.

title: Bayesian Symbolic Regression with Entropic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Symbolic regression is the problem of finding an algebraic expression describing a stochastic dependence of a target variable on a set of inputs. Unlike forms of regression that fit parameters assuming a fixed model structure, symbolic regression is a search problem over the space of expressions, represented, for example, as abstract syntax trees using a library of operators. Symbolic regression is typically used in settings with limited, noisy data in the natural sciences. However, searching for a single best-fitting expression fails to capture the epistemic uncertainty about the expression, which motivates a Bayesian perspective that enables uncertainty quantification and specification of natural priors to constrain the search space. In this work, we propose ERRLESS (Entropy-Regularized Reinforcement Learning for Expression Structure Sampling), a scalable approach for sampling from the posterior distribution over expressions given data using maximum-entropy reinforcement learning. ERRLESS learns a neural policy that constructs expressions sequentially by building up their abstract syntax trees. At convergence, the policy samples expressions from the posterior. At test time, expressions can be sampled by rollouts of this policy. We demonstrate that ERRLESS achieves competitive results on the Feynman benchmark while producing short and interpretable expressions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the mean of the posterior predictive approximated by ERRLESS achieves a high coefficient of determination ($R^2$) compared to an SMC baseline, highlighting the benefits of the Bayesian perspective in symbolic regression.

AI.tldr: ERRLESS is a Bayesian symbolic regression method that uses entropy-regularized reinforcement learning to sample from the posterior distribution over mathematical expressions, enabling uncertainty quantification while maintaining interpretability.
AI.motivation: Traditional symbolic regression only finds single best-fitting expressions, failing to capture epistemic uncertainty. A Bayesian approach is needed for uncertainty quantification and to constrain search space with natural priors, especially useful for noisy, limited scientific data.
AI.method: ERRLESS uses maximum-entropy reinforcement learning to train a neural policy that sequentially constructs expressions as abstract syntax trees. The learned policy samples expressions from the posterior distribution at convergence.
AI.result: Achieves competitive performance on Feynman benchmark with short, interpretable expressions. The posterior predictive mean achieves high R² compared to SMC baselines, demonstrating Bayesian advantages.
AI.conclusion: ERRLESS provides a scalable Bayesian approach to symbolic regression that enables uncertainty quantification while maintaining interpretability, showing benefits over single-expression optimization methods.

title: A Multi-Scale Temporal Framework with Dynamic Fusion for EEG-Based Emotion Recognition
comment: The paper has been accepted at: IEEE | 2026 9th International Conference on Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence (PRAI 2026)
summary: Mixed emotions represent a clinically relevant but still underexplored target for automatic emotion recognition. EEG provides millisecond-level access to neural activity, yet most EEG pipelines analyze the signal through a single temporal window, thereby fixing the temporal structure available to the model. This study introduces a multi-scale temporal framework for EEG-based emotion recognition. The EEG waveform is decomposed into windows of one or several durations, processed by a shared attention-based encoder, and integrated through a dynamic fusion module that assigns sample-specific weights across temporal scales. The framework is evaluated under a subject-independent protocol in binary and three-class settings, with the three-class task including the mixed affective category. The best results are 65.22% for the two-class task and 45.43% for the three-class task. Both are obtained with three-scale dynamic-fusion configurations and remain substantially above the full-signal baseline. The best-performing temporal scales differ between the two tasks. Dynamic fusion outperforms concatenation in the highest-scoring two-class configuration and slightly exceeds it in the highest-scoring three-class configuration, although these multi-scale settings require substantially more computation than the full-signal baseline.

AI.tldr: A multi-scale temporal framework for EEG-based emotion recognition that decomposes EEG signals into multiple temporal windows, processes them with an attention-based encoder, and fuses them dynamically, achieving improved performance over single-window baselines for both binary and three-class emotion classification (including mixed emotions).
AI.motivation: Mixed emotions are clinically relevant but underexplored in automatic emotion recognition. Traditional EEG pipelines use a single temporal window, fixing the temporal structure available to models and potentially limiting performance for complex affective states like mixed emotions.
AI.method: 1) Decompose EEG waveforms into windows of multiple durations; 2) Process each window with a shared attention-based encoder; 3) Integrate information through a dynamic fusion module that assigns sample-specific weights across temporal scales; 4) Evaluate under subject-independent protocols.
AI.result: Achieved 65.22% accuracy for binary classification and 45.43% for three-class classification (including mixed emotions) with three-scale dynamic-fusion configurations. Performance remained substantially above full-signal baseline. Best temporal scales differed between tasks. Dynamic fusion outperformed concatenation in binary task and slightly exceeded it in three-class task.
AI.conclusion: Multi-scale temporal analysis improves EEG-based emotion recognition, particularly for complex affective states like mixed emotions. The dynamic fusion approach effectively integrates information across different temporal scales, though it requires substantially more computation than single-window approaches.

title: Satellite Trajectory Optimization via Proximal Policy Optimization for Space Debris Avoidance
comment: 18 pages, 16 figures. Published in IEEE Access, vol. 14, pp. 18138-18154, 2026
summary: Collision avoidance systems are commonly used to avoid fragmentation events occurring in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) and Geosynchronous Equatorial Orbit (GEO). However, these events have been growing in frequency as orbital congestion worsens with the launch of megaconstellations. Consequently, conjunction alerts and collision risks are becoming increasingly common. Current practices, which are commonly manual or rule-based, have difficulty scaling to these worsening dynamic environments. To address this intensifying situation, we propose a reinforcement-learning policy for autonomous collision avoidance, trained via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) along with an open-source, high-fidelity astrodynamics simulator for training and evaluation. In 1,000 deterministic GEO episodes, our agent achieves a 97.5% collision avoidance success rate, outperforming traditional controllers such as a rule-based baseline (20.7% success) and an impulsive delta-v planner baseline (27.5% success). To achieve these results, we designed a simulator to train and evaluate our agent, using real-world and simulated debris. We simulate Newtonian two-body dynamics using Sun/Moon third-body perturbations, fuel-dependent thrust, and configurable debris fields. The agent is trained with curriculum learning and shaped rewards oriented toward encouraging survival, adequate projected miss distance, and delta-v conservation. Finally, our evaluation consisted of a fully deterministic pipeline, including shared seeds, per-episode logs, and telemetry exports. Our work is a publicly available framework at https://purl.org/sat-trajectory-avoidance

AI.tldr: A reinforcement learning system for autonomous satellite collision avoidance in GEO outperforms traditional rule-based and impulsive delta-v planners with 97.5% success rate.
AI.motivation: Collision avoidance systems struggle to scale with increasing orbital congestion from megaconstellations. Current manual or rule-based methods are insufficient for the growing frequency of conjunction alerts and collision risks in dynamic LEO and GEO environments.
AI.method: Uses Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) reinforcement learning trained with an open-source high-fidelity astrodynamics simulator. Includes Newtonian two-body dynamics with Sun/Moon third-body perturbations, fuel-dependent thrust, configurable debris fields, curriculum learning, and shaped rewards for survival, miss distance, and delta-v conservation.
AI.result: In 1,000 deterministic GEO episodes, the RL agent achieved 97.5% collision avoidance success rate, significantly outperforming rule-based baseline (20.7%) and impulsive delta-v planner baseline (27.5%).
AI.conclusion: The proposed reinforcement learning framework provides an effective solution for autonomous collision avoidance that scales better than traditional methods in increasingly congested orbital environments, with publicly available code for further development.

title: Who Bridges Safety? Identifying and Targeting Cross-Lingual Shared Safety Pathways
summary: Uncovering the internal mechanisms underlying the safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for developing trustworthy artificial intelligence. Currently, mechanistic interpretability studies on multilingual safety are largely confined to local components, such as isolated neurons. However, this static and fragmented perspective overlooks the synergy among components and fails to elucidate how safety signals dynamically propagate within the model to drive safety decisions ultimately. In this work, we move beyond isolated neurons to identify and target the cross-layer functional pathways formed during safety signal propagation, thereby uncovering the mechanisms driving the cross-lingual safety gap. Specifically, we first identify monolingual safety pathways and validate their impact on refusing harmful requests. Subsequent cross-lingual analyses reveal a sparse subset of cross-lingual shared safety pathways, confirming that this intersection acts as the internal bridge transferring safety capabilities from high-resource (HR) languages to non-high-resource (NHR) languages. Building on these mechanistic findings, we propose a pathways-targeted alignment method based on the cross-lingual shared safety pathways. Experimental results show that updating only a small fraction of pathway parameters significantly improves safety in NHR languages while largely preserving the model's general capabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies cross-layer functional pathways that transfer safety capabilities between languages in LLMs and proposes a targeted alignment method to improve safety in non-high-resource languages.
AI.motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability studies on multilingual safety focus too narrowly on isolated components, missing the dynamic synergy and safety signal propagation pathways that ultimately drive safety decisions. There's a need to understand the internal mechanisms behind cross-lingual safety gaps in LLMs.
AI.method: 1. Identify monolingual safety pathways and validate their impact on refusing harmful requests. 2. Conduct cross-lingual analyses to find sparse subsets of cross-lingual shared safety pathways. 3. Propose pathways-targeted alignment method based on cross-lingual shared safety pathways, updating only a small fraction of pathway parameters.
AI.result: Experimental results show that updating only a small fraction of pathway parameters significantly improves safety in non-high-resource languages while largely preserving the model's general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals that cross-lingual shared safety pathways act as internal bridges transferring safety capabilities from high-resource to non-high-resource languages, and targeted intervention on these pathways can effectively improve safety performance without compromising general capabilities.

title: Deep Learning Imputation of Missing Radius of Maximum Winds (Rmax) Values in Tropical Cyclone Best-Track Data
summary: Probabilistic coastal hazard assessments require accurate characterization of tropical cyclone (TC) parameters, yet datasets often contain missing records for the radius of maximum winds (Rmax), a key variable in Joint Probability Method analyses. This study evaluates data-driven approaches for Rmax imputation, including one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks (1DCNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and conventional machine learning models. We examine physics-informed input augmentation, temporal modeling, and transfer learning using synthetic RAFT and STORM datasets for pre-training and observational IBTrACS data for fine-tuning. Including the radius of 34-knot winds (R34) substantially improves performance across all model types. Temporal models achieve higher average correlations than non-temporal models despite using approximately an order of magnitude fewer samples, indicating better preservation of relative Rmax variability across storms. This advantage is more pronounced when R34 is unavailable, suggesting temporal information can partially compensate for missing storm-size predictors. Transfer learning does not improve performance, likely because synthetic datasets have lower and less variable Rmax distributions than IBTrACS. These findings demonstrate the potential of temporal deep learning for reconstructing incomplete TC records and highlight the importance of physics-informed inputs, observational data availability, and distributional consistency in coastal hazard assessment.

AI.tldr: Deep learning temporal models outperform conventional ML for imputing missing tropical cyclone radius data, with physics-informed inputs and storm temporal patterns being key factors.
AI.motivation: Coastal hazard assessments need accurate tropical cyclone parameters, but critical radius of maximum winds (Rmax) data is often missing from datasets, requiring effective imputation methods.
AI.method: Evaluated 1D CNNs, LSTMs, and conventional ML models for Rmax imputation; tested physics-informed inputs, temporal modeling, and transfer learning using synthetic datasets (RAFT/STORM) for pre-training and observational IBTrACS data for fine-tuning.
AI.result: Including radius of 34-knot winds (R34) improved all models; temporal models achieved higher correlations despite using fewer samples, especially when R34 was unavailable; transfer learning didn't help due to distribution differences between synthetic and real data.
AI.conclusion: Temporal deep learning shows promise for reconstructing incomplete tropical cyclone records, emphasizing the importance of physics-informed inputs, observational data availability, and distributional consistency in coastal hazard assessment.

title: Different Feedback, Different Updates: Selective Self-Learning from User Interactions for Large Language Models
summary: User feedback offers natural supervision for persistent LLM improvement, but a single message may support multiple behavioral changes with different scopes of generalization. We introduce SLIFT, a selective self-learning framework built on a task-relative view of user feedback. SLIFT decomposes each feedback message into atomic components and interprets each component relative to the original task as Fix, Spec, or Null: requirements for task validity, compatible condition-specific refinements, or content with no reliable positive update direction. To incorporate each change at the appropriate scope, SLIFT trains two complementary LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone: a Generalist that consolidates Fix requirements into default behavior through feedback-conditioned self-distillation, and a Specialist that observes only the task and Generalist response to supply residual guidance for applicable, unmet Spec refinements. Null components induce no positive update. Across backbones, SLIFT achieves strong performance on both MemoryBench and WildFB, with targeted analyses further examining its underlying mechanisms. We release our code at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SLIFT.

AI.tldr: SLIFT is a selective self-learning framework that decomposes user feedback into atomic components (Fix, Spec, Null) and trains complementary LoRA adapters to incorporate changes at appropriate generalization scopes for persistent LLM improvement.
AI.motivation: User feedback provides natural supervision for LLM improvement, but single messages often support multiple behavioral changes with different generalization scopes, requiring careful selective learning approaches.
AI.method: SLIFT decomposes feedback into atomic components interpreted relative to original tasks as Fix (task validity requirements), Spec (compatible condition-specific refinements), or Null (no reliable update direction). It trains two complementary LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone: a Generalist that consolidates Fix requirements through feedback-conditioned self-distillation, and a Specialist that provides residual guidance for unmet Spec refinements.
AI.result: SLIFT achieves strong performance across backbones on both MemoryBench and WildFB benchmarks, with targeted analyses examining its underlying mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: SLIFT provides an effective framework for selective self-learning from user feedback by properly decomposing feedback into components with different generalization scopes and training complementary adapters to incorporate appropriate changes.

title: FedOrbit: Adaptive Personalized Federated Learning for Non-IID LEO Satellite Constellations
summary: Federated learning (FL) in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations is affected by non-IID data and irregular ground-station visibility, both driven by orbital geometry. Global aggregation performs poorly when orbit-level class distributions are disjoint, while strong personalisation can be excessive when these distributions overlap. We present FedOrbit, which combines continuous orbit-level training over inter-satellite links, class-aware hierarchical aggregation, quality-weighted feature aggregation with return-rate dampening, and adaptive feature decomposition based on inter-orbit class similarity. Across three remote-sensing benchmarks and two non-IID partitions, FedOrbit achieves the highest accuracy in five of six settings and is within $0.9$ percentage points of the best result in the sixth. The gains over the strongest baseline reach $16.1$ percentage points under Dirichlet partitioning and $8.6$ under pathological partitioning, with the smallest per-orbit accuracy spread in five of six settings.

AI.tldr: FedOrbit improves federated learning in LEO satellite constellations by addressing non-IID data and irregular visibility through orbit-level training, hierarchical aggregation, and adaptive feature decomposition.
AI.motivation: Federated learning in LEO satellite constellations faces challenges from non-IID data (driven by orbital geometry) and irregular ground-station visibility. Global aggregation performs poorly when orbit-level class distributions are disjoint, while strong personalization can be excessive when distributions overlap.
AI.method: FedOrbit combines: 1) continuous orbit-level training over inter-satellite links, 2) class-aware hierarchical aggregation, 3) quality-weighted feature aggregation with return-rate dampening, and 4) adaptive feature decomposition based on inter-orbit class similarity.
AI.result: Across three remote-sensing benchmarks and two non-IID partitions, FedOrbit achieves highest accuracy in 5/6 settings and is within 0.9 percentage points in the sixth. Gains over strongest baseline reach 16.1% under Dirichlet partitioning and 8.6% under pathological partitioning, with smallest per-orbit accuracy spread in 5/6 settings.
AI.conclusion: FedOrbit effectively addresses the unique challenges of federated learning in LEO satellite constellations, providing a robust solution that adapts to orbital geometry-driven data heterogeneity and connectivity constraints while achieving superior performance across various non-IID scenarios.

title: RAVEN-Eval: Rubric-Guided Automatic Evaluation for AI Video Generation Models Based on LMM Preference Judgement
summary: AI video generation has advanced rapidly and entered widespread commercial use. As a result, quality differences among videos produced by state-of-the-art AI video generation models~(AIVGMs) have become increasingly difficult to discern using conventional evaluation criteria, such as visual fidelity and semantic instruction following. Meanwhile, human evaluation now requires more expertise and sustained attention, substantially increasing annotation costs. This calls for automated evaluation that can reliably distinguish fine-grained differences among advanced AIVGMs with minimal human intervention. To address this challenge, we present RAVEN-Eval, a rubric-guided automated evaluation framework for AIVGMs, built primarily on the LMM-as-a-judge paradigm. Through an automatic task curation and quality-filtering pipeline, RAVEN-Eval curates 150 text-to-video~(T2V) tasks and 100 image-to-video~(I2V) tasks, and systematically collects more than 4,500 AIGVs. At its core, RAVEN-Eval adopts rubric-guided automated LMM preference judgement, in which LMM judges conduct pairwise comparisons according to task-specific rubrics. It further introduces an anchor-based model insertion approach to reduce the evaluation cost of incorporating new models. Finally, we evaluate 20 high-performance AIVGMs, as well as the judging capabilities of 13 LMM judges, and establish the RAVEN-Eval Leaderboards. Overall, RAVEN-Eval paves a scalable path for automatic and trustworthy evaluation of rapidly evolving AIVGMs.

AI.tldr: RAVEN-Eval is a rubric-guided automated evaluation framework for AI video generation models that uses LMM-as-a-judge paradigm to distinguish fine-grained quality differences among advanced models, reducing the need for expensive human evaluation.
AI.motivation: As AI video generation models advance rapidly and enter commercial use, quality differences between state-of-the-art models have become difficult to discern using conventional metrics. Human evaluation has become more expensive, requiring expertise and sustained attention. There's a need for automated evaluation that can reliably distinguish fine-grained differences among advanced AI video generation models with minimal human intervention.
AI.method: RAVEN-Eval uses rubric-guided automated LMM preference judgement where LMM judges conduct pairwise comparisons according to task-specific rubrics. It includes: 1) automatic task curation and quality-filtering pipeline that curates 150 text-to-video and 100 image-to-video tasks, collecting over 4,500 AI-generated videos; 2) rubric-guided automated evaluation; 3) anchor-based model insertion approach to reduce evaluation costs when incorporating new models.
AI.result: The framework successfully evaluated 20 high-performance AI video generation models and assessed the judging capabilities of 13 LMM judges. It established the RAVEN-Eval Leaderboards, providing a comprehensive evaluation system. The approach demonstrated scalability and trustworthiness for evaluating rapidly evolving AI video generation models.
AI.conclusion: RAVEN-Eval provides a scalable and automated solution for evaluating advanced AI video generation models, addressing the limitations of traditional metrics and expensive human evaluation. The framework paves the way for automatic, trustworthy evaluation of rapidly evolving AI video generation technologies.

title: Confusion-Geometry Rebalancing for Long-Tailed Adversarial Training
summary: Adversarial training under long tailed distributions suffers from a dual imbalance: the class imbalance skews the training objective toward head classes, and the adversarial inner maximization may further amplify this bias. Existing methods mitigate this issue by correcting class priors or adapting class wise robust supervision, yet they treat each class in isolation and fail to identify which boundaries drive long tailed collapse. We propose a Confusion Geometry Rebalancing method (CGRm) for long tail adversarial training, a plug in framework that leverages directed robust errors as training signals. CGRm leverages periodic robust evaluations to derive source class loss weights, class wise robust coefficients, and a directed confusion geometry graph. The method then couples feedback weighted robust optimization with graph guided margin correction, thereby boosting the robustness of vulnerable classes and sharpening the critical boundaries that drive long tailed performance degradation. Experiments on long tailed benchmarks show that CGRm achieves consistent robust performance gains over existing methods, with ablations validating the contribution of each component. We provide the code in the supplement.

AI.tldr: CGRm: A confusion geometry rebalancing method for long-tail adversarial training that uses directed robust errors and graph-guided margin correction to address dual imbalance in adversarial training on imbalanced datasets.
AI.motivation: Adversarial training under long-tailed distributions suffers from dual imbalance: class imbalance skews training toward head classes, and adversarial inner maximization amplifies this bias. Existing methods fail to identify which boundaries drive long-tailed collapse and treat classes in isolation.
AI.method: Proposes CGRm method that leverages periodic robust evaluations to derive source class loss weights, class-wise robust coefficients, and a directed confusion geometry graph. Couples feedback-weighted robust optimization with graph-guided margin correction to boost robustness of vulnerable classes and sharpen critical boundaries.
AI.result: Experiments on long-tailed benchmarks show CGRm achieves consistent robust performance gains over existing methods, with ablations validating the contribution of each component.
AI.conclusion: CGRm effectively addresses the dual imbalance in long-tail adversarial training by using directed robust errors and confusion geometry to identify and correct critical boundaries, leading to improved robustness across all classes.

title: Motif 3: Technical Report
summary: We introduce Motif 3, a decoder-only Mixture-of-Experts language model with 314 billion total parameters and 13.2 billion activated per token. Each sparse MoE layer contains 384 routed experts, with eight selected per token. This fine-grained sparsity provides substantial expert capacity while limiting computation. Motif 3 is built around Grouped Differential Latent Attention (GDLA), which integrates grouped differential attention with the compressed key-value representation of Multi-head Latent Attention. The architecture further incorporates modified manifold-constrained hyper-connections, Expert Specific PolyNorm activations, and multi-token prediction to improve optimization stability, expert specialization, and inference efficiency. We pretrain Motif 3 on approximately 12.5 trillion tokens spanning web documents, STEM, code, mathematics, multilingual content, and domain-specialized corpora. Expert-balancing and numerical-stabilization techniques support stable training at scale, while selective MXFP8 computation and communication, memory-efficient fused kernels, and window-aware context parallelism enable training with context lengths up to 256K tokens. Our post-training pipeline combines general supervised fine-tuning, six specialist teachers trained with reinforcement learning, a software-engineering teacher trained with supervised fine-tuning, and Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation. The resulting unified model consolidates complementary capabilities in reasoning, coding, tool use, professional work, long-context understanding, calibrated abstention, and instruction following. Across a broad evaluation suite, Motif 3 demonstrates competitive performance against leading open weight models, including strong results on long-horizon agentic tasks, mathematical reasoning, scientific knowledge, and hallucination-sensitive evaluation.

AI.tldr: Motif 3 is a 314B parameter sparse MoE language model with only 13.2B activated parameters per token, featuring novel architectural innovations like GDLA attention and specialized training techniques that achieve strong performance across diverse tasks.
AI.motivation: To develop a large-scale language model that efficiently combines expert capacity with computational efficiency through sparse activation, while consolidating diverse capabilities including reasoning, coding, tool use, and long-context understanding into a unified model.
AI.method: Decoder-only Mixture-of-Experts architecture with 384 experts per layer (8 selected per token), Grouped Differential Latent Attention, modified manifold-constrained hyper-connections, Expert Specific PolyNorm activations, and multi-token prediction. Trained on 12.5T tokens using expert-balancing and numerical-stabilization techniques with up to 256K context length support.
AI.result: The model demonstrates competitive performance against leading open weight models, with strong results on long-horizon agentic tasks, mathematical reasoning, scientific knowledge, and hallucination-sensitive evaluations, while consolidating diverse capabilities into a unified system.
AI.conclusion: Motif 3 successfully achieves efficient large-scale modeling through sparse expert activation and architectural innovations, demonstrating that careful architectural design combined with comprehensive training and distillation can produce a versatile model capable of handling diverse real-world applications.

title: Recurrent Neural Networks Beyond Time: Learning from Multiple Ordered Projections
summary: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are widely used for sequence learning, yet their application is commonly associated with temporal data, although recurrent computation fundamentally operates on ordered sequences rather than on time itself. Building on this observation, we introduce the Ordered Structural Dependency Hypothesis (OSDH), which proposes that multiple admissible orderings of the same observations may reveal complementary structural dependencies inaccessible through a single sequential organization. To operationalize this hypothesis, we propose the Independent Structural Expert Principle (ISEP), whereby projection-specific sequence models are trained independently before their learned representations are integrated through a dedicated fusion model. As a concrete realization, we present Structural Evolution RNNs (SE-RNNs), which employ conventional RNNs as projection-specific structural experts while preserving the underlying recurrent computation unchanged. Proof-of-concept experiments on three synthetic datasets with substantially different levels of structural complexity demonstrate that the proposed architecture consistently benefits from multiple ordered projections when hidden structural dependencies are present, while remaining competitive on simpler datasets. Since OSDH is independent of the underlying sequence-processing model, the proposed framework naturally extends beyond recurrent networks and may be instantiated using alternative architectures. The results suggest a general computational perspective for exploiting complementary ordered representations across diverse structured learning problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that multiple orderings of sequence data can reveal complementary structural dependencies, introducing the Ordered Structural Dependency Hypothesis and Independent Structural Expert Principle, with Structural Evolution RNNs as a concrete implementation showing benefits on complex structural data.
AI.motivation: Current RNN applications focus primarily on temporal data, but recurrent computation fundamentally operates on ordered sequences rather than time itself. The authors argue that considering multiple admissible orderings of the same observations could reveal complementary structural dependencies that are inaccessible through a single sequential organization.
AI.method: The paper introduces the Ordered Structural Dependency Hypothesis (OSDH) and Independent Structural Expert Principle (ISEP), where projection-specific sequence models are trained independently before their representations are integrated through a fusion model. They implement this as Structural Evolution RNNs (SE-RNNs), which use conventional RNNs as projection-specific structural experts while keeping the recurrent computation unchanged.
AI.result: Proof-of-concept experiments on three synthetic datasets with different structural complexity levels show that the proposed architecture consistently benefits from multiple ordered projections when hidden structural dependencies exist, while remaining competitive on simpler datasets.
AI.conclusion: The Ordered Structural Dependency Hypothesis provides a general computational perspective for exploiting complementary ordered representations across diverse structured learning problems, with the framework being extensible beyond recurrent networks to alternative architectures.

title: MELLON - Multimodal Enhanced LLM for Online Navigation
summary: Web navigation agents are capable of addressing various types of tasks on different websites. Current baselines on web navigation are either unimodal or lack strong reasoning abilities given multimodal inputs. Focusing on the WebShop benchmark, a real-world website simulation, we explore the alignment of text and images, as well as multimodal reasoning and planning abilities, to enhance the performance of web navigation agents. We propose three innovative multimodal enhancements: Multimodal Enhanced LLM for Online Navigation (MELLON), VQAgent, and Multimodal Ranker. MELLON demonstrates a significant improvement in task completion accuracy, with a 9.26% increase after just one epoch of training. Our findings suggest the necessity of further exploration into multimodal approaches, with a focus on more extensive training and alignment strategies to enhance the effectiveness of web navigation agents.

AI.tldr: Multimodal web navigation agents that combine text and image understanding achieve significantly better performance on real-world website navigation tasks like WebShop, with one method showing 9.26% accuracy improvement after minimal training.
AI.motivation: Current web navigation baselines are either unimodal (text-only) or lack strong reasoning abilities with multimodal inputs, limiting their performance on real-world websites that contain both text and visual elements.
AI.method: Proposed three multimodal enhancements: MELLON (Multimodal Enhanced LLM for Online Navigation), VQAgent, and Multimodal Ranker, focusing on aligning text and images while improving multimodal reasoning and planning abilities.
AI.result: MELLON demonstrated significant improvement with 9.26% increase in task completion accuracy after just one epoch of training on the WebShop benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal approaches are necessary for effective web navigation agents, and further exploration with more extensive training and better alignment strategies is needed to enhance their effectiveness.

title: Evaluating Generative Time-Series Models on Data with Point Masses
summary: Many of the series that generative time-series models are benchmarked on place a large probability mass on a single value --- it does not rain, no ride is requested, no part is ordered. We report what happens when such data is evaluated carefully. First, the standard rolling-origin protocol can score a model on a window whose atom structure bears no resemblance to the dataset: on one benchmark the dataset is $42\%$ zeros and the evaluation windows are $13\%$, on another $47\%$ against $5\%$. This is not a cosmetic problem --- it reversed one of our own conclusions, turning the strongest occurrence model in our study into what looked like a cautionary tale. Second, we give a control in which CRPS is invariant \emph{by construction} while the temporal coupling is destroyed, which measures exactly how much that coupling contributes to a chosen statistic. Third, benchmarking seven models on a matched protocol over five seeds, an autoregressive hurdle beats a conditional flow on five of six datasets, by up to a factor of $153$, while the flow's own occurrence statistics vary by up to $62\%$ across training seeds and every baseline is deterministic. Finally, the model ordering is not the same under five different occurrence statistics, and the two that do not share a construction agree with each other least.

AI.tldr: Standard evaluation protocols for time-series models with many zeros are flawed, with mismatched zero frequencies between training and test windows. A careful analysis shows these issues can reverse conclusions about model performance, and autoregressive models outperform flows on most datasets.
AI.motivation: Many time-series datasets have high probability mass on single values (e.g., zero for no rain, no ride requests), but standard evaluation protocols don't account for this properly. The authors discovered that the standard rolling-origin evaluation creates windows with atom structures that don't match the dataset distribution, which can lead to misleading conclusions about model performance.
AI.method: 1) Analyzed the rolling-origin protocol's mismatch between dataset and evaluation window atom structures. 2) Created a control where CRPS is invariant by construction while destroying temporal coupling to measure its contribution. 3) Benchmarked seven models using a matched protocol across five seeds on six datasets, comparing autoregressive hurdle models vs conditional flows.
AI.result: 1) Rolling-origin windows had dramatically different zero frequencies than datasets (42% vs 13% and 47% vs 5%). 2) This protocol issue reversed their own conclusion about the best model. 3) Autoregressive hurdle beat conditional flow on 5 of 6 datasets by up to 153x. 4) Flow model occurrence statistics varied by 62% across training seeds. 5) Model ordering differed across five occurrence statistics, with the two that don't share construction agreeing least.
AI.conclusion: Current time-series evaluation protocols for datasets with many zeros are flawed and can produce misleading results. Careful matching of evaluation windows to dataset structure is essential, and autoregressive models generally outperform flow models for such data. The choice of evaluation statistic significantly affects model rankings.

title: RISE-RL: Rubric-Informed Selective Exploration for Open-Ended Reinforcement Learning
summary: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) for open-ended tasks is challenging because responses must satisfy multidimensional criteria without following a single correct generation trajectory. Existing rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) methods compress fine-grained criterion-level feedback into scalar rewards, making persistent capability gaps difficult to target under limited on-policy exploration. We propose $\textbf{RISE-RL}$ (Rubric-Informed Selective Exploration), which uses repeatedly missed rubric criteria to elicit privileged trajectories that are difficult to discover through unguided exploration alone. RISE-RL retains only trajectories whose complete-rubric reward exceeds the mean reward of natural rollouts, and then re-evaluates them under the original prompt to emphasize behaviors that remain weakly supported by the natural policy. The resulting guidance signal is optimized through a separate auxiliary objective and removed once its additional benefit diminishes. Experiments with 4B and 14B models across writing, chat, health, and science show that RISE-RL achieves the highest mean score on every evaluated benchmark under guidance-free evaluation. Compared with standard Rubric-RL, it improves the average score by 1.3 points at the 4B scale and $\textbf{3.3 points at the 14B scale}$, including a $\textbf{6.0-point}$ gain on CreativeWriting-V3. It also improves creative-writing diversity and yields gains on objectively scored medical and scientific benchmarks. These results indicate that selective internalization through reward filtering and policy support shaping is effective for open-ended reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: RISE-RL improves LLM alignment by using rubric criteria to generate privileged trajectories for challenging aspects, filtering them based on rubric rewards, and optimizing guidance through an auxiliary objective that's removed once benefits diminish.
AI.motivation: Existing rubric-based RL methods compress fine-grained criterion-level feedback into scalar rewards, making persistent capability gaps difficult to target under limited on-policy exploration for open-ended LLM tasks.
AI.method: RISE-RL uses repeatedly missed rubric criteria to elicit privileged trajectories, retains only those whose complete-rubric reward exceeds mean natural rollout reward, re-evaluates them under original prompts, and optimizes guidance through a separate auxiliary objective that's removed once benefits diminish.
AI.result: Achieves highest mean score on every evaluated benchmark (writing, chat, health, science) with 4B and 14B models; improves average score by 1.3 points at 4B scale and 3.3 points at 14B scale, including 6.0-point gain on CreativeWriting-V3; improves creative-writing diversity and yields gains on medical and scientific benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Selective internalization through reward filtering and policy support shaping is effective for open-ended reinforcement learning with LLMs.

title: PET/CT Radiogenomic Mutation Prediction in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Using Multi-Label Learning
summary: Lung cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer- related mortality worldwide. Although targeted therapies have improved outcomes for patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), they rely on mutation profiling through tissue biopsy, an invasive procedure with several limitations. This study investigates PET/CT-based radio- genomic prediction of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), tumour protein 53 (TP53), and Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene (KRAS) mutations using deep learning. We further evaluate whether pairwise multi-label learning improves mutation prediction compared with conventional single-gene classification. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first studies to systematically investigate multi-label learning for PET/CT radiogenomic mutation prediction in NSCLC. Experiments were conducted on a novel UK-based radiogenomics cohort. Joint pre- diction of KRAS and TP53 improved AUC from 0.58 to 0.64 for KRAS and from 0.69 to 0.71 for TP53. For the EGFR/KRAS pair, only EGFR benefited from joint learning, while no improvement was observed for the EGFR/TP53 pair. These findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of multi-label learning depends on the specific combination of gene mutations being modelled, suggesting that mutation-specific modelling strategies may be preferable for PET/CT radiogenomic prediction.

AI.tldr: Deep learning approach using PET/CT radiomics to predict NSCLC gene mutations (EGFR, TP53, KRAS) shows that multi-label learning improves prediction for some gene pairs but not all, suggesting mutation-specific strategies are needed.
AI.motivation: Current targeted therapies for NSCLC require invasive tissue biopsies for mutation profiling. The paper aims to develop a non-invasive alternative using PET/CT radiomics with deep learning to predict key gene mutations.
AI.method: Used deep learning on PET/CT radiomics data from a novel UK-based radiogenomics cohort. Compared conventional single-gene classification with pairwise multi-label learning for predicting EGFR, TP53, and KRAS mutations in NSCLC patients.
AI.result: Joint prediction improved performance for certain gene pairs: KRAS/TP53 pair improved AUC from 0.58 to 0.64 for KRAS and from 0.69 to 0.71 for TP53. EGFR/KRAS pair only benefited EGFR prediction. No improvement for EGFR/TP53 pair.
AI.conclusion: Multi-label learning effectiveness depends on specific gene mutation combinations, suggesting that mutation-specific modeling strategies may be preferable over general approaches for PET/CT radiogenomic prediction in NSCLC.

title: ChronoState: Hidden Elapsed-Time Conditioning for Temporal-State Action Selection in Frozen-Backbone Language Models
comment: Submitted to SPIE Defense and Commercial Sensing 2027
summary: Temporal decisions in language-model systems often depend on both symbolic task state and elapsed wall-clock time, such as cache expiration, job completion, quota resets, deadlines, or stale sessions. We study whether elapsed time can be supplied as a non-token, system-side scalar and composed with visible symbolic state by a frozen-backbone language model. We introduce ChronoState, a compositional temporal-state benchmark in which symbolic state appears in the prompt, elapsed seconds tau are supplied through a hidden chronometric-injection channel, and the model selects a forced-choice temporal action. Here, "hidden" means hidden from the user-visible token sequence, not from model computation. Using Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as a frozen bf16 backbone with a 31-dimensional sinusoidal-plus-log time encoding, gated FiLM residual modulation, and a rank-8 LoRA action surface, hidden-time CI reaches 0.9305 +/- 0.0134 accuracy and 0.9410 +/- 0.0103 balanced accuracy. No-time and shuffled-time controls fall to 0.5511 +/- 0.0042 and 0.3323 +/- 0.0097, respectively, with high shuffled-time wrong-state consistency supporting causal dependence on the injected scalar within the trained distribution. Generalization remains strong for held-out templates, durations, and multi-constraint compositions, but held-out quota-family transfer is weak at 0.5065 +/- 0.0559, while a fair prompt+LoRA timestamp baseline reaches 0.9893 +/- 0.0052. Thus, ChronoState supports a narrow conclusion: hidden elapsed time can be composed with symbolic task state under direct supervision, but does not establish autonomous time tracking, broad unseen-family abstraction, or superiority over prompt-injected timestamps.

AI.tldr: A study shows that language models can be trained to combine symbolic task state with elapsed time information when time is provided through a hidden system channel, achieving high accuracy but with limited generalization to unseen scenarios.
AI.motivation: Temporal decisions in language-model systems often require both symbolic task state and elapsed wall-clock time (e.g., cache expiration, deadlines, quota resets). The paper investigates whether elapsed time can be supplied as a non-token, system-side scalar that can be composed with visible symbolic state by a frozen language model.
AI.method: Introduced ChronoState, a compositional temporal-state benchmark where symbolic state appears in prompts, elapsed seconds are supplied through a hidden chronometric-injection channel, and models select forced-choice temporal actions. Used Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct as frozen backbone with 31-dimensional sinusoidal-plus-log time encoding, gated FiLM residual modulation, and rank-8 LoRA action surface. Compared no-time and shuffled-time controls, and tested generalization across templates, durations, multi-constraint compositions, and quota-family transfer.
AI.result: Hidden-time chronometric injection achieved 0.9305 accuracy and 0.9410 balanced accuracy. No-time and shuffled-time controls dropped to 0.5511 and 0.3323 respectively, with high shuffled-time wrong-state consistency indicating causal dependence on injected time. Generalization was strong for held-out templates, durations, and multi-constraint compositions, but quota-family transfer was weak at 0.5065, while prompt+LoRA timestamp baseline reached 0.9893.
AI.conclusion: Hidden elapsed time can be composed with symbolic task state under direct supervision, but does not establish autonomous time tracking, broad unseen-family abstraction, or superiority over prompt-injected timestamps. The ChronoState benchmark supports narrow conclusions about time-state composition in supervised settings.

title: Rethinking Factor Sharing in Federated LoRA: A Rank-Aware Adaptive Approach
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) represents large language model (LLM) updates with two compact matrix factors, i.e., $A$ and $B$, providing an efficient way to fine-tune large models in federated learning paradigm. Inspired by the asymmetric roles of the LoRA factors, we study whether $A$ should be shared across clients while $B$ remains client-specific (Share-A/Local-B), or whether $B$ should instead be shared while $A$ remains client-specific (Share-B/Local-A). With a least-squares surrogate, we reveal that Share-A/Local-B requires the client-specific LoRA update matrices to use a common rank-$r$ input-side space, whereas Share-B/Local-A requires a common rank-$r$ output-side space. The two strategies therefore incur different projection residuals, indicating that the preferred strategy is the one with the smaller aggregate residual across clients. With this insight, we propose Federated Adaptive Factor Sharing Low-Rank Adaptation (FedAS-LoRA), which selects the sharing side before training to enhance fine-tuning performance. To enable adaptive factor selection before training, we design a Rank-Aware Shared-Subspace Sufficiency (RSS) metric, which effectively assesses whether a shared rank-$r$ input subspace is sufficient for the local data distributions using representations extracted from a frozen LLM backbone. Experiments across different tasks, data distributions, LoRA ranks, and participation settings confirm the effectiveness of RSS and the superior performance of FedAS-LoRA.

AI.tldr: FedAS-LoRA: An adaptive approach for federated learning that intelligently chooses whether to share LoRA factor A or B across clients based on which minimizes aggregate projection residuals, using a novel RSS metric for pre-training selection.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently fine-tuning large language models in federated learning using LoRA. While LoRA reduces communication costs by representing model updates with two compact matrices (A and B), the authors identify that the asymmetric roles of these factors raise an important question: which factor should be shared across clients and which should remain client-specific to optimize federated fine-tuning performance?
AI.method: The authors propose FedAS-LoRA (Federated Adaptive Factor Sharing Low-Rank Adaptation) which: 1) Analyzes the mathematical properties of sharing either factor A or B using a least-squares surrogate model; 2) Shows that Share-A/Local-B requires common rank-r input-side space while Share-B/Local-A requires common rank-r output-side space; 3) Designs a Rank-Aware Shared-Subspace Sufficiency (RSS) metric to assess whether a shared rank-r input subspace is sufficient for local data distributions using frozen LLM representations; 4) Selects the sharing side adaptively before training based on which strategy minimizes aggregate projection residuals.
AI.result: Experiments across different tasks, data distributions, LoRA ranks, and participation settings demonstrate: 1) The RSS metric effectively predicts which sharing strategy will perform better; 2) FedAS-LoRA achieves superior performance compared to fixed sharing strategies; 3) The approach is validated across diverse experimental conditions confirming its effectiveness and robustness.
AI.conclusion: The asymmetric roles of LoRA factors A and B have significant implications for federated learning. The optimal sharing strategy depends on which factor sharing minimizes aggregate projection residuals across clients. FedAS-LoRA provides an adaptive, principled approach to select the better sharing strategy before training using the RSS metric, leading to improved federated fine-tuning performance for large language models.

title: TRACE: TRajectory Attribution for Automated Context Engineering
summary:
Production AI agents fail when their context sources -- system prompts, knowledge bases, tool descriptions, and procedural skills -- contain errors or gaps. Current maintenance relies on manual log review and ad-hoc debugging, creating a scalability bottleneck as interaction volume grows.
  We present TRACE (TRajectory Attribution for Automated Context Engineering), an automated feedback loop that mines historical agent trajectories to diagnose and remediate context failures. Our key insight is that trajectories are rich with implicit dissatisfaction signals -- user corrections, rephrasing, abandonment cues -- that reveal precisely where context sources failed, without explicit feedback collection. Unlike model fine-tuning, TRACE operates on the context layer, enabling rapid iteration without retraining.
  We make four contributions: (1) a trajectory mining framework that systematically extracts diagnostic information from historical agent executions; (2) multi-component causal attribution that extends textual gradients from monolithic prompt optimization to heterogeneous context sources (skills, knowledge bases, tools, prompts); (3) exploratory verification, where agents actively read context sources to distinguish content gaps requiring CREATE from stale content requiring UPDATE, achieving 96% operation accuracy; and (4) a reusable simulation methodology and verifiable benchmark addressing the absence of open datasets for context debugging, with a six-category fault taxonomy, ground truth annotations, and a cross-layer verification protocol.
  On 60 dissatisfaction traces spanning three complexity tiers (up to 16 execution nodes), TRACE achieves 72.7% root cause attribution and 82% end-to-end fix effectiveness, showing that over 80% of context-layer failures can be automatically diagnosed and remediated by mining historical trajectories, an overlooked resource in production systems.

AI.tldr: TRACE is an automated system that mines historical AI agent trajectories to diagnose and fix context source failures without requiring explicit user feedback or model retraining.
AI.motivation: Production AI agents fail when their context sources (prompts, knowledge bases, tools, skills) contain errors or gaps. Current manual debugging approaches don't scale with growing interaction volume, creating a maintenance bottleneck.
AI.method: TRACE uses four key components: (1) trajectory mining framework extracting diagnostics from historical executions, (2) multi-component causal attribution for heterogeneous context sources, (3) exploratory verification where agents read context to distinguish content gaps (CREATE) from stale content (UPDATE), and (4) simulation methodology with fault taxonomy and cross-layer verification.
AI.result: On 60 dissatisfaction traces across three complexity tiers, TRACE achieves 72.7% root cause attribution and 82% end-to-end fix effectiveness, with exploratory verification achieving 96% operation accuracy for distinguishing content gaps vs. stale content.
AI.conclusion: Over 80% of context-layer failures can be automatically diagnosed and remediated by mining historical trajectories, demonstrating that these overlooked resources in production systems contain valuable implicit dissatisfaction signals for automated debugging.

title: SR-OPSD: Self-Referenced On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) converts feedback into dense token-level supervision on trajectories generated by the policy to be optimized, providing a useful complement to reinforcement learning with sparse outcome rewards. However, the self-teacher policy used in OPSD is typically a stop-gradient or exponential-moving-average copy of the policy conditioned on additional context information, and thus co-evolves with both the student policy and its on-policy context distribution. Directly matching such a moving target with a fixed projection objective can lead to unstable optimization or excessive distributional concentration. This nature of OPSD motivates the proposed \emph{Self-Referenced On-Policy Self-Distillation (SR-OPSD)}. At fixed student-generated contexts, a token-level variational characterization identifies the effective distillation target as a geometric interpolation between the self-teacher policy and a reference policy.
